# **Exterior Binding of the Volume**

<image-desc>The image displays the front cover and spine of a large historical book. The binding is in the "half-leather" style: the spine and the outer corners are reinforced with dark brown leather, while the main boards are covered in marbled paper. The marbled pattern is a classic "snail" or "shell" design, characterized by tight spirals and wavy lines in colors of terracotta red, charcoal grey, and pale ochre. The leather spine has raised bands decorated with horizontal gold-tooled lines. A small red leather label is affixed to the upper section of the spine, though the gold-leaf lettering is illegible due to the angle and wear.</image-desc>

<term>Half-binding</term> <note>A method of bookbinding where the spine and corners are covered in leather for durability, while the rest of the cover is finished with paper or cloth.</note>

<term>Marbled paper</term> <note>Decorative paper produced by floating pigments on a liquid surface and transferring the pattern to paper; the "snail" or "shell" pattern seen here was popular from the 17th century onward.</note>

<term>Gold-tooling</term> <note>The process of pressing heated metal tools into leather through gold leaf to create decorative designs or titles.</note>

<term>Spine label</term> <note>A thin piece of contrasting leather glued to the spine to display the book's title and author.</note>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page begins the "Editor's Preface," written by Stephen Wren, the grandson of Sir Christopher Wren. It follows the list of subscribers and introduces the motivations behind the publication of *Parentalia*.</meta>

## THE EDITOR’S
# PREFACE.

---

A respect for the memory of worthy ancestors and a desire to communicate useful knowledge to the public were the motives that prompted my father to compile this work—partly biographical and partly scientific. This work is honorable to the deceased, as it places their virtues in a fair light and preserves their compositions <note>original: "Composures"; refers to literary or written works</note>. It also tends toward the advancement of literature, not only by their treatises and letters but by their example—a strong incentive, as it shows what limitless achievements are to be obtained by study and contemplation <note>original: "Speculation"; here meaning intellectual inquiry or abstract study</note>.

The variety of subjects contained in this performance evidences in the compiler an extensive range of knowledge in both the languages and sciences, as well as the accuracy of judgment necessary to avoid errors and confusion. It further demonstrates the skill required to regularly conduct such a multitude of facts and detached particulars to a proper conclusion <note>original: "just Period"; meaning a fitting end or a well-ordered completion</note>, without inserting anything trivial or unnecessary.

<summary>Stephen Wren introduces the preface to "Parentalia," explaining that his father, Christopher Wren Jr., compiled the work to honor their ancestors (specifically Sir Christopher Wren) and to provide a scholarly resource through their letters and scientific treatises.</summary>
<keywords>Stephen Wren, Christopher Wren Jr., Sir Christopher Wren, Parentalia, biography, scientific treatises, family history, 18th-century publishing</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Editor's Preface" by Stephen Wren. He explains the practical reasons for publishing his father's manuscript, including the threat of unauthorized versions and his commitment to high production quality.</meta>

# PREFACE.

Besides the motives mentioned above (to which I am not indifferent <note>original: "insensible"</note>), several additional reasons—by no means to be ignored—determined me to fulfill my father’s intention and publish his manuscript. I am referring to the requests <note>original: "solicitations"</note> of people of letters and the prevention of a fake counterfeit, which would have been a deception <note>original: "imposition"</note> of the public and an injury to the honored subjects of these papers [the Wren family]; such a scheme had already been underway <note>original: "in agitation"</note>.

As the glory of God and the good of mankind were the goals toward which these excellent people directed their studies, research, and actions, their memory seems entitled to a kind reception from the public. I leave this monument, erected to their memory, to the public's fairness <note>original: "candour"; in the 18th century, this meant an impartial or kindly disposition</note>, without speaking at length to further praise the subject matter or style. Any such praise <note>original: "encomiums"</note>, however well-deserved, may be seen as biased when coming from a descendant, even if supported by many prominent examples. Yet I surely cannot be criticized for stating that I have spared no necessary expense—not only on the copper-plate engravings for the use and illustration of the mathematical and architectural <note>original: "architectonical"</note> parts, but also in the beauty and elegance of the book overall. This was done out of gratitude to the generous subscribers (though they are few) and so that virtue and science might make their public appearance in a dignified dress <note>original: "decent habit"</note>.

I can truly declare <note>original: "protest"</note> that financial profit <note>original: "interest"</note> played so small a part in this undertaking that if the book

<summary>Stephen Wren explains that he published "Parentalia" to fulfill his father's wishes, satisfy scholarly demand, and prevent the release of a low-quality counterfeit version. He emphasizes his investment in high-quality engravings and printing to honor the subjects' contributions to science and architecture.</summary>
<keywords>Stephen Wren, publishing history, copper-plate engravings, architectural illustration, 18th-century books, Parentalia, intellectual property</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page concludes the "Editor's Preface" by Stephen Wren. It continues from the previous page where the author discussed the expenses incurred in publishing the work.</meta>

-># PREFACE.<-

...covers its expenses <note>original: "clears its Charges"</note>, my financial goals <note>original: "pecuniary Views"</note> are fully satisfied.

It is a particular pleasure to acknowledge my greatest debt of gratitude to the Right Honorable *Arthur Onslow*, Esq., Speaker of the Honorable House of Commons. I could say a great deal about the pleasure of being honored by his attention; however, it would be pointless to single out any one generous act by a person whose entire life is a constant series of them.

I hope that closing this preface with an elegant quotation from the preface of Sir *Robert Cotton’s* posthumous works—which is very relevant <note>original: "apposite"</note> to our current subject—will not be met with any criticism <note>original: "censure"</note>.

> “Among the Greeks and Romans—the two lights <note>original: "Luminaries"</note> that first spread the rays of knowledge and civilization <note>original: "Civility"</note> through these northwestern regions—anyone who preserved the memory and works of virtuous men from decay <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note> and the rust of time by bringing them into the light for the public good was considered among the best of patriots.

> “The memory of some men is like the rose and other fragrant <note>original: "odoriferous"</note> flowers, which give off a sweeter and stronger scent after they are plucked. The memory of others may be compared to the poppy and similar plants that make a colorful and grand display while they remain on the stem,

<meta>catchword: but</meta>

<summary>In this concluding section of the preface, Stephen Wren expresses his financial disinterestedness in the project and acknowledges the support of Arthur Onslow before quoting Sir Robert Cotton on the importance of preserving the history of virtuous men.</summary>

<keywords>Arthur Onslow, Sir Robert Cotton, House of Commons, historical preservation, patriotism, posthumous works, Parentalia, Stephen Wren</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page concludes the "Editor's Preface" by Stephen Wren. It finishes the block quotation from Sir Robert Cotton comparing the reputations of virtuous men to fragrant flowers, and ends with a Latin aphorism from Seneca.</meta>

# PREFACE.

> “but when they are cut and gathered, they have an unpleasant <note>original: "ill-favoured"</note> smell. The worthy people featured in these records can be compared to the first kind—both for the sweet reputation <note>original: "Odor of a good Name"</note> they had while they lived, and after they were taken by the common blow of death <note>original: "Stroke of Mortality"</note>.
>
> “To increase the fragrance of their virtues and memory, these memoirs—which might be called, quite appropriately, a bouquet <note>original: "Posy"</note> of various different flowers—have been collected.
>
> “The journey is long by way of instructions, but short and effective by way of examples <note>original Latin: "Longum iter est per præcepta : breve et efficax per exempla."</note> — Seneca, *Epistle VI*.”

->STEPHEN WREN.<-

# INTRODUCTION.

The family of the name of *Wren*, of note and antiquity, from which the eminent persons specified and distinguished in these memorials were descended, has been seated, occasionally, at *Sherborne House*, *Billy Hall*, and *Binchester*, in the Bishopric of *Durham*; but came originally from *Denmark*.

<margin>
Burton on Antoninus's Itinerary, page 46.
</margin>
<margin>
Camden's *Britannia*, Volume 2, 2nd Edition, by Bishop Gibson, page 945.
</margin>
> "Binchester—called by *Antoninus*, *Vinovium*, and by *Ptolemy*, *Bi-novium*—was a city of old and a *Roman station*, situated on the brow of a hill which overlooks the River *Wear*, and near *Bishop Auckland*. It is much noted by the neighbors thereabouts for the debris and ruins of old walls, and also for the *Roman coins* often dug up in it, which country people call *Binchester pennies*; and for *Roman inscriptions*, one of which, cut into an altar dedicated to the *Mother Goddess*, is thus described by Mr. *Camden*."

<margin>
* Sertorius Ursatus, *On Roman Abbreviations* <note>original: *De Notis Romanorum*</note>.
</margin>
Namely: *To the Mother Goddesses, Claudius Quintianus, a beneficiary of the consul, willingly and deservedly fulfilled his vow.* <note>original Latin: *Scilicet Deabus Matribus Claudius Quintianus, beneficiarius consulis, votum solvit lubens merito.* A "beneficiary" in this context was a soldier exempt from menial duties by favor of a high-ranking officer.</note>

# INTRODUCTION.

The antiquities of this place have been carefully researched by the current owner, Mr. *Charles Wren*. Among other curiosities, he discovered a carnelian <note>A reddish-brown semi-precious gemstone often used in signet rings.</note> and, in another area, a fine urn enclosed within a circular wall, which contained a wooden vessel.

<margin>From the ancestral papers of C.W. <note>original: *Ex Schedis avitis C. W.*</note></margin>
*Geoffry Wren*, brother of *William Wren* of *Sherborne House*, was a man of very remarkable character. He served as the confessor and privy counselor to two successive kings, *Henry VII* and *Henry VIII*. In 1515, he was appointed a canon of the Royal Chapel of *St. George* at *Windsor* and was the founder of the seventh stall there. He died in 1527 and lies buried in the north aisle of the choir. His grave is marked by a large marble stone featuring his image in brass, surrounded by ornate canopy-work <note>original: "tabernacle-work," referring to decorative carved booths for statues.</note>, located near the Earl of *Huntingdon’s* tomb.

<margin>
In the Treasury of the College of Windsor.
Ashmole’s *History of the Garter*, page 151.
</margin>
His anniversary, or memorial service <note>original: "Obit"</note>, was previously held and celebrated on the fifth of April.

<margin>In the Acts of the Chapel of Windsor.</margin>
*While Lord Richard Sydnor, the acting dean, was presiding over the court, there appeared the gentlemen Francis and Anthony, brothers of the venerable Geoffry Wren, a canon of this chapel and founder of the seventh stall (who served as confessor and counselor to Kings Henry VII and Henry VIII). They requested that they be granted the authority to administer the estate of the said Lord Geoffry, who recently died.* <note>original Latin: *Sedente pro tribunali Domino Richardo Sydnor, locum tenente decani, comparuerunt generosi viri Franciscus et Antonius fratres venerabilis viri Galfridi Wren, hujus capellæ canonici: septimæ sedis fundatoris: [R. <margin>From the ancestral papers of C.W.</margin>
*Francis Wren*, mentioned above as one of the two younger brothers of *Geoffry*, served as the steward to *Mary*, Queen of *Scots* and Dowager of *France*, during the time she lived in *England*.

<margin>Dugdale’s *Antiquities of Warwickshire*, page 140.</margin>

# INTRODUCTION.

Christopher Wren, Esquire (the compiler of the following work) and the eldest son of Sir *Christopher Wren*, was born on *February 18, 1675*. He received his early education at *Eton School*, and in 1691, he was admitted to *Pembroke Hall* in *Cambridge*. In 1694, he was appointed Deputy Clerk Engrosser <note>A legal clerk responsible for writing out official documents in a large, clear hand.</note>, and in 1698, he traveled through *Holland, France, and Italy*. He was twice elected as a Member of Parliament for *Windsor* in 1712 and 1714. He first married *Mary Musard*, daughter of Mr. *Philip Musard*, who was the jeweler to *Queen Anne*; they had one son, *Christopher*, who is still living. He later married Lady *Constance Burgoyne*, the widow of Sir *Roger Burgoyne*, Baronet, and daughter of Sir *Thomas Middleton*, Knight, of *Stanstead-Mountfitchet* in *Essex*. They had one son, *Stephen*, who is the publisher of this book. He was a learned and pious man, a skilled antiquary <note>A student of history and ancient artifacts.</note>, and was beloved by all who knew him for his generous and helpful nature. He published a work on ancient coins titled *A Collection of Ancient Coins* <note>original: *Numismatum Antiquorum Sylloge*</note>. After a life well-spent, he died on *August 24, 1747*, at the age of 72, and lies interred at his country estate at *Wroxhall* in *Warwickshire*.

The title he designed for this book was: “PARENTALIA. *Memorials of the Lives of the Right Reverend Father in God Matthew Wren, Doctor of Divinity, Lord Bishop of Ely; Christopher Wren, Doctor of Divinity, Dean of Windsor; and Sir Christopher Wren, Knight, Surveyor-General of the Royal Buildings. With Collections of Records and original Papers.*”

<margin>Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44.</margin>
“*Let us now praise famous men, and our fathers who fathered us: who were honored in their generations, and were the glory of their times.*” Of these men, let his memorial be blessed, “*who built the house, and set up a holy temple to the Lord:—who raised up for us the walls that were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and rebuilt our ruins.*” 

<margin>Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49.</margin>

<margin>
Ausonius, 
Preface to 
*Parentalia*
</margin>
“*The title of this little book is PARENTALIA* <note>A Roman festival honoring deceased relatives.</note>; *this is a name from ancient times, established ever since the reign of Numa* <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome.</note> *for the funeral rites of kindred. Nor does the reverence of survivors hold anything more sacred than to remember the lost with veneration.*”

> “*The buried ashes rejoice to hear their names spoken; I have laid them all to rest in happiness; now I alone remain.*” <note>original: “*Gaudent compositi cineres sua nomina dici, Omnes composui fœlices, nunc ego resto.*” From the poet Ausonius.</note>

->[C. W. *July 1741*.]<-

<margin>
† Trefoil <note>original: *Trifolium*</note>
</margin>
make it a matter of wonder that † Garden Clover <note>original: "Claver"</note> will hide its stalk when the sun shows brightly, which is nothing but a full expansion of the leaves."

<margin>
‡ In a manuscript in the possession of the Collector. <note>original: *In MS. penes Collectorem*</note>
</margin>
Upon this passage, Dr. *Christopher Wren*, Dean of *Windsor* (in his ‡ experimental observations and additions to the work of the said noble author), has the following note: "Regarding the Clover, it is no wonder that in the hot sun it will hide the stalk by expanding its leaves. The greater wonder is that always before stormy weather, the flower and leaves will shrink up close to the stalk, as if to hide itself. The causes of this opening and closing are, like the effects themselves, opposites; for as the opening proceeds from the sun’s beneficial heat, so the shutting comes from a natural dread of the approaching storm. This shrinking is the more admirable because it comes close to the natural power of foreknowledge <note>original: "Presage"</note> found in the higher order of sentient creatures, such as ravens, crows, cocks, and perhaps most eminently in those little birds, the Wrens. For this reason, some of the ancestors of our family [of the *Wrens*], placed over the paternal coat of arms a *Wren* in its natural colors <note>original: "proper"</note> as the crest, holding in its foot a *Trefoil* <note>A three-leafed clover.</note>, with this motto—

->*He survives the storms, foreknowing them by heaven's guidance.*<-
<note>original: *Turbinibus superest, cælo duce præscius.*</note>

"This emblem, together with the motto and coat of arms, stood in the south window of those lodgings located at the northwest corner of the inner cloister at *Windsor* College in the year 1643. It had stood there for a full 116 years—that is, from *April* 1527, the year and month in which *Geoffry Wren* died, after he had served as Canon of the said chapel for twelve years;

“Founder of the seventh stall, Privy Counselor to the two Kings, Henry VII and VIII, etc.”

Again, in his note on the nature of the *Trefoil* <note>Clover or a three-leafed plant.</note>, “Geoffrey Wren <note>original: Galfridus Wren</note> was among the founders of the chapel at Windsor; and was a counselor to Kings Henry VII and VIII; for the crest of his family shield, he had a Goldcrest bird <note>original: Regulum, likely a pun on the family name Wren, traditionally called the 'king of birds'</note>, holding a Trefoil with its foot raised: signifying by both that reason provides the best omens <note>original: optima auguria</note>.”

<margin>* Consult also Century 9, page 211. In my possession, C. W. <note>original: Consule item Cent. 1x. p. 211. Penes me C. W.</note></margin>

One of the ancestors of this family, having gained much honor and estate by his valor against the *Scots*, wrote under his coat of arms —

->*With God leading, fortune followed.* <note>original: Ducente Deo fortuna secuta est.</note><-

The crest and mottos have been since varied: the motto chosen by Sir *Christopher Wren*, well adapted to a mathematician, was —

->*By number, weight, and measure.* <note>original: Numero, pondere, et mensura.</note><-

The print of Bishop *Wren* is from an original picture of him, before his advancement to the prelacy <note>The office of a high-ranking church official, such as a bishop.</note>, being about thirty years of age. *A wise man can be pressed by evils, but not crushed* <note>original: Sapiens malis premi, sed non opprimi potest</note>, was not the Bishop’s motto; but is only an inscription, alluding to the serenity and fortitude with which he bore all the injurious attacks of his enemies, and an imprisonment of eighteen years.

The resemblance is as perfectly retained in the print of Dr. *Christopher Wren*, as in the former; being also from an original. *Fortune is the companion of virtue* <note>original: Virtuti fortuna comes</note>, intimates the honors to which his distinguished qualities raised him; the Doctor’s own motto (and a very excellent one) being, *If all is right within, do not worry.* <note>original: Si rectè intus, ne labora.</note>

->Concerning the *Wren* family and their heraldic insignia.<-

<meta>This page continues the genealogical and heraldic history of the Wren family, following the account of Geoffrey Wren and the family's service to the Tudor kings. # INTRODUCTION.

...moved, with the title and privileges of a Prince Palatine: and Christopher, successor to his brother in the same deanery, appointed by King Charles; and elevated to the honorary office of the Most Noble Order of the Garter <note>original: periscelidis-aureæ</note>, serving as both Secretary and Registrar; they acknowledge their father Francis of London: their grandfather Cuthbert of Durham; Lord of Newbald-Revel, of the Monks of Kirby <margin>† In the County of Warwickshire.</margin>, so-called: their great-grandfather Lord William, of Shirborne-house in the bishopric of Durham, and originally of Billy-hall: their great-great-grandfather Francis, or Anthony (for the first name is in doubt), in the same family, descending from a long line of ancestors; for all of whom the family insignia were:

<margin>
* A Chevron.
† A Chief.
‡ Cross-crosslets.
|| A Wreath.
§ Mantle.
** Doubled, i. e. lined throughout.
</margin>

On a silver shield, a black * chevron is surrounded on both sides by three erased purple lions' heads (two above, one below); above these, on a crimson † chief crossing the shield, are three gold ‡ cross-crosslets. On the helmet, beneath a twisted silver and crimson || wreath, a crimson § mantle is draped around the shield, lined ** with silver. Above the wreath is a silver lion’s head, erased, pierced by the tip of a bloody spear and encircled by a gold collar, like a leader captured in war but killed by his wounds. All of these signify the nobility of the family, illustrious for magnificent buildings (marked by the chevron); an affinity with nobles (noted by the purple lions' heads); and especially an alliance contracted with high-ranking prelates (as the gold crosses woven into the crimson garment signify). For heralds did not then, as they do now, paint insignia obtained by petition and price, but those won by virtue (which alone is true nobility). Above all, it displays an icon of fortitude and an unconquered spirit in military service, signified by the erased head of a lion, the <term>protome</term> <note>A representation of the upper part of an animal or person.</note> of a certain prince from Scotland, captured and slain in battle.

<margin>‡‡ Chevron.</margin>

In the modern shield, the colors are varied in some part; specifically, the ‡‡ chevron is blue, as are the three blue lions' heads, and the blue lion's head upon the helmet; and it is without the gold collar.

## MATTHEW WREN, D. D.
### LORD BISHOP of *ELY*.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'D' decorated with floral patterns and foliage within a square border.</image-desc>

DOCTOR Matthew Wren, Lord Bishop of *Ely* and Count-Palatine (eldest son of *Francis Wren*, citizen and mercer of *London*, only son of *Cuthbert Wren* of *Monk’s-Kirby* in the county of *Warwick*, second son of *William Wren* of *Sherborne-House* and of *Billy-Hall* in the Bishopric of *Durham*), was born in the parish of *St. Peter’s-Cheap*, *London*, in the year 1585.

<margin>
From a funeral oration by John Pearson, Doctor of Divinity and Master of Trinity College, in manuscript.
</margin>
Being an eminent scholar in his youth, of great promise and more than ordinary potential, he became first a student in *Pembroke Hall* in the University of *Cambridge*; then a Greek scholar, and on November 9, 1605, was elected a Fellow of that house; and (which was a happy omen of his future fortunes) he had been invited and drawn there by Dr. *Lancelot Andrewes*, the most learned, pious, and worthy Master of that *Hall*, who later became Bishop

THE LIFE OF

of *Winchester*; by him first planted in that fruitful soil of *Bishops*; always observed by his vigilance and circumspection, encouraged by his support and favor, and directed by his advice; so that devoting himself to the study of the best learning, he, in a short time, grew famous for his skill in the arts and languages; performed the university exercises with general credit and applause; was a strict observer of its rights and customs; a punctual enforcer of its discipline; a zealous asserter of its privileges; and became so great a lover of that place, that neither the length of his days, nor the injuries of the times could obliterate or diminish his affection.

After he had enriched and adorned himself with the most useful knowledge, and all the accomplishments of human learning, he came with these fair advantages, besides a singular desire and most passionate affection, into the service and ministry of the Church. Indeed, divinity has the best title to the sharpest wits and most fortunate dispositions, and may challenge a right to whatever virtue and excellence either the felicity of nature or the success of industry can bestow upon men. For the strength and vigor of our minds, the finest parts, and most ready faculties, all our choicest acquisitions and whole stock of improvements can never be employed or spent better than in promoting the interest of piety, adorning the beauty of holiness, and bringing credit to religion.

While he was engaged in these noble designs (being, by a rare combination, one of the most knowledgeable and also most devout persons of his age) and equally endeavoring the advancement of both the university and the clergy; though he seemed to conceal himself within the walls of his college, for which he had so great a respect; or else did adhere with all fidelity and observance to Bishop *Andrews*, his very good lord and patron (to whom he became chaplain in the year 1615, and then Rector of *Teversham* in *Cambridgeshire*); yet even then, men's expectations concerning him were very high; and it was the general opinion that there was nothing so great or significant which might not be achieved and accomplished by one so eminently qualified.

Nor was it possible for him any longer to escape the quick and piercing eye of King *James*, the reputation of whose wisdom could not now be consistent with his private condition, since our public schools had formerly given him opportunities to know and understand his worth. Therefore, at that point in time, when the family of his Royal Highness *Charles*, Prince of *Wales*, needed a true son of the Church of *England*, and one of the most approved fidelity, this was the man whom above all others, his *Majesty*, out of his own inclination and guided by his own exquisite judgment, was pleased (in the year 1621) to appoint chaplain to his son. To which gracious favor it was no small addition of honor that the affair was carried out so privately as to make it doubtful whether he was assigned by the *King* himself or petitioned for by the *Prince*; which ambiguity was still happily improved, in that he was equally acceptable to *them both*: But this was only the prelude to a greater and deeper mystery.

For it is most remarkable that this prudent *monarch* had entertained and settled in his mind a firm intention to practice such a riddle of policy, which not only distracted and puzzled the world while it was taking place, but will never cease to be a wonder, now that it has become history. Since those men of the most curious and inquisitive minds, whose business and ambition is to dive into the depths of princes, to search and discuss the intrigues of public negotiations, and examine all reasons of *state*, after they have run through a maze of uncertainty and tired their thoughts in this subtle speculation, find themselves still as much in the dark as when they first set out in their very first conjectures.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Matthew Wren, detailing his role as chaplain and counselor to Prince Charles (the future King Charles I) during the 1623 journey to Spain.</meta>

### MATTHEW WREN, D. D.

It was resolved then by this most judicious and shrewd *Prince* to send his only *Son*, the Heir of three *Kingdoms*, the dearest *Offspring* of a most affectionate and indulgent *Father*, the Delight and Hope of the Royal Family, into the territories of *Spain*. This was to trust him with a cunning and wily nation of a reserved temperament, given to hidden and secret machinations, and of which we had until then no other knowledge or experience than what we derived from its craftiness and pride, and the perpetual hatred it bore us. This was done, moreover, not at the head of an army, nor in the midst of his naval forces, nor in any such military posture in which the *English* used to make their visits to *Spain*. In a word, it was to venture him upon their faith and honor (of which we had good reason to be suspicious) without any other guard or security than his own princely wisdom and discretion.

When therefore this select *person*, in so dangerous an expedition, became chaplain—or shall I say, counselor—to this excellent *Prince* (for where the power of godliness has once established itself, and sincere discretion has wholly taken hold of the heart, there is little or no distinction between these two roles, which among others are kept at a wide distance), then, wherever he went, he unfolded the foundations and articles of our religion with such clarity and lucidity. He maintained and defended them with such strength and spirit, and privately unraveled all those sly and knotty schemes which some of their most eminent churchmen had twisted to entangle the *Prince’s* affairs. He did this with such great acuteness and dexterity that no other means whatsoever, no artifice or expedient, could claim a greater share in opening the avenues and passages for his Royal *Highness’s* safe return.

> " (to which he had been too long accustomed) deprived him of his own reason, judgment, and understanding, and gave way to that unaccountable voyage, which became a fertile subject of fear and jealousy to ourselves at home, and of amazement, as well as laughter, to the rest of Europe. Never were a pair sent abroad to be exposed to the censure of a foreign and capricious nation so ill-suited.
" The Prince was of a grave and steady demeanor, adapted to the genius of the Spanish nation, which had gained him universal love there; the Marquis (then made a Duke) was of a light and Frenchified dress and behavior, and given to his pleasures, and generally thought to be lacking those clear and quick-sighted intellectual qualities which were required for the management of that high concern.
" Innumerable were the mischiefs King James was involved in by this rash and hot-headed voyage to Spain; and the King lived to see himself a true prophet, the match being dashed to pieces by that very means. For while the Earl of Bristol—the greatest statesman we had then left, and who negotiated the match—proceeded with slow and wary, yet as sure steps as the subtle and intriguing genius of the Spaniard, and the different interests and sentiments of the Pope, Emperor, and Duke of Bavaria (who all had their parts to play in this affair as well as the King of Spain) would permit, there was some solid though slippery ground for the King and Prince to set their feet on. The articles of religion were agreed upon, and temporal articles were near a conclusion; but by the Prince’s and Duke’s arrival in Spain, all was unraveled, and the subtle Spaniard would not easily grant that any match had been seriously treated of or intended before. So everything had to begin again, and the whole affair rested on the Duke’s shoulders, which (God knows) were too feeble to bear the weight of it. He therefore turned to a work more suitable to his temper and strength, and pursuing his revenge for the insults he received in Spain, he alienated his old master to the highest degree (at least in that King’s opinion) by snatching his darling match from him and delivering it up to his Parliament, who made short work of it and immediately tore it to pieces."

<margin>Dr. Welwood's Memoirs, p. 22.</margin>
King James, in order to obtain from the Emperor the restoration of his son-in-law, the King of Bohemia, was coaxed into that inglorious plan of sending Prince Charles into Spain for a marriage with the Infanta that was either never intended for him or came too late. And it was more owing to King Philip the Third's generosity than to King James's politics that he ever saw England again.

<margin>P. 69.</margin>
Prince Charles in his temper was brave, magnificent, liberal, and constant. It was his noble and generous behavior that so impressed the King of Spain when he went there to court the Infanta, that he rejected the repeated requests of his council to seize him, and paid him more respect than could have been well expected even if he had been King of England at that time.

<margin>P. 24, 27.</margin>

And when several princes were about to enter into a league for the recovery of the Palatinate, and the House of Austria was beginning to doubt their success, Gondomar used this tactic, among others, to break their measures by proposing a match with the Infanta of Spain for the Prince of Wales as the easiest and surest way to restore the Palatine family; which, like all the rest, was only to distract King

The ills that attended this affair were these: that thereby “the Protestant religion was entirely rooted out of *Bohemia*, the electoral dignity transferred from the *Palatine* family, the *Palatinate* itself lost, the liberty of *Germany* overthrown, and the famous library of *Heidelberg* was carried to *Rome*, to the irreparable prejudice of learning.”

So that *Gondomar* had good reason to say, in one of his letters to the Duke of *Lerma*, printed in the history of that Duke’s life, *p.* 28. “That he had lulled King *James* so fast asleep, that he hoped neither the cries of his daughter, nor her children, nor the repeated solicitations of his Parliament and subjects in their behalf, should be able to awaken him.”

<margin>Remark of Spanhemius.</margin>
The learned *Spanhemius* in his history of *Louise Juliane*, Electress Palatine (daughter of *William*, Prince of *Orange*, and mother to the King of *Bohemia*, who outlived her son and was one of the greatest patterns of virtue that any age has produced), sums up what relates to this affair with this remark: “That never prince was more obliged to a sister than King *Charles* the First was to the Queen of *Bohemia*; since it was only the confederation of *her* and *her children*, who were then the next heirs after him to the crown of *England*, that prevailed with the court of *Spain* to permit him to see *England* again.”

In opposition to these accounts, generally received of the *Spanish* Match and *Palatinate*, this passage in our noble historian, <note>Lord *Clarendon*</note> is to be taken notice of.

<margin>Clarendon’s History of the Rebellion, Book I. p. 27.</margin>
“Sir *Francis Cottington*, who was secretary to the Prince and not grown courtier enough to dissemble his opinion, had given the Duke <note>of *Buckingham*</note> offense before his journey into *Spain* \*, — and improved that prejudice after his coming there, by disposing the Prince all he could to the marriage of the *Infanta*; and by his behavior after his return, in justifying to King *James* (who had a very good opinion of him) the sincerity of the *Spaniard* in the treaty of the marriage: *That they did in truth desire it, and were fully resolved to gratify his Majesty in the business of the Palatinate; and only desired in the manner of it, to gratify the Emperor and the Duke of Bavaria all they could, which would take up very little time.*” All which being so contrary to the Duke’s purposes and resolutions, his displeasure toward *Cottington* <note>afterwards Lord *Cottington* and Chancellor of the Exchequer</note> was sufficiently manifest.

But to conclude; the account of the *Spanish* affairs and the journey to *Spain*, given solemnly by the Prince himself and the Duke at a conference between the *two houses* of Parliament (which conference his Royal *Highness* and the Duke were desired to manage), required in all reason and good manners to be judged by that age and posterity as most credible and authentic, namely:

<margin>Clarendon’s History of the Rebellion, Book I. p. 17. and the Duke’s account of the Spanish Match to the Parliament.</margin>

What follows next in the Duke’s account confirms and illustrates the wise conduct of *Dr. Wren*, under *Divine assistance*, in the guardianship of the *Prince’s* conscience, as seen in his *Royal Highness’s* defense and steady maintenance of his religion against all the most strenuous attacks of the Church of *Rome*. “Instead of proceeding,” continues the Duke, “upon the articles which had been claimed to be concluded, they urged nothing but new demands; and in matters of *religion* so peremptorily, that the *principal* clergymen and the *most eminent* of that King’s preachers had frequent conferences with the Prince to persuade him to change his *religion* and become a *Papist*. In order to move him more successfully to this, they procured the Pope to write a letter himself to his *Highness*, reminding him of the religion of his *ancestors* and *progenitors*, and conjuring him to return to the same faith. However, it pleased God not only to give the *Prince* a constant and unshaken heart in his *religion*, but *such wonderful abilities to defend the same in his discourses and arguments, that they stood amazed to hear him, and in effect, confessed that they were not able to answer him*,” etc.

"Persons of Honor were eye and ear-witnesses to this, having had the happiness to attend him there."

The common rumor in *Spain* was that the Prince had come (as they called it) to become a Christian; and the Prime Minister *Olivarez*, at his first visit, told him that the match should be made immediately, and that the Kings of *Spain* and *England* should divide the world between them; for he did not doubt that he came there to join their religion. To which the *Prince* answered, "**He did not come there for religion, but for a wife**." After every effort was used to allure the *Prince* to Popery—by Popish books, Popish pictures, and by carrying him to religious houses and to persons famous for pretended miracles, etc.—his Highness remained steadfast and showed no sign of changing.

<margin>Page 19.</margin>
The conference ended with great applause in both Houses for the Prince’s and Duke’s behavior and conduct throughout the affair, and in a hasty resolution to dissuade the *King* from entertaining any further proposals toward the match, and to frankly and resolutely enter into a war with *Spain*.

The famous library of *Heidelberg* having been mentioned before from a quotation by *Spanhemius*, it might be an omission not to insert this curious record, as it falls in our way.

<margin>In the year 1622, from the papers of C. W. and Helvicus's Chronology, p. 158.</margin>
*The Heidelberg Library, famous throughout almost all of Europe, containing an epistle written by Saint Paul’s own hand, was transported partly to Rome and partly elsewhere. Besides this epistle of Saint Paul, they say a manuscript of the Pentateuch of such great antiquity that the Jews would kneel to kiss it was also transferred to Rome from there, along with other excellent monuments.*

<margin>Jenkins's Reasonableness of the Christian Religion, Vol. II, p. 99.</margin>
The *Alexandrian MS* in the King's Library is believed to be as old as the one in the *Vatican*, which is acknowledged to be twelve hundred years old.

There is a copy of *St. Paul's Epistles* in the *French* King's Library, and another in the library of the *Benedictines* of *St. Germain*, which are concluded to be at least a thousand years old.

By the details in the preceding conference between the *two Houses of Parliament*, it is evident that *King James* was not mistaken in the prudent choice he had made of *Dr. Wren* for the office of preceptor and spiritual guide to his *son* in *Spain*. By his learning and skill in all ecclesiastical affairs and the most important controversies between us and the Church of *Rome*, and by a rational instruction of his Royal Highness in the fundamental truths of the *Protestant faith*, the Prince stood like a rock, firm and immovable in the true religion; and in the end, he triumphed over all the efforts, policies, and machinations of the *Roman* churchmen and the courts of *Rome* and *Spain*.

It was a notorious instance of the great injustice and uncharitableness of the times that followed, and of the *Calvinist faction*, that this orthodox divine—who, from his earliest appearance in the world, did on all occasions, as well as during the *Prince's* journey to *Spain*, defend and maintain the sound doctrine of the Church of *England* with great learning, vigilance, Christian courage, and resolution against Popery, superstition, and innovation—should himself (as will appear) be accused and publicly impeached in *Parliament* under the hateful charge of being a *Papist, idolater*, and *innovator*.

<margin>Clarendon's History of the Rebellion, Book I, p. 74.</margin>
"—*Innovation* in religion (says a great historian) was an unlucky word, and deceived very many honest men into apprehensions very prejudicial to the King and to the Church." Moreover, it was the usual maxim and practice of the Puritans and the *factious party*, in their malice against the government of the Church by *Bishops*, to call every man they did not love a *Papist*.

From this deviation we now return to the purpose, in chronological order.

<margin>In 1624, Dr. Wren was made Rector of Bingham in Nottinghamshire, and Prebend of Winchester.</margin>
In the year 1624, Dr. *Wren* was presented to the Rectory of *Bingham* in *Nottinghamshire*, and a Prebend of *Winchester*. In 1625, he was called rather than preferred to the Mastership of *St. Peter's College* in *Cambridge*; where he exercised such prudence and moderation in his government that he reduced all the Fellows to one sacred bond of unity and concord, and inspired the scholars to constancy and diligence in their studies. Moreover, <margin>In 1625, made Master of St. Peter's College, Cambridge.</margin> he built a great part of the college from the ground, rescued their writings and ancient records from dust and worms, and by indefatigable industry organized them into a good method and order. But seeing the public offices of religion less decently performed, and the service of God depending upon the courtesy of others for want of a convenient oratory within the walls of the college; what he then could not do at his own expense, he accomplished by his influence with well-disposed persons elsewhere, and procured such considerable sums of money that he built and beautified a complete chapel, which he dedicated *March* 17, 1632.

<margin>Nov. 4, 1628.</margin>
Being made Vice-Chancellor of *Cambridge*, he asserted the privileges, restored the discipline, kept all close to their respective duties, and taught the university at length to consider and understand itself.

<margin>July 24, 1628.</margin>
In 1628, he was promoted to the dignity of Dean of *Windsor* and *Wolverhampton*, and Register <note>The official recorder or registrar.</note> of the most honorable and noble *Order of the Garter*; in which office he discharged his duty with remarkable gravity, prudence, and authority; bestowed many accurate writings of his own on the society; and to his honor <margin>Ashmole's Order of the Garter, p. 201.</margin> "it is to be remembered, that from the institution of the most noble Order, until he was chosen for the office of Register, the annals of the Order were at no time recorded by a pen nearly so judicious and elegant, whose excellent pattern his worthy brother and successor in that office, Doctor *Christopher Wren*, exactly copied."

<margin>Ashmole, p. 175.</margin>
To observe by the way: — At the solemnity of ratifying the peace between King *Charles* and *Louis* XIII, King of *France*, *September* 6, 1629, in the Chapel of *St. George* at *Windsor*, he (as Dean) gave the oath to the Marquis of *Châteauneuf*, the *French* King's Ambassador, and not the Archbishop of *Canterbury*, though he was then present. It is no small privilege, that if the Archbishop of *Canterbury* be present at the Chapel of *Windsor*, he still sits below the *Dean*, nor can he consecrate there without his license.

<margin>In 1633, made Bishop of Hereford, Clerk of the Closet, and Prebend of Westminster.</margin>
In 1633, the King (who after so many trials in every promotion, had found him a most loyal subject, and an approved son of the *Church*, born as it were, and ordained from his youth for the government of it) conferred on him the Bishopric of *Hereford*; the position of Clerk of the Closet; and a Prebend of *Westminster*: and although he did not long enjoy the See of *Hereford*, yet in that short space of time, he settled that *Church* by accurate and certain statutes, which before was governed by useless, obsolete, and papistical <note>Relating to the Roman Catholic Church; often used in this period to denote practices deemed overly ceremonial or superstitious.</note> customs.

May 14, 1634, he was chosen a governor of *Sutton's-Hospital*, called the *Charter-house*.

<margin>*In 1635, transferred to the Bishopric of Norwich.*</margin> In 1635, the Bishopric of *Norwich* became vacant. At that time, it required a prelate who was no less resolute than he was wise and skillful, as it was a large and expansive diocese and was then shaken by schism and faction. Therefore, he was translated from *Hereford* to *Norwich* as the most suitable man for such a difficult province. There, for a period of over two years, he uncovered impostures, restrained restless and seditious efforts, and broke the spirits of all stubborn schismatics.

<margin>*Lord Clarendon's History of the Rebellion, Vol. II. p. 74.*</margin> A noble historian, and *others following him*, relate "That in the diocese of *Norwich*, he proceeded so passionately and fervently against the dissenting congregations that many left the kingdom, which diminished the wealthy manufacture there of kerseys and narrow cloths; and what was worse, it transported that trade secret to foreign parts." <note>Kerseys are a type of coarse woolen cloth.</note> But this departure of the *Norwich* weavers was *chiefly* brought about through the policy and management of the *Dutch*, who, lacking that manufacture (which had been improved to great perfection there), left no method untried to persuade these weavers to settle in their towns, promising full liberty of conscience and greater advantages and privileges than they had obtained in *England*. His *Lordship's* zeal for the service of God in the Church of *England*; his courage and resolution in impartially putting into practice legal ecclesiastical discipline during a most dissolute and hypocritical age; his warm opposition to the *Socinian* doctrine and the *Calvinist* party; and his firm handling of the *Puritans* and *Presbyterians* raised an implacable hatred against him. This first promoted slanders and libels, which were soon followed by long and grievous oppressions. Regarding the view of *him* as a disciplinarian, it is believed the *noble author* quoted earlier described him as having a *severe and sour nature*; but, at the same time, he acknowledged him to be "a very learned man, and particularly well-versed in the ancient liturgies of the *Greek* and *Latin* churches."

<margin>*Clarendon, Vol. I. p. 83.*</margin> In truth, the character given by that *excellent writer* to Archbishop *Laud* can also be very justly ascribed, in every respect, to his *Lordship*. "That he proposed no goal in all his actions and designs except those that were pious and just; and that no man ever had a heart more devoted to the King, the Church, or his country."

But among all his virtues, there were two especially worthy of remembrance and imitation: his *modesty* and *humility*. He never asked for the slightest reward; he never solicited any man by word or letter; he never sought any dignity he enjoyed, but always obtained what he never sued for. He was always offered what he never requested and was promoted to every station not by persistence but by merit. He disdained the methods of those ambitious and troublesome persons who greedily pursue the dignities of the Church, lay siege to the doors of great men, and extort rather than obtain promotion from <margin>*Appendix to the Life of Dr. Barwick. p. 462.*</margin> their patrons. "I have always been of the opinion," said Lord Chancellor *Hyde* (in his letter from *Brussels* during the King's exile), "that the method observed by Bishop *Andrews* and the Bishop of *Ely* [*Wren*] is the correct one; and if I could help it, if the *King* were at *Whitehall* tomorrow, he should never promote any man in the Church who sought it. And I think I have reason to believe the *King* is of that mind."

<margin>*In 1636, made Dean of His Majesty's Chapel.*</margin> In 1636, upon Bishop *Juxon's* advancement to the *Treasurer's Staff*, he succeeded him as Dean of *His Majesty's Chapel*, one of the highest dignities of the Court because it is closest to the *King*. Suddenly, when the diocese and palatinate of *Ely* required a man experienced in all ecclesiastical affairs—one not ignorant of civil law and secular transactions, and expert also in our university statutes and customs (all of which accomplishments were concentrated in him)—he was translated from *Norwich* to this see, for which he was so exactly

Thus, by his great virtues and abilities, he arrived at this high and honorable preferment, to plentiful and fair revenues, and to the bosom of a most gracious prince, during the most flourishing season of both Church and State.

If the nation had understood itself, the happiness of that age would have been too great; God, at that time, had granted blessings which could no longer coexist with the wickedness of an ungrateful people, nor with the allowance of his injured goodness; that very happiness which corrupted the nation destroyed it; the mercies which were abused became its ruin.

For suddenly, an unexpected storm from the *North* disjointed the whole body of the kingdom, and a violent sickness seized all its members. Wretched men, under the disguise of piety and religion, shook the very foundations and pillars of the *Church*. They committed outrages against all the *Bishops*, but especially *those* most endeared to the *King*, designing the extirpation of both *them* and *him*. They stirred up the multitude, promoted murmurs and discontent, spread malice in the people’s minds, and forged bitter *Articles* against them, so that the hatred of it all might fall on the *King*.

<margin>Accusation of Bishop Wren in Parliament, December 19, 1640. (Rushworth)</margin>
On December 19, 1640, the day after the impeachment of Archbishop *Laud*, Mr. *Hampden* was sent with a message to the *House of Peers* to inform their *Lordships* that the *Commons* had received information of a very high nature against *Matthew Wren*, Lord Bishop of *Ely*, for establishing idolatry and superstition in various places and performing some acts of that nature himself. He also indicated that because they heard of his attempt to escape the kingdom, he was commanded to request that some course be taken for him to provide security to remain present and abide by the judgment of Parliament.

<margin>Gives £10,000 bail for his daily appearance. December 23, 1640, gives the same security for standing the judgment of the House.</margin>
Thereupon, the said Bishop being commanded to withdraw, the Lords ordered him to provide £10,000 bail; and being called in, he consented to it, hoping to find friends to be bound with him. For the present, he gave a £10,000 bond for his daily appearance; and on the following December 23, the Bishops of *Bangor*, *Peterborough*, and *Llandaff* became bound with him in the same penalty for his forthcoming and standing the judgment of the House of Lords.

<margin>July 5, 1641. August 1641.</margin>
As the only crime of this excellent prelate was the extreme grace and favor of his *Prince*, the slanders and reproaches of malicious sycophants were received with great applause. All those who would clamor loudest against him were encouraged and abetted, not with regard for the truth, but for the effectiveness of their charge. Finally, in *July* following, a mark of *impeachment* was fixed on him for *high crimes and misdemeanors*, which soon after was followed by an *impeachment* of twelve more bishops, together with the Archbishop of *Canterbury*, for making constitutions and canons in the *Convocation* of 1640.

III. His order for the *Communion Table* to be placed altar-wise and to be railed in; and his kneeling and consecrating the bread and wine at the west side of the *Communion Table*, with his back toward the people, and bowing toward or before the *same*.

V. Arranging all the pews or seats so that the people were forced to kneel with their faces toward the east.

VI. He used his power to restrain *effective preaching*, forbidding all sermons on Sunday afternoons or on weekdays without his license. Fearing that explaining the *Catechism* and the *Book of Common Prayer* might be as influential as preaching (as he and some of his officers said), he prohibited any kind of explanation and mandated only the simple question and answer found in the *Book of Common Prayer*.

VII. To prevent people from knowing where sermons were being held, he commanded all ringing of bells to be the same, so that people could not distinguish between a service with a sermon and one with only prayers.

VIII. He allowed no prayer to be said before the sermon except the one directed in the 39th Canon, which has no legal authority; and after the sermon, he permitted no prayer at all except the *Gloria Patri*, etc.

IX. He published a Book of Articles to which the *churchwardens* were required to swear. These 39 *Articles* contained at least 897 questions, one of which was: *Does any man speak profanely during meals regarding religion or the Holy Scriptures?* Another: *Does the minister explain the Holy Scripture according to the interpretation of the early Church Fathers?*

After some time spent debating these articles, it was resolved and voted that it is the opinion of *this House* that *Matthew Wren*, Bishop of *Ely*, is unworthy and unfit to hold or exercise any office or dignity in the *Church* or *Commonwealth*; and that a *message* be sent to the Lords to request that they join with the *Commons* in petitioning His *Majesty* to remove Bishop *Wren* from both his personal presence and his service.

### Articles of Impeachment of the Commons assembled in Parliament in the name of themselves, and of all the Commons of England, against MATTHEW WREN, late Bishop of Norwich, and now Bishop of Ely.

<margin>Preamble.</margin> **T**HAT the said *Matthew Wren*, being popishly and superstiously inclined, did—upon first becoming Bishop of *Norwich* in the year 1635—endeavor by various ways and means to suppress the powerful and diligent preaching of the Word of God. He introduced several orders and injunctions tending toward superstition and idolatry, and he disturbed the orderly and settled condition of the ministers, people, and churches of that diocese. This caused great harm to His *Majesty* and great grief, unrest, and risk to the property, consciences, and lives of many of His *Majesty's* loyal subjects there, clearly leading to an increase in profanity, ignorance, and disobedience among the common people, as may be seen in the following details.

<margin>
Articles of Impeachment against Bishop Wren, July 20, 1641.
</margin>

I. Whereas many chancels of churches during Queen *Elizabeth's* reign, and ever since, were flat and ordered to continue as they were by the Rubric, he, while Bishop of *Norwich* and without any lawful authority, enjoined in 1636 that they should be raised with two or three, and sometimes with four steps, so that the Communion Table, placed altar-wise, might be seen by the people.

II. In the same year, he ordered that the Communion Table, which was appointed by the Rubric to be placed in the body of the church, should instead be set at the east end of the chancel.

III. In the same year, he enjoined that a rail should be set around the table, within which only the minister should enter, as if it were too holy for the people; some of whom, such as *Daniel Wayman* and others, were punished for going inside it.

IV. To further advance blind superstition, he caused all the pews in the churches to be so altered in the same year that all the people might kneel with their faces eastward toward the Communion Table, which was set altar-wise.

V. In the same year, he enjoined that after part of the Morning Prayer was read at the reading desk, the minister should go to the table as a more holy place and read part of the Communion Service (now called the "second service"), even though no Communion was to be administered. By this, the consciences of many—both ministers and people—have been grieved, and the service rendered unprofitable because the people were unable to hear it from that place.

VI. Both he and his chaplains, as well as other clergy following his example, used so many bowings and acts of adoration toward the table after it was so placed that they have given great scandal to sincere and well-affected Christians.

VII. In the same year, he enjoined all persons to receive the Sacrament while kneeling at the said rail, and ordered that ministers should not give the Communion in any other way. This caused many good people, for fear of idolatry, to avoid the Sacrament, yet they were excommunicated for not receiving it.

VIII. In the same year, he enjoined that there should be no sermons on the Lord's Day in the afternoons, or on weekdays, without his license. He also ordered that there should be no catechizing other than the questions and answers contained in the *Book of Common Prayer*, not allowing the ministers to explain them to the listeners. Furthermore, to encourage the people in profaning the Lord's Day, he enjoined the ministers to publicly read a book in the churches that allowed sports on that day; for not doing so, several were suspended by him, such as Mr. *William Leigh*, etc., and some were deprived of their positions, such as Mr. *Jeremy Burroughs* and others.

IX. Whereas there had formerly been a different way of ringing the bells when there was a sermon compared to when there were only prayers, he ordered in the same year that this difference should be discontinued to hinder the people's edification.

X. Whereas many godly ministers used to preach a preparation sermon two or three days before the Communion to prevent the unworthy receiving of the Lord's Supper, he prohibited the ministers of his diocese from doing so any longer.

XI. Endeavoring to suppress the power and effectiveness of prayer, he enjoined in the same year that no minister should pray before a sermon, but only move the people to pray using the words of the 55th Canon, which is not authorized by law. When he was present where a preacher did pray, he used to show his disapproval by sitting in his seat without showing any reverence.

<meta>This page continues the specific articles of impeachment against Matthew Wren, proceeding from Article XII through Article XXIV, detailing his enforcement of religious rituals, his persecution of clergy and tradesmen, and his alleged financial extortions.</meta>

XII. To further alienate the people's hearts from hearing sermons, he, in that same year, commanded all ministers to preach in their hood and surplice—a practice not previously used in the diocese—and caused prayers to be omitted for two Sundays in the church of *Knatshall* because of the lack of a surplice.

XIII. During his time as Bishop of *Norwich*, which lasted about two years and four months, he caused fifty pious ministers to be excommunicated, suspended, or deprived of their positions for not reading the service at the communion table; for not reading the *Book of Sports*; for using extemporaneous prayers; and for not complying with other illegal innovations. This led to the ruin of their families, and some were forced to flee overseas.

XIV. By unlawful and harassing methods, he forced the parishes within his diocese to contribute to the unnecessary expenses of raising the floors of their chancels and railing in the communion table, among other things.

XV. He harassed and troubled many of his Majesty's subjects in several ways through fees, excommunications, penances, and other censures for not approaching and kneeling at the rail when receiving Communion, for not standing up at the Gospel, and for other similar reasons.

XVI. Through rigorous prosecutions and other means, he caused 3,000 of the King's subjects (many of whom were tradesmen who each employed 100 poor people) to go to *Holland* and other places overseas. There, they established and taught their manufactures, which greatly hindered trade and impoverished the people of this kingdom.

XVII. Finding that the people disliked his innovations, he often publicly claimed that he introduced them by the King's command, thereby attempting to create a bad opinion of his Majesty in the hearts of his subjects.

XVIII. In the same year, 1636, in a church at *Ipswich*, he practiced idolatrous actions while administering the Lord's Supper: consecrating the bread and wine with his face toward the east and his back toward the people, lifting them so high that they could be seen above his shoulders, and bowing low either toward or before them when they were set down on the table.

XIX. To demonstrate his Popish sympathies, he caused a crucifix to be engraved on his episcopal seal in that same year.

XX. He has employed men as his commissioners and officials whom he knew were inclined toward his Popish superstitions and were unsound in their judgment and practice.

XXI. By filling vacancies with his own chaplains and associates, he has greatly oppressed several patrons, forcing them into expensive lawsuits to recover their own rights—and sometimes doing so even after he had promised the contrary *in verbo Sacerdotis* <note>on the word of a priest</note>.

XXII. He imposed penance on several churchwardens for not reporting people according to a "Book of Articles" (many of which were ridiculous) that he designed to increase the profits of his visitations. These churchwardens were forced to have their reports written by clerks appointed for that purpose, who charged extravagant rates for them, causing grievous oppression to his Majesty's poor subjects.

XXIII. By various forceful means, he forced the inhabitants of *Norwich* to pay two shillings in the pound of their rents as tithes, which was contrary to the laws of the realm and the ancient customs of that city.

XXIV. He assumed arbitrary power to compel the people of his diocese to pay excessive wages to parish clerks, threatening to prosecute those who refused in the High Commission Court.

To these misdemeanors, the Commons requested that the said *Matthew Wren*, now Bishop of *Ely*, should answer and receive such punishment as law and justice require.

The substance of this preceding charge seems to have been taken from *Mr. Prynne's* libel against the *Bishop*, when he was in the see of *Norwich*, entitled *News from Ipswich*.

The putting the laws into execution, and nothing but what was warrantable by law, against preachers of schism and sedition (who contended with obstinacy and affected sanctity to seduce the people from the orthodox religion established in *England*, and to withdraw the hearts of the subjects from their love and allegiance to their sovereign) was, in the language of those times, interpreted as the persecuting of godly, painstaking ministers; restraining powerful preaching, and the advancing of Popery and superstition.

> “Surely, if it is decent and fit for God’s service, it may stand so (if authority please) in any church. But if it advances or ushers in any superstition and Popery, it ought to stand so in none. Nor does any King’s Chapel have any prerogative (if that may be called one) above any ordinary church to disserve God in, by any superstitious rites.

> “Secondly, this also appears by the canon, or rule of the Church of *England*; for it is plain in the last injunction of the Queen that the holy table ought to stand at the upper end of the choir, North and South, or altar-wise. For the words of the Queen’s injunctions are these: — *The holy table in every church (mark it, I pray, not in the Royal Chapel or cathedrals only, but in every church) shall be decently made and set in the place where the altar stood.* Now the altar stood at the upper end of the choir, North and South, as appears before by the practice of the church. And to set it otherwise there is to set it across the place, not in the place where the altar stood. And so *stulti dum vitant vitia* <note>fools while avoiding vices [run into the opposite]</note>, weak men run into one superstition while they would avoid another; for they run into the superstition of the cross while they seek to avoid the superstition of the altar. So you see, here is neither Popery nor innovation in all the practice of Queen *Elizabeth*, or since.

# MATTHEW WREN, D. D.

"And in the daily prayers of the Church of *England*, this was retained at the Reformation; and that Psalm in which is *venite, adoremus* <note>Come, let us worship</note>, is commanded to begin the Morning Service every day. And for all I know, the priest may as well leave out the *venite* as the *adoremus*—the calling of the people to their duty as much as the duty itself once they have come. Therefore, even according to the Service Book of the Church of *England*, both the priest and the people are called upon for external and bodily reverence and the worship of God in His church. Therefore, those who do it do not innovate; and yet the government is so moderate (God grant it is not too loose meanwhile) that no man is constrained, no man questioned, but only religiously called upon: *venite adoremus*, 'Come, let us worship, etc.'"

<margin>P. 127.</margin>
"In Bishop *Jewel*’s reply to *Harding*’s answer, where *Harding* names various ceremonies, and particularly bowing themselves and adoring at the Sacrament—I say, adoring at the Sacrament, not adoring the Sacrament—there Bishop *Jewel* approves of everything, both the kneeling and the bowing. And he further adds, *That they are commendable gestures and tokens of devotion, as long as the people understand what they mean and apply them to God.* Now with us, the people always understood them fully and applied them to God, and to none but God, until these factious spirits and those like them—to the great disservice of God and His church—went about to persuade them that they are superstitious, if not idolatrous gestures; as they make everything else out to be where God is not served slovenly."

Further to recite the expressions of the same prelate (used upon another occasion) in defense of the external worship of God: "Ever since I came into office, I have worked for nothing more than that the external worship of God (so much slighted in various parts of this kingdom) might be preserved, and that with as much decency and uniformity as possible. For I clearly saw that the public neglect of God’s service in its outward appearance, and the shameful state of many places dedicated to that service, had almost cast a damp upon the true and inward worship of God. While we live in the body, inward worship needs external helps, and even all those are scarcely enough to keep it in vigor. And this I did to the utmost of my knowledge, according to both law and canon, etc."

It must surely appear very strange and unaccountable in all future times that "the contriving of pews in churches to face the East; the regulating of prayers and sermons and the ringing of bells; enquiries into whether any persons talk profanely of religion or the Holy Scriptures at mealtimes; whether ministers explain the Holy Scriptures in the sense of the primitive Fathers"—all necessary branches of pastoral care and authority in a diocese—should be deemed highly criminal in a Christian bishop by a sect claiming Christian purity and the name of Saints.

# THE LIFE OF

[A] friend, for advice on certain forms and points of law: The person thus entrusted, discovering (upon review) matters of such importance that he believed might be very helpful for the prosecutors to be warned of; betrayed his trust, and to ingratiate himself, treacherously delivered up *all* the *Bishop's papers* to the primary persons in power within the governing faction. The consequence of this was—that the decision which had been taken to bring him to trial for his life was suddenly canceled, and an order was made by the *House of Commons* to keep him in prison at their pleasure. He endured this with patience and resignation until (it pleased God) their tyranny had passed. In this manner, the Bishop, who had been prosecuted out of *malice*, was preserved by *treachery*.

The true reasons for the persecution of the Bishop and some others in the *hierarchy* are briefly noted by Archbishop *Laud*, referring to himself and those of his brothers who were fellow laborers for the good government of the Church and the maintenance of the orthodox faith practiced within it. Among these, no one was more diligent than Bishop *Wren*, who constantly assisted in all his councils for ecclesiastical affairs.

# MATTHEW WREN, D. D.

In a short time, these misguiding, hypocritical zealots obtained their seditious ends to their heart’s desire; they saw the *Church* in the greatest outward desolation, her truth questioned, her glory vanished, her buildings falling, her revenues devoured, and one of her chief prelates for dignity and learning driven from the See and Palatinate of *Ely* into a close, melancholy prison, under continual threats of a violent death: The Metropolitan and Primate of all *England* <note>Archbishop William Laud</note>, one of the most innocent, devout, and magnificent men of that age, beheaded in the view of forty thousand men; and too many of them were so inhuman as to rejoice at the death of a Bishop, against whom their chief objection was his being a Bishop. So certain it is that an erroneous devil in the understanding becomes a *furious devil in men’s practice*.

The grand charge of "innovation" so fiercely urged against Archbishop *Laud*, Bishop *Wren*, and the orthodox clergy of the *English* Church in those times of fanaticism was no more than what has been occasionally taken up and made use of in the service of blind zeal and illiterate and obstinate bigotry. —

### Sir Thomas Widdrington’s *Speech* (noted previously, p. 12) at a conference between both Houses on Tuesday, the 20th of July, 1641, at the transmission of the impeachment against Matthew Wren, Doctor in Divinity, late Bishop of Norwich, and now Bishop of Ely.

->My Lords,<-

I am commanded by the knights, citizens, and burgesses now assembled for the Commons in Parliament to deliver these articles against the Bishop of *Ely*.

May it please your Lordships first to hear them read.

->My Lords,<-

These articles are dipped in those colors in which this Bishop rendered himself to the Diocese of *Norwich*; they need no gloss or varnish: In them you may behold the spirit and disposition of this Bishop; hear the groans and cries of the people; and see a shepherd scattering (I had almost said) devouring his own flock. He that desired to paint Hercules thought he had done enough when he made a resemblance of the lion’s skin, which he was accustomed to carry about him as a trophy of his honor.

I will not say that in these you will find a resemblance of the lion’s skin; I am sure you will find the resemblance of the skins—that is to say, the tattered and ruined fortunes of poor, innocent lambs who have extremely suffered by the violence of this Bishop.

# THE LIFE OF A M...

In the year 1635, this man was created Bishop of *Norwich*; he was no sooner there than he began to march furiously.

In the creation of the world, light was one of the first productions; the first visible action of this bishop, after his appointment to this See, was to put out many burning and shining lights by suspending various able, learned, and conscientious ministers. He, who should have been the golden snuffer of these lights, became their extinguisher; and when these are taken away, where will poor men light their candles?

My Lords, this was not all.

He put out lights and set up firebrands in their places; he suspended hardworking <note>The original text uses "painful," which in the 17th century meant painstaking or industrious.</note> ministers and set up idle, factious, and superstitious priests (to use their own language) in their places. Yet it is the fortune of these men at this time, like rivers in the ocean, to be buried in the extreme activity of their diocesan.

He made a scourge, not of small cords, but of new injunctions and numerous articles, tied together with a strong twist of a most dangerous oath; and with this, he whipped out not the buyers and sellers, but the faithful dispensers of the Word—out of their churches, out of their estates, and out of their dear country.

This *Noah* (if I may so call him without offense), as soon as he entered into the ark of this diocese, sent—nay, forced—doves to fly out of this ark; and when they returned to him with olive branches in their mouths, representing peaceable and humble submissions, he would not receive them into this ark again unless, like ravens, they would feed upon the carrion of his new inventions. They were not permitted to have any footing there; he stood like a flaming sword to keep such people out of his diocese.

My Lords, unless he had done this, he could never have hoped to bring that great work, which he undoubtedly aimed at, to any perfection.

While the *Palladium* of *Troy* stood, that city was impregnable; the *Greeks* had no sooner stolen it away than they instantly won the city. So then, he first put out the candles, and then had the opportunity to shuffle in his works of darkness. He first beat off the watchmen and seers; then, what the impiety of some was pleased to style the "piety of the times" was likely to follow.

This being done, he then began to dress up God’s worship according to his own fancy. He expressed this in injunctions and directions—the Minervas <note>In mythology, Minerva was born fully formed from the head of Jupiter; here it refers to the Bishop's own sudden and personal decrees.</note> of his own creation. We find them styled *regales injunctiones Domini Episcopi* <note>"Royal injunctions of the Lord Bishop"</note>; a title too sacred with which to baptize his "brats." I shall be bold to call them *tyrannicas injunctiones Domini Episcopi* <note>"Tyrannical injunctions of the Lord Bishop"</note>. History affords no more barbarous cruelty than to join a dead and a living body together, where the one is miserably killed by the stench of the other. This bishop, who like *Aaron* should have stood between the living and the dead, has joined to living ordinances many dead and poisonous ceremonies, which have no other life than what they received from the breath of his injunctions. These are pressed upon the consciences of the people; even these must be observed as moral laws.

An arbitrary government in the church is more dangerous and more grievous than one in the state; it is exercised upon men’s consciences—the most tender part—and is the very pinnacle of tyranny, and of all others the most intolerable. A blow that would hardly be felt on the arm will put out the eye.

My Lords, in the time of King *Richard I*, one of this man’s predecessors—a valiant bishop—went to the *Holy War*. This bishop has raised a war at home, in his own diocese; a war not against *Saracens, barbarians, Turks, or infidels*, but against good and well-disposed people. I know not what
