# MATTHEW WREN, D. D.

What style to give this war; without doubt, my Lords, this was no holy war.

The weapons of this warfare were thirty-eight injunctions and one hundred thirty-nine articles, containing eight hundred seventy-nine questions.

The soldiers were chancellors, commissaries, officials, commissioners, rural deans, etc.

He himself commanded in chief.

The ways of assault and killing were by excommunications, suspensions, and deprivations—I stop here: *Mille modis morimur mortales* <note>Mortals die in a thousand ways.</note>.

The storehouse where all these were originally hatched and kept was the superstitious and malicious breast of this bishop.

This diocese was the stage where the direful tragedies of this war were acted for the space of two years and more.

<margin>1 Samuel 8:11, etc.</margin>
Thus did he trouble *Israel* in the time of peace; indeed, by these actions, he put some of the chariots and horsemen of *Israel* to flight. From these, he raised a fee of 500 pounds for his primary visitation; if it is considered *cum pertinentiis* <note>with all associated fees and rights</note>, it was not cheap, yet it was well-increased, for it was formerly only 40 pounds in the time of some of his predecessors.

Will it please your Lordships to patiently cast your eyes upon the model of this bishop’s zeal, piety, and religion? Let his affection for prayer and preaching speak for all the rest.

*First*, regarding prayer. It was his chance to find a prayer which is no prayer, pretended to be prescribed by a canon which is no canon—I mean the 55th Canon, set forth in the year 1603—and no other prayer must be used in his diocese before sermons. That monster of <term>conceived prayer</term> <note>Extemporaneous or spontaneous prayer, as opposed to set liturgical forms.</note> (pardon the expression, it’s not my own) seemed as bad to him as a spell or charm; it must not be used on any occasion. Without doubt, he would never have been so strict and severe in this particular if he had only dreamed of the predicament which a minister, a friend of his, was put in by this rule; the story is short.

A butcher was gored in the belly by an ox; the wound was cured, and the man desired a public thanksgiving in the congregation. The minister, finding no form for that purpose, read the <term>Collects for the Churching of Women</term> <note>A prayer service specifically for women after childbirth.</note>.

Next, regarding preaching. That he is most capable in this regard is agreed by all; but that he ever preached in this diocese, except once, I never heard affirmed by anyone.

His next care was that others should not preach too often; if they did, they were put on his blacklist. He changed that golden sentence of *Væ mihi, si non prædicavero* <note>Woe to me if I do not preach.</note> into *Væ aliis, si prædicaverint* <note>Woe to others if they preach.</note>. He was so far from the practice of St. *Paul*, the great preacher of the Gentiles—who, we read, preached until midnight—that he decreed there must be no sermons in the afternoon; there may be—indeed, there must be—sports and pastimes then. And, as if he stood in fear of the wordless language of bells, which might foretell a sermon, he cannot endure to hear the sound of a sermon in the toll of a bell.

In a word, he adorned churches at the expense of other men and ruined pulpits, which ought to have been the greatest part of his own responsibility.

My Lords, you have now had presented to your Lordships a brother—indeed, one whose position engaged him to be a father of the clergy—yet one who, like *Joseph’s* brothers, has taken the coats from *Joseph*. Indeed, they were forced to flee from him as *Joseph* fled from his mistress, or else they must taste of his forbidden waters; but in their leaving, he tears their skirts—indeed, their whole garments and livelihoods—from them. He has taken the locks from

<margin>16 Henry III. F. Waste, 128.</margin> In the time of King *Henry III*, we find a tenant in dower punished in an action of waste because she had destroyed two rich <term>villains</term> <note>Feudal tenants or serfs</note> and made them beggars.

He robbed souls of that sweet manna which is *pabulum animarum* <note>food of souls</note>, the Word of God.

My Lords, I have not yet recounted all his robberies; he has robbed God of part of His day; he makes part of that a day of sports. He has robbed the subjects of their indubitable birthright: the laws of the kingdom.

The citizens of *Norwich* must pay tithes for the rents of houses; there is no law in *England* nor custom in *Norwich* for it. Nay, and so that they may be sure to be robbed of justice too, the lawsuit for these tithes must be in his own consistory, from which there can be no appeal and no prohibition.

The true patrons of churches are robbed of their right to present clergy; others, who had no claim or only a small pretense of right, are admitted upon this unhallowed maxim: that if he should institute those who had the right, the pretender was without remedy. By this, he inverted a fundamental law of this nation, granting unjust possessions to those with remediless rights.

My Lords, I cannot tell you everything, but you can measure a lion by its paw.

I am commanded to lay this great malefactor at your doors—one who has been a great opponent of the life and liberty of religion, and who set a "brand of infamy" (to use his own words) upon *Ipswich* education.

In short, he is a complete mirror of innovation, superstition, and oppression; he is now caught in the snare of those articles which were the work of his own hands.

The rod of *Moses* at a distance was a serpent; it was a rod again when it was taken into his hands. This Bishop was a serpent, a devouring serpent in the diocese of *Norwich*. Your Lordships, perhaps, will by handling him make him a rod again; or, if not, I do not doubt but your Lordships will chastise him with such rods as his crimes deserve.

My Lords, I am commanded by the House of Commons to request your Lordships that this Bishop may be required to answer these articles, and that there may be such proceedings against him as the course and justice of Parliament admit.

> "Most gracious and dread Sovereign,

"You have before your Majesty’s eyes the representative body of the poor town of *Berwick*, yet a town (for *fuimus Troes* <note>Latin: "We were once Trojans," a literary allusion meaning "our glory is a thing of the past."</note>) that has been the delight, indeed, the ransom of kings; a true *Helena*, for which many bloody battles have been fought, lost, and regained several times within the span of a single century. A town, the strongest fortress of both your Majesty’s most flourishing kingdoms, yet upon every discord and dissension, tossed like a ball between them; if held in the hands of one, then thrown by the other kingdom—a ball that never found rest until the happy Union.

"A town, which today is as useless as weapons in a time of peace, yet may serve for your Majesty to look upon as a little map of both your great kingdoms, as sharing the nature of both, yet doubtful whether it is more beyond the ordinary limits of the one or outside the jurisdiction of the other kingdom, but prominent in the sight of both. A town neither wholly regulated by *English* or *Scottish* laws, but by customs and usages in some things different from both; yet rather inclined to *English* laws, and more affected by *Scottish* fashions and language, as it is more often addressed by the official decrees of the one and more often sees and hears the other.

"Although it is now *English*, and has been so since the time of King *Edward* IV, yet such is our distance from the center of the kingdom that the lines of those blessings now enjoyed by that kingdom—through your Majesty’s happy government and residence there—do not so fortunately converge in us.

"We well know (as indeed who does not?) that the royal blood running in your Majesty’s veins is drawn from the most renowned kings of both these kingdoms. And by those kings (most revered Sovereign), especially your Royal Father of ever-blessed and happy memory, this town—though on the borders of either kingdom—has been richly adorned with many privileges, franchises, and immunities; and, therefore, we do not doubt that your Majesty—in whom every man may behold the worth of all your ancestors, you being no less the rightful heir of their virtues than of their crowns—will graciously maintain what they have so kindly granted.

"But it is best to use few words with kings, especially when they are spoken by an unskilled orator. We dare boldly say (most gracious and mighty King) that our hearts are better than our tongues, being most of all unfortunate in this: that they are linked with such poor expressions.

"Yet we hope that your Majesty may see in our faces what you do not hear fully expressed by our tongues; we humbly beg your free pardon for the one, and your gracious interpretation of the other.

"Your Majesty is now going to place a crown upon your most sacred head, which God and your own right have long since given into your hands.

"Our humble prayers are that not only that, but all your other crowns, may be for your Majesty crowns of roses, without any mixture of thorns.

"And we most affectionately wish that the throne of King *Charles*—the great and wise son of our *British Solomon*—may be like that of King *David*, the father of *Solomon*, established before the *Lord* forever."

<meta>This page continues the account of Matthew Wren's life, moving from his activities during the King's progress to the intense political and religious persecution he faced leading up to the English Civil War.</meta>

<margin>Dr. Stillingfleet’s Grounds of Protestant Religion. Dedication.</margin>
...most strangely succeeded by the bitter, virulent, and unchristian *invective* (cited above) against the Bishop of *Ely* in 1641, which was received by the seditious with great applause and became the immediate *prelude* to the imprisonment and oppression of his *lordship* and of others, his brethren; and, in the end, to the abolition of *Episcopacy* and the total subversion of *Church and State*. That they should *both* fall together was a certain and unavoidable consequence; for *loyalty* to the crown is embedded in the very foundations of the reformed *Church of England*, which stands on those two grand principles of religion and government: “giving to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.” When, by the providence of *God*, upon the happy *Restoration* of the monarchy, the *Church of England*—which before had been triumphed over as if dead—obtained a glorious *resurrection*, it was with the *influence* of supreme *authority*. This has caused so close a union and combination of *interests* between them that the *Church of England* and the *Crown* have, like *Hippocrates’s* twins, both wept and rejoiced together. And nothing argues for the excellent constitution of our *Church* more than that the purity of *Christian doctrine* is joined therein with the acknowledgment of the regal power and supremacy. —— But to proceed,

The Bishop of *Ely* bore all this persecution and storm, raised by the factious and fomented by Parliament, with a sedate and composed mind, supported by his innocence. He resolved that if he perished, it should be without his own weakness or any poor desertion of himself; he privately prepared a just *apology and defense*, which, being fortunately discovered by the treachery of his *counsel*, proved the miraculous means of his preservation. Thus, he who was accused by falsehood and malice was saved and protected by perfidiousness.

Therefore, without any visible reason or even the bare formality of an open trial, they committed him to the *Tower of London*, relying on the plausibility of their conspiracy that had gained so many noted abettors, and taking no other evidence against him but the unjust prejudices of their own associates. Then they had free leisure to invent crimes that might affect both his life and estate; and lest any way should be left for his relief, they finally proceeded to a public sentence so that they might exclude him from all hopes or possibility of favor.

<margin>Short View of the Troubles of England, and Treaty of Uxbridge, p. 741. Oxford 1681.</margin>
Among the propositions agreed upon by the mutual advice and consent of the Parliaments of both kingdoms—united by the solemn *League and Covenant* and tendered to his *Majesty* at the Treaty of *Uxbridge* on November 23, 1644—it was stated:

> “ *First*, That the persons who shall expect no pardon be *Rupert* and *Maurice*, Counts Palatine of the *Rhine*; *James*, Earl of *Derby*; *John*, Earl of *Bristol*; *William*, Earl of *Newcastle*; *Francis*, Lord *Cottington*; *John*, Lord *Powlet*; *George*, Lord *Digby*; *Edward*, Lord *Littleton*; *William Laud*, Archbishop of *Canterbury*; *Matthew Wren*, Bishop of *Ely*; with many others, lords and gentlemen of eminent quality in the two kingdoms.”

Thus was he loaded with calumnies and malicious imputations and debarred of all means to vindicate and defend himself. Oppressed with violence and tyranny, exposed to the mercy of rapine and sacrilege, divested and stripped of all his fortunes, and abridged and deprived of his liberty, he was condemned to the solitude of a close and tedious imprisonment in the *Tower* (where he continued for nearly eighteen years). And yet, in all these trials, he behaved himself like one who was made to bring afflictions into repute. The Church beheld his sufferings and saw through him that nothing in Christianity was impracticable, and the world almost pardoned his enemies for the pleasure and benefit of his example.

<meta>This page continues the account of Matthew Wren's steadfastness during his long imprisonment, highlighting his virtuous character under trial and his interactions with fellow prisoners like George Monk.</meta>

-># MATTHEW WREN, D. D.<-

Such cruel treatment and barbarous indignities as these were to be pitied and lamented by all, except him who endured them; for the wisest and best of men have a greater sense of baseness than misfortune, and are accustomed to be more affected by their own failings than by the injuries of others. It pleased Divine Providence that those latent virtues, which are less conspicuous amidst the smiles and compliments of fortune and almost disappear in a smooth and undisturbed course of felicity, being (as it were) kindled by this fiery trial, should break forth into a more glorious flame to enlighten and adorn the darker side of adversity.

For he stepped forth and appeared with an innate ability to undergo the greatest extremities; to slight and scorn all menaces and terrors, being as well inured and hardened by discipline and custom as by nature and constitution, made and framed for this noble experiment. And, so that we may not question but that he was brought into these circumstances by the special appointment of heaven, he was of such an impregnable spirit, of such incredible constancy and resolution, buoyed up with a most certain and fruitful hope, exalted with an earnest and cheerful expectation, and prepared to meet the utmost effects of cruelty. He was always apt and forward to anticipate events, and that with the great assurance of a more pleasant scene and happy state of affairs; so that by the aids and encouragements of conscience, and the secret testimonies of his own integrity, he blasted the villainies which had been hatched against him, and disgraced and shamed all the affronts that were offered him.

If it happened that anyone had the curiosity to visit a person so bravely miserable, or if anyone felt a desire (more prevalent than the danger that accompanied it) to behold virtue struggling with calamity, he met with only one man, a most upright and elevated soul, who built and bore itself up upon its own foundation; and all the hopes and confidence of the kingdom, the prospect and expectation of better times, were reduced into one corner and miraculously preserved in the breast of one single person.

Notwithstanding the grievances and anxieties of a close restraint, he heightened and improved the incomparable greatness of his mind by the solace and delight of study. When he was destitute of the advantage of books, he betook himself to the explanation of the Holy Scriptures, assisted only by the strength of his own abilities, the solidity of his judgment, and that stock of learning which he had treasured and maintained in a faithful memory. Accounting that which others call imprisonment to be an opportunity for study, he bestowed all his time in meditation, writing, and searching into the sacred mysteries (using his skill in three languages) and committed to paper an infinite number of annotations. This Covenant, as it deserved, had no better treatment in the *Complaint* or *Remonstrance of the University of Cambridge, namely:*

<margin>Querela Cantabrigiensis, p. 204. 5th Edition. London, 1732.</margin>
> A Covenant with Hell, begun between *Munster* and *Mecca*, by the help of a Jesuit, the most impious and unchristian confederacy that their grand master the *Devil* could contrive; the chief end of which is to dethrone the *Lord's anointed*, and throw down the Church and its apostolical government; and to force not only their fellow subjects to contradict their oaths of allegiance and supremacy, but even their most gracious Sovereign to perjury, by violating his sacred oath which he solemnly made at his coronation. And to complete their most horrid and heinous sin, to join in arms with a *foreign nation*, to lay desolate their own native country, to stain this earth with the blood of their own countrymen and fellow subjects, and to expose the treasures of *England*, the cream of these fruitful valleys, to the empty and hungry maw of a rebellious *Scot*, and then vow never to have peace, except that which shall be written in the blood of their enemies (his *Majesty* and his loyal subjects); and lastly, most cruelly and wickedly to exhort and solicit all Protestants in the *Christian world* to undertake the same course as them by rising in rebellious arms, thereby exposing the throats and lives of all our brethren, the Protestants of *France* and elsewhere, to the just jealousy of their several princes: and yet this *Covenant* is made the foundation of the great work of their glorious *Reformation*. The contrivers of this *scheme of iniquity* have reduced this renowned *University* almost to a mere *Munster*, and have done more in less than three years than the apostate *Julian* could effect in all his reign, namely: broken the heartstrings of learning and learned men, and thereby dislocated <note>The original word "luxated" means dislocated or put out of joint.</note> all the joints of Christianity in the kingdom.

The end of this *Scottish Covenant*, which had caused such incredible miseries to the nation for many years, was this.

->Monday, May 20, in the year 1661.<-

<margin>Bishop Kennet's Register, p. 450.</margin>
> THE Lords in Parliament assembled, having considered a paper sent to them from the House of Commons for the burning of an instrument or writing called the *Solemn League and Covenant* by the hand of the common hangman, do order that the same instrument or writing, called the *Solemn League and Covenant*, be burned by the hand of the common hangman in the *New Palace Yard* at *Westminster*, in *Cheapside*, and before the *Old Exchange*, on *Wednesday* the 22nd of this instant, *May*. And that the said Covenant be immediately taken off the record in the House of Peers and in all other courts and places where it is recorded; and that all copies of it be taken down from all churches, chapels, and other places within *England*, *Wales*, and the town of *Berwick-upon-Tweed* where they are set up. Printed by order of the House of Lords, 1661.

But, previous to this happy occurrence (while the *Bishop* was wholly dedicating himself to the service of *God* and his *King*), the yoke of tyranny began to sit loose; and the new models of the upstart politicians began to fail and fall apart; and all those happy things were accomplished which he had framed and fashioned in his thoughts—which he alone had the prudence to foresee and the courage to hope for. While impudent and wicked men, highly conscious of their own desperate exploits, reflected at last upon what they had formerly committed, and seemed to be ashamed of their share in villainy, the

The secluded members of the Long Parliament being restored to their seats in the House (*Feb.* 21, 1659-60)—that great step towards the settlement of the peace of the nation—among the first transactions of importance, which were the apparent dawnings of a glorious change, it was ordered on *March* 15th following, *that Dr.* Wren, *Bishop of* Ely, *be discharged from his imprisonment; and that the Lieutenant of the* Tower *of* London *be, and is hereby required to discharge him accordingly.*

Yet for all this, he was not admitted to his own palace, but exposed to an uncertain and hired habitation, and seemed rather to enjoy an enlargement than a restoration, until King *Charles* II—whose return was the great desire and whose appearance was the solid joy of all loyal hearts—came armed with majesty and power, and sat down upon his father's throne.

In the beginning of the great rebellion and confusions, several persons continued to make a regular presentation of their clerks to the bishop of the diocese: and the bishop gave them institution, though without power of giving them possession.

<margin>See the Register of the Bishop of Ely.</margin>
This was instanced in the diocese of *Ely*, even while the *bishop* was a prisoner in the *Tower of London*.

<margin>Bishop Kennet's Register, p. 885.</margin>
From the register of Bishop *Wren* of *Ely*, for the first three years following the Restoration, we know several matters of fact relating to patrons, clerks, and benefices, of singular use and application in the knowledge of things, times, and men. And one particular will appear: that there were but very few of the parochial clergy deprived within this diocese in 1662 for not submitting to the Act of Uniformity, though more of the old legal incumbents had been sequestered about the year 1644 than, in proportion, within any other diocese (this being one of the associated counties) under the early pretended reformation made by the then prevailing powers; and though the zeal of this *bishop* was distinguished above all his brethren in purging his diocese of disaffected ministers—a zeal that was apt to carry him beyond the bounds of the law.

<margin>Said to be Mr. Rogers.</margin>
There is at least one instance of it in the case of the rectory of *Leverington* in the Isle of *Ely*, which had been possessed for some years by a worthy person, Mr. *Richard Reynolds*, M.A. Having been episcopally ordained, having no surviving predecessor, and conforming to the *Act*, he had a lawful title to it; and yet the bishop, not liking the man because he had come in without his patronage, gave a new collation on *Feb.* 9, 1662, to Mr. *John Randolph*, M.A. When he was denied admittance, Randolph commenced a suit against Mr. *Reynolds*, who in the end obtained a legal recovery of his rightful title. In the meantime, he got a friend to complain to the King of the needless and expensive vexation given to him; and his Majesty was so gracious as to speak to the bishop to give no further disturbance. But his lordship was so unyielding as to insist upon defending the rights of his see; and when the King seemed to expect to be obeyed, the bishop bluntly said, *Sir, I know the way to the Tower*; for which his former long confinement and his now declining years might be some apology for his hasty humor.

<margin>Kennet.</margin>

> "There is an impropriate rectory—the name of the place I know not—of three hundred pounds per *annum*, belonging to the Bishop of *Hereford*, within four miles of that city, with a very good house upon it, which was let for 'lives'; and there was but one life remaining when the current Bishop of *Ely* was Bishop *there*; and though his Lordship was offered a thousand marks, and believes he might have had a thousand pounds to renew the lease, yet he refused it, on purpose that it might be reserved as a demesne for the Bishop for the time to come; and accordingly he gave his late *Majesty* an account of it, who very much approved of what he had done, and gave command to *Dr. Theophilus Field* and *Bishop Cooke* successively not to renew it; so that in all probability it has now clearly expired and may be a good improvement to that bishopric."

William Prynne's libel against Bishop Wren, and the Bishop, the nation, King, Queen, and Court.

The noted *William Prynne*—a stigmatized Presbyterian, a busy, meddling, restless man, and an inveterate enemy against the hierarchy of bishops—wrote a scandalous libel, suiting the uncharitableness of those seditious times, entitled *News from Ipswich*; printed three times in 1636, and another time in 1641, intended chiefly against Doctor *Wren* when he was Bishop of *Norwich* and had taken up his dwelling in that town. He fell as scandalously foul on the Archbishop himself, and some of the other bishops also, and those who acted under them. For therein he commented very sharply (as he conceived) on the Archbishop himself, with his Arch-Piety, Arch-Charity, Arch-Agent for the Devil, etc. With similar reproach he attacked the bishops, generally calling them *Luciferian Lords Bishops, execrable traitors, devouring wolves, etc.*, with many other odious names not fit to be used by a Christian, and more particularly on Bishop *Wren*; and yet this very man, who by his numerous vile writings, especially his *Histrio-mastix*

--- Page 60 ---
<meta>This page continues the account of the legal consequences for William Prynne and his associates, their eventual release by the Long Parliament, and the restoration of Matthew Wren and other bishops following the return of King Charles II.</meta>

[Histrio]mastix had disgraced the Nation, defamed the Church, its Discipline, and its Members, dishonored the King and Queen, and reproached the Court with some things that were thought to tend toward the destruction of his *Majesty's* person. Thereupon, he had been justly sentenced to a fine, the pillory, and imprisonment. However, in the year 1641, by an order of the *Blessed House of Commons* (as it was called by the *godly party*), he was released from his prison. On his journey back to town, he was met and caressed by multitudes in several parts of *England* and brought triumphantly into *London*, to the great defiance and contempt of authority and justice. At length, this snarling zealot—when it was too late, and he had seen fully to what great woe, misery, and confusion the *godly party* had brought the King and the Nation—heartily repented. He wished that when they had cut off his ears, they had cut off his head instead. In the end, to make some atonement for his former crimes, he became, in some manner, instrumental in the most happy *Restoration*.

<margin>
Rushworth,
Part II.
Vol. I. p. 463.
</margin>
*John Lilburne* and *John Warton*, the two printers and publishers of Mr. *Prynne's* seditious libel cited above, called *News from Ipswich*, were deservedly punished by censure in the *Star-Chamber*, upon information preferred in that high court by the King's Attorney-General.

The barbarous invectives of the two other great incendiaries of the *time*, Dr. *Bastwick* and Mr. *Burton*, were all of a piece with the malice and venom of *Prynne* against the hierarchy of the Church, wherein the *Archbishop* and the Bishop of *Ely* were principally targeted. Dr. *Bastwick*, in his answer to the charge against him in the *Star-Chamber*, has these abominable passages:

<margin>
Rushworth,
Part II.
Vol I. p. 381.
</margin>
> "That the Prelates were invaders of the King's royal prerogative, contemners and despisers of the whole Scriptures, advancers of Popery, superstition, idolatry, and profaneness; also, that they abused the King's authority to the oppression of his loyal subjects, and therein expressed great cruelty, tyranny, and injustice; and in the execution of this impious performance, they showed neither wit, honesty, nor moderation; nor were they either servants of God or of the King (as they ought to be indeed), but of the Devil, being enemies of God and the King, and of every living thing that was good; all which he declared he was ready to maintain."

For these and similar horrid defamations and slanders, the three delinquents—*Prynne*, *Bastwick*, and *Burton*—were sentenced by the court, consistent with law and justice, though some misguided people thought with too much rigor. As an additional mark on *Prynne*, more than the others, it was decreed that he should be stigmatized on both cheeks with the letters S. L., signifying a "seditious libeller." It was very fortunate for this man that he lived to repent publicly (and, it is to be hoped, sincerely) of his seditious and rebellious practices, and to see an end to the most abject slavery and distress of his country in a miraculous deliverance by the blessed *Restoration*.

<margin>
September,
1660.
</margin>
Upon the glorious scene and alteration of affairs in Church and State, by the long-wished-for return of the King, the Bishop of *Ely*, along with the *eight other surviving prelates (who had outlived the persecution and confusion of the times), were restored. But no man's restitution seemed of so great importance as his; for into his breast the Church of *England* betook herself, as to the only man who had the skill and courage to repair and reinforce her.

# MATTHEW WREN, D. D.

diffused, and reeling forgotten discipline. When, therefore, he was courted by the highest preferments, and the concerns of the *Church* could not well be managed by a lesser wisdom and authority than his, even then he was void of all ambitious thoughts; he sought not advancement but restoration, contented to recover, restrain, and die in his own former dignity. In the greatest affluence of prosperity and plenty, he gave no way to pleasure, but studied and practiced the highest degrees of temperance and anxiety; he drank no wine for almost twenty years (except that of the sacred chalice) and would eat on no other than a wooden trencher; he persevered to macerate his body with abstinence and fasting, indulgent enough to others, as if he had been weary of this life and made haste to eternity. Nor, though his own family was most dear to him, did he ever exceed the bounds of his usual moderation in providing for it; he did not catch at other men's estates to augment his own, but many times receded from his lawful rights; and particularly to his successor, he left not some few gleanings, but a large harvest of fines. The first money he received after his restitution, he bestowed on *Pembroke Hall*, and to the honor of Almighty God, to whose service he had wholly devoted himself; for the ornament of the university, which he always affected with a fervent and passionate love; and in a grateful remembrance of his first education, which was in that place received and thankfully acknowledged, he built that most elegant *Chapel* there, at the expense of above *five thousand pounds*, completely finished, and endowed it with *perpetual revenues* for *repairs*. This, however noble and magnificent, is the least of those monuments he has left to posterity.

It is not to be forgotten that the only bodily exercise he could obtain during his long imprisonment, and which in some degree might conduce to his health, was walking on the leads of the *Tower* (by the connivance of his warder) where, upon a just computation, he walked round the world.

<margin>Heylyn's Geography, p. 22.</margin>
> "The earth is affirmed by the best writers to be 21,600 miles in compass, which is demonstrable enough: for since there are in each of the greater circles 360 degrees, and every degree is reckoned at 60 miles, let 360 be multiplied by 60, and the product will be 21,600, as was said before. So that, if it were possible to make a path around the earth, an able footman going constantly 24 miles a day would compass it in 900 days; and so in proportion of time and miles."

A remarkable instance (among many) should not be passed over in silence, of *his magnanimity, resolution*, and *contempt of adversity*, which may convey a further idea of *his character*. Some time before the decease of *Oliver Cromwell*, Mr. *Christopher Wren* (only son of Dr. *Christopher Wren*, and nephew of the Bishop of *Ely*) became acquainted with Mr. *Claypole*, who married the Usurper's favorite daughter. This gentleman, being a lover of mathematics, had conceived a great esteem for him and took all occasions to cultivate his friendship and to court his conversation, particularly by frequent invitations to his house and table. It happened upon one of these invitations that *Cromwell* came into the company as they sat at dinner, and without any ceremony (as his usual way was in his own family), took his place. After a little time, fixing his eyes on Mr. *Wren*, "Your uncle," says he, "has been long confined in the *Tower*." "He has so, Sir, but bears his afflictions with great patience and resignation." — "He may come out if he will." — "Will your Highness (as he was called) permit me to tell him this from your own mouth?" — "Yes, you may."

<meta>This page concludes the account of Matthew Wren’s steadfastness during his imprisonment and describes his death and burial in 1667.</meta>

As soon as he could decently retire, he hastened with no little joy to the Tower and informed the *Bishop* of all the details of this interview with *Cromwell*. Upon this, his Lordship expressed himself warmly to this effect:
> "That this was not the first time he had received a similar hint from that *miscreant*, but he disdained the terms proposed for his release, which were to be a humble acknowledgment of *his* favor and an abject submission to his detestable tyranny. That he was determined patiently to wait for the *Lord’s leisure* and owe his deliverance (which he trusted was not far off) *to him alone*."

<margin>*Acts, Chapter 16*</margin>
Such was the exemplary courage and resolute behavior of St. *Paul* and *Silas* in the prison toward the magistrates of *Philippi*, when "they sent their sergeants, saying, 'Let those men go.'" And the keeper of the prison told this saying to Paul: "The magistrates have sent to let you go." But Paul said to them, "They have openly cast us into prison uncondemned, and now do they thrust us out secretly? No, truly; let them come themselves and fetch us out."

He paid his last debt to nature at *Ely House* in *Holborn, London*, on the 24th of *April* in the year 1667, aged 81 and upwards. His body was conveyed to *Cambridge* by the heralds with all decent pomp and ceremony, and deposited in a stone coffin in a vault under his own chapel. The Vice-Chancellor, heads of colleges, and the whole university attended the solemnity of his funeral rites; and the very eminent and learned Doctor *John Pearson*, then Master of *Trinity College* (afterwards Bishop of *Chester*), gave his funeral oration in *Latin*. From a manuscript of that oration, the preceding descriptions and other significant passages of his life (with some additional memoirs interspersed) have been transcribed here.

## NUMB. II.

<margin>Year 1667.</margin>
An oration delivered at Cambridge, in Pembroke Chapel, at the funeral of the right reverend father in Christ, MATTHEW WREN, Bishop of Ely.

By JOHN PEARSON, D. D. and Master of Trinity College.

*Most reverend lord, lord vice-chancellor; most noble youths; most distinguished and esteemed men,*

IF I have ever had to hope in any business of the republic of letters that it would turn out successfully, and that the outcome should match the duty so auspiciously undertaken, it certainly seems most necessary at this time to pray with all my heart that an oration worthy of us and worthy of the prelate should be achieved; lest either the reputation of the university, or the honor and dignity of the church, should lose its value through the weakness of my mind, the poverty of my words, or the infirmity of my judgment.

For until now, no more fitting occasion has been granted to this most ample home of the arts where we live to raise itself up, nor has a more illustrious splendor of the religion we cultivate ever shone forth, than in the life, deeds, and varied fortunes of that bishop whose funeral we celebrate with solemnity: in whom alone, if this seat of the muses did not exhibit everything honest, noble, and glorious it could show; in whom, if the fame most deservedly elicited and even extorted from all did not redound most greatly to us, then we must utterly despair of claiming honor for letters forever.

Behold the sacred miters placed before your eyes as if in a school; think of these insignia of the episcopacy as trophies brought back to Athens, but especially recall in your soul and memory your prelate Matthew, whose bier did not more clearly carry and sustain these ornaments than he himself, while he lived, supported, refined, and adorned that sacred order and dignity.

<page-num>40</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF</header>
<meta>catchword: fictâ</meta>

It will therefore be worthwhile, most distinguished men, both for you to recall with grateful thought and for me to explain with the thread of a clear oration, under what auspices he undertook all his most perfect works; by what steps he ascended, and through what windings and diversions he passed; so that, tracking his footsteps and led by his example, adorned with his virtues, we may learn to follow such a great leader and long for such arduous and glorious things.

To pass over his remarkably ancient and sufficiently noble family, and other things which can less easily be drawn as an example, he came to the university as a youth of the greatest promise, sent not with common expectation nor in the manner of others, but (which was a most happy omen) sought out, summoned, and brought by Lancelot Andrewes, the most praised Master of this Hall. First placed by Andrewes’s hand in this fertile soil of bishops, diligently observed by his care, continually instructed by his advice, and spurred on by his constant favor, he gave himself entirely to the study of good literature. He cultivated his mind with perpetual vigils, while he weakened, wore down, and exhausted his body.

In a short time, being most well-known for his remarkable skill in arts and languages, and having performed the public duties and exercises of the university with the highest praise, he observed religious rites most devoutly, exercised discipline most sharply, and defended privileges most gravely. He conceived and fixed such a deep love for these seats in his mind that neither the length of his age nor the injustice of the times could erase or diminish it.

After he had emerged learned, cultivated, and polished in all the humanities and most liberal studies, he applied himself to the Church with his whole mind and with all the force of his soul. And indeed, theology claims for itself, as if by its own right, extraordinary and sharp wits, and men most flourishing in every kind of learning and the gifts of some illustrious mark; for all the powers of the mind cannot be better exercised and spent than in cultivating piety, in adorning the worship of God, and in celebrating divine matters.

While this man was engaged in these things—by a rare combination both most learned and most pious, and equally intent on promoting the goals of the university and the Church—although he seemed to hide within these walls which he so greatly cherished, or adhered most faithfully and obediently to his Lancelot, he began to be held in the highest expectation. There was nothing so great that everyone did not judge it could be accomplished and obtained by him.

Nor could he remain hidden from the perceptive eye of the most wise King JAMES, to whom he was already sufficiently known and understood, even from our own academic benches. Therefore, at that moment in time when the Prince's household required a true son of the Church of England and a man of well-tested faith, the King, of his own accord and by his own judgment (that is, the greatest judgment), assigned him as chaplain to his CHARLES. To this matter, an additional heap of honor was added: the transaction was carried out so secretly that it remained in doubt whether he was given by the King or requested by the Prince. This doubt has even now been most happily increased because he was equally dear to both; and in that secret, this was certainly clear and evident: it was a prelude to a greater mystery.

For behold, there settled deeply in the mind of the most prudent King a very certain plan for conducting an affair, which was a miracle to the whole world when it was happening, and perhaps, after it was done, it will never cease to be so. So much are the wits of men fatigued and darkened as they busy themselves and strive to pry into the secrets of princes, discuss the causes of public business, and thoroughly understand their reasons.

It was determined by the most skillful of kings to send his only son, the heir of a triple kingdom, the hope and comfort of his father's house, CHARLES, the most beloved offspring of a most indulgent father, to the shores of Spain. He committed him to a nation most prudent in secret plans, known to us until now for craftiness, pride, and long-standing enmity; not surrounded by an army, nor armed with a fleet (the kind of preparation with which the English used to seek out the Spanish), but committed to their sufficiently suspect faith, fortified only by his own prudence.

When, therefore, your Matthew was chaplain (should I say secretary?) to the best of princes in a most dangerous business: (for where true piety has taken root, and a heart not

<header>MATTHEW WREN, D. D.</header>

...steeped in a false religion; these things, which differ so widely among others, differ little or not at all here.)

Then, indeed, he so eloquently explained the foundations of our religion everywhere and defended them so vigorously, and privately untied the knots tied by churchmen to entangle the prince's affairs with such sharp insight, that the path for the prince’s return to his father was more clearly opened than by any other means.

Furthermore, if we wish to consider any evidence (most grave men) of how much our university was esteemed at that time, I believe no better conjecture can be made than that the prince loved it so ardently that he flew here upon his return: **CHARLES** deigned to care for it with such devotion, pursued it with such indulgence, or sent Matthew from his own side to adorn it.

I pass over the richness of the benefit with which he was immediately rewarded; the dignity of the prebend with which he was honored; and his appointment—or rather elevation—to the governance of Peterhouse <note>the College of St. Peter</note>. There, through his moderation of mind and command, he brought all the fellows into the greatest harmony; he inspired the youth toward the study of good literature; he even erected new buildings. He rescued the college archives from moths and bookworms, shaking off the dust and organizing them into a brilliant order with the greatest industry. Seeing that the duties of piety were being performed with less decorum because of a lack of sacred meetings within the college, and a certain borrowed license to serve God outside its walls, he arranged for a chapel to be built and decorated—not being able to do so at his own expense at that time, he used the funds of others but his own authority among good men.

Having been made Vice-Chancellor, he restored collapsed discipline, kept everyone to their duty, and taught the university itself to finally understand its own nature.

But truly, the most serene King could not bear for him to be away for long or to struggle in academic dust. Therefore, he appointed him Clerk of the Private Oratory and made him Dean of his chapel at Windsor. There, he served not only to ensure that divine offices were performed properly and decorously but also to uphold the dignity and splendor of this highest empire (which consists in the most famous Order of the Garter <note>periscelidis</note>). He ruled this order not only with remarkable gravity, wisdom, and authority but also adorned it with his most accurately polished writings, leaving an ample place for his brother and an example for all posterity.

When the King saw—no longer by conjecture but through many proofs—that he was born and prepared for the public government of the church, he moved him to the Bishopric of Hereford. You would hardly believe he had touched it, were it not for the fact that in that very short space of time, he stabilized a church fluctuating with ambiguous, useless, or unauthorized statutes, and adorned it with accurate and elegant ones.

Behold, the see of the Diocese of Norwich became vacant—a large and wide one, yet shaken and broken by schism. It demanded a skillful, wise, brave, and learned bishop. Therefore, he who alone seemed equal to such a great task was transferred there from Hereford. There, for two years and more, he uncovered the frauds of the schismatics, repressed their attempts, and broke their spirits.

Meanwhile, he moved to the Deanery of the Royal Chapel, the highest position one can ascend to in the court (that is, no closer access to the King). And since the correct administration of the Bishopric of Ely requires not only skill in ecclesiastical matters but also a knowledge of civil laws combined with academic institutions; and since all these things clearly met in that one man, he occupied that see as well, for which he seemed to have been made.

Thus, at last, through great virtues, he attained the height of dignity, the most abundant revenues, and the favor of a most indulgent prince, during the most flourishing time of both the empire and the church.

Meanwhile, not in the last place to be set down, and especially to be remembered among you, were his modesty and moderation. He never asked anyone for anything, nor did he solicit anyone even with a small word; he never sought any honor that he obtained. What was not sought was always granted; what was not requested was offered.

<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>42</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

Away with those who gape after church honors, who besiege the doors of the powerful or of prelates, and who do not so much earn dignity as seize it. I judge that he should be preferred before you, whom his own desires did not promote, but his merits; who stood at the very peak of happiness with a chosen wife and a numerous family, a great example of a most favoring divine power.

Truly, (members of the university) we were too happy in that age. God had then indulged us with things that neither the crimes of an ungrateful nation could bear, nor the long-suffering of the most merciful God could endure any longer. Happiness itself corrupted those whom it ruined; prosperity itself brought down those whom it depraved.

For suddenly, a storm rising from the north <note>Likely referring to the Scottish Covenanters or the start of the civil unrest in Scotland.</note> immediately loosened the structure of the kingdom, and a plague pervaded every limb. Under the mask of piety, most wicked men uprooted the church. They flew at all the bishops, but especially those dear to the King, because they sought not so much the bishops as **CHARLES** himself. They scraped together accusations, stirred up the mob, fueled envy, and instigated hatred, solely for the purpose of transferring these attacks to the King.

First, they accused our prelate, making him out to be wicked only because of his prince's favor and criminal because of his grace. They did not care how truly they spoke, but how boldly they might slander him. They exposed his alleged crimes before the supreme tribunal and demanded the ultimate punishment.

Meanwhile, the prelate, possessing a most exalted mind and relying on his innocence—certain that he was perishing by no fault of his own—quietly prepared himself for a just defense. This defense preserved him with such wonderful success that he, whom fraud had accused, was protected by the very treachery of the times.

Therefore, they threw him into prison without a trial, trusting in the notoriety of their conspiracy and their own reputation. They charged him with his life and all his fortunes; by public decree, they excluded him from all hope or expectation of mercy.

Thus, burdened with slanders, stripped of his defense, oppressed by power, exposed to robbery, deprived of all goods, pierced by the decree, robbed of liberty, shut away in hiding places, and defiled by the filth of a perpetual prison, he became a spectacle and an example worthy not only of the church but of the whole world.

These were indeed shameful things—sorrowful, pitiable, and to be wept over by everyone except the man who suffered them.

Wise men are moved by shame, not by misfortune, and by their own faults, not by the injuries of others. Divine providence willed that his other virtues—which were less conspicuous in a prosperous, steady, and perpetual fortune—might finally shine out as if ignited by this flame, glowing with more illustrious rays.

For he proved himself capable of bravely enduring the hardest trials and despising threats with an innate firmness; he was not so much instructed as he was born and formed for this.

And lest we doubt that he was placed in these straits by divine power, he was of such a steadfast mind, incredible constancy, and unheard-of equanimity—supported by a most certain hope, always upright in expectation, and ready to endure the cruelest suffering. He was so ready to anticipate the best and most joyful outcomes with great confidence that he put the injuries to shame through the conscience of a righteous will and the protection of his honor.

If anyone were ever seized by a desire to see a man so bravely miserable—if the desire to witness unhappy virtue should lure them more powerfully than the danger itself—they would see one man sustaining a most upright mind by himself alone. The entire hope of the kingdom and the expectation of better times were reduced to a single corner and preserved in a single heart.

Furthermore, he nourished this unshakable firmness of mind with the solace of study. Although almost all his library resources had failed him, he applied his mind to illustrating the sacred scriptures through his own talent, insight, learning, judgment, and memory. What others called imprisonment, he considered a "liberal leisure," spending himself entirely on meditation and writing. Having searched for the deepest meanings of the sacred text with his skill in three languages, he secretly wrote innumerable pages and completed so many volumes that posterity will easily believe he spent more than eighteen years in prison.

# MATTHEW WREN, D. D.

*All these things he elegantly and accurately drafted himself, and he provided in his will that they should be published for the public—if it seemed appropriate to the judgment of his most learned friends.*

*While he was entirely occupied with these matters, the yoke of tyranny began gradually to collapse, and the rudders of the new republic began to fail. Everything he had conceived in his mind, and which he alone had hoped for and foreseen, came to pass. While wicked men, fully conscious of their crimes, reflected on what they had done and wished it could be undone, he was snatched from prison so suddenly and unexpectedly that, amidst the general change of affairs, his own liberation was the only thing that caught him by surprise. Attributing this to a singular instance of divine mercy, he left the Tower of London almost reluctantly on the same day he had arranged for the consecration of the chapel at Peterhouse.*

*Not yet restored to his own home, but exposed to an uncertain hearth, he seemed more like someone cast out of prison than truly liberated—until* **CHARLES**, *sought by the prayers of all and received with the joy of all good men, stood armed with supreme authority and placed upon his father's throne.*

*How shall I remember that transformed state of affairs? Although this sight might be sad and mournful, I believe there is no one who has not been refreshed for a while from this grief by the memory of that day.*

*He returned with the others—though they were few—but his return was of no small importance. The shattered church fled to his protection; he was one of the few who both knew how and dared to renew the collapsed and extinguished discipline. In him almost alone, its liberty, safety, and security were founded.*

*Therefore, when the highest matters demanded him, and it seemed the church could be sustained in no other way than upon his shoulders, he did not aspire to higher positions at all. Not eager for promotion, but content to be restored, he desired to remain in his own see, to grow old, and to fall asleep.*

*Amidst a great abundance and flow of goods, he indulged in no pleasure. He had set his mind to observe the utmost restraint and temperance; for nearly twenty years, he did not swallow or even taste a single drop of wine.*

*He continued to weaken his body with fasting and abstinence; indulgent enough toward others, he was cruel only to himself, as if weary of this life and hurrying toward heaven.*

*Nor did he look too much after his own family, in which he took such great delight; he studied to show the same restraint in providing for them. He did not seize the property of others to enrich them, nor did he snatch up everything that belonged to him.*

*To his successors, he intentionally left not just the gleanings, but an ample harvest.*

*Moreover, he adopted this college <note>Referring to Peterhouse, Cambridge.</note> into his family and took it as his heir; the money first received from his revenues he sent ahead into this treasury.*

*Here, to the honor of God Almighty, to whose constant veneration he had always dedicated himself entirely; for the glory of the university, which he followed with incredible care and a certain burning love; and in memory of his first education, which he recalled daily with a most grateful mind—he built this chapel at enormous expense, endowed it with perpetual revenues, and duly consecrated it with his prayers. Beneath it, he built a tomb; to this, he finally entrusted his body. This is indeed an illustrious monument, yet the least of those he left behind.*

### *Extracts from Mr.* Atwood's *Memoirs, <note>Fellow of Pembroke Hall</note> relating to Bishop* Wren.

He brought a short history of the masters and all the fellows <note>of Pembroke Hall</note>, written with the greatest faithfulness, zeal, and skill from the beginning of the college's era, nearly down to his own times.

In the Bishop's Diary, in his own hand, December 25, 1585: I was born in London. Have mercy, O God! March 10, 1614: I responded in philosophy before King James, by order of the Cambridge Senate. <note>With the highest praise.</note>

Although the Bishop was born in London, he was descended from an ancient family, the Wrens of Binchester in the County of Durham. Because that place had been a Roman station, it might have inspired his interest in antiquities; for he was a true antiquary, and can be traced by his collections wherever he went: at Pembroke Hall, where he was a Fellow; at Peterhouse, where he was Master; at Windsor, where he was Dean; and at Ely, where he was Bishop. I <note>Atwood</note> have seen several of these collections. Besides his register, which seems to have been partly drafted by himself (and several parts of which bear his personal touch), it is quite remarkable that he kept a register while he was a prisoner in the Tower, where he could have had no assistance.

His charities were great; his chapel at Pembroke Hall is said to have cost him nearly £4,000 <note>over £5,000</note>, which he endowed with an estate at Hardwick, in the County of Cambridge, for repairs, etc. And yet, although he had provided well for a large family, his family is extinct in the male line, though it continues in the female line.

It must be admitted that he was arbitrary to the last <note>with reason and justice</note>, as appears by his admitting † Dr. Beaumont to the Mastership of Peterhouse as a Visitor through a stretch of power, despite the college having nominated Dr. Luke Skippon and Dr. Isaac Barrow, two deserving people.

The manner of his burial may be found in Mr. Worthington’s account, taken from the Heralds' Office.

*Christopher Wren, Bachelor of Divinity of Oxford. Incorporated at Cambridge, July 5, in the year 1630, Register of the University of Cambridge.*

*Christopher Wren, Doctor of Divinity at Cambridge, in the year 1630. Ibid [The same].*

This was probably in order to succeed his brother Matthew Wren as Master of Peterhouse; for on February 6, 1634, the Fellows of Peterhouse nominated to the Bishop of Ely: Christopher Wren, Doctor of Divinity, from the southern part of England, and John Cosin, Doctor of Divinity, from the northern part. But although Dr. Wren was first in the nomination, the Bishop <note>Francis</note> preferred Dr. Cosin, probably the more so because he was from his own college, namely Caius. On February 8, 1634, John Cosin, Doctor of Divinity, was admitted as Master by Francis, Bishop of Ely, as recorded in the Register of Peterhouse.

Throughout all the duties of life, Matthew Wren, Bishop of Ely, conducted himself with such gravity and integrity of character, with such remarkable piety, and finally with such observance of apostolic discipline, that wicked men did not fear him more than they hated him. From this source flowed all those things which he suffered, etc. He was thrown into the Tower of London—and finally, when he had fought strenuously, I might almost say, with beasts for about eighteen years, he was released from prison and restored in the year 1660.

Behold, however, a most clear sign of a truly great mind! Although he necessarily suffered huge losses and damages during that storm, yet in the year he was freed from custody—

...the fifth year had not yet passed before he consecrated to God the Savior that chapel, that most elegant glory of Pembroke, founded, built, excellently decorated, and endowed at his own expense. Even to such an extent, true virtue is incapable of being defeated. <note>Well done!</note>
This most missed man died April 24, 1667, over eighty years old, and with the university itself solemnly celebrating the funeral rites, he was laid to rest near the altar in the chapel built by him not so long before. (This was noted before.)

->From the MS. History of Pembroke Hall in Cambridge. By an uncertain hand.<-

Matthew Wren, Greek Scholar, B.A., chosen Fellow, Nov. 5, 1605. M.A. Junior Treasurer 1610, Senior Treasurer 1611. When James I made a royal progress to Cambridge, Wren maintained the philosophy act with great applause. Bursar 1621. President of the College 1616. Had a testimonial, June 30, 1618. Chaplain to Bishop Andrews. Chaplain to Prince Charles on his voyage to Spain. Doctor of Divinity. Resigned his fellowship, Nov. 8, 1624. Vice-Chancellor, 1628. Master of Peterhouse. Dean of Windsor. Bishop of Hereford. Bishop of Norwich. Dean of the King's Chapel. Bishop of Ely. He was severely handled by the Long Parliament and imprisoned in the Tower for almost twenty years, without ever being brought to a trial for his alleged misdemeanors. In 1660, he was restored to his episcopal function. He was a very great benefactor to the college in money and books; but especially in erecting at his own expense (it cost him nearly £4,000) that goodly building, the new chapel, the altar of which he furnished with his own chapel plate and endowed with the manor of Hardwick in this county to keep it in repair. He died in the year 1667.

*A Transcript of a certain narrative, written by the late Bishop of Ely <note>Dr. Matthew Wren</note> with his own hand, of that remarkable conference which, after his return from Spain with Prince Charles (in the year 1623), he had with Dr. Neale, then Bishop of Durham; Dr. Andrews, Bishop of Winchester; and Dr. Laud, Bishop of St. David's, regarding the said Prince; at which time, something prophetic was then said by that Reverend Bishop of Winchester.*

After our return from Spain, my Lord of Winchester (among other great expressions of his respect for me) made me promise to him that, on every occasion of my coming to London (for I still lived at Cambridge), I would stay with him; to which end, he had three rooms near the garden prepared and reserved for me; and twice or thrice I had stayed there.
And at another time, arriving suddenly and late in London, I stayed at my sister’s in Friday Street, and the next day, being Friday, I went to Winchester House for dinner and asked his Lordship's pardon that I did not stay there; because my business was to negotiate with some country gentlemen who were staying in Holborn, whom I could not meet with except in the evening and morning, when it would not be safe for me to cross the bridge or the Thames; and so after dinner I took my leave of him, hoping to return to Cambridge on Monday.

But on *Saturday*, going to do my duty to my Lords of *Durham* and St. *David's*, and telling them of my sudden return, they insisted on overruling me and made me promise them that, though I had taken leave of my Lord of *Winchester*, I would still meet them the next day at *Whitehall*, at my Lord's chambers, for dinner. I did so, and there we sat, after dinner, for over an hour. And then, as I showed them that on the morrow my business would be dispatched and I would be gone on *Tuesday*, I took my leave again of them all. But on *Monday* morning by break of day (before they were usually stirring in *Friday Street*), there was a great knocking at the door where I stayed; and at last an apprentice, who slept in the shop, came up to my bedside and told me there was a messenger from *Winchester House* to speak with me. The business was to let me know that my Lord, when he came from court last night, had charged his steward to arrange it so that I might be spoken with and required, as if from him without fail, to dine with him on *Monday* next—to be at *Winchester House* by ten o'clock—which I wondered at all the more, his Lordship not being accustomed to come from his study until near twelve.

My business would hardly permit this; yet because of his Lordship's urgency, I got up immediately and went into *Holborn*, and there made such dispatch that soon after ten o'clock I took a boat and went to *Winchester House*, where I found the steward at the water-gate, waiting to let me know that my Lord had called twice to know if I had arrived. I asked where his Lordship was. He answered, in his great gallery (a place where I knew his Lordship scarcely came once a year); and as I went there, the door was locked; but upon my lifting the latch, my Lord of St. *David's* opened the door and, letting me in, locked it again.

There I found none but those three Lords, who, causing me to sit down by them, my Lord of *Durham* began by saying to me,

> “*Doctor*, your Lord here will have it so; I, who am the least fit person, must be the speaker. But thus it is: after you left us yesterday at *Whitehall*, as we entered into further discourse on those things which we foresee and conceive will before long come to pass, we resolved again to speak to you before you left here. We must know from you what your thoughts are concerning your master, the *Prince*. You have now been his servant for over two years, and you were with him in *Spain*; we know he respects you well, and we know you are no fool but can observe how things are likely to go.”

“What things, my Lord?” I asked. “In brief,” said he, “how the *Prince's* heart stands toward the *Church of England*, so that when God brings him to the *Crown*, we may know what to hope for.”

My reply was to this effect: that although I was the least fit of any to give my opinion in this matter—attending him only two months in the year, and then at a great distance, only in the closet and at meals—since they so pressed me, I would speak my mind freely. So I said,

> “I know my master's learning is not equal to his father's; yet I know his judgment to be very sound. And as for his affections in these particulars which your Lordships have pointed out—for upholding the doctrine, discipline, and the rightful state of the Church—I have more confidence in him than in his father, in whom they say (better than I can) there is much inconstancy in some particular cases.”

Upon this, my Lords of *Durham* and St. *David's* began to argue the point with me and required me to let them know upon what ground I came to think thus of the *Prince*. I gave them my reasons at length, and after many replies (for over an hour together), then my Lord of *Winchester* (who had said nothing all the while) spoke to me in these words:

### INDORSEMENT.
*Archbishop Laud's certificate to the King [Charles I] touching Norwich Diocese, and the King's notes upon the same, 1636.—Extract from the principal register of the archiepiscopal see of Canterbury.*

FOR this diocese, my Lord [of *Norwich*] has given me a very care- <gloss>Dr. Matthew Wren, Bishop.</gloss> ful and punctual account, very large, and in all particulars very considerable; and I shall return it to your Majesty as briefly as I can reduce it.
And first, he has for this summer, though by your Majesty's leave, lived (away from both his episcopal houses) in *Ipswich*, partly because he was informed that that side of his diocese did most need his presence, and he found it so; and partly because the chapel at his house in *Norwich* was possessed by the French congregation; but warning has been given them to provide elsewhere by *Easter* next.

His Lordship found a general lack of catechizing throughout the diocese, but has settled it; and in *Norwich*, where there are thirty-four churches, there was no sermon on the *Sunday morning*, except only in four, but all were put off to the *afternoon*, and so there was no catechizing. But now he has ordered that there shall be a sermon every *morning*, and catechizing in the *afternoon* in every church.

For *lectures*, they abounded in *Suffolk*, and many were set up by private gentlemen, even without so much as the knowledge of the Ordinary, and without any due observation of the canons or discipline of the Church. Several of these, his Lordship has carefully regulated according to order, especially in *St. Edmund's Bury*, and to their very good satisfaction; and he suspended no *lecturer* from whom he might obtain conformity. And at *Ipswich*, it was not unknown to them that Mr. *Ward* currently stands censured in the High Commission and does not obey; yet the Bishop was ready to have allowed them another, if they would have sought him, but they are resolved to have Mr. *Ward* or none, and that (as is conceived) in spite of the censure of the Court.

At *Yarmouth*, where there was great division previously for many years, their *lecturer* having been censured in the High Commission about two years ago, went into *New England*; since which time there has been no lecture, and much peace in the town, and all ecclesiastical orders well observed. But in *Norwich*, one Mr. *Bridge*, rather than he would conform, has left <gloss>Let him go, we are well rid of him.</gloss> his *lectures* and two curacies, and has gone into *Holland*. The *lecturers* in the country generally observe no church orders at all; and yet the Bishop has

has handled it with moderation, and upon their promise and his hopes of conformity, he has inhibited only three in *Norfolk*, and as many in *Suffolk*, of which one is not a graduate and has been a common stage-player.

His Lordship humbly requests direction as to what he shall do with such scholars (some in holy orders, and some not) as knights and private gentlemen keep in their houses under the pretense of teaching their children. <margin>I approve your judgment in this; I only add, that care must be taken that even those qualified by law keep none but conformable men.</margin>
For my part, I think it very fit that the beneficed men were immediately commanded to reside at their parishes; and for the rest, your Majesty's instructions allow none to keep chaplains except those who are qualified by law. All of which, notwithstanding, I most humbly submit (as the Bishop does) to your Majesty's judgment.

<margin>Bishop's certificates in this case must be the most unquestionable evidence.</margin>
For Recusants, whereas formerly there were usually only two or three reported, his Lordship has caused above forty to be indicted in *Norwich* at the last sessions; and at the assizes in *Suffolk*, he delivered a list of those who were reported upon the oath of the churchwardens to the Lord Chief Justice, and his Lordship to the Grand Jury; but they dismissed it, claiming the Bishop's certificate was not evidence. But the true reason is believed to be because he had also included those who had been reported to him as Recusant separatists, as well as Recusant Romanists.

His Lordship's care has been such that, although there are over 1,500 clergymen in that diocese and many disorders, yet there are not thirty excommunicated or suspended; of these, some are for stubbornness and will not yet submit; some for an obstinate refusal to publish your Majesty's declaration; and some for contemning all the orders and rites of the church and intruding themselves without a license from the Ordinary <note>A church official, usually the Bishop, with jurisdictional authority.</note> for many years together.

Last of all, he found that half of the churches in his diocese did not have a clerk able to read and to answer the minister in Divine Service; by which means the people were completely out of practice in joining with the priest, and in many places they did not even say, *Amen*. But concerning this, his Lordship has strictly enjoined a reformation.

<margin>His request is granted; and assuredly his negative consequence shall follow.</margin>
If this account given by the Bishop of *Norwich* is true, as I believe it is (and ought to believe it, until it can be disproved), he has served the Church of *England* very well and has been very poorly rewarded for it. His humble suit to your Majesty is that you will be graciously pleased, in your own good time, to hear the complaints that have been made against him, so that he may not be overwhelmed by an outcry for performing his duty.

### WINCHESTER.

Lancelot Andrewes: After the Prince's return from Spain, Dr. *Wren*, who was there with him, was still staying (when he was in *London*) at *Winchester House*, where he had three rooms reserved for him. But being required to go to *Cambridge* by break of day, he went the night before to his sister's house in *Friday Street*, having taken his leave of the Bishop. While King *James* lived, it was not easy to share this, nor afterward, except in private to intimate friends, such as my tutors Dr. *Hierom Beal*, Dean *Mason*, and my brother, and perhaps to Dr. *Cosin* and Dr. *Duncan*. Since the event, I have told it to many, not thinking it fit to conceal it any longer." He told it to me at *Ely House*, not long before his death, and I earnestly desired him to put it in writing.

->HEREFORD, NORWICH, ELY.<-

MATTHEW Wren. He was chaplain to Prince *Charles* and went with him into *Spain*. He went with him too, when he was King, into *Scotland* in *May* 1633, and came back in *July*. At the end of *August*, Bishop *Laud* having been made Archbishop, and the Bishop of *London*, *Juxon*, succeeding him in the deanery of the King’s Chapel, the King appointed Dr. *Wren* to be Clerk of his Closet, but gave him time to move his family.

He came to *London* on that morning that *James*, Duke of *York*, was born. The next day, the King said to him, "Now that you are at my side, there will be many schemes to set the Archbishop and you at odds; but I warn you of it, so that you do not allow such a trick to be played upon you. And therefore, I require you both, by that faith which I am sure you both will keep toward me, to bind yourselves mutually: neither of you is to believe any report against the other; and if you encounter any such thing, even though you do not believe it, you shall immediately share it with each other." This was done with much alacrity.

In *November*, Dr. *Hacket*, coming to serve at Court as chaplain and with much skill congratulating the Clerk of the Closet’s closer access to the King, began to tell him what hopes he and many others had that he (Dr. *Wren*) would have been Bishop of *London*, and that the King had first intended it, had the Archbishop not intervened, claiming that the Bishop of *London* should be a man of

whom the Archbishop has experience of, and upon whom he may rely; and so he obtained **London** for the Bishop of **Hereford**. Dr. **Wren** paid no attention to Dr. **Hacket**'s foolishness, suspecting it to be a scheme by Bishop **Williams** to create in him a dislike of the Archbishop; but resolving to keep his faith with the King and Archbishop, he immediately informed him of all that passed between himself and Dr. **Hacket**. The King approved well of his handling of the matter and told him there was no truth in the report, nor anything but a plot to stir up trouble between the two of them.

In November of the next year, Bishop **Lindsell** died, and the Archbishop sent Mr. **Dell** to tell him that the King would grant **Hereford** to him, and the Deanery of **Windsor** to his brother. He was elected Bishop of **Hereford** on December 5, 1634. But because the Archbishop's chapel at **Lambeth** was not ready, his ordination was delayed until the second week in Lent, March 8.

Immediately after this, his spare time was occupied in framing a liturgy for the consecration of a church at **Dore** in **Herefordshire**, and converting the impropriation into a rectory. This was the gift of the noble and pious **John**, Lord **Scudamore**, whose journey as ambassador to **France** was delayed until the completion of this task, which was carried out by the Bishop of St. **David**'s.

Next, he prepared for a visitation of that diocese, and requesting the statutes, they sent him two books. One was of some antiquity, though without a date, very imperfect, and of no authority, inscribed *Haes leges & consuetudines ecclesiae Herefordens* <note>These laws and customs of the church of Hereford.</note>. The other was a body of statutes compiled by Bishop **Whitgift**, then of **Worcester**, upon a mandate from the Queen, but never confirmed by her. Thus, there was reasonable doubt how men could be required to take any oaths based on such statutes, or be censured for not observing them. The Archbishop told him that Bishop **Lindsell** had the same scruples, and therefore advised him to take those books along to the **New Forest** (where the King was going to hunt) and—from them and such observations of his own as he could not lack (having served Bishop **Andrewes** for so long, and having been President of **Pembroke Hall**, Master of **Peter House**, Dean of **Windsor** and **Wolverhampton**, and a prebendary of **Winchester** and **Westminster**) —to compile one entire body of statutes for the future government of that church and the college of vicars and hospitals belonging to it. He did so.

But about August 20, the King, without any warning, moved to **Oatlands**; seeing that the Bishop arrived there the next day, he smiled and said, "I will reward your diligence. I hear the Bishop of **Norwich** is dead, and I will transfer you there," (giving him his hand to kiss), "but I want you to go and finish the visitation you have announced at **Hereford** before you move."

The Bishop implored his Majesty not to require that of him, for besides the fact that it would be interpreted as a point of great arrogance in him, it would ruin him financially as well. Having postponed the business of all tenants who desired to renew their leases until he should come down among them, if he went now, he would receive nothing (though it would cost him £100) nor be able to perform his promise to them, as his Majesty had ordered that no bishop, after being named for a transfer, should issue any lease. "I will trust you," said the King. "How many tenants have been with you?" He said five. "I give you leave," said the King, "to contract for them."

During his visitation, Dr. **Richardson**, the Dean, served an inhibition upon him from the Archbishop's court, thinking his unique jurisdiction would be compromised. The Bishop was quite glad of it, for this shortened his stay, and he forced the Dean to be visited by his chancellor the week before he moved.

He spent three days visiting the chapter, finding there several very reverend and learned men, far from the rigid Puritanism with which they had been slandered. He left them the book of statutes he had compiled, to be
