considered; contracted with four of the five tenants, received from them £500, and returned in a fortnight and gave the King an account of everything.

"But what have you done with the fifth lease?" said the King. "Reserved it for your Majesty's wisdom," said the Bishop. The case was this: *Mr. Geeres* of *London*, the fifth tenant of the impropriation of *Dilvin*, had moved to add a "life" to his lease. But before the Bishop arrived there, a second life having ended, his agents offered £1000 for a new lease for three such lives as they would name. But the Bishop considered that it was worth £300 *per annum*, with a convenient house upon it within three or four miles of *Hereford*. The remaining life (*Dr. Robotham's* widow) was above 60 years old, so that there could never be a fairer opportunity to augment the bishopric, if the King would see to it that no succeeding bishop should lease it out, but instead hold it only as *demesnes* during his time. The King was mightily pleased and told the Bishop he had acted like an honest churchman, and began to reveal to him a resolution he had in mind to augment the lesser bishoprics if he fairly could. And he immediately gave such an order that not only was *Bishop Field* stopped from renewing that lease, but *Bishop Cook* after him as well; though his brother *Sir John Cook* was much aggrieved at *Bishop Wren* for it.

About a fortnight after his return, *Dr. Kerry*, the senior residentiary (80 years old), and *Dr. Skinner*, the Chancellor, came to him in *London* in the name of the Chapter to thank him for the Book of Statutes which he had left them. Although it was somewhat to the particular loss of some of them (the old doctor especially), the statutes were in general so much for the public good of the Church that they craved his mediation with the King to confirm that book as their rule forever. He asked to be excused from this, as he had written the book himself and was now moving away from them. So they went to the Archbishop's palace, and the Archbishop—after examining a few things objected to by the Dean and hearing the Bishop's answers—had the whole book confirmed under the Great Seal of *England* and sent to them. Within three months after his translation to *Norwich*, the King made him Dean of his Chapel, the Bishop of *London* having been made Lord Treasurer. He sat at *Norwich* for two and a half years; during that time there was a foul riot at *Ipswich*, with which they tried to scare him. *Sir John Banks* prosecuted them for it in the *Star-chamber*. There was also a conspiracy against his life discovered in *Holland* by *Sir William Boswell*, whose letters the King commanded Secretary *Windebank* to convey to him by post that very day, as he was then at *Ludham* in *Norfolk*. Two petitions against him from *Ipswich* and *Norwich* were secretly delivered into the King's hand by some high-ranking individuals. But the King answered them with a sharp enough rebuke, and afterward sent the petitions to the Bishop and told him who had delivered them.

In April 1638, the King, by his letters from *Newmarket*, moved him to *Ely*; but he told him one day that he would have an account from him concerning the Bishopric of *Norwich* and its state. He answered that there would be an opportunity (when he was in his grave, but the King, by God's grace, still living to effect it) to make it one of the best bishoprics in *England*; or rather (if he should see it more for the public good) to divide that overly large diocese (having in it above 1200 titles) and to make two competent ones out of it. A cathedral for *Suffolk* might be either *Sudbury* or *St. Edmund's-bury*; there are two archdeaconries in it, and a dean and four prebends might, without great difficulty, be raised from benefices and some other particulars in that county within the gift of his Majesty and the Archbishop. And for a supply of maintenance, he said, there is a lease of the greatest part of the Bishopric of *Norwich*, containing about eighty parcels, granted at very low rents to *Queen Elizabeth* by *Dr. Scambler*

-> GOOD SIR, <- -> *Christ Church, Sept. 14, 1734.* <-

<margin>Letter to the *Rev. Mr. Bateman.*</margin>
By Barn’s *Oxford* wagon, which arrives at the *King's Head* in the *Old Change* on Tuesday night, I have sent a box of papers relating to Bishop *Wren*, addressed to yourself and to be left in the warehouse until called for. Therefore, I must ask you to send some trustworthy person to inquire there for them and to convey them to Mr. *Wren*, whose residence I do not know.

He has full liberty to transcribe them or make whatever use of them he pleases.

I believe the Bishop's answer to the articles of impeachment is so well written and such an effective reply to all the outcry raised against that prelate that it should be printed; indeed, a great part of the other papers are merely materials for that defense. I have also had transcribed two remarkable passages out of some manuscripts of Archbishop *Sancroft* relating to Bishop *Wren*, which I think were never printed.

I am certain I have several other letters and papers belonging to this Bishop; but I have unfortunately left the catalog of my manuscripts behind me in *Wales*, so I do not know where to find them until I can receive it from there.

This Bishop was certainly a person of great capacity for business and of vast industry; I have seen exact abridgments of all the registers and institution books in the Bishop's offices at *Norwich* and *Ely*, written in his own hand.* I think some of them are at *Ely House*.

I have some letters from Sir *Christopher Wren* and schemes of his regarding the rebuilding of St. *Paul's*, bound up in a folio collection of papers belonging to that church, which I lent last year to the Lord Bishop of *Chichester*, and he still has it with him. Mr. *Wren* may use the book when his Lordship comes to town.

Dr. *Knight*, Prebendary of *Ely*, has a very good portrait of Dr. *Christopher Wren*, Dean of *Windsor*.

### N U M B. III.

MATTHEW Wren, the eldest son of Dr. Matthew Wren, Lord Bishop of Ely, was originally a student at *Cambridge*, and afterwards for several years (during the time of the Usurpation) at the University of *Oxford*—not in a college or hall, but in a private house. After his Majesty’s Restoration, he became secretary to Edward, Earl of *Clarendon*; he was elected a Burgess for *St. Michael’s* in *Cornwall*, to serve in that Parliament which began at *Westminster*, May 8, 1661. <margin>*Fast. Oxon. Vol. II. p. 819.*</margin> After the fall of Lord *Clarendon*, he was made secretary to his Royal Highness *James*, Duke of *York*, in whose service he continued until the time of his death, which happened in 1672 at the age of about 42 years. His body was conveyed to *Cambridge* and buried there in *Pembroke Hall* Chapel, in the same vault where his father had been laid five years before.

This ingenious person has written:

I. *Considerations on Mr. Harrington’s Commonwealth of Oceana, restricted to the first part of the Preliminaries, London, 1657.* —— Before these *Considerations* is a long letter sent by the author to Dr. *John Wilkins*, Warden of *Wadham* College (afterwards Bishop of *Chester*), by whom the said author was requested to give his judgment concerning the *Commonwealth of Oceana*.

II. *Monarchy Asserted: Or the State of Monarchical and Popular Government; in Vindication of the Considerations on Mr. Harrington’s Oceana, London, 1659 and 1660.*

III. *Increpatio Bar-jesu; sive polemicae adsertiones locorum aliquot s. scripturae ab imposturis perversionum in catechesi Racoviana; collectae hinc inde ex opere praegrandi medit. critic. in S. Paginam conscript. a patre suo episcopo Eliensi in solitudine sua carceraria.*

The Reverend Dr. Barwick had recommended that Mr. Matthew Wren answer the pernicious *Leviathan* of Mr. Hobbes, from which Mr. Wren excused himself as being insufficient, and wished it to be undertaken by some professional divine.

### *From the same Hand to Dr. Barwick.*
->*Brussels, July 25, 1659.*<-

<margin>Appendix to Dr. Barwick's Life, p. 429.</margin>
> “ I hope it is only modesty in Mr. *Wren* that makes him hesitate to undertake the work you have recommended to him; for I dare swear, based on what I have seen of his, that he is well-equipped to answer every detail of it—I mean, every part that requires an answer. Nor is there a need for a professional theologian to defend the Creator from the claim of making man more of a beast than any of those in the field, or to defend Scripture from his licentious interpretation. I dare say he will find something in Mr. *Hobbes* himself—I mean in his former books—that contradicts what he puts forward in this one, specifically in that part where he considers himself most precise: his beloved *philosophy*. And surely, something is owed to *Aristotle*, *Tully* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>, and our *universities* to clear them of his insults; and it is high time, if what I hear is true, that some tutors are reading his *Leviathan* to their pupils instead of the *others*. Mr. *Hobbes* is my old friend, yet I cannot excuse him for the mischief he has done to the King, the Church, the laws, and the nation. Surely, enough can be said against the *politics* of a man who, having reduced all religion, wisdom, and honesty into an implicit obedience to established laws, writes a book of political theory which I may boldly say must be condemned as impious and seditious by the established laws of any kingdom or province in *Europe*. Therefore, it would be very strange if its fundamental principles could not be overthrown. But I must ask your and Mr. *Wren’s* pardon for speaking at such length and anticipating the criticisms he will make of it.”

<header>MATTHEW WREN, D. D.</header>

<margin>*Oxford Fasti, page 180.*</margin>
Doctor *Thomas Wren*, the second son of *Matthew*, Bishop of *Ely*, and formerly a student of *Cambridge*, was created a Doctor of Medicine on August 2, 1660, by virtue of the Chancellor's letters. These letters state, "That by the force of the late unhappy times, he was constrained to leave the University of *Cambridge* (in various colleges of which his father was *Visitor*) and for his proficiency in studies, was obliged to settle himself in the vicinity of the University of *Oxford*: That the hardships under which his *father* lay for seventeen years together were such that (his estate having been taken away) he could not allow his children bread, much less cover their expenses for living in colleges and taking their degrees, except to have the benefit of the public library, etc." This person, who was very fond of music while he studied in *Oxford* (which was for about eight years), was made Archdeacon of *Ely* by his father after his Majesty's Restoration, and held other ecclesiastical positions. He died in 1679 at *Wilberton* in the Isle of *Ely*.

After the Restoration of his Majesty King *Charles* the Second, it was his pleasure, as well as that of the Marquis of *Hertford*, Chancellor of the University of *Oxford*, and of Sir *Edward Hyde*, who succeeded to that office in the year 1660, that there should be a granting of degrees in all faculties to those who had suffered for his *Majesty's* cause and had been expelled from the university by the visitors appointed by Parliament in the years 1648 and 1649. Among these, *Charles Wren*, the third son, and Sir *William Wren*, the fourth son of *Matthew*, Bishop of *Ely*, were made Masters of Arts on August 2, 1660. *Charles Wren* was afterwards a Member of Parliament for the town of *Cambridge* in the year 1685.

# NUMBER IV. (*e*)

<margin>*Oxford Fasti, page 807.*</margin>
KING *Charles* the First, by a foreknowledge like that of *Bishop Andrewes* and by divine instinct, after he was condemned, told Colonel *Tomlinson*, * "That he believed the *English* monarchy was now at an end." About half an hour later, he told the colonel, "That now he had an assurance, by a strong impulse on his spirit, that his son should reign after him." † His Majesty meekly resigned himself to God, both his own private cause and the public cause; and by a divine spirit, foretold the happy recovery of both. *Nemo vir magnus, sine aliquo afflatu divino unquam fuit* <note>"No man was ever great without some divine inspiration."</note>, was the observation of *Tully* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>.

<margin>*Virgil's Poetry.*</margin>
This foreknowledge in great minds proceeds from wisdom, holiness, and a divine impulse, the only source of true prophecy; nevertheless, it is very remarkable that a preview of this King's misfortunes occurred from a quite different cause and a far distant source, so consistent that (without any forced interpretation) it gave an account of his troubles:

1. Under a most unnatural rebellion and destructive civil war, and to infer.
2. That he should be driven from his capital city, palaces, forts, and estates.
3. Be torn away from the embrace of his Queen and children.
4. Be compelled by the necessity of his affairs to implore foreign aid.
5. Be constrained to see the miserable persecution and cruel slaughter of his friends and loyal subjects.

† Doctor *Sprat's* sermon before the House of Commons, *January* 30, 1677-8, *page* 41.

<margin>Oracles in Virgil's Language.</margin>
These modern instances of *Virgilian prophecy* give occasion, for the sake of curiosity, to extend this narration and to recollect what great honor and veneration, in almost all ages, has been paid to this divine poet; for Virgil's prognostications were not only taken in the usual way of opening his book at random and lighting upon whatever passage first came to sight, but the oracles of the gods in their temples were solemnly delivered in his verse:

Thus St. *Augustine*, upon hearing a voice saying, *take up and read* (tolle, lege), took up his Bible and turned to the 13th chapter of St. *Paul's* Epistle to the Romans and the 13th verse: *Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, etc.* and reformed his

# THE LIFE OF

his conduct accordingly. Moreover, it was sometimes a custom that those who intended to test their fortunes did not casually open and inspect the books of Holy Scripture themselves in the usual way, but took the omens from the words of the deacon reading in the church.

But however trifling and uncertain practices of this kind may generally appear, there have been examples where portions of Scripture have happened to occur so relevant to the occasion that it may be no sign of superstition to believe they could not have happened *sine numine*, without a special providence. To mention one or two of the most significant instances:

<margin>Echard's History of England, Vol. 2, p. 643. Clarendon's History of the Rebellion, Book 4, p. 29.</margin>
The second lesson appointed in the liturgy of the Church of England on the 30th day of January is the 27th chapter of St. Matthew's Gospel, containing the history of our Savior's death. When Dr. Juxon, Bishop of London, read this to King Charles I on that day—the day of his martyrdom—and immediately before he ascended the scaffold, His Majesty took particular notice of it. Supposing it had been selected on purpose, he thanked him for his timely choice; but the Bishop modestly told him it was the lesson directed by the calendar for that day. This highly pleased the King as a providential preparation for his passion.

On the eleventh day of January, many thousands of the seditious citizens and the London rabble marched in a tumultuous manner to Westminster, insulting the majesty of King Charles I and supporting the factious party of the Parliament. The Psalms for both morning and evening service for that day are 56, 57, 58, etc., and they serve as prophecies of the troubles that followed.

<margin>Dr. Sprat's Sermon before the House of Commons, Jan. 30, 1677/8, p. 44.</margin>
The text of the sermon preached before King Charles I at his coronation, though it might have seemed ill-timed, proved prophetic; it was the latter part of those words from Revelation 2:10: *Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.*

<margin>Lassels' Voyage to Italy, Part 2, p. 109.</margin>
Francis I, King of France, having been defeated and taken prisoner at the Battle of Pavia by the Emperor Charles V in the year 1525, was conducted to a Carthusian monastery. The monks happened to be at their devotions, chanting a portion of the 119th Psalm. As the King entered the chapel, he found them at this verse: "*Coagulatum est sicut lac cor eorum, ego vero legem tuam meditatus sum*" <note>"Their heart is as callous as fat, but I delight in your law."</note>. Whereupon, he joined them in the very next verse, which was most applicable to his current condition, and sang aloud with a piety as great as his loss: "*Bonum est mihi quia humiliasti me, ut discam justificationes tuas*" <note>"It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I might learn your statutes."</note>.

<margin>Writers of the Augustan History on the Virgilian Lots. From Spartianus's Life of Hadrian.</margin>
But to return to the <term>Sortes Virgilianae</term> and review them as they appear in antiquity from the *Augustan History*.

The Emperor Trajan, a Spaniard by birth from the town of Italica in Andalusia, was adopted by Nerva and reached the throne as an old man. Hadrian, sent to deliver the congratulations of the army, was transferred to Upper Germany, from where he hurried to Trajan so that he might be the first to announce the death of Nerva. At that time, being anxious about the Emperor's judgment of him and his own succession in the empire, he consulted the *Virgilian Lots*, and this fate fell out:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 6.</margin>
> "But who is he that stands apart, distinguished by the olive branches,
> carrying the sacred vessels? I recognize the hair and the gray beard
> of the Roman King, who shall first establish the city with laws,
> sent from the small Cures and a poor land
> into a great empire; whom then another shall succeed."

Furthermore, such a lot is said to have come to him from the Sibylline verses. He also had a premonition of his future reign from an oracle given at the temple of Jupiter Nicephorus. [Thus do subtle minds agree.]

<margin>According to Julius Capitolinus, in Albinus.</margin>
When *Clodius Albinus Caesar* drew a lot concerning his fate in the temple of the Cumaean Apollo, he was answered with these verses:
<margin>Aeneid, Book 6</margin>
> "This knight, amidst a great and disturbing tumult,
> "Shall restore the Roman state; he shall strike down the Carthaginians and the rebellious Gaul."

It is well-known that he did indeed subdue many nations in *Gaul*. However, he himself suspected that the prophecy *he shall strike down the Carthaginians* was predicted of the Emperor *Septimius Severus*, because *Severus* was an African.

<margin>According to Aelius Lampridius, in Severus Alexander.</margin>
For the Emperor *Severus Alexander*—whose mother was Mamaea, and who was beloved by all men—this lot appeared in the temple of Fortune at Praeneste while Heliogabalus was plotting against him:
> "—————— If you can break through the harshness of fate,
> "You shall be Marcellus."

Also, when at his parent's urging he turned his mind from philosophy and music to other arts, he was enlightened by these Virgilian lots:
> "Others, I believe, will shape breathing bronzes more delicately;
> "They will draw living faces from marble;
> "They will plead causes better, and describe the paths of heaven
> "With a rod, and tell of the rising stars:
> "But you, Roman, remember to rule the nations with authority;
> "These shall be your arts: to impose the way of peace,
> "To spare the conquered, and to crush the proud."

<margin>According to Trebellius Pollio, in Claudius.</margin>
*Aurelius Claudius Gothicus*, when he had become emperor and consulted the lots in the Apennines about how long he would rule, received this answer:————
> "Until a third summer should see him reigning in Latium."

He died in the third year of his reign.
Likewise, when he consulted about his descendants:
> "For these I set neither bounds of space nor time."

Likewise, when he consulted about his brother *Quintillus*, whom he wished to have as a partner in the empire, the answer was:
> "The fates will only show this man to the earth.——"

He was killed in a military riot on the seventeenth day of his reign.

"In this type of divination," says Cicero, "rashness and chance, not reason and wisdom, prevail."

> Victory was gained, though he was then at *Jerusalem*, at the distance of a two days' journey from the field of battle. The former, they say, was revealed to him in a *dream of the night*, and the other by a *voice from heaven*, which the *Jews* call *Bath-Kol*, i.e., *The Daughter of a Voice*, or the *Daughter Voice*. For the *Jewish writers* hold that there were three sorts of revelations anciently among them. The first by *Urim* and *Thummim*; the second by the *Spirit of Prophecy*; and the third by *Bath-Kol*. The first, they say, was in use from the erecting of the Tabernacle to the building of the Temple. The second from the beginning of the world (but mostly under the first Temple) until the death of *Malachi* under the second Temple. But after the death of *Malachi*, the Spirit of Prophecy wholly ceased in *Israel*; and from then on, they had *Bath-Kol* in its stead, which, they say, was a *voice from heaven*. That they called it *Bath-Kol*, i.e., *The Daughter Voice*, or the *Daughter of a Voice* (for it may be interpreted both ways), seems to be with respect to the oracular voice delivered from the Mercy-seat, when God was there consulted by *Urim* and *Thummim*. That was the grand and primary voice of revelation; this was of a secondary dignity, and inferior to it, as the daughter is to the mother, and therefore in respect to it, and as succeeding in its stead, it is called the Daughter Voice, the other being to it as the mother in precedence, both of time and dignity. So that it may be understood what kind of oracle this was, I shall here give the reader one instance of it out of the *Talmud*; it is as follows.

Rabbi Jochanan and Rabbi Simeon, Ben Lachish, desiring to see the face of R. Samuel, a *Babylonian doctor*, said, "Let us follow the hearing of *Bath-Kol*." Traveling therefore near a school, they heard the voice of a boy reading these words from the first book of Samuel, 25:1, *and Samuel died*; they observed this and inferred from this that their friend Samuel was dead, and so they found it had happened. For Samuel of Babylon was then dead. "Many

The ancient heathens had five special ways of divination: the first was *Afflatu Dei*, or by *inspiration*; the second, by *oracles* from the *tripos* in the temples; the third, by the *burning* of *laurel*; the fourth, by the *stars* or *astrology*; the fifth, by *observation* of birds, or *augury*. All these, with great elegance and brevity, are comprised by *Virgil* in three lines, in the address of *Aeneas* to *Helenus*, a king, priest, and prophet.

### NUMB. VII.

*Extracts from Lord Clarendon's* History of the Rebellion, *concerning the* Scottish Liturgy *and* Canons. *Book II. Page 83, etc.*

<margin>Regarding the Scottish Liturgy and Canons, revised by Archbishop Laud, Bishop Juxton, and Bishop Wren. Commissioned by the King.</margin>

IT was toward the end of the year 1633, when the King returned from
*Scotland*, having left it to the care of some of his bishops there to
provide such a liturgy and such a book of canons as might best suit the
nature and temperament of the better sort of those people, to which the
rest would easily submit; and that, as fast as they made them ready, they should
send them to the Archbishop of *Canterbury*, to whose assistance the
King joined the Bishop of *London* (Dr. *Juxton*) and Doctor *Wren*, who by
that time had become Bishop of *Norwich*; a man of a severe, sour na-
ture, but very learned, and particularly well-versed in the old liturgies of the
*Greek* and *Latin* churches. And after His Majesty was informed in this way of
what was sent, he would recommend and enjoin the practice
and use of both to that, his native kingdom.

It was now two years, or very nearly so, before the bishops in *Scot-
land* had prepared anything to offer to the King toward their intend-
ed reformation; and then they reversed the proper method and first pre-
sented a body of canons to precede the liturgy, which was not yet ready,
choosing to finish the shorter work first. The King referred the con-
sideration, as he had before resolved to do, to the Archbishop and the other
two bishops—(Dr. *Juxton*) the Bishop of *London* and (Dr. *Wren*) the Bishop
of *Norwich*—who, after their perusal of them and some alterations made,

The text also details Wren's appointment by King Charles I to help revise the Scottish Liturgy and Canons alongside Archbishop Laud.</summary>

--- Page 93 ---
<meta>This page continues the account of the introduction of the new Canons and Liturgy in Scotland, detailing the procedural errors made by the King and the bishops—specifically Laud, Juxton, and Wren—and the resulting civil unrest in Edinburgh.</meta>

<page-num>65</page-num>
<header>MATTHEW WREN, D. D.</header>

...with the consent of those bishops who brought them from *Scotland*, returned them to the King; and his Majesty, impatient to see the good work entered upon, without any other ceremony (after having given his royal approval), issued his royal proclamation for the proper observation of them within his kingdom of *Scotland*.

It was a fatal oversight that these Canons, neither before nor after they were sent to the King, had ever been seen by the Assembly or any Convocation of the Clergy, who were so strictly obliged to observe them; nor were they even communicated to the Lords of the Council of that kingdom. It is almost impossible that any new discipline could be introduced into the Church without significantly affecting the government of the State, and even encroaching upon or referring to the municipal laws of the kingdom.

In the next place, it was just as strange that the Canons should be published before the Liturgy was prepared (which was not ready for about a year afterward, or thereabouts), when three or four of the Canons were primarily for the observation of and punctual compliance with the Liturgy. All the clergy were to be sworn to submit to it, and to pay all obedience to what was enjoined by it, before they even knew what it contained. Whereas if the Liturgy had been published first with all proper circumstances, it is possible that it might have found a better reception, and the Canons might have been less scrutinized.

It was about the month of *July* in the year 1637 that the Liturgy (after it had been sent out of *Scotland*, perused by the three bishops in *England* <note>Laud, Juxton, and Wren</note>, and then approved and confirmed by the King) was published and appointed to be read in all the churches. In this particular, there was the same deliberate and premeditated omission as there had been in the preparation and publication of the Canons; the clergy were not consulted at all, and—what was more strange—not all the bishops were made acquainted with it. This was less criticized afterward, when some of them renounced their office and became ordinary presbyters as soon as they saw the trend of the times. The Privy Council had no more notice of it than the rest of the kingdom did until the *Sunday* before, when it was declared, "That next *Sunday* the Liturgy should be read"; because of this, they were less concerned to foresee or prevent any obstructions that might happen.

On the *Sunday* morning appointed for reading the Liturgy, it was received in the Cathedral of *Edinburgh* with riot and disorder, in defiance of all authority; and it fared no better in the other churches of the city, but was met by the seditious rabble with shouting and outcries, threatening the men whose office it was to read it with bitter curses against bishops and popery.

The first actors in these tumults and confusions were truly from the lowest classes of the people, but soon after, more significant persons—and at length, some of the highest quality—declared themselves to be of the party against the bishops. They united themselves by subscribing to a Covenant, raised an army under its obligation, and began a rebellion; and this was the first alarm *England* received regarding any trouble, after it had enjoyed for so many years the most uninterrupted prosperity, in a full and plentiful peace, that any nation could be blessed with.

<margin>*Rushworth's Historical Collections, Part II, Vol. I, p. 717.*</margin>

No question but there is a great concurrence between them" (meaning the *Scottish* Covenanters)

Among the reasons published by his Majesty for imposing the Liturgy in *Scotland* was this: “That its substance was composed no differently from that of *England*, so that the *Roman* party might not upbraid us with any material differences in our Liturgies;” and yet, by having some few alterations that differed from it, “it might be truly considered a book of that Church’s own composing, and established by his royal authority as King of *Scotland*.”

<margin>Ibid. 387.</margin>
Together with this service book (which in substance, structure, and composition was conformable to the decency and uniformity of God’s worship in the Church of *England*), his Majesty sent certain instructions to the bishops of *Scotland*: “That although he had established it by his authority, they should nonetheless proceed with all moderation, and excuse those who found things contained in the book that they were either not well-convinced of, or wished to be informed about, or for which they hoped that time and reason might lead them to a better belief.”

The excellence of the liturgy's composition, accompanied by such cautious and wise advice and direction for its peaceful reception and use, clearly vindicates his Majesty and his three *English* prelates. Consequently, the misfortunes that followed were apparently due to the weak, impolitic, and unseasonable conduct of the *Scottish* bishops, upon whom the Lords of the Council (in their complaint to the King regarding the riots) did not hesitate to place the greatest blame.

## NUMBER VIII.

### A memorable Feast of Saint George, celebrated at Windsor in the 4th year of the reign of the most serene King Charles I, and supreme head of the most noble order of the garter. Dr. Matthew Wren performing the office of registrar.

THE year was now 1628 from the birth of Christ. It was the 23rd day of September when the Sovereign, residing at Windsor for the commencement of the solemnity of Saint George (which he had postponed until this day by three successive edicts for urgent reasons, and especially because of the naval expedition to the support of the people of La Rochelle), granted a dispensation (according to custom) for the absence of five companions: the Earls of Northumberland, Derby, Arundel, Somerset, and Banbury.

The King of Denmark, | 
--- | ---
The Prince Palatine, | } *Foreigners, and*
The Duke of Chevereux, | } *occupied with their own affairs.*

The Earl of Mar and the Earl of Carlisle were serving the Sovereign in Scottish affairs or on an embassy to foreign parts.
The King of Sweden, the Prince of Orange, and the Earl of Suffolk, who were previously elected to the places of the Duke of Brunswick and the deceased Earls of Suffolk and Leicester, but were not yet installed.
The Duke of Buckingham (oh, the crime and the sorrow!), and the Earl of Worcester, an elderly hero, had recently passed away.
The Earl of Mulgrave, the Earl of Sussex, and the Earl of Rutland were absent for uncertain reasons.

Therefore, at four o'clock in the afternoon of that day, the most honorable lords from among the companions themselves assembled in the Sovereign's inner chamber (all dressed in the solemn vestments of the order, according to each man's rank).
William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke, Lord Steward of the King’s <unclear>ni</unclear> household.
Philip Herbert, Earl of Montgomery, Lord Chamberlain of the same household.
Thomas Erskine, Earl of Kellie.
Edward Sackville, Earl of Dorset.
Henry Rich, Earl of Holland, recently elected Chancellor of Cambridge.
Thomas Howard, Earl of Berkshire.
Among the officers, indeed, were the Reverend Father in Christ, Richard Neile (who had climbed through the sees of Rochester, Lichfield, Lincoln, and Durham, and finally to the chair of Winchester and the King's more sacred councils), Prelate of the order.
The most distinguished man Sir Francis Crane, Knight, and of the King’s inner chamber, Chancellor of the order.
Matthew Wren, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Master of Peterhouse, Cambridge (whom the Sovereign, while still Prince of Wales, had made his private chaplain and a participant in his Spanish journey, and had recently gifted, among other things, the Deanery of Windsor), Registrar of the order.
The most distinguished man Sir William Segar, Knight, King of Arms or herald, commonly called Garter.
Finally, the excellent man James Maxwell, of the King’s most intimate bedchamber, Black Rod or Usher of the order.

After a short wait, the Sovereign comes forth to them, shining in the appropriate robes of the order; and after all the other nobles and courtiers present there were ordered to leave, he takes the throne and happily begins the St. George’s solemnity.

There, first, the registrar or scribe, with knees bent toward the throne, is bound by the oath of the order, while the Black Rod <note>The Usher of the Black Rod</note> presents the holy books on his knees for him to touch while swearing, and the King of Arms recites the words of the oath itself from the ancient register of the order.

Then the prelate likewise takes the oath of his office; and after him, the chancellor is at last bound by the same oath, which had been omitted for a year and a half or more because there was no scribe who could lead the words of the oath (as the new scribe now did for both him and the prelate).

When these things were finished, they immediately descended through that most august gallery which hangs on the northern edge of the Windsor hill to St. George's Chapel; the poor knights and the canons of the church walked before them in solemn dress and procession.

There, while the evening services were performed with most devout hymns, the insignia of the Duke of Brunswick and the Earls of Suffolk and Leicester were offered by the companions present (according to their rank), with the prelate standing at the altar on one side and two canons on the other.

It is not right to be silent here about what provided a wonderful festivity to the Sovereign and the others; for while the musical organs and a large choir of singers, producing the highest harmony, almost shook the chapel itself, a most clever little bird (called a robin or redbreast), perched upon the banners here and there, was constantly and fearlessly present not only that evening, but also during the services of the following days; it raised its songs so beautifully and clearly as if (under such great judges) it had resolved to contend with the entire choir for the victory of divine praise.

After the insignia were offered, Pembroke and Montgomery went out and introduced the most honorable Lord Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Cleveland, into the choir as the deputy of the most powerful Gustavus Adolphus, King of the Swedes, Goths, and Vandals, Grand Prince of Finland, Duke of Estonia and Karelia, and Lord of Ingria (by the assignment of the Sovereign). He carried the robe of the order only upon his arm, and after the rituals of respect were duly performed near the seat destined for King Gustavus himself, they placed him there. As he stood there (for a deputy is not permitted to sit), the scribe charged him with the oath of the order upon the soul of the King himself.

The most honorable Lord Dudley Carleton, Viscount Dorchester and the King’s Vice-Chamberlain, was introduced second by Kelly and Salisbury; he was the deputy of the most high Prince Henry, Prince of Orange (as was clear from the principal letters written in French), and he took a similar oath, with the scribe likewise leading the form of the words.

The third to enter was the most honorable Lord Theophilus Howard, Earl of Suffolk and Warden of the Cinque Ports; having been placed in his seat by the guidance of Dorset and Holland, he put on the robes of the order there and took the oath.

Not long after the divine services were finished, they all ascended in order to the palace, and lamps lit everywhere put to flight the evening shadows. Suffolk indeed went away to St. George’s Hall to dine with the rest of the companions, but the deputies immediately set aside the characters they were representing.

On the following morning, at about the ninth hour, the Sovereign descended on foot to St. George’s Chapel through the front courtyards of the palace, with a very long line of companions, officers, and many followers of the order walking before him under a portable canopy of all-silk clearly interwoven with gold; and immediately the morning prayers began.

When the litany had begun, they led the Sovereign from the choir through the nave of the church, with the sacred singers dressed in dalmatics walking before everyone else. Then, in a most devout procession of supplication, they went around the entire cemetery that lies to the south of the chapel; they finally returned into the chapel through the eastern cloister, and when it was finished, at last

With the usual offerings also during the second liturgy, they returned again to the palace with the same pomp.

The most serene Queen, throughout the time that the offerings and procession were taking place, watched from various windows of the chapel. The Ambassadors of both Venice and the United Netherlands were also present and watched with great reverence; for them, the Dean of Windsor had prepared a convenient gallery on each side of the choir opposite the oratory, as was appropriate for the occasion and the time.

In the afternoon, at almost four o'clock, the Sovereign went with his fellow knights to the chapter house of the chapel and asked if there was anything that required a present consultation.

There, (among other things) the scribe of the order pointed out the lack of sacred vessels for the table of the chapel, which according to previous decrees of the chapter ought to have been supplied long ago. Therefore, by a unanimous vote of all, it was decreed that all fellow knights shall ensure that before the next anniversary of St. George (and all future knights hereafter, within a year after their election), at least twenty pounds shall be paid to the Dean and Chapter of Windsor to be spent on the use of the altar (under a strict account to be given to the commissioners whenever they command). Moreover, when the Sovereign was asked by the fellow knights that he himself (as an example to all) should confer some gift, he most willingly agreed.

It was also decreed that in the offerings to be made from then on, following the example of the Sovereign himself (which was most devout, O God, and supremely pious!), each individual should most humbly bend their knees. They all confirmed this by their word at present, and on the following day, they most holily confirmed it by their action (to the extraordinary glory of God, and as a singular testimony of their obedience and Christian piety).

Finally, the Sovereign added that two places in the order were now vacant: one from the death of the elderly Earl of Worcester, and the other from the unhappy fate of the Duke of Buckingham (whom the parricidal knife of an assassin, summoned from Acheron <note>A river in the underworld; used here to signify the depths of hell or ultimate evil</note> itself, had snatched away a month ago). However, he said he did not intend to propose any foreign prince at this time, and so they were free to proceed now to the election.

They went, therefore, into the choir, and there while the hymn was being sung after the second lesson, the Chancellor began the scrutiny <note>The formal examination or counting of votes</note>. When the evening services were finally finished late in the evening, a great number of lamps were lit, and they returned to the palace.

On Thursday, at the hour of morning prayer, they went again through the northern walk to the chapter house, where the Chancellor presented to the Sovereign the scrutiny of the election received the day before.

Therefore, having weighed the scrutiny, the Sovereign pronounced the most honorable Lord William Compton, Earl of Northampton and President of Wales, as elected (reserving the second vacancy for another time). Pembroke and Montgomery immediately introduced him into the chapter house; and as he was present and prostrated on his knees with thanksgiving, the Sovereign himself invested him with the blue silk ribbon with the image of Saint George hanging from it. Then Pembroke bound the Garter of the order to his leg.

Going from there into the choir, Northampton preceded them (but without the habit of the order) and stood before the seat assigned to him with his head uncovered while all the sacred rites and offerings were performed.

Having finally received the blessing, they all returned to the palace.

The place of the Prelate was then vacant due to the death of the distinguished Bishop of Winchester, Lancelot Andrewes, *the Great* <note>The Greek phrase "Τῶ Πάνυ" refers to his supreme renown</note>, whose incomparable holiness, learning, integrity, charity, and constancy every age will deservedly admire; the Bishop of Durham was filling his duties.

In the year 1627, April 22. As the Solemnity of St. George approached, the Sovereign went to the Whitehall chapel at Westminster for evening prayers, and dined publicly that night with his fellow knights.

On the next day, which was St. George’s Day, they again went solemnly to the chapel, and from there, in a most devout procession, they walked around the outer courtyard of the palace (while the most serene Queen watched from a window) and returned to make the sacred offerings.

Before evening prayers that day, the Sovereign declared in the chapter that, since three places were now vacant, it pleased him that for the foreign princes (whose nomination belongs to him alone), they should elect the King of Sweden and the Prince of Orange; the third place, however, was left to their own judgment and choice.

They immediately went to the chapel, where, while the hymn [*Magnificat anima*] <note>The Magnificat, or Song of Mary</note> was being sung, the scrutiny of the election was begun by the Chancellor in this form.

## NUMB. IX.

MAY 11, 1633. *His Majesty began a journey toward Scotland, attended by a huge courtly procession numbering four thousand people or more.*
*Present from the most noble order were the most honorable lords Pembroke, Montgomery, Arundel, Surrey, Salisbury, Carlisle, Holland, Suffolk, Portland, Hamilton, and Lennox. Among the officers were the Dean of Windsor as scribe, and Maxwell the usher, who most lavishly hosted many of the nobles in his house at Berwick on the first arrival, and likewise hosted the King himself upon his return from Scotland.*
*June 13. The Sovereign reaches Edinburgh. On the 18th, he is crowned with a sacred and most august rite. On the 20th, the assembly called parliament began, and eight days later it was most successfully concluded.*
*On the first day of July, the Sovereign left Edinburgh to visit various small towns of the kingdom, and returned on the tenth day.*
*On July 16, having returned to Berwick and set out from there the next day, traveling by relay horses and carriages at a very rapid pace (by the favor of God the Best and Greatest, his protector, guide, and restorer), he reached Greenwich on Saturday afternoon, which was July 20.*

## NUMBER 10.

March 25. MATTHEW WREN, *Bishop of Hereford, upon leaving the Deanery of Windsor, also voluntarily resigned the office of Scribe of the Order into the most sacred hands of the Sovereign; however, his brother* CHRISTOPHER WREN, *Doctor of Divinity and domestic chaplain to the King, was appointed to both positions by the Sovereign's favor. In the year of our Lord 1635, the 11th year of King Charles.*

For the new scribe of these perennial annals, the first things to be recorded are the auspicious beginnings of the reign of Charles (March 27), shining forth in its eleventh year.

*It was a sign of a favorable omen to begin the history of the most honorable order under their guidance thereafter.*

*For there soon followed that memorable embassy of Lord* Johan Baron Skytte, *who was sent with the mandates of his most serene lady,* Christina, *Queen of the Swedes, so that he might most humbly resign into the most sacred hands of the Sovereign the decorations and insignia of the most illustrious order, which the most invincible King* Gustavus Adolphus *had laid down along with his life; and thus he not only satisfied the prescribed laws of the order, but also excused the delay.*

*He added, moreover, that the most serene Queen, together with the entire Swedish nation, held the Sovereign's unusual affection in conferring these honors in such high regard that she would never cease to provide those things which might lead to the amplification of the splendor of the Sovereign himself and of the British nation.*

*The brevity of these annals does not permit a review of that copious and rich store of arguments with which that most noble ambassador, out of his singular eloquence, accurately detailed all the honors of the Order of the Garter.*

*On the other hand, to have passed over these very things in silence would have been a matter not so much of laziness as of a crime. For no greater glory is found to have ever accrued to the most august order from the virtues and merits of any foreign fellow-member than that which the heroic deeds of that prince added to it.*

*After a brief response was given, the Sovereign entrusted to Mr.* Francis Crane, *Chancellor of the Order, the duty of expressing his mind more explicitly.*

*But as for that truly august method by which the Sovereign ordered the ambassador to be introduced into his chamber by two leading fellow-members; by which the ornaments themselves were restored; and by which the duties attending so great a business were arranged; since it was exactly recorded by the master of ceremonies, Mr.* John Finet, *a most refined man, and the forms of the speeches themselves were collected by him, I deliberately omit it.*

->To the Right Honorable the Lords Spiritual and Temporal in the High Court of Parliament.<-

*The most humble Answer of Matthew Wren, Bishop of Ely, to the Articles of Impeachment presented against him by the Honorable House of Commons for several Crimes and Misdemeanors.*

THE said Bishop of Ely is weighed down with very great sorrow and grief of heart that so honorable an assembly as the House of Commons should hold him worthy of so heavy and sore a charge. Nevertheless, because in the integrity of his own heart and conscience he is assured he is not guilty of being—or ever having been—popishly or superstitiously inclined, or of endeavoring to suppress powerful and diligent preaching, or of introducing anything that tended toward superstition or idolatry, or of disturbing the estates of the ministers, people, and churches of the *Norwich* Diocese when he was Bishop there; or of disquieting and endangering the estates, consciences, and lives of any of his Majesty's subjects there, or of bringing profaneness, ignorance, or disobedience to the people: but rather that the true aim and intention of all his actions was only to promote the glory of God by the increase of devotion, decency, and uniformity in the Church. He is thereby encouraged to make and present this, his modest, just, and humble answer before your Honors, of whose high wisdom, justice, moderation, and nobility he is, by long and daily experience, so fully assured, that he does, with all readiness and humble trust, submit himself and his whole cause to the good pleasure of Almighty God and to your Lordships' most honorable examination and judgment.

*The charge consists of twenty-five articles; he makes his several and distinct answers to every one of them in the same order in which they are charged against him, humbly requesting the accustomed benefit that he may be permitted to make further explanations and proof as the occasion shall require.*

TO the first article, this defendant answers and says that it is not possible for him to make any just reply here unless it is first declared how many churches and <term>chancels</term> are intended by the said article, and which ones they are.

He further says that, since it has now been almost six years since he was made Bishop of *Norwich*, he can neither affirm nor deny what was ordered or enjoined by him regarding the raising of any particular chancels; but he humbly refers himself to such acts and registries of the Consistory in that matter as shall be produced against him.

Nevertheless, he says that he never ordered that any chancel should be raised three or four steps; but he remembers that in St. *Margaret’s* Church in *Ipswich*, finding a tomb which had been placed (not more than twenty years before, and without any license from the <term>Ordinary</term>) at the entry into the

He also denies that the chancels in which any step was raised while he was Bishop there had remained level and flat throughout the reign of Queen *Elizabeth*, or that they ought to have remained so. The Rubric indeed, which was made in the 1st year of *Elizabeth*, orders that the chancels shall remain as they have in times past, meaning by that (as the defendant humbly supposes) that the chancels should not be demolished or defaced, but should be preserved for the use of the parish; yet it does not forbid anything being done there tending toward decency and the convenience of the administration. How else is it that any tombs have been placed or any seats erected in chancels since the first year of *Elizabeth*?

He also humbly believes that, just as steps may be raised at the reading desk and at the pulpit for the greater convenience of those administrations at the discretion of the Ordinary, so also in the chancels, where the Communion service is to be read and the holy Sacrament administered, a step or two might be raised without offense so that the minister might thereby be more conveniently heard by the parishioners during his administration there.

Lastly, he says that finding most of the chancels he viewed in that diocese were already so conveniently raised before he arrived there, he commended them for their convenience. And whether the Table were seen or not seen, this Defendant never concerned himself; but so that the Minister in his administration there might be the better seen and heard by the people, and the people seen by the Minister, he conceived it so meet and requisite that he did enquire in his Articles (*Cap.* 3. *Art.* 13.) whether the view of the Church or Chancel were hindered; and afterwards gave his directions to the contrary. [*Direct.* 21.]

To the second Article, he answers and denies that he did, in the year 1636, order that the Communion Table should be set at the East end of the Chancel altar-wise, and not be removed from there.

And he says that he was always so far from having any thought or intention of resembling the Popish manner of altars, that he believes he never once, by any words of his own, so much as named the word *Altar* in any of his articles or directions; much less did he ever term the Table an Altar.

And whereas he mentioned the North end of the Communion Table, he humbly conceives that (even by that) he did the more distinguish it from an altar: for since altars are very nearly equilateral, or four-square, the North end or South end of an altar has never been heard of. Only in the first year of Elizabeth (1 *Eliz.*), when the use of altars was but as yesterday out of their eyes, and the name of altars but newly out of their mouths, the custom of speech led them to call the North end, or North part of the table, the North side of it, as they had been used to call it the North side of the altar. And he rather believes this to be so because in the second year of Elizabeth (2 *Eliz.*), when they best understood their own meaning, the Queen, causing the Liturgy to be translated into *Latin*, the Rubric before the Communion service reads it *Ad septentrionalem mensæ partem stans* <note>Standing at the north part of the table</note>, and not *ad septentrionale latus* <note>at the north side</note>, so that North part, North side, and North end were all one.

He further says that it was necessary the Rubric should appoint the Table at the time of the Communion to stand in the body of the Church or the Chancel, where Morning and Evening Prayer were appointed to be said; for otherwise, in various places where they had no Chancel, they would not have had any Table, or any Communion or divine service.

But where Chancels existed, it was by law, as he humbly conceives, appointed that the Table should stand up at the East end of the Chancel. The words of the Queen’s Injunctions (issued in 2 *Eliz.* 1559) being that the Holy Table in every church shall be set in the place where the altar stood; and that, if for more convenience at the time of the distribution of the Communion it were set in any other place of the Chancel, yet after the Communion was done, it should be placed where it stood before from time to time. Now these Injunctions are allowed and confirmed by the Queen’s Advertisements, *Cap.* 1. *Art.* 3. And those Advertisements are authorized by law, 1 *Eliz. Cap.* 2. *Sect. penult.*

He also says that his directing to have the Communion Table placed at the East end of the Chancel was done by him as much for uniformity with all cathedral and collegiate churches—which he conceived received the usage that had been in them from the beginning of the Reformation—and all the King's chapels, and many parish churches where it had never been otherwise; as also for a double convenience, especially of the smaller churches and parishes. Inasmuch as by the metropolitical injunction they were to make rails for the Communion Tables, setting the said tables in this way tended both to less cost and less encumbrance; for if the said tables should have been placed anywhere else in the Chancel, they would have taken up both more room and more cost in the railing.

He further adds that an Act of State made at the Council Board by the King himself, with the advice of the Metropolitan and the rest of the Privy Council (who were all Commissioners for ecclesiastical causes) regarding the placing of the Table in that manner at *St. Gregory's Church* in London, in the year *1633*, served as a rule to guide this Defendant (as being the Ordinary) to give directions for the same. This is especially true considering that the aforementioned Advertisements of *7 Eliz.* directly imply that the Table should stand there, even at the time of the Communion. <note>Item, they shall decently cover the Table with a carpet, and with a fair linen cloth at the time of the ministration, and shall set the Ten Commandments upon the east wall over the said Table, Chapter 2, Article 7.</note> For if they were over it at the time of ministration, then the Table was to stand under the said east wall at that time.

Nevertheless, he humbly supposes that both by his articles inquiring only whether the Table did ordinarily stand up at the east end, and by his directions that the Table should always stand there unless the Ordinary gave directions otherwise, he thereby suggested that the Communion Table might and should be removed upon any appropriate occasion for more convenient hearing or receiving of communion—not only at the time of Communion, but at other times when there was no Communion. To this end, he expressed himself afterwards regarding some churches in the said Diocese, such as at *St. Edmundsbury*, *Lavenham*, and other places, where it was certified that the end of the chancels was too far distant from the people in the church. And at *Yarmouth* (from the beginning), he had given orders for the greater convenience of the people that, although a rail had been placed toward the east end of the said chancel by the Vicar-general’s appointment, the Communion Table should always stand outside and below the said rail, in the body of the said church.

To the third article, this Defendant answers and denies that in the year *1636* he enjoined that there should be a rail before the Table.

But he says that it being reported by most of the presentments in his primary visitation that the Vicar-general had, in the Archbishop’s metropolitical visitation, enjoined them to set up rails, and many people coming to this Defendant asking for direction on what manner and style the said rails should most appropriately be, this Defendant did, after his visitation was past, give a general direction that it was most appropriate to set them from one side of the chancel to the other—thereby aiming for the least possible expense.

He also denies that he considered the place within the rail too holy for the people; and he is heartily sorry that those who gave this information to the Honorable House of Commons consider God’s people to be as dogs. For such were the only words of this Defendant’s direction: that the rails should be so thick with pillars that dogs might not get in. Against such an abominable profanation of dogs coming to defile the Lord’s Table, he humbly conceives that no care or provision can be too much. He is ready to prove that in a poor country parish in his diocese, on a *Christmas Day*, while the minister was preaching a sermon concerning the participation of the Communion, a dog came into the chancel and, leaping upon the Communion Table (which was not railed in), took the bread prepared for the Communion in his mouth and ran away with it. Because of this, they could have no Communion that day, as there was not another loaf of white bread in the town, except for that which the dog had defiled.

Indeed, he further says that the said rails preserve the Lord’s Table from various other inconveniences and profane abuses, not only from boys rioting, leaning

He also says that rails and enclosures in front of the communion table were not a *thing* newly or recently adopted. For in the great churches of *St. Paul*, *Westminster*, *York*, *Norwich*, and various other cathedral churches; also in *St. Gregory’s*, *St. Edmund’s*, *St. Margaret’s*, and *St. Michael’s*, and other parish churches in *Norwich*, and in *St. Margaret’s* at *Westminster*; *St. Martin’s in campis*; *St. Michael’s* in *Crooked-lane*, *St. Saviour’s*, *St. Giles* at *Cripplegate*, and many more in *London*, there have been rails at the communion table time out of mind. Also at *Hadley*, *Boxford*, *Wilby*, and many other churches in the Diocese of *Norwich*.

Therefore, it never entered this defendant’s mind to doubt that the <term>Metropolitan</term> might by law enjoin things of such use and convenience. This is considering that the canons of our Church made in 1571 charge the churchwardens <note>To see that all things are diligently observed which pertain to their offices, and which are conceived in the Queen’s Injunctions and in the Book of Advertisements; and that shall be set forth by the archbishops and bishops in every one of their visitations, for the use of the churches, Chapter 5, Paragraph 11.</note> And they also charge deans <note>To ensure that all injunctions set forth by the Queen, or enjoined by the bishop in his visitation, are diligently observed, Chapter 2, Paragraph 6.</note> We also have the printed injunctions of *Richard Cox*, Bishop of *Ely*, around 1570, and of *Thomas Cooper*, Bishop of *Lincoln*, in the year 1571, and of some others. So, it appeared to have been usual since the Reformation, and lawful for archbishops and bishops, at their visitations, to enjoin things convenient and useful for the Church.

Lastly, as for the claim that some people were punished for stepping within the rail—God knows who they were, by whom they were punished, and where and when it occurred. But this defendant says that one *Daniel Whayman*, of *Monks-Soham* in *Suffolk*, was in great danger of punishment before His Majesty’s commissioners for having disturbed the minister in a very grievous manner during the administration of the Holy Communion, until it pleased the court to refer the matter to this defendant as <term>Ordinary</term> there. Upon the said *Whayman’s* submission, he was easily induced to entreat the court that he might be dismissed from any further punishment.

To the fourth article, this defendant answers and denies that in the year 1636, he ordered all pews to be altered so that people might kneel with their faces eastward toward the table set altar-wise; much less did he do so to further blind superstition, or order that there should be no seats around or level with the communion table.

But he says that whereas the arrangement of seats in churches by right belongs to the <term>Ordinary</term>, he only inquired in his visitation articles about the manner in which the said pews and seats in their churches and chancels were arranged. He did this as a preventative measure for the future, so that the gentle suggestion provided by such an inquiry might remind men hereafter to avoid both a foul disorder and a great profanation, which he had observed in many places. The disorder was that everyone had taken it upon themselves to build seats in churches according to their own fancy, in terms of style and height, observing neither uniformity nor decency—which is a very beautiful thing in men’s private houses, and even more fitting for the house of God. The profanation was that he had found the seats in some churches arranged in such a way that people could not conveniently kneel down during prayer to worship the Lord.

THE LIFE OF

Therefore, to promote holiness and Christian devotion rather than blind superstition, these were the goals he aimed for through the specific details of that inquiry. First, that in God's house, by observing proper order and outward decency, men might be reminded of the beauty of inward holiness. Secondly, that since God's house was ordained as a house of prayer, the people might have an opportunity (and no obstacle) to place themselves in the posture of prayer: to kneel and humble themselves in God's service. Thirdly, that as much as is convenient, they might look or turn their faces in the same direction. This is a practice (as he humbly believes) that is very advantageous, because otherwise men's devotions are much disturbed by gazing into one another's faces during prayer. This has created an unseemly custom in many people of hiding their eyes with their hands or holding their hats before their faces, as if they were ashamed of the worship of God.

Based on that assumption, then—that to avoid this inconvenience and to promote uniformity—it would be appropriate to arrange future or altered seating so that the people (as far as convenience would permit) might all kneel in the same direction. What direction was then more suitable to choose than eastward? For has not all *Christendom* generally observed it from the beginning, by building churches facing the east in all nations? This was done even though, by doing so, they did what the pagans had done before them in building their idolatrous temples, and contrary to what the *Jews* (who in their time were the true Church of God) had always observed. It was also the constant practice of the early Church to kneel toward the east during the time of prayer. <note>"We turn toward the East," says *Gregory Nyssen* in *Lib. de Orat.* and *St. Augustine* in *Lib. ii. de Serm. Dom. Cap. 19*. "We worship toward the East," says *Athanasius* in *Quaest. Necess. 14*. "We look to the East when we pray," says *St. Basil* in *Lib. de Spir. Cap. 27*; and also *Epiphanius* in *Lib. I. Tom. I. Cap. 19*.</note> That this was the custom here in *England* after the Reformation is shown by the old forms of the seats in many churches, and by Mr. *Cartwright's* complaint that the minister during prayer was in the chancel with his back to the people; and also by the rubric before the *Te Deum*, which appoints the minister, when he reads the lessons, to stand and turn himself so that he may best be heard.

Therefore, this defendant could have no other intention in that inquiry but this: that since the east is the highest end of the church and the holy table stands there, by kneeling in that direction, people would not offend or disturb one another and would also better hear and see what the minister said and did during his administration.

And for the same purpose—that during the holy communion, men's thoughts might be less disturbed by other objects, the minister himself and his administration be less liable to disturbance, and the place itself be clearer for that holy service and for the communicants to approach—he inquired whether any seats were above the table or even with it. He considered this, in his own judgment (subject to correction), to be very inappropriate for several reasons.

To the fifth article, this defendant answers and denies that he ordered the minister, after some part of Morning Prayer, to go to the table set altar-wise as if to a holier place. For he always considered it to be table-wise and all parts of the church to be equally holy.

But he says this: that the Church by law has directed various parts of the divine service to be performed in different parts and places of the church. For example, baptism is to be performed at the font <note>Rubric before Baptism</note>; matrimony is to begin in the body of the church <note>Rubric before Matrimony</note> and be finished at the Lord's table <note>Rubric after the Blessing</note>. The order of burial is to begin at the church gate and so proceed either into the church,

He also denies claiming the communion table is holier than other parts of the church, asserting that different services are assigned to different locations by law.</summary>

or toward the grave, <note>Rubric before Burial.</note> The Thanksgiving for Women after Childbirth is to be at the table, <note>Rubric before it.</note> The Commination is to be partly in the pulpit, <note>Rubric before the Commination.</note> and partly where they are accustomed to say the Litany, <note>Rubric before the Psalm Miserere.</note> As for that part of the Morning Prayer which is called the Communion service, the rubric before the Communion appoints that it shall be said at the table; and the rubric after the Collects orders that upon Holy Days, if there be no Communion, yet all shall be said that is appointed at the Communion until the end of the homily. And where then shall the Communion service be said, but at the Communion table? If not, how does it then happen that for the sermon or homily (whether there is a Communion or none) they go to the place for the sermon—that is, into the pulpit—except that it was settled thus upon the Reformation? This appears by the constant custom ever observed in all cathedral and collegiate churches, and in many parochial churches, time out of mind, and also in the King’s Chapel. (*Mr. Thomas Foster*, parson of St. *Matthew’s* in *Ipswich*, a man of great age, affirmed in open synod there that for many years after he was first a minister there, the Ten Commandments and the rest of the service were never read otherwise than at the table.) This is also shown by the testimony of various elderly men who were ministers above fifty years ago, and by Mr. *Cartwright’s* own complaint in these words: “After Morning Prayer, the minister, to say other prayers, climbs up to the far end of the chancel, as far as the wall will let him.” <note>Page 105, line 1.</note>

He further says that the practice which he saw of this usage in the presence of the Supreme Governor of the Church, before this defendant came into his daily attendance—namely, in the journey into *Scotland* in the year 1633, and in all parish churches where His Majesty came in his summer progresses—might be inducement enough, if not warrant, to this defendant to give that direction which he did in this matter.

But he also alleges that Queen *Elizabeth’s* Advertisements say that the Common Prayer shall be said or sung in such a place as the Ordinary shall think fit, considering the largeness or narrowness of the church and choir, so that the people may be most edified. Also, the first rubric before the Morning Prayer says that the prayers shall be used in the accustomed place of the church, chapel, or chancel, unless it shall be otherwise determined by the Ordinary. Now, the accustomed place of prayer when that rubric was made was the choir in all churches that had choirs, as appears by the first rubric; for the Common Prayer Book of King *Edward VI* says, the priest standing in the choir shall begin the Matins. Queen *Elizabeth* also ordered in her Injunctions that to say the Litany, the priest, with others of the choir, shall come and kneel in the middle of the church, which is as much as to say they shall come out of the choir or chancel. He therefore humbly conceives that if the Ordinary has power by law to determine where the Common Prayer shall be said, and also to remove it out of the accustomed place when he thinks fit, how much more might this defendant give direction to have it read in the place which he saw approved of by such great examples, and which he found to be the accustomed place when that law and rubric were made—that is to say, at the table? And how could the consciences of either minister or people (if they had any conscience for obedience) be justly offended and grieved that a thing so consistent with law and good example was put into practice?

For if the reason for the offense is that the service itself was unprofitable to the people, who could not hear (as this charge says) what was said or prayed there, this defendant humbly answers that he

He was so careful of all convenience in that regard that where the minister (raising his voice as he ought to do, though some, with evil intent, would not) was not fully heard there, he should move closer to the people. The Table also, if necessary, should be placed further down, as at *St. Edmund’s-bury*, *Lavenham*, and other places; and at *Yarmouth*, for this very reason, the minister, even when there was no Communion, should not go to the Table to read the service there. And this, during the Visitation, was often said by the Commissioners: that if any church were too large, upon proper information being given, direction should be provided as to where to stand so that they might be sufficiently heard.

And therefore, he humbly prays that consideration on this point may be granted thus far, since the complaint is made because the people could not hear the said Communion service, and that the said complaint can only apply to a very few people, such as those who sat very far away and in the outermost parts of some very large churches (scarcely one such in forty throughout the Diocese). How it must necessarily be inferred that in every congregation it could not but be very profitable to all the people, in a far greater measure than it had been before this defendant came into that Diocese; because then, in not even one church in forty did any of the people hear a word of the said service. For generally, it was not read at all in the churches; but after the Second Lesson, they sang a psalm, and so the sermon began, and that was all they did (a few places excepted), leaving out the whole Communion service, or the most part of it, when there was no Communion.

Regarding the general correction of this, brought about by this defendant’s care, he is ready to make it appear—as well by letters of joy, applause, and thanks written by the Dean and Canons, the Chancellor, various gentlemen, and grave ministers, as also by the testimony of many other godly and worthy men—how far their consciences were from being offended; and on the contrary, how much they rejoiced for the due reverence and complete observance of God’s service.

Lastly, therefore, he humbly prays that it may be observed that the Preface to the Book of Common Prayer says that for the resolution of all doubts concerning the manner of how to understand, do, and execute the things contained in the service book, the Bishop of the Diocese shall, at his discretion, give orders for the same, provided that his order is not contrary to anything contained in the same. And if the Bishop is in doubt, he may have a resolution from the Archbishop. This Preface being (as he humbly conceives) confirmed by law, and the Archbishop’s resolution therein being also publicly known, this defendant hopes that he did nothing in this point (especially for the reasons before alleged) but what was legally warrantable.

To the Sixth Article, this defendant answers and denies that the bowings and adorations which he used were superstitious gestures, or that they were dangerous examples to lead others to do the same; or that they are any scandal or offense to sound, sincere, or well-disposed Christians; or that his chaplains or others followed his example of bowing after the Table was set altar-wise.

But this he humbly acknowledges: that when he enters any church or chapel consecrated to God’s service, or departs from it; as also when he approaches the Lord’s Table or recedes from it; and when during the Divine Service the Lord Jesus is mentioned, he performs an adoration by lowly and reverently bowing his body. He humbly offers the reason for all of this in the following arguments.

He began to do so by the example of that learned and holy prelate, Bishop *Andrews*, now with God, under whom this defendant was brought up from his youth, and had depended upon him for more than forty years. Bishop *Andrews* constantly and religiously practiced the same upon all occasions; this defendant therefore, even then, considering with himself that the said Bishop—being an ancient, grave divine of high account for his piety, knowledge, and great learning, and one who had conversed with most of those holy fathers who lived in this Church at the beginning of the Reformation under Queen *Elizabeth*—it could not be otherwise than that he had received the same from their usage and practice.

As his own years and studies increased, he found, first, that bowing at the name of the Lord Jesus had not only been practiced by the clergy, but had also been enjoined upon all the people ever since the first Reformation, as appears by the Injunctions, *1º Eliz. Cap. 52.*, thereby to testify our due acknowledgment that the Lord Jesus Christ, the true and eternal Son of God, is the only Savior of the world, in whom alone the mercies, graces, and promises of God to mankind, for this life and the life to come, are fully and wholly comprised, *1º Jac. Can. 18.*

Secondly, bowing before the holy table had been anciently used in the Church of *England* by the clergy, as appears by the rule which the most noble Lords of the Garter set for themselves when they began to use the same gesture under King *Henry V.*: that they would do it *humiliter & ad modum ecclesiasticorum virorum* <note>humbly and in the manner of clergymen</note>. That this usage might continue still in the Church of *England* after the Reformation appears from Bishop *Jewell*, who in his *Reply* to *Harding*, allows it as a commendable gesture and a token of devotion, *Art. 3. Div. 29.* Neither was it forbidden by the Injunctions of King *Edward* or Queen *Elizabeth*, in both of which other gestures are prohibited. And as for any fear of popish superstition, Bishop *Morton*, in his defense of this gesture, shows that this cannot be; for the Papists only use it because of their opinion of transubstantiation and would deride us for doing it in any other respect. *Book of Sacram. p. 463.*

Lastly, because this defendant always humbly conceived that no Christian would deny that bowing or performing adoration was to be used as a part of God's worship—the affirmative act being necessarily included in the negative precept, *non adorabis ea : ergo adorabis me* <note>you shall not worship them: therefore you shall worship me</note>, to say nothing of the frequent exhortations in Holy Scripture to do so—and because he found in antiquity that it was the constant practice of the Church of Christ to always use an act of adoration when they entered into God’s house. For which purpose *venite adoremus* <note>O come, let us worship</note> seems to have been placed at the very beginning of our Morning Prayer; therefore he himself was further induced to observe the same, although no canon enjoined it, seeing that reason, piety, and the constant practice of antiquity commend it.

Also, this defendant considered that lifting up of the hands, or casting down of the eyes, or smiting the breast, or giving a sigh, or any other similar gestures—which are as liable to just offense as bowing is—are in no way prohibited. And he could never understand why the using of this particular reverence should not be as free as using no kind of reverence at all. Especially when no exception (of which he has heard) has ever yet been brought against it which would not be just as applicable against uncovering the head at the entrance into God's house, or against kneeling down in the church at a seat, or against men holding their hats before their faces while praying.

Civilly also, he saw the same done at every approach to the earthly majesty and at every departure from it *toties quoties* <note>as often as it happens</note>. And it is held as no mockery in that time, but a sign of duty and loyalty, when the King is not present, to ex-
