[To ex]hibit a solemn reverence toward the Chair of State in his Presence Chamber, or in the House of Parliament, or toward his Majesty’s seat at *Windsor* Chapel and elsewhere. No more, as he humbly conceives, is it any superstition, but a sign of devotion and of an awful apprehension of God’s divine presence, to do him reverence upon approaching the House of God or the Lord’s Table.

For this defendant professes that he never does it otherwise than as a sign of his habitual intention and preparation of heart to be ever, if it were possible, in perpetual adoration of the majesty of God. But because he cannot do this—he cannot imitate the twenty-four elders, who have no rest day or night from falling down and worshipping before the throne (*Apoc. 4*), nor is it possible for the weak, finite, and limited nature of man to subsist if he should do nothing but adore—therefore he contents himself to do it as he does for prayers, thanksgivings, and spiritual rejoicings: at some special and chief times instead of the rest. And those times are whenever his outward sense, in some special way, reminds him of God’s divine presence.

Since then those things which (besides being dedicated to the worship of God) also expressly bear the name of God, do thereby, at the very sight of them, more especially remind him of God’s divine grace and presence, he therefore takes them as the occasions and limits for performing adoration to God’s eternal majesty.

Now, churches and other consecrated places are named and called the House of God. Therefore, this defendant humbly adores the Lord of the house whenever he enters into that house of His; and in performing this, the prayerful utterance of his poor soul is ["*God be merciful to me a sinner*"] or ["*Thou, O Lord, art worthy to receive all honor and glory*"]. And this he would do even if there were no table at all in the church.

But yet, the Communion Table being also called the Lord’s Table and God’s Board, he is again induced to do his adorations to God when he comes before it or recedes from it. However, as Bishop *Andrewes* said of prayers which the saints used to make at the graves of martyrs, *Sepulcrum ipsum* <note>the grave itself</note>, and so in this case, *mensam ipsam non magis adorans quam parietem* <note>worshipping the table itself no more than a wall</note>. *ad Apol. Cap. 1. Par. 51.*

So then, God is present everywhere, yet by more special promise and assistance in places dedicated to His holy worship. They are higher than other places, not by any inherent holiness, but by a relative holiness because of the holy use to which they refer. In which kind, no doubt, He is also present at the font and in the pulpits, as well as at the table; but because the table bears God’s name and particularly suggests the memorial of Christ’s death and passion (*Bishop Jewel, Art. 8. Div. 22.*), therefore this defendant limited himself to the forenamed occasions only for performing such adoration unto the Lord Almighty.

As for Mr. *Nowell*, Mr. *Guest*, and Mr. *Duncon*, this defendant humbly answers that they are of age and good understanding, very able to answer for themselves, and as he believes, ready to show that they used the same gestures before they became his chaplains. He is sure that he used that form of humility and adoration long before he directed any table to be set up at the East wall, and before he was Bishop of *Norwich* or anywhere else. Therefore, his setting of the table (as is alleged) had no such intent and was no inducement for him to perform that reverence.

->### MATTHEW WREN, D. D.<-

To the Seventh Article, this Defendant answers and denies that he enjoined all the people to do reverence before the holy table placed altarwise.

But he says that by his Articles he only inquired whether the communicants came up reverently before the Lord’s Table, and did not sit still in their pews to be sought throughout the church. And afterwards, understanding by the presentments that in most of the churches there was (by the Vicar-general’s order) a rail before the table, then his direction, based on that assumption, was necessarily that all communicants should come up reverently and kneel before the rail to receive the holy communion.

And this he did upon these grounds:

1. For conformity and obedience to the rules of the church, as he humbly conceives; for the words of the invitation before the sacrament are [*to draw near*], and then, if there is a rail, that implies an approach to the rail. For this exhortation [*to draw near*] is not to be understood as being made to the people down in the church, for them to come nearer—that is, to come up into the chancel. Rather, it was made when, by occasion of having offered, the communicants were all present in the chancel and ready to communicate, and yet they are required to draw nearer. This appears by the rubric after the offertory in King *Edward's* service-book, directing that as many as do not intend to receive the communion shall depart out of the choir into the church; but the communicants shall stay there still, near it, and therefore to those who stood there, that exhortation is afterward spoken [*draw near*]. It is also expressly called "coming to the table" by our service-book. As in the prayer before the consecration: *we do not presume to come to this your table*; and before that in the third exhortation: *bewail your sins, or come not to this holy table*; and before that in the second rubric for the order of administration: *in no way presume to come to the Lord's table, etc.*

2. For uniformity among themselves; for where most of the parishioners voluntarily came up before the table to receive the blessed sacrament, he humbly conceives it might reasonably be desired of all the rest that they would do so too, *ne esset schisma* <note>lest there be a schism</note>, to take away all occasion for difference and division, especially in this holy business.

3. For great convenience. 
1. Thereby to avoid all risk of spilling the bread and wine consecrated for the holy communion, which often happened when carrying them around. 
—— 2. Thereby to discover *recusants*: for in large and numerous congregations, the churchwardens had no readier way to find out who never took communion than to stand by and take notice of those who came before the table to receive. 
3. Thereby to discover those who refused to kneel reverently at the receiving, as well as those who, after the delivery of the bread and wine to them, still would not partake of them. 
4. To avoid all other kinds of improper behavior, with which some had been charged, committed when the sacrament was carried to private seats. 
5. For a faster completion of the service, experience having shown them that in large parishes, where one man was to administer to two or three hundred people, they finished sooner by an hour or more by doing it thus, which was a great relief to both the minister and the communicants. 
6. For the greater convenience of the communicants. For whereas the injunctions of Queen *Elizabeth* take care to have the table ordered so that the communicants may more conveniently, and in greater numbers, receive communion with the minister, this direction to have the people come up before the table contributed much to that goal. But if they might stay where they wished and expect to have the sacrament brought to them, then no care would need to be taken regarding where the table should stand.

He further believes in all humbleness that drawing the people up to the table to receive the holy Sacrament there might rather have been an argument to lessen their fear or fancy of an altar. For tables are for eating and drinking at them, but from altars, they used to carry that which was to be eaten and drunk to other parts and places of the temples. In all other reformed churches as well, the communicants come to the table (and the bread and wine are not carried to them), and we never heard of any objection against it.

How, therefore, it should be an offense to the consciences of many, or of any, this defendant does not understand, seeing it is a thing grounded upon so much reason and has also been practiced without offense (since time out of mind) in many places of the land. Such as at *St. Giles* without *Cripplegate* and at *Allhallows Barking, London*, at *St. Edmund's* as well, and at *St. Michael's Coslany* in *Norwich*, and in various other parishes besides the cathedral and collegiate churches. And he denies that there was any idolatry or superstition in it, or any fear of such justly given by him.

He also humbly believes that if he had, by his episcopal authority, assigned any other place in the church or chancel where they should all come and kneel at the Sacrament, just as great a pretense for objection would have been found, and some quarrelsome way picked against it. But regardless, the rules and rubrics of the church having designated a special place or part of the chancel for it, by the words of the preface cited before, <note>at Article 5, near the end</note>, it was left to the <term>Ordinary</term> (as he believes) to be ordered by him according to his discretion and for the greatest convenience.

He further denies that he gave direction to the minister not to administer the Communion to such people who would not come up and perform such reverence. For he never gave any direction therein about their performing any reverence. But if by performing reverence they mean kneeling, he then answers that the direction was not his, but the law's. For the rubric after the consecration enjoins <note>that the minister shall deliver the Communion in both kinds to the people in their hands, kneeling</note>. And the 27th Canon of *James I* prohibited every minister from administering to anyone but those who kneeled, under pain of suspension.

He likewise says that he, by his letters once and again, expressly advised the chancellor not to cite or call into the court those who stayed in the chancels and would not come up to the rail. <note>See his letters of May 7, 1637, and mine, May 23, 1637.</note> As for any who presented themselves upon their knees in the chancel and did not have the Communion delivered to them, but yet were afterward excommunicated for not receiving it, this defendant says that he excommunicated no man, nor did he give any order to have them excommunicated. Nor does he believe that any of those who are named in this article were excommunicated while he was bishop there, and much less for that reason. He therefore refers to the acts of the court, as he is informed that *Fisher* was never cited at all; also, that *Newton, Bedwell*, and *Duncon* were invited by the minister to come into the chancel, but they would not. Whereupon he told them that he would come down to them after he had administered to the rest, but they went out of the church and would not stay. As for *Shyming* and *Fromar*, this defendant never heard of them; and *Edmund Dey* has long since been dead.

To many people, he personally gave directions on how they should do it for the best benefit and edification of the poor people. Mr. *White of ——* has reported to others that this defendant gave not only allowance, but also direction and charge to them to expound the words of the Catechism; he therefore believes that no man was ever questioned for expounding it.

He further says, that he did direct that the said catechizing should be performed according to the Catechism of the Church of *England* only. This Catechism is proposed by the law of the land in the rubrics of the service book as the rule of examination for the Bishop to follow, and it is the best form that ever was compiled for laying the foundation and grounds of religion in the hearts and minds of unlearned Christians. He considered also that the great variety of catechisms, which every man in former times pushed out at his own pleasure, distracted and corrupted the minds of the people more than anything else, sowing in them the seeds of both error and faction. And he conceived it an unreasonable thing that any catechizing should be publicly practiced in the Church except according to the Catechism which the Church of *England* allows in her liturgy. The proper observation of this was so far from suppressing knowledge or introducing ignorance that the defendant is humbly confident it produced the exact opposite effects. For some godly and hardworking ministers (namely, as he remembers, one Mr. *Crackenthoyr*, then parson of *Burton-magna* in *Suffolk*, and another from a neighboring diocese with him, men otherwise unknown to this defendant) came to visit him and told him that they blessed God for the good success which, after half a year's experience, they had found therein. As for the offensive claim that explaining the catechism might be as bad as a sermon, this defendant cannot help but wonder how any man who presents himself as a Christian dared to inform the Honorable House of Commons that the Bishop ever made such an assertion; neither can he believe that any subordinate official could be so unwise as to claim the same.

He further says that the book concerning the sports to be allowed was a declaration first published by King *James*, of blessed memory, in the year 1618, and then repeated, ratified, and published again by the King's Majesty who now reigns, with a command to all Justices of the Peace, and to the judges and Justices of Assize, to observe it. And his Majesty further willed that a public announcement of it should be made by order from the bishops through all the parish churches of their dioceses. In obedience to this, after it was certified to this defendant that the majority of the ministers of the diocese had already published it, and since his Majesty is the <term>supreme Ordinary</term> and governor in the administration of the Church, who was this defendant that he should have failed to give the order (as was required)? And to whom could he give the order in every parish church but to the <term>incumbent</term> there? But he believes that no man was ever deprived of his position for not reading it.

Yet this defendant says that he carried out nothing in this matter by himself or in his own person, but referred it all entirely to the Chancellor of the diocese. To the Chancellor—by a patent confirmed by the <term>Dean and Chapter</term>—the entire administration of the diocese had been committed by this defendant's predecessors. Therefore, this defendant had no command, nor any coercive or <term>coarctative</term> power over him to compel him by force or fear to do anything except what he himself thought fit to do. (The Chancellor, by the purpose of his position, was joined to the bishop and by patent was imposed upon him as a judge of the law to inform the bishop and to see that nothing was done but what was right and lawful.) And in this matter, although by letters to this defendant, the said Chancellor first informed him that specific men (by name) refused to obey specific orders (the reading of this book being one of them) and asked for direction on what to do with them, this defendant did, in his reply of private letters, urge him to proceed according to what was right and the duty of his position in censuring them for it. Yet he humbly believes that whatever was illegally or unjustly done by the Chancellor as a result cannot rightfully affect this defendant, who himself gave no sentence upon anyone and whose private advice was based on the Chancellor’s reports. It also remained within the Chancellor's power and choice to reject that advice if he found it was not consistent with what was right.

The case therefore being such that this defendant must presume the Chancellor (who was the primary and sole agent in the matter) did nothing but what was right and according to law; and if he did otherwise, it is still not a case where the law involves the abettors, counselors, procurers, or <term>fautors</term> in the crime along with the main actor. This defendant humbly prays that the said Chancellor alone may be <term>responsal</term> for it. This is especially because this defendant has reason to believe that the Chancellor can and will show that there were also other defaults found in those who were suspended; and that those suspensions were soon lifted, and that no man at all was deprived of his position for this reason—particularly not any of those mentioned in the article.

<header>MATTHEW WREN, D. D.</header>

To the ninth Article, this defendant answers and says that he directed there should be no difference in bell ringing for church when there was a sermon compared to when there was none, except for funeral knells. And he humbly believes that it was very much in accordance with reason, prudence, piety, and good order to do so. By doing so, he intended to remove, as much as possible, that evil custom which many had adopted—making a division between the use of public prayer and preaching. He finds that *Richard*, Bishop of *London*, inquired specifically about this fault in his articles in the year 1605. For, by the distinction they made between those two, they worked to prefer one over the other, whereas they ought always to be held in equal holy esteem together.

He therefore denies that this was done to hinder the people in their good desires of serving God and edifying their souls; on the contrary, it was to further and benefit them in that goal. For the practice of giving different notice with the bells had been used by indiscreet and divisive people as an opportunity to express their contempt for the Divine Service of the church and to separate themselves from their brethren in the holy service of God, to the great hazard of their souls and to the clear dishonor of Almighty God.

This defendant therefore, considering that all people were bound by the law (of both God and man) to go to their parish churches at all appointed times; and that once there, the sermon could reasonably be no less welcome to them—but rather more welcome—even if they did not know about it beforehand because of any distinction in ringing. He could in no way doubt that his episcopal authority and discretion could properly establish a rule for the ringing of bells, a matter which every sexton thought himself fit to decide at his own pleasure. And many of the ministers had already taken that same order for ringing themselves, thereby keeping their people from wandering to other parishes.

Regarding the claim that people used the notice from the bells to devote themselves to God's service in places where both prayer and preaching were held: this defendant answers that this excuse has no validity at all in the country parishes, nor in any part of the diocese, except for *Ipswich*, *Norwich*, and one or two other towns. In those places, there being several parish churches, they might easily leave one and go to another; yet he humbly believes the law does not allow this. And he is the bolder to call it an excuse because the true use made of that distinction in ringing was not to come to the service of God at all if there were no sermon, but to stay at home or to go to private <term>conventicles</term> and unlawful assemblies. Nevertheless, the order which this defendant directed was general, and therefore it concerned churches where there was no sermon no more than those where there was constant preaching every *Sunday*.

As for sermons and preaching, the high value this defendant placed on them appears (as he hopes) from this and all his other directions; for he always considered the sermon as a true and proper part of God’s divine worship and of the public service. Based on this, he often advised that after the sermon, the <term>collect</term> should always be said:

->[*Grant, we beseech you, that the words which we have heard this day with our outward ears, etc.*]<-

He also humbly conceives, that the 55th Canon of 1603 was justly urged by him in this behalf. He also believes, that there was never any public Prayer permitted in the Church of God for 1500 Years, except such as was first publicly considered and allowed by the Church to be used. And the Reason follows, *ne forte aliquid contra fidem, vel per ignorantiam, vel per minus studium, sit compositum.* <note>lest by chance something be composed against the faith, either through ignorance or through lack of study.</note> And of this, whatever was the particular Occasion then in those Times, yet the Danger always remains, and (God knows) it is nowadays too often met with in our Pulpits. And for this he humbly conceived that the Form of bidding Prayer, or of moving to pray, might be the more allowable, and was ordained to be used in the Pulpit, rather than any other set Prayer.

<meta>This page continues Matthew Wren's defense regarding his restrictions on pulpit prayer, arguing that the authority to lead worship is not inherent to an individual but granted through specific ecclesiastical office and calling.</meta>

...conceived by himself) for the worshipping of God, was a thing, the power of which was never given to him. For neither at holy orders, nor by institution and induction, nor by any license granted, is such power given. And it is rightly observed by the learned upon 1 Corinthians 12, that the grace, or enabling gift, is not immediately to induce the operation or act in the Church of God, unless the administration—that is, the office or calling—be also given. By that rule, therefore, to which *Christ* himself submitted, as Saint *Paul* says, *No man takes this honor upon himself*. Just as no man (no matter how able he is to perform it) ought to take upon himself any office in God's service, so he should not take up any function of that office until he is called to it—that is, until he is appointed to it by an express power given to him.

However, it is not denied by this defendant that some private, conceived prayers have been used by many learned divines in the pulpit in a good and godly manner; yet he humbly conceives that it was necessary that the rule for how men should pray there in the pulpit should be general and certain, not arbitrary. This is because those who are most unable to do so will take the same liberty that others have, whereby many, by venting their own undigested conceptions in the pulpit, have greatly offended God and the Church, and brought a scandal on those two most divine offices: praying and preaching.

He thought it therefore fitting to adhere to the ancient usage of our Church, as he found it both prescribed in the Canon and practiced also, not only by Bishop *Latimer*, but also by Bishop *Jewel*, whose form is found in his book that is appointed to be kept in all churches. He did this especially because Bishop *Andrewes* and the late Dr. *Montfort* had often affirmed to this defendant and others that, until Mr. *Cartwright's* time, it was never otherwise in this Church. But then, a dislike of the prescribed form of public prayer established by law burst forth in both their preaching and writing, until the State began to question them for it. When they found it was not safe to preach or print any more against the liturgy, they resorted to the use of these newly formed prayers in the pulpit, thereby continuing the people in a dislike and neglect of the prescribed form.

He further answers and denies that at the sermon in *Ipswich*, when the preacher made his prayer, he showed no reverence by kneeling or otherwise, as if to discourage the said prayer. For he sat with his head uncovered and did very reverently and diligently attend to what was said; at the close of all, he did humbly kneel down and pray. He had long observed this practice in the university, it being usually done there in his time by the doctors and heads of the houses: to attend to what the preacher would pray for, and then to kneel down at the Lord's Prayer. In this, he did more than that whole congregation generally used to do (though there were above 500 present), until some of them were induced by this defendant to show more reverence. For ordinarily, no one but those of his company (whether man or woman) was seen to kneel at any part of the prayers from their first coming into the church until their going out. But the reason why this defendant did not kneel during all the said pulpit prayer was because he did not dare join in those extemporary prayers until he had heard and gathered what they would pray for, as he had many times encountered passages that were not only ill-advised or confused, but also erroneous, scandalous, seditious, and dangerous, uttered in such a kind of praying. Some have prayed for "holy Machiavellianism"; some that their original sins might at last be forgiven them; some regularly slandered the King and Queen; some took it upon themselves to distinguish the nobility as "true-hearted" or not; and so on.

But to reinforce what was practiced at the beginning, and to bring things back to what they were before, was merely to remove the said scandal by a fair and regular rejection of that innovation. Just as when the *Papists* call us *Protestants* *novatores* <note>Latin: innovators</note> and charge us with innovation in areas where we differ from them, our true answer is that the innovation is on their part, as they have brought those things into the Church which were not in use in the pure and primitive times, to which times the reformed *Church of England* endeavors to conform. And so it is now with those who have had recourse to the beginnings of the Reformation here, thereby avoiding some exotic customs lately introduced; departing from those customs cannot now be rightly charged as being an innovation.

He also denies that any ministers were forced by him to depart this realm for *Holland* or into other parts beyond the sea, or to remove into other dioceses; much less that any were so prosecuted by him as to be the cause of their deaths, or of leaving their cures <note>The spiritual charge or parish responsibilities of a clergyman.</note> and going away. Neither does he believe that there was any just and true cause given to them by anyone to do so, as far as he was ever informed by certificate or letters from the chancellor or commissary regarding the said ministers.

But as to the parties named in this article, this defendant—referring himself otherwise to the records of the court—humbly answers that:

Mr. *Thomas Scott* being under suspension, the first thing that this defendant did after coming personally into the said diocese was to hold a court, and there, with all tender and respectful treatment, to absolve the said Mr. *Scott* for three months; after that, he directed that he be granted forbearance for six months more; and after that for eight or nine months longer. Within that time, he received several letters from the said Mr. *Scott* expressing great acknowledgment of the favor he found from this defendant. He also says that the said Mr. *Scott* was in his usual health and alive for more than a year after this defendant left the See of *Norwich*. For he did not die until about *Whitsuntide* 1640, which was about two years later.

Mr. *William Powell* (as was certified to this defendant) was suspended for many violations of the canons and was granted absolution soon after (without coming for it himself) via his proctor <note>A legal representative in ecclesiastical courts.</note>, Mr. *Edward Trott*.

Mr. *Richard Raymund* likewise was so suspended, and shortly after so absolved, namely, in the person of Mr. *Richard Pert*, his proctor.

This defendant had a good opinion of Mr. *John Carter*, a curate in *Norwich*, until he was informed otherwise of him by frequent letters over the course of a year from the chancellor—specifically on *April* 22, 1636; *May* 3, 1636; *June* 22, 24, and 27; *October* 20; *December* 7; *February* 5 and 17; and *March* 10—to whom he wholly referred him.

Mr. *Nicholas Beard*, a curate in *Ipswich*, was suspended by the visitors for other defaults and also for refusing to present and show (which is required by law at all visitations) his letters of orders <note>Documents proving a person has been ordained as a priest or deacon.</note>, which would prove he was a minister, and his license to serve there, which would prove he was of that diocese. This defendant was not personally hasty to restore him because he had previously (within a few years prior) heard him speak very bitterly in a sermon against the state and against a noble earl of this land, who was then a high officer. He was also informed by honest men that the said Mr. *Beard* was of a very turbulent spirit, whom they suspected of being the secret instigator of a great riot committed suddenly one evening by a dangerous assembly of common people against this defendant.

Mr. *Hudson* (as this defendant was informed) was suspended at the visitation but was restored again a short while later. This defendant never knew or heard anything more of him.

To his recollection, this defendant never heard of Mr. *Robert Kent*; but now, upon inquiry, he finds that he was a minister in *Norwich* (though now deceased) whom the chancellor suspended on some occasion around 10 o'clock in the morning and absolved before three o'clock in the afternoon of the same day, without his paying a penny fee for his dismissal. Mr. *William Bridge*, having some intention beforehand to leave *Norwich*, was excommunicated for not appearing at the visitation (in which he was presented for many dangerous doctrines), and so he immediately departed for *Holland*, as the chancellor wrote to this defendant. Mr. Warren was cited, although he had no license to preach in that diocese; neither had his orders yet been shown to anyone, nor had any complaint been brought to this defendant (who was then an inhabitant of that town and lived not far from that church, though the said Mr. Manning would take no notice of him) that he not only neglected all the orders of the church, but also the rules of the divine service, and had quoted many dangerous passages in the pulpit tending to the disparagement of the state and the disquiet of the people. He also says that preaching without a sufficient license has at all times been punishable and investigated within the Church of England.

Concerning Mr. Eades, this defendant does not remember that he ever heard of such a man until reports were recently brought to him of some very seditious sermons preached by him.

*[*The counsel are desired to consider and insist upon this: that the chancellor and the commissary inflicted all these previously mentioned censures, although this defendant was made acquainted with most of them through letters or meetings before they were done, and did consent to or advise them. For he could not doubt that they, being men of the law, could best judge what was law and right; and being sworn men (their oath is that they will, to the utmost of their understanding, deal uprightly and justly in their office without respect or favor—Canon 127, 10 James I) to act uprightly, and holding their positions for life, they could in no way be induced by him to do anything other than what he had always desired them to do.*

*However, for the honor of his position and out of zeal for the service of the church, it was necessary for him to maintain a correspondence of letters and consultations with them. This was especially important because of the annual account that had to be made to the King regarding the state of all affairs in the diocese, as the King had commanded; for this, he (living outside the diocese) could not have done except through that exchange of letters between himself and the officials.]*

Lastly, this defendant says that notwithstanding the non-residence of those six, for which they were deprived (as previously stated) and the long desertion of their cures, and the patient waiting both before and after their citation, their deprivation did not proceed until this defendant, in his account to the King through the Archbishop in December 1637, had given notice of their situation and had humbly prayed to be directed on what he should do. In answer to this, in the following January, he was told to see the King’s pleasure on record in the Archbishop’s office, from where he received a schedule as follows:

> “*My Lord of Norwich has been very careful of all your Majesty’s instructions. Of those who have stood under episcopal censure, or who fled to avoid censure, there are no more than three or four who have submitted themselves; yet his lordship has had patience (notwithstanding the peremptory citations sent out) to wait for them until now. But now he must proceed to deprivation, or suffer scorn and contempt to follow all his injunctions. Nevertheless, in this he humbly craves direction; and so do I, if it please your Majesty to give it.*”

To which the King had written in the margin of the schedule with his own hand:

*Let him proceed to deprivation.*

So this defendant, transmitting a copy of all this to the chancellor (as he conceived himself bound to do), the said chancellor, after a stay of two months longer, did proceed to their deprivation.

But this defendant humbly shows that in the aforesaid deprivations (and in all other censures of which he was made aware), he aimed at nothing except discharging his own duty and preserving the good order of the Church. As for any advantage to his own benefit, he was so far from admitting the least pretense of it that, although Mr. *Case*, parson of *Erpingham*, was no less at fault for nonconformity and desertion of his cure than some of the rest, this defendant rather overlooked some trickery between the said *Case* and the under-officers to avoid censure, lest it might be suspected that he aimed at his benefice, of which the Bishop of *Norwich* was the patron.

He also humbly conceives that it may well be taken as an argument of just and right proceedings against the previously named ministers that not one of them would ever appeal the sentence of the consistory, and thereby bring their cause to be discussed and judged in the *Archbishop’s Court*. From there, if they had found any grievance, there lay an appeal to the King, and so by delegated judges (assigned by the Lord Keeper), they might have obtained such relief as was due to them with much less trouble and damage.

To the fourteenth article, this defendant answers and denies that he unlawfully compelled the inhabitants of that diocese to raise the floors of the chancels, rail the communion tables, remove seats, and make other alterations at an expense of over £5,000, or that he harassed by presentments, citations, censures, journeys, and attendance at the courts those who did not obey.

For proof of this, first he humbly refers to what he has answered to the first, third, and fourth articles, and also in the eighth and thirteenth articles. He further believes that the churchwardens of some parishes (for certain private motives) might have been persuaded to spend money on these things, and that in other parishes they may have included in this account everything that was voluntarily spent by them for repairing and beautifying their churches in whatever other way.

As to the town of *Ipswich*, he further says that in a petition which they sent to the King, who was then at *Tudbury* (to which His Majesty gave an answer at *Woodstock*, when this defendant was not present in His Majesty’s attendance), the first point of it was a complaint against this defendant and the officers of the jurisdiction for putting the petitioners to expense by causing some chancels to be adorned and various pews to be removed or altered. But His Majesty was pleased to mark that particular item with a cross and then commanded the Master of the Requests to give the petitioners no other answer but this: that His Majesty would hear no more of that complaint, for nothing was done in that regard but what His Majesty expected to be done and well approved of. He also directed that the said petition should be delivered to this defendant, which was done at *Oxford* within two days; and so notice of the said answer was given to this defendant, both by Sir *Edward Powell* and also by the King himself in the hearing of the Archbishop.

And he humbly hopes that the chancellor and commissaries (for there are no officials belonging to the bishop) will be able to clear themselves from having used any unlawful courses or unjust harassments in these matters. <meta>This page continues Bishop Matthew Wren’s defense against the articles of impeachment. It moves from specific financial disputes regarding church repairs in Norwich to a broader theological and legal argument defining "innovation" versus "restoration."</meta>

<page-num>99</page-num>
# MATTHEW WREN, D. D.
<meta>catchword: But</meta>

The defendant, who played no part in this matter at all, was certainly neither the first mover nor the final agent in it. He therefore refers himself to such proofs as shall be truly brought regarding anything done by him, and will not refuse to pay all such charges as appear to have been unjustly placed upon them by him, provided that he may have the materials delivered to him safe and sound. He is also informed that *Thomas Dixon* and *Alexander Harrison*, churchwardens of *St. Edmund's* in *Norwich*, being required to provide a note of such charges as the parish incurred due to this defendant's visitation, returned only 13s. 4d. This was rejected, and they were sent back to bring a larger sum, with Alderman *Parrot* reproaching them and saying, "What, no more? Well, we perceive you would willingly have Popery come in again." The account for the years besides that of the visitation was taken and included in the information given to the honorable House of Commons; and he does not doubt that the same was done in many other places.

To the fifteenth article, this defendant answers and denies that he proposed any unlawful innovations or injunctions, or that anyone was harassed in their estates or consciences for not coming to the rail and kneeling before the table set altar-wise, or for not standing up during the Gospel. For further answer on this matter, he refers to what has already been answered in the 7th article.

And he further humbly conceives that restoring the forms and rites of the Church which were in use during the reign of *Queen Elizabeth*, and drawing the people to a proper obedience to those ordinances of the Church, should not now be justly called an innovation, but rather part of a reformation or renovation. This is because, at those times, the opposite practice was styled and reputed to be an innovation. For he finds this in the inquiry which the Bishop of *London* made in the year 1583: <note>Does your minister teach any doctrine of innovation to withdraw the people from due obedience to the ordinances of the Church? Article 6.</note> And again: <note>Does your minister in his ministration use the precise form and rites which are prescribed, without innovation or alteration of the same? Article 31.</note> Similarly, the Bishop of *Chichester* in the year 1600 inquired: <note>Are there any who preach any doctrine of innovation in your parish to withdraw the people from their due obedience, or are there any new presbyteries or private conventicles and schismatical dealings among you? Article 42.</note> King *James* also, in the conference at *Hampton Court*, termed those things an innovation which were then insisted upon against the orders of the Church [page 47]; and in his proclamation for the uniformity of common prayer, he says that he will not admit innovations in things once settled by mature deliberation, meaning the rites of the Church, in the 10th year of *James*.

Speaking, therefore, of the religion and ceremonies in the Church of *England*, since "new" and "old" are relative terms and are only used in relation to earlier or later things, he humbly conceives it necessary first to designate the time periods by which the state of our Church is to be bounded, and to which we intend to refer when we say (with the holy Fathers in Council): Τά ἀρχαῖα ἔθη Κρατείτω. — *Let the old usages prevail.* And he humbly conceives those times to be the blessed era of the Reformation [the 6th year of *Edward VI* and the 1st year of *Elizabeth*], along with the times immediately following. Therefore, whatever can be shown to have been in use in our Church then (though perhaps in some way since then discontinued), the taking up of those practices again cannot—except by mistake and very improperly—be termed an innovation, and has no crime at all in it; especially where the general rules of devotion, decency, and uniformity also guide us in matters of discretion and practice.

To the sixteenth article, this defendant answers and denies that ignorance, superstition, or profaneness were introduced by him. He humbly conceives that the contrary—namely, the means of knowledge, true religion, and holiness—were promoted and cherished by him in both action and true intention. He labored, as much as in him lay, to draw Christian people to the love and practice of the worship of God established here by law, and to an humble and awe-filled reverence for His divine majesty. He was careful that through the profitable method of diligent and faithful catechizing, those of a lower status should be brought to a better knowledge of God and to a true understanding of the grounds of the Christian religion.

He therefore denies that he suppressed prayer, which he endeavored so much to bring into holy estimation and use, or that he forbade sermons. He did not refuse to license anyone who desired to preach in an orderly way, and he was (for that very reason) inclined to consent to the removal of those obstinate non-residents. He feared that it might be objected against him that he had allowed several parishes to remain for so long neglected and deprived of the holy Word, the prayers, and the sacraments. For further proof of this, he also alleges that, whereas in the city of Norwich itself there are thirty-four churches and there used not to be more than three or four sermons at them all on Sunday mornings—because, under the pretense of going to the cathedral church, people of all ages and sexes were left to do what they would—this defendant had no rest in his mind until he convinced the Chancellor to order that in every church of the said city there should be a sermon (if possible) on Sunday mornings and catechizing in the afternoon.

He likewise says that to that part of the charge concerning the putting down of lectures, no answer can be expected unless the particular place or the men had been named, as well as when and by whom it was done. But he further says that at St. Edmund's Bury the clergy had discontinued a lecture on their own which they previously held collectively on Mondays. As soon as he had notice of this, he readily gave his consent and directions for resuming it again. He likewise ordered and confirmed the two single lectures there on Wednesdays and Fridays. At Bungay they also had a lecture; and at Ipswich they might have had one if they had desired anyone but the man whom this defendant could not allow, as he was suspended during the King's pleasure by sentence of the High Commission, and they would choose no one else. And there, into *New England*, of those who are named in this article, went *Francis Lawes*, a poor and lowly weaver; *John Dicks*, a poor joiner; *Nicholas Busby*, a poor weaver; *Michael Metcalf*, and *Nicholas* his son, a dornick weaver <note>A weaver of dornick, a type of checked or figured linen or wool cloth.</note> (he alone had some wealth), but he was called into question for some words against the King, and so slipped away. *John Durant* is supposed to be the same person as *John Berant*, a poor weaver who went into the *Low Countries*; and to that same place went *Richard Cook*, a draper newly established, who kept only one apprentice.

And this defendant denies that the departure into *Holland* of those who practiced the trades of wool manufacturing either began in the year 1636, at which time this defendant’s visitation of the Diocese of *Norwich* was held, or that it ended with the year 1637, at which time this defendant was transferred from that diocese. For they began to go to *Rotterdam* and *Arnhem* and other places there in the year 1633, and so also in 1638 they went there in great abundance. So that out of one port in that diocese in the year 1635, one hundred and forty-six persons left; and in 1638, one hundred and fifty persons; whereas out of the same port in the years 1636 and 1637, there went in total no more than one hundred persons. And out of another port in the same diocese, from Michaelmas <note>September 29</note> 1637 to the Annunciation <note>March 25</note> 1638, only one hundred and ten persons left; whereas in the next half-year (which was after this defendant had left the see), more than two hundred and thirty persons went.

This defendant therefore humbly believes that the chief cause of their departure was the small wages given to the poor workmen, by which the master-craftsmen grew rich but the workmen were kept very poor. And then, that occasioning the poor quality and bad manufacture of those goods, the *Dutch*, desirous to learn the trade for their own advantage as well as for the better production of the commodities, did for a time invite our people there by giving much higher wages for work than were given here; so that it was generally reported in *Norwich* that they could get 15 shillings in *Holland* for work that here yielded not 10 shillings. To this must also be added that in the year 1636, the danger of the plague in *London* stopped the weekly trade of fabrics and other commodities from *Norwich*, and thereby men stopped hiring as many workers as they had done before when the weekly exchange was open. And so that forced the poor to complain and to go seek a means of living abroad.

And as proof of this, he humbly offers that while frequent complaints of this matter were brought to the Council Board—that the trade was being carried into *Holland*, and many things were requested for the remedying of the same—yet

It was never even once mentioned, or in any way suggested to their Lordships, that any harsh treatment in ecclesiastical matters in that Diocese was the cause or the occasion for it. And this defendant hopes to prove that of the many hundreds who went to *Holland* in those times—they then taking their oaths before the King's officers and declaring the reason for their going—not one of them all ever mentioned any of those things which are claimed in this article; instead, very many of them answered that they went to work at their trades there, to increase their skill, and to find better means of living.

And indeed, why would they need to go there for any church proceedings here (had that been the true cause), when it would have been a much shorter and easier journey for poor workmen simply to have moved into some other diocese? And if any of the wealthier sort (such as those who employed a hundred workers) went away only for that reason, why did they not appeal instead? Seeing that they might have obtained an inhibition (for 7 or 8 shillings) which would have immediately halted the consistory court, no sentence of which was to be in force until—after fifteen days—the parties themselves confirmed it by their own default in not appealing. The poorer sort, therefore, went chiefly for profit and means of life; the wealthier sort might also be led away by that which was operative in any diocese, as in the Diocese of *Norwich* (excepting always that the *Norwich* Diocese had a better opportunity for sudden and easy shipping across the sea); and that was the utter dislike of all church government, and of the doctrine and discipline established here by law.

To the seventeenth article, this defendant answers and denies that, contrary to the duty of his office and the duty of a good subject, or to clear himself of blame, or to raise a bad opinion of the King in the hearts of his subjects, he ever declared that what he did was by his Majesty's command. But quite to the contrary, to testify to his own dutifulness, to encourage the obedience of his Majesty's good subjects, to settle peace in their minds, to show the legality and authority of those particular things which were in practice, and to reveal the evil and disloyal dispositions of some of those who have now been informers to the Honorable House of Commons, he felt bound in all duty that he should not refrain (when the occasion arose) from making the King's pleasure known to the rest of his Majesty's honest and faithful subjects in the following manner.

Returning to *Suffolk* from attending his Majesty in the year 1636, he was led to understand that although the answer the King gave (in this defendant's absence) to a petition from *Ipswich*—wherein they complained of the alteration of the seats in their chancels and of setting up the communion tables there, namely, that his Majesty would hear no more of any complaint of this kind and that the Bishop had done only his duty therein, as his Majesty expected from him, as is previously set forth in the answer to the fourteenth article of this charge—had been fully reported by the Masters of Requests to one *Peter Fisher* of *Ipswich*, who attended court regarding the said petition; yet he, conspiring with some other of the petitioners, had for many weeks concealed his Majesty's pleasure from all but a few of themselves, and had not made it known to their neighbors, whom it chiefly concerned. This defendant, therefore, held it fit to give notice of his Majesty's royal pleasure in this matter, and caused the petition itself, which the Master of Requests had delivered to this defendant at the King's command, to be produced in open court for the satisfaction and contentment of the good people, who had asked to be excused only until they might hear what answer the King would give to their said petition.

He further says, that a Petition having been likewise put up to his Majesty by some of *Norwich* complaining of the setting up of the Tables in the Chancels, and of reading the Communion Service there, and of some other Orders of the Church; and his Majesty being afterwards pleased not only to tell this Defendant of it, and how he had dismissed them accordingly as he had done those of *Ipswich*, but also to require this Defendant to be careful of his Duty in the Observation of the said Orders: he, as in Duty he ought, did share the same with the Chancellor, and with some others of *Norwich* who came to him; as not doubting, but that the King's supreme Authority in all things ecclesiastical, and the Knowledge of his good Pleasure in these Matters, would settle a right Opinion, and Conformity, and Peace in the Minds of all Men.

in reading the words without stop or interruption, and without danger of spilling the bread and wine, he did in Tower Church in *Ipswich*, in the year 1636, turn toward the west side of the table; but it was only while he repeated the previously mentioned Collect, in which he was to take the bread and wine, and at no other time.

And he humbly believes that although the Rubric says that the minister shall stand at the north side of the table, yet it is not meant to be interpreted as if he should never step away from it during the entire Communion time. For it is common to go before the table to read the Epistle and Gospel, and necessary to go from the table to the pulpit to preach, and with the basin to receive the offerings, if there are any, and with the bread and wine to distribute them to the communicants. Inasmuch, therefore, as he did stand at the north side all the while before he came to that Collect in which he was to take the bread and wine into his hands, and returned there as soon as that was done, he humbly believes it is a clear demonstration that he came to the west side only for the greater convenience of performing his office, and in no way out of any superstition, much less in any imitation of the *Romish* priests. For they place themselves there during all the service before and all after, with no less strictness than at the time of their consecrating the bread and wine.

But he denies that he ever used any elevating of the bread and wine, much less that he made any elevation so high that the bread and wine might be seen over his shoulders. Abundant testimony regarding this will be provided by many (*above all exception*) who were then present and well observed all actions and gestures, namely: Mr. *Lany*, Mr. *Keene*, Mr. *Norwich*, Mr. *Novell*, Mr. *Mapletoft*, and others. He therefore says that only in repeating the Words of Institution did he take the silver plate, in which the bread was, into his hand to break the bread and to say, *Take, eat, etc.* But then he never lifted his hand from the table whereon it rested; and he did no differently with the cup also. Whereas in the Popish church the custom is that the priest, after the consecration, elevating the bread and the chalice, does it so that it is not only seen over his shoulder, but holds it up over his head, meaning that he then sacrifices Christ's body, which he has transubstantiated there, and therefore elevates it for that purpose, so that the people beholding it may fall down and adore it. This defendant is ready, according to the decision used in such cases in the ancient Councils, to pronounce *Anathema* <note>A formal curse or excommunication.</note> to any superstitious or idolatrous usages or intentions ever held by him in that kind, and to profess that he faithfully and totally adheres to the Article of the Church of *England*. [That the Sacrament is not to be carried about, lifted up, or worshipped, *Article 28*.]

Regarding bowing at his arrival at or his departure from the Lord's table, whether the Lord's Supper is celebrated there or not, he humbly refers himself to that which he has answered regarding the sixth article of this charge. He adds this: that since the bread and wine are then upon the table, it cannot be otherwise than that the reverence which he then uses must be before them, or after they are set upon the said table. But he further says that as soon as he had ended the Collect of Consecration, his bowing low was a kneeling down at the table to receive the bread and wine himself. Now, because he always uses to kneel upon the floor during the holy action, and not upon any pesse <note>A footstool, hassock, or thick mat for kneeling.</note>, after he had taken the bread and was then to set the plate back upon the table so that he might likewise take the cup, he could not help but lift the said plate—not only as high as his shoulder, but as high as his head also—because while he continued kneeling in that way, his head was as low as the table, if not lower.

To the nineteenth Article, this Defendant answers and denies that he caused the Figure of Christ upon the Cross to be engraved upon his episcopal Seal, thereby the more to manifest his popish affection. And he says that he utterly denies all popish affections; and that the figure of Christ upon the Cross may be had without any popish affection; and that the said figure upon his seal did itself declare what affection it was to manifest. For there was this motto engraved with it [Εν ᾧ Κόσμος ἐμοὶ κἀγὼ τῷ Κόσμῳ.] being taken out of St. Paul, *Gal. vi. 14.* and being applied to the same purpose, and used with the same affection (be it humbly spoken) that St. Paul used there: *God forbid* (said St. Paul) *that I should rejoice, but in the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, whereby the World is crucified unto me, and I unto the World.* In a holy imitation of this, this Defendant bears various coats of arms (as is the custom) upon the said seal: namely, the arms of the See of *Norwich*, and the arms of the See of *Hereford*, and of the Deanery of *Windsor*, and of the Mastership of *Peter-house*, together with his own paternal coat of an ancient descent. He considered within himself that these were all emblems and badges only of worldly and temporal glories; and desiring that the world should have a right understanding of him, and to testify that he did in no way glory in anything of this transitory world, but humbly endeavored to wean himself from all temporal and vain rejoicings, he therefore caused such a small figure of Christ on the Cross to be set over all the said coats. By that he professed that as he was only to *preach Christ crucified*, 1 Cor. i. 21. *and that as he esteemed not to know anything but Jesus Christ, and him crucified*, 1 Cor. ii. 2. so much more, he had, and still would strive to take joy in none of these his honors and preferments, as they were human and worldly, but only would use them as if he had them not, and as if he were dead and crucified to them, and they to him; but that his whole study, and rest, and rejoicing, should be in the Cross of our Lord Jesus, and that unto it he would cause all his worldly estate (public and private) to stoop and do service.

This was all the affection which this Defendant intended to manifest by this; and he humbly conceives it was holy and truly Christian. For the expressing of this to the world, those coats of arms gave him a good opportunity; and for the assuring and impressing of so much into his own soul, he alluded to those words of the heavenly Spouse to his Church, *Pone me ut sigillum super cor tuum* <note>Place me as a seal upon your heart</note>, Cant. viii. 6. Therefore he (who never had nor used a crucifix anywhere else in the world) thought it no harm at all, nor in any way popish in him, to use it upon his seal.

And he humbly prays that it may be well considered how it can rightly be suspected that he had any popish affection in that, or in himself at all; whereas during the Assizes for the county, following soon after his primary visitation in *Suffolk*, he caused the presentments of the said county (being about five hundred) to be sent to him from *Norwich*. Having himself perused them all and extracted the names of all such as, by the oaths of the churchwardens and other sworn men, had been presented for popish recusants, he caused the same to be clearly written out, alphabetically, on parchment, comprising the Christian names and surnames of two hundred persons or thereabouts, and then affixed to it this very seal named before, and so sent the same to the Lord Chief Justice, *sedente curiâ* <note>while the court was in session</note>, at the Assizes at St. *Edmund’s-bury*. As this was a voluntary act of his, never used before by any other Bishop, so it then testified under that seal his true zeal and care for the religion established here in England; and so he hopes it may rightly be alleged now to show that the figure of Christ upon the Cross in the seal—

To the twentieth Article, this Defendant answers and denies that he employed such men as his commissioners, rural deans, and household chaplains whom he knew to be inclined toward innovative courses and popish superstition, or to be erroneous and unsound in practice and judgment.
And he further says that he believes there was not a visitation, whether metropolitan or diocesan, held in that diocese or in any other of this province within the memory of man, conducted by commissioners more numerous or more worthy in quality or reputation than those persons were whom he employed for his primary visitation, namely: the Chancellor of *Norwich*, the Dean of *Norwich*, Dr. *Jones*, Dr. *Goad*, Dr. *Warren*, Dr. *Franklin*, Dr. *Paule*, Dr. *Eden*, Mr. *Britten*, Mr. *Nouell*, and Mr. *Mapletoft*.

Now, the choice of the men employed was this: a few of them this Defendant himself knew; others, upon some inquiry, had been recommended to him as grave, judicious, and orderly men; and others of them he found had long before been made surrogates under the seal of the Chancellor to execute his office for him. To the twenty-first Article, this Defendant answers and denies that he very much oppressed various patrons of churches, unless it is meant by his constant care to discover simoniacal compacts, if there were any; for he claimed nothing among them but the right of institution.

He also admitted the said *John Duncon* to the rectory of *Sutton* upon the presentation of His Majesty the King; but because he suspected the validity of the title, he caused him to refrain from his induction and, after further discussion, to surrender his institution.

Mr. *Geast* was also instituted by him to the rectory of *Garboldsham*, but it was following a judgment against another person who had intruded.

He instituted no other of his chaplains, nor any other clerks when any controversy arose, except—as nearly as he could judge upon hearing counsel—those with the strongest title. Thus, he believes that of all the admissions he granted while he was Bishop there, although very many of them were litigious, such was his care to admit according to the truest right that not six of them in total were afterwards evicted by law.

He also denies that, against his priestly word given, *in verbo sacerdotis*, he put *Mr. Rivett* (though he was the true and right patron) to an expensive lawsuit to evict the incumbent. For proof of this, he refers himself to the records in Chancery, where the said *Rivett* filed a bill against this defendant with the said false and scandalous imputation of breaking his priestly word; the court first caused the said words to be expunged and erased out of the bill, and afterward, upon a demurrer, dismissed the bill itself as well.

*Mr. Chute* was counsel for this defendant in it.

The case was this. To the parsonage of *Beldeston*, *Mr. William Rivett* presented *Jo. Ashley*, clerk; before admittance was given to him, *George Anton* entered a caveat for his interest, and then presented *John Cornelius*, clerk. Upon a day appointed, the parties appeared before this defendant, and the case was pleaded at length by *Mr. Fountain* for *Mr. Rivett*, and by *Mr. Hoburn* for *Mr. Anton*. The rectory proved to be appendant to the manor, and the competing patrons were then in a lawsuit about the said manor. *Rivett* pleaded a lease of 100 years. *Anton* produced a defeasance upon condition of paying £3000, which he pleaded was all paid to within £140. Many other exceptions were alleged by *Mr. Fountain*, but so fully answered by *Mr. Hoburn* that (in this defendant's understanding) the true right seemed to be in *Anton*. So they rose, the Bishop saying that now he had heard what could be said by their counsel, he would consider it, and (if necessary) advise with his own counsel about it; for he claimed nothing but the right of institution.

They did not request any writ, *de jure patronatûs*; nor did either of them make it appear who presented last; but both parties promised that in the meantime they would wait and not bring any writ of *ne admittas*. When the company had departed, this defendant showed to *Mr. Fountain* and *Mr. Rivett's* brother the reason why *Rivett's* clerk was not admitted at first, before *Anton* came in for his right: namely, that he had received three certificates from *Mr. Stubbin*, a minister in *Suffolk*, charging *Mr. Ashley* with nonconformity and various other misdemeanors, besides many complaints formerly made against him at the primary visitation. When *Mr. Fountain* had read all of these, he declared that he would write to *Mr. Rivett* and cause him to change his clerk, if the Bishop would not proceed in the meantime. To whom this defendant replied, "I do not know how long you may stay; but you know what I said a while ago to you both, and you may be assured upon my word that notice shall be given to you before I do anything." He made no other promise, nor used any other words.

The next day, being informed that (contrary to their promise) they were bringing a writ of *ne admittas* against *Cornelius*, this defendant sent to *Westminster Hall* to tell *Mr. Fountain* about it, and to show that he took it so poorly that he now held himself free from any kind of promise. He said he would admit *Anton's* clerk, to whom the right (as he conceived) belonged, unless the said *Mr. Fountain* would take it upon himself to guarantee that no writ of *ne admittas* should be brought; but if he would promise that, then this defendant would still wait and have the cause examined again. The answer was brought that *Mr. Fountain* disavowed knowledge of any such intention to bring it, but yet, being urged, he plainly refused to guarantee that no writ would be brought; whereupon *Anton's* clerk was admitted.

As for the things in lawsuit, the said *Cornelius* and *Ashley* came to a voluntary settlement regarding all demands; and so *Cornelius* allowed a judgment to pass, and *Ashley* received the benefice. After examination and calculation, finding that the due and lawful payments would amount to about £570—as appears by the account written below—and not counting the uncertain fees for absences, proxies, suspensions, dismissals, etc., which could not be less than £100, this defendant, willing to save the labor of sending his own collectors as well as to show that courtesy to the Registers, was content to accept £470 from them, so leaving to them above £200 for the costs and their own labor in the same.

He also further says that some of his predecessors before him had a higher settlement than that which he took, and so did his successor by a great deal. He humbly asks leave to say that it is not the size of such a sum, but only the size of the diocese that should be considered here; in comparison, the lawful profits of the visitation in smaller dioceses are far greater than in this. For, considering first that the visitation in *Norwich* Diocese is held only once in seven years, and in other dioceses twice in six years, the said Diocese of *Norwich* is ten times as large as the Diocese of *Ely* in its number of parishes and titles; and yet the profits of every visitation at *Ely* are worth more than £60. And it is four times larger than *Hereford* Diocese, and yet the profits of a triennial visitation there are honestly worth £150.

He therefore denies that his Books of Articles were ever intended for the better benefit of the Register, or other farmer at *Norwich*, as he had none but the Register, who was to attend the Visitation, because the said book was prepared long before and was essentially the same as the one he used in the Diocese of *Hereford*, which was in no way complained about there.

And regarding the number of the articles in the said book, he humbly conceives that those who informed the honorable House of Commons had, of all people, the least reason to find fault with this Defendant; for, by giving them a greater scope, he also gave them more advantage in picking quarrels against him. But he further says that by being truly careful to follow in the steps of his ancestors, and to that end, laying before him the Visitation Articles of many godly and worthy Prelates—such as Bishops *Coxe*, *Cooper*, *Grindal*, *Elmer*, *Watson*, *Bancroft*, *Bilson*, *Mountague*, *Abbot*, *Andrewes*, *Overall*, *White*, and several others—and gathering from them what he found in each for the compiling of his own book, it resulted in scarcely an article being included that he did not borrow from some others; thus, the number of his articles was somewhat increased above others. And yet, he finds that the Bishop of *London* in the third year of King *James* had above one hundred articles in his book, at which time there was, perhaps, much less need of such inquiries than now. So also did the Archdeacon of *Middlesex* in the year 1620, and the Bishop of *London* in the year 1621 had above one hundred and twenty articles. And in the year 1628, he had above one hundred and thirty, and no quarrel was ever made at any of these. A second occasion for the length arose by dividing his book (as others had done, and as was best for organization) into chapters, under various heads and titles; for, by this, it happened that the same things, in several respects, were set down in this book of his and inquired about more than once, as will easily appear by comparing the second, fourth, sixth, and seventh chapters, and so by that, the number of articles appeared to increase. Thirdly, he was willing to make more articles and questions out of them, thereby to better provide for the serenity of men's consciences and the securing of men's minds; considering well that the plain country people are not as able by themselves to discern what particulars are comprised and intended under general questions; therefore, so they might be safe and sure in their own understandings and without fear of mistake, he divided the same into more particulars; as appears in the chapter concerning Matrimony, where that is distributed into ten articles, which many others have comprised in two or three.

He further says that it made him more diligent in his inquiry because he knew that he was not to visit there again until seven years later; whereas other bishops visit every third year. But he was enjoined to give the King an account of the state of the diocese every year, through the Metropolitan, and that also necessarily made him more careful to be fully informed at first, according to the wise man's rule, *Vidisti hominem diligentem in opere suo; ipse stabit coram regibus*, Prov. xxii. 29 <note>"Do you see a man diligent in his work? He shall stand before kings."</note>.

And how could he have it be arbitrary and at his own pleasure if he brought it into a court that could regulate both him and them?

But this he says: that he considered how necessary a parish clerk was for the performance of the Church's divine service—besides various other duties of that position or office—to make audible responses in all those parts of the divine service as required by the rule of the Book of Common Prayer, and so to lead the humble and ignorant people, and in a way to encourage and instruct them to join in making those responses with him as the Book requires. Finding also that not only the canons of the Church required having a clerk in every parish, but also the rubrics of the liturgy assumed, when they were made, that there was at least one clerk in every parish (namely: the *rubric of Matrimony* after hands are joined; *ibid.*, the *rubric for going to the Table*; the *rubric for the Order of Burial*, first and second; and the *rubric of the Commination before the 51st Psalm*), this Defendant therefore was much grieved to see that in many places of that diocese, they neither had nor cared to have a clerk. Thereupon, by his own frequent exhortations and by recommending the matter to the chancellor, he labored to correct this failure. Therefore, regarding such parishes where men of sufficient abilities were available for that service, but the parishioners would allow only very meager wages or none at all, and would not pay any rates which the churchwardens set for the wages of a clerk, it may well be that he said he would, in that case, implore the aid of the King’s commissioners for ecclesiastical causes <note>The High Commission court</note>, so that they might take such order in the matter as the said court thought fitting.

Regarding the towns named in the Articles, this Defendant remembers nothing at all concerning *Congham*. If the honorable House of Commons had understood with how much violence and injustice these outcries have been raised, as this Defendant humbly believes, he is confident that this impeachment would not have been brought against him. But since they do not have the power to conduct examinations under oath, he was forced to refer his entire defense to the cognizance of the noble peers of this House.

Had there been any corruption, extortion, simony, or bribery—any advantage or gain to this Defendant by anything that was done—he would consider himself worthy of such a serious impeachment. But since malice itself has not dared to pretend any pretense of that, and since he gained nothing but labor for his pains and hatred for his good will, he humbly believes that he may in justice be excused if, upon a severe examination, any error is thought to have occurred in that which was honestly, religiously, and dutifully intended by him.

Therefore, since those Articles are now charged against him criminally and by way of public impeachment, he humbly prays that it may be stated which law or statute each and every one of these particular offenses is supposed to have violated, so that he may have the common benefit of the law and justice in pleading his humble and lawful defense.

He also further humbly craves the noble favor and justice of this honorable House, so that—to avoid being caught by surprise regarding his defense—he may, by order of this House, be allowed to see all letters, papers, records, and other writings that happen to be alleged as evidence against him, with a convenient amount of time for his learned counsel to review them. He also asks that it be ordered for him to review all records, registry books, and other notes and writings that his counsel thinks necessary for his modest, humble, and just defense against these impeachments.

## A SERMON by Bishop WREN.
---
->PROV. xxiv. 21.<-
->*Fear God my Son, and the King.*<-

**NOLI** æmulari <note>Do not be envious</note>, *Do not fret because of the ungodly, nor be envious of the evil-doer,* says *King David* the father, *Psalm* xxxvii. 1. *And do not let your heart be envious of the evil-doer,* says *King Solomon* the son, *Prov.* xxiii. 17. Why, you will say the son learned it from his father; or it was a good and a godly lesson, and it is no wonder then if both of the wise kings included it among their holy advice.

Yes, but *do not be envious of the evil-doer,* says *King Solomon* again at the fourth verse of this chapter. What, again! And so soon, with so few verses between? Surely then there is some extraordinary importance in it; it is not only one of his good counsels, but it is a special one—one that he would have heeded and learned before many, and above any other.

It would seem so indeed, for *noli æmulari* <note>do not be envious</note>, *Do not fret because of the ungodly, nor be envious of the evil-doer,* he says once more in the verses just before my text. For fear it should not make as deep an impression on men's minds as was fitting, he presents it a third time, as if loath to leave it until it is thoroughly settled and fastened in their hearts; but *Tertia jam vice* <note>now for the third time</note>, 2 *Cor.* xiii. 1. says the Apostle, *firmum erit omne verbum* <note>every word shall be established</note>; the admonition thrice repeated will make it sure and immovable.

Now, in the name of God, who is that evil-doer of whom he warns us so often? Or what is it the wise man would have us do to show that we are not envious of him? Why, the Spirit has set that down too, and repeatedly; in the preceding chapter, verse 17, it is: *Do not let your heart be envious of the evil-doer, but let it always be in the fear of the Lord; Timor domini* <note>the fear of the Lord</note>, that is the general rule for it. But lest that might prove not specific enough, he says it over again, more particularly here in my text: *Do not be envious of the evil-doer, but fear God, my son, and the king.* And then that is enough; *Timor Dei & Regis* <note>fear of God and the King</note>. When he had said that, there was likely no need for more instruction. The distinct performance of these two duties, and the strict avoidance of those who do not perform them—of presumptuous and reckless sinners, and of contemptuous and lawless subjects—a *noli æmulari* <note>do not be envious</note> for both of these, not to associate or align ourselves with them; neither with those who do not fear God, nor with those who pretend, forsooth, to fear God but yet do not fear the king. This is the very last and greatest lesson of all, the one which *Solomon*, it seems, in his wisdom chose to close his own book of *Proverbs* with.

For, although he indeed spoke three thousand proverbs in total (1 *Kings* iv. 32) and this text now makes up no more than seven hundred, yet as it appears both by the verse after my text ("these things also belong to the wise") and by the first verse of the following chapter ("these are also proverbs of Solomon, which Hezekiah’s men copied out"), it is more than probable that this book of Proverbs went no further than this: to *fear God and the king*, and then he was finished. All that now follows from my text to the end of the book were but fragments collected out of his other works—gatherings and gleanings which other men afterwards brought together and, when they had them, added them to this book. But with this he himself ended it at first, as the very sum, crown, and conclusion of all: *Time Deum, fili mi, & regem; fear God my son, and the king.*

He argues that this dual obedience is the true conclusion of the original Book of Proverbs and warns against associating with those who disregard either divine or royal authority.</summary>
