<meta>This page continues Bishop Matthew Wren’s sermon on Proverbs 24:21, transitioning from the introduction to an analysis of the first part of the verse: "Fear God."</meta>

<page-num>116</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF</header>
<meta>catchword: of</meta>

Now the words, you see, are in total scarcely six; yet at once they present us with three chief persons and three great relations. The persons are no less than God, the Lord of all; God’s deputy, the King; and all who call God Father, all the people. The relations are first *Personae* <note>persons</note>, the reference in which all these persons stand to one another: God to the King and people, the King to the people and God, and the people to God and the King. Secondly, *Operae* <note>works or duties</note>, what must be done as a duty from the people to both: *Timere* <note>to fear</note>, they are to fear them. Lastly, *Causae* <note>causes</note>, why it must be done; yes, and *Modi* <note>manners</note> too, how it must be done—*quia filii* <note>because they are sons</note> and *quâ filii* <note>as sons</note>—because they are sons, and as sons, fear them therefore; fear them in that manner and in that order too, as sons to both God and the King. Yet as sons first to God and then to the King: all these are particularly encircled within this narrow compass: *Fear God, my Son, and the King*.

Of which, so that I may speak in a way that God’s people may learn to fear God and the King rightly, I humbly beseech you that we may here address ourselves to God—that holy, blessed, and glorious Trinity, *etc.*

->*Fear God, my Son, and the King.*<-

You see what first meets us at the very door of the text; and there our beginning must be, at *Timere* <note>to fear</note>, at the duty of fear, and in that, at *Dei* <note>of God</note> before *Regis* <note>of the King</note>, at the fear of the Lord first; for that is the best beginning there can be.
To begin with God is natural: Εϰ Διος ἀρχώμεθα <note>Let us begin with Zeus</note>, says one of their poets, and *a Jove principium* <note>from Jove is the beginning</note>, says another. But the fear of God belongs to a wisdom above nature: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom*, says the Psalmist, *Psalm 111:10*; and as it begins, so it continues: *it is the increase of wisdom also*, says Solomon, *Proverbs 15:33*. Yes, it is the very end of all, the sum of all that can be said or done: *Ecclesiastes 12:13, Let us hear the end of everything: fear God, for this is the whole duty of man. Hoc est totum hominis* <note>This is the whole of man</note>; every man must do this, or else he does nothing; and no man needs to do more than this: it will be more than enough for him if he truly fears God.

## *Timor Dei* <note>The Fear of God</note>.

Why else does the Spirit so often tell us to fear God, rather than any other Christian duty? *My son, love God*, or *my son, obey God*, or *my son, trust in God*; all these would have been holy and good charges, but none of them all would have been as significant. However, *my son, fear God* is a precept and a promise of them all; for fear is a universal duty that runs through all other duties and keeps them in tune. It is God’s *praepositus* <note>overseer or provost</note> in the school of graces; it ensures that none of them are out of order or in any way faulty.
It makes us look well to our ear, for fear we should hear unprofitably; to our eye, for fear we should glance irreverently; to our love, for fear anything should slip from us which God may take as unkind or unloving; to our obedience, for fear we grow careless or presumptuous; to our faith, for fear we become doubting or desperate; to our joy, for fear it should be immoderate; to our grief, for fear it be unjustifiable; to our devotion, for fear it be hypocritical; to our religion, for fear it be superstitious; to our whole life, for fear it be licentious. For fear is like the *Inquisitor Major* <note>chief inspector or inquisitor</note> over all the rest; when it is right, all other offices are right; all is well, if God is but rightly feared.
Let it be no wonder, then, that the Prophet attributes fear to Christ himself, and that at the end of various other virtues, as a sure guide and director of

of them all, the *Spirit of the Lord upon him*, says he, *Isaiah 11:2.* But what Spirit? *The Spirit of Wisdom, and of Understanding; the Spirit of Counsel and of Strength; the Spirit of Knowledge, and of the Fear of the Lord:* without that indeed the rest (as great as they are) would be little or nothing; and concerning that, therefore, the next verse adds yet further, *Et odorabitur timorem Domini*; besides his having the Spirit of Fear, he *shall also hunt and seek after it above all the rest*; indeed, *odorabitur*, it shall be the very *breath of his nostrils, the life and soul of all other gifts in him, the fear of the Lord.*

And to this suits well that excellent meditation that *Irenæus* has about it. “Such things (says he) as were so strictly charged upon our forefathers in the old Law, as merely slavish and servile, all those indeed the liberty of the Gospel pared off at once: but then natural things, and such as comply with ingenuity and freedom (as the knowing of God, the loving of him, the following of his Word, and the subduing of our own lusts) these were to be expanded by the Gospel, and not dissolved; so far from abolition, that they received a far greater increase. And from this it comes (says he) that our fear of God (that is what he principally chooses to insist upon) has grown much more now than ever the Law could expect it: and why? Because it is natural (says he) that sons should fear more than servants; the very liberty of sons being as a lodestone to allure, and as a whetstone to increase, and as a touchstone to try their love; and their inbred affection setting such an edge on the reverence and fear which they bear him, as no slavery of the Law could ever achieve.”

<margin>Sermon on the Holy Lights.</margin>
That *we have not then, since Christ, received the spirit of bondage to fear anymore*, St. Paul says correctly in *Romans 8:15*, because *such fear as that* (the fear that was of old) *carries torment*, 1 *John* 4; it only vexed and afflicted those who had it. But yet by the blessing of the Gospel the fear of the Lord is highly improved for us; for it is the Spirit of Adoption now, and only combines with joy and pleasure, *taking delight rather than being burdened*, says Pantaleon; it is such a reverent and free disposition in us toward God our Father, that though we were sure he should never know of our offense, or could possibly say to us, "I know it, and it offends me, but yet I will not punish it," even then we would strive the more against it, as being loath to displease so good a Father, and having more care not to go astray than not to smart for it, and performing duty not for fear of suffering vengeance, but for fear of neglecting that duty, and of wronging so much love as he and we are mutually engaged in.

And now by this I know (says St. *Hilary*, on *Psalm 127*) what King *David* meant when he called the faithful to school with him, *Come, my children, and listen to me, and I will teach you the fear of the Lord, Psalm 34:11.* For what need is there for that (says he) if there were nothing else to it? Who teaches the lamb to fear the wolf? Or who reads lessons against the kite to the chickens? But the fear of the Lord comes by holy rule and instruction; it is not what nature trembles at, but what grace directs us to; and it is not perfectly possessed except from the lessons of love—such love as obliges us to beware of all offending.

Now the Psalmist indeed does not set it down there; but if any profess they have come to learn it, I dare close up this point with an answer to that other question of his, *quis est vir? Psalm 25.* *Who is the man who fears the Lord?* For a man may soon know him now, or at least he may easily know whether he himself is that man: if he finds in his soul so pure and devoted an affection to God his Father, that his joy is only to please him, and his study is to avoid offending him, his whole contentment is that God loves him, and he rests himself securely upon the favor that God has for him. *Hic vir hic est*—this man may be confident that he is a good student, and that he has thoroughly learned the fear of the Lord.

<summary>Wren defines the "fear of the Lord" not as a tormenting or slavish terror, but as a "Spirit of Adoption" and a learned discipline rooted in love. Drawing on Irenæus and King David, he argues that a true believer obeys God out of a desire to please a loving Father rather than a fear of punishment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Bishop Matthew Wren’s sermon on the fear of God, moving from the theoretical nature of fear to the necessity of its outward, practical expression in the life of a believer.</meta>

<page-num>118</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

But yet this is not enough, even for the *Fear God* <note>Latin: *Time Deum*</note> here in my text: that there is such a thing as fear; and that it is now in a more liberal and son-like condition than when *Solomon* spoke of it; and that the mind of man may be, and ought to be entirely affected with it; and that God alone must be the object of it. In speculation indeed it comes to no more; the *Fear of the Lord* <note>Latin: *Timor Domini*</note> is only this, and these particulars make up the full theory of the fear of the Lord.

But yet there goes something more to the perfect duty of it. For this *Fear God*, as a present and particular precept, aims also at the practicing of it; it implies the action as well as the mind, all actual and outward expressions of it, besides the inward and habitual affection.

->*The Expression of Fear.*<- <note>Latin: *Expressio Timoris.*</note>

So that is the next thing which we must look at here. If a man’s spirit is right in the fear of God, and the right spirit of God’s fear is upon him, what demonstration he must also make of the same, and how it must be acted, so that it may appear God is thus feared.

For *but you have prepared a body for me*, <note>Latin: *corpus autem aptasti mihi*</note> if ever you notice it, you know it is not omitted by our Savior himself, that God having ordained him a body, in that body he was to perform his will. *Heb. 10:9.* And it is much more so with us; we being bodies also, and not only spirits, the spirit alone will not suffice us. It is not enough that our minds and affections are inwardly endowed with it, but we must also make such expressions so that the performance of the duty may be witnessed. The duty we acknowledge is that we do fear God; but by that which is to be read by our outward behavior, neither God nor man will bear us witness that we fear him.

Neither God nor man, I say. For expressions, I shall show you, there are of both kinds, both to God and to man. To man, so that he may know it, and (when need arises) acknowledge it, and glorify God for it, or benefit himself by it; to God only, that he may be pleased to acknowledge it, though he knew it not long before—for he knows what is in man better than man himself. And for this reason it is brought in with a *Now* to *Abraham* (that father not of the faithful alone, but of the fearful too, for he is the first who is ever said to fear the Lord) *Gen. 22:12. Now I know that you fear God.* <note>Latin: *Nunc cognovi quod timeas.*</note> What? Not until now, Lord? Was *Abraham’s* mind unknown to you before? Could not God tell long ago whether *Abraham* feared him? Yes; as *St. Peter* answered Christ’s third question, whether he loved him, with *Lord you know all things; you know that I love you:* and yet Christ the third time said to him, *Feed my sheep, John 21.* As if to say, never be sorry, *Simon*, that I ask you so often, and never doubt but I perfectly know you; but I will not acknowledge it until you express it this way. For however God requires truth in the inward parts, yet the inward parts alone are not all he requires; he will not acknowledge that he is loved unless that love appears outwardly; and we must make an expression of our fear, or else he will not acknowledge that we fear him.

->*To God Himself.*<- <note>Latin: *Ipsi Deo.*</note>

Now what expression of it can we make to God? *Abraham’s* case, mentioned before, shows us that upon special commands there may be special ways of it, even to the sacrificing of an only son, if God so requires. But the ordinary way that lies open for all men, the very word itself here will show us, that we must express our fear to God by acts of religion; for so the word fear ordinarily implies in Scripture.

<summary>Wren argues that the fear of God must transition from an internal sentiment to an outward practice. Using the examples of Abraham and St. Peter, he explains that God requires external acts of religion and obedience as a witness of one's internal devotion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Bishop Matthew Wren’s discourse on the fear of God, moving from the internal requirement of fear to the biblical and etymological evidence that links "fear" directly with the physical and ritual acts of "worship."</meta>

<page-num>119</page-num>
<header>MATTHEW WREN, D. D.</header>

When Moses had at large described the whole duty of God’s worship, his conclusion is, *And now Israel, what does the Lord require of you, but to fear him*, Deut. x. 12. That special command which God sent against worshipping strange gods was, *Fear not the gods of the land where you dwell*, Judges vi. 10. And the complaint which the prophet makes of *Israel*, *That the fear wherewith they feared God, was in precepts of men’s teaching*, Isaiah xxix. 13. By Christ himself, it is expounded as corrupting God’s worship, *Mat.* xv. 9. *In vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the precepts of men.*

And in this sense I can tell what to make of it, that when the articles were to be sworn to between the two great princes, *Laban* and *Jacob*—how *Jacob* should treat *Laban*’s daughters whom he had as wives, and how *Laban* should keep a faithful league with *Jacob*—*Laban* indeed swore by his idols, but *Jacob* swore a strong oath, *per timorem patris Isaac* <note>Latin: by the fear of his father Isaac</note>, by the fear of his father Isaac, Gen. xxxi. What was that? Why, *Laban* swore according to his religion, and *Jacob* according to his, by the worth and truth thereof, and by that Deity whom his father and he feared, namely, the God of Heaven, whom they worshipped.

<margin>Phavorinus.</margin>
And with a reference to this also, we must take what is recorded in Holy Writ of religious *Obadiah*, holy *Job*, devout *Cornelius*, and various others—always how they feared God. For as it appears by the wise man, *Eccles.* i. 30. θεοσέβεια <note>Greek: godliness/piety</note>, and θεοῦ φόβος <note>Greek: fear of God</note>, the fear of God and the worship of God, are all one in the language of the Spirit; and the grammarians themselves have noted it so, that Λατρεία <note>Greek: Latreia; divine service/worship</note>, the most peculiar word for worship (coming from Λα as an intensive and Τρεῖν), in its nature imports nothing else but an ancient fear; so that these two will always go together, and where there is any true fearing of God, there will be withal due worshipping of him.

And does not King *David* himself lead to this, in plain terms explaining his own mind? *But as for me*, says he, *I will come into your house, Psal.* v. 7. His meaning is, *I will come and worship you*; for that was all the coming into God’s house in those days; when they came, they came to worship, and worship God they did. Whenever they came there, they were neither too holy nor too stately, neither too fine nor too foolish to cast themselves down when they came into God’s presence. But to make it certain, he goes on in the next words there, *And in your fear will I worship in your holy temple*, he says; there we have them both expressly, not worship put alone, nor fear alone put for worship, though either would have been enough: "I will worship you," or "I will show my fear of you in your temple," but both together: "when I am there, in your fear will I worship." That is, I will adore you with such expressions of humility and reverence as by right belong to a Creator from his creature.

And how fully then does this meet with the widespread profanation of our times, that will now weave a distinction between this fear and perfect worship, between a religion and a due devotion, between holiness and holiness? Plenty of holiness, indeed, in heart and in mind; religion in the belly and the brain; oh, we are so full of that, we are ready to burst with it! It runs out many times at our mouths with "stand further off, I am holier than you." Yes, and we are "good men," you must know, and "exceedingly godly," such as fear God and hear his word duly. That is true; we have a great deal of religion in our ears too; but yet higher or lower, we have none—none upon our heads for a due reverence before him, none in our knees to bow at his blessed name, none for our bodies to cast them down and worship.

He criticizes contemporary believers who claim inward holiness but refuse to show outward humility or bodily devotion in God's presence.</summary>

<header>THE LIFE OF AM</header>

Especially not in His house, in the most sacred presence of our God; no, the less fuss there, the better, the less superstition. Just come in confidently, and without any more stir, sit down and keep your hat on, and listen—and who dares say that we do not fear God? Whatever is more than this, regarding adoration or any "beauty of holiness," let King *David* say what he will of it, yet it is but δεισιδαιμονία <note>Greek: deisidaimonia; a word often translated as superstition or an excessive, misplaced fear of the divine</note>, a superstitious over-fearing of God. For where does He require, many of us ask, any of these expressions and external actions in His worship?

But to these unsavory fancies, the prophet *Malachi* may be allowed to reply; many passages of his first chapter, *mutatis mutandis* <note>Latin: with the necessary changes having been made</note>, fit these times as well as they did those for which they were written. And they are not at all distant from my text either, for they are all about expressions of fear in the service of God; at the sixth verse: *If I be a father, where is my honor? And if I be a master, where is my fear? says God to you who despise my name.*

But they wondered why He should complain; they were sure they feared Him and honored Him as they should, and it may well be they meant as we do—within our hearts, forsooth! Therefore they reply again: *Despise! How have we despised you?* (Verse 7). God tells them: in that you say, *the table of the Lord is not to be regarded.* There is one specific instance for them of the lack of fear and honor. And are there not some among us who say the same? The table of the Lord, the house of the Lord, and the presence of the Lord—would you know how some of us regard them, or what distinction we make between them and any other places? A great deal less, I am sure, than some others. For the King’s presence, and the places where our superiors are, receive a great deal more reverence and respect from us; and we ourselves expect a great deal more in the presence of our inferiors.

And yet that is God’s express argument against us there—unless we nowadays are able to teach God better logic. *Go and do the same to your prince now, and see if he will be pleased with you, says God* (Verse 8). Do not show respect when you enter his presence; beg nothing of him on your knee; do not bow down in honor of him; but be "Jack Fellow" <note>An old expression meaning to act with over-familiarity or as an equal to one's superior</note>, sit still, or keep your hat on when he has anything to do with you, and will he accept you? *And yet I am the greatest King of all, says the Lord of Hosts, in that same chapter.*

But at this we sniff and cry, *Ecce labor!* <note>Latin: Behold, what a labor! or Look, what a lot of work!</note> Oh, here is a fuss indeed for uncovering the head, and standing, and kneeling, and bowing. But what reason is there that we should be put to so much inconvenience and weariness in serving God, who—as He Himself is a spirit—requires only to be worshipped in spirit and truth, and He knows our hearts well enough? And was not that the very objection of the *Jews* then also? *But you have said, "It is a weariness," Ecce labor, and you have sniffed at it, says the Lord of Hosts* (Verse 13). And then, what is the conclusion? *Therefore my name is and shall be fearsome among the heathen, He says in the 14th verse.* God upbraids and threatens them with the heathen, their neighbors, whose idolatrous religion expressed more fear of a God than theirs did. We may be just as well upbraided and threatened too by the erroneous religions that neighbor us; for they are far more careful to show the holy signs of fear than we are. And by that, to speak truly, they now stand. The opinion, affection, and devotion of the people—I speak from some experience—in liking them and boasting of ours, is carried away by nothing so much as by outward worship and reverence.

I would only wrong our nation of old, when they first became *English*, if I did not make this a note of the excellent spirit which then possessed them: that as they lost almost all words of their own language to signify this passion of the mind which we mean by "fear," they borrowed none from other languages, except only this word "fear," and that they brought

derived from the Latin, *Vereri*, to show that at first their noble affections knew no fear but the fear of God—filial and reverential fear alone, such as God himself (we see) would have his worship performed by, and our religion expressed by.

And if we ever come to lose that fear in our religion, we shall soon come to lose religion and everything else, however much we soothe ourselves; for that is the way to hold even the right religion as well. St. Paul says flatly in Hebrews 12:28: *Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom* (he means the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as we have received no other kingdom), *let us hold the grace fast.* True; that is good advice: but how shall we do that? How shall we hold it? It follows: *In serving him acceptably to his mind;* and how is that? *With reverence* (says he) *and holy fear.*

And whoever thinks himself wiser than this, let him go try it with David, who does not think him so. *For holy and reverend is God’s name*, says he; and then such a fear as this—one which performs a holy reverence to him and to his blessed name—that is *the fear of the Lord, and the beginning of wisdom* (Psalm 111:10). *And a good understanding have all they that do thereafter:* they alone understand rightly what religion and holiness and the true fear of the Lord is; those who, without any hypocrisy, have it truly within their hearts and, without any profane contempt, also express it duly in the outward worship of him.

->To men in general.<-

And in this way, we make the expression of our fear of God to God himself. But yet there are other expressions of the same fear toward man. In general, first, there is the commerce that passes between us and others: the justice and righteousness, the mercy and charity, the truth and honesty which we show toward all men. These are like broad seals to prove it to them, and the letters patent that testify to it and justify us in our fear of God.

That unrighteous judge who did not fear God, but gave justice to the poor widow only to avoid trouble, nevertheless confessed—even by denying to do it out of any fear of God or man—that the chief thing which should have moved him to it was the fear of God (Luke 18:4). And why was it that Abraham could look for nothing better than murder and rape among the Philistines, fearing they would kill him and violate his wife, but *because he thought surely the fear of God was not in that place* (Genesis 20:11)? But Joseph, on the other hand, aiming to satisfy his brothers' minds and to make them not doubt his fair and honest dealing, makes that fear the reason and assurance of it: *Do this and live*, says he, *for I fear God* (Genesis 42:18).

And in this regard, it is worth observing that when God was pleased to take the Devil's own verdict concerning Job's fearing of God, although Job was excellent at both expressions—at acts of religion, in his holy and daily worshipping of God, and at acts of honesty, in his upright dealing with all men—yet God questions the Devil not about the former (his religious fear of him), but only the other (his righteous fear of him): *Have you not considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth in the fearing of God?* (Job 1:8). But how was that to appear to Satan? He does not say, "because he prays this much, he preaches this often, he sacrifices daily, or he professes continually"; but rather, *For he is an upright and just man, and shuns wrong and evil*, says God. These are signs able to convince the Devil himself, who, not daring to deny it based on those proofs, only sought to blemish it with a slander of ulterior motives: *Timet, sed an gratis?* "It is true, Job fears God, I see that; but *does he fear God for nothing?*" (at the 9th verse).

<summary>Matthew Wren argues that true religion requires both internal reverential fear and outward expressions of worship and ethical conduct. He uses biblical examples like David, Job, and Joseph to show that a genuine fear of God is proven through justice, honesty, and upright behavior toward others.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse by Bishop Matthew Wren on the dual nature of the fear of God, which must be expressed through both internal holiness toward God and external righteousness toward fellow men.</meta>

The point is so clear, regardless of what some talkers among us might say, that I would only do you a disservice by trying to illustrate it. I shall better conclude it with this instruction: that these two expressions of our fear—to God by our holiness, and to man by our righteousness—must never be confused, nor their relationships misplaced. However, because of our worship of God, men may well hope that we fear him; and by our uprightness with man, God takes notice of how well we do fear him. Yet we mistake it greatly if we think we may spare one of them, and that either expression may serve well enough for both.

It was, therefore, only done in vain by the proud, holy Pharisee to tell God—by not being like the tax collector—that he was no extortioner, nor unjust, nor an adulterer; and by his frequent fasting, that he was no glutton; and by his faithful paying of tithes, that he was no church robber. But in the meantime, he stood on his own terms with God, trusting in his own righteousness, standing up as though he challenged God, *and praying with himself*, says the text in *Luke 18:11*, as though he scorned to do anything more for God. He let God know what he was, as though God were indebted to him; and if such things as those would serve God, then fine; but otherwise, in the pride of his heart, he expressed no reverence, nor worship, nor any fear of God at all in his presence.

And just as futile is that other Pharisaical trick, which has now become the sign of a saint among many of us: to pay little regard to that which our Savior calls the weightier matters of the Law—justice, mercy, and fidelity. He means conscientious honesty, such as is regulated by the glorious law written in our hearts, and not by the outward law of *Westminster Hall* or of a bishop’s court. Instead, many have no qualms about bursting in private with envy and malice, hatred and all uncharitableness; to backbite and slander, to cross and hinder, to censure and condemn; to wallow also in oppression and usury, in falsehood and wrongdoing, in lust and uncleanness, in pride and hypocrisy, in contempt and disobedience, in schism and faction, both ecclesiastical and civil. And yet, despite all this, they fully expect that our running to church and crying out for sermons, our defying the devil and railing against Antichrist, our pretending of conscience and finding fault with the state and times, our singing of psalms and talking of scripture, our casting up of the eyes and making sour faces, must be proof enough to any man that we fear God extraordinarily.

Alas, no; it is a universal rule, like the one St. *James* gives for our faith, and it equally extends to all our affections (*James 2:18*): *Show me your faith by your works, and your hope by your works, and your love by your works, and your fear by your works.* But if you would have me see them and glorify God in them, or edify myself by them, you must show them to me in that way or not at all—by your works. And what works? Not those of godliness and devotions, not by your fair but empty show of holiness. No, we highly esteem all holy conduct, but *God will be the judge of it* <note>Latin: viderit Deus</note>, for we leave God to judge it because the heart of man is so deceitful that the ministers of Satan can, in that respect, transform themselves into angels of light (*2 Corinthians 11:14*). Rather, it is by mercy and charity, by piety and equity, and such other human duties; the Apostle was expressly treating of such works there, and by them you must show men, and let them judge, whether you fear God or not.

<meta>This page continues Bishop Matthew Wren’s discourse on the dual nature of fear, specifically examining how the fear of God is intrinsically linked to the fear of the King.</meta>

# MATTHEW WREN, D. D.

At the very least, by way of gathering them all together, let us take God's way here; let us express one by the other that is closest to it, the fear of God by the fear of the King. The text, you see, joins them so closely that it makes but one and the same act for two objects, God and the King; two persons, but conjoined in one act of our fear, both made one in that: *Fear God, my son, and the King*. This is to make us know that, whatever holy pretenses are made for it, God is not feared if the King is not. The lack of performance in the one implies imperfection in the other, and the lack of truth in the one confirms hypocrisy in the other. No fear of the King, no fear of God. God himself has purposely joined them together here, and it is to make God a liar and a man himself sacrilegious if any dare take either from the other or put them asunder.

And the reason for it is unshakeably sound, or else the blessed Spirit in St. *John* was but a poor logician. For did you ever notice how he enforces the absolute necessity of brotherly love among us? He has two arguments together for it in 1 *John* 4:20: *If any man says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar; for how can he who does not love his brother whom he has seen, love God whom he has not seen?* That is the first, and it is a <term>topic rule</term> that is particularly applied by him on this ground: because of the general image of God which is upon a man’s brother. He does not see God, but he sees God’s image in him; and God he does not see, except in some image of him, and the liveliest image of God is in his brother. *Therefore*, in very good reason then, *how can he who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, love God, whom he has not seen?* No, he cannot; the question, *how can he?* only makes the denial more forceful; it is an impossible thing in very reason.

The other argument of St. *John* is <term>ab authoritate</term>, a sufficient reason in itself because we are commanded it; but yet it is guided by the nature of another <term>topic rule</term> also, because where one thing is ordained to be with another, the one is not as it should be without the other. *Now this commandment we have from him, he says: That we should love our brother?* No, that is not enough; *But that he who loves God should love his brother also*, Verse 21. That is the second.

Keep then these two arguments in mind, and anyone may conclude for my text and the King, and the Spirit here will warrant him; but let whoever can reply or deny, for the Spirit will confound him. As good as those arguments are in St. *John* for his purpose—for the love of our brother—I dare boldly say (and let me disregard my education and judgment too if I do not make it appear to any honest man’s conscience) that they are far more compelling here for our purpose: for the fear of the King.

I begin with the first, and I apply it expressly: if any man says, "I fear God," and does not fear the King, he is a liar. and Lord! What a holy army of liars might we then quickly muster up? But what is the reason? For how can he? That is, it is impossible for him who does not fear the King, whom he has seen, to fear God, whom he has not seen. And why so? How does that follow? It follows from the very same ground as before: because of the image of God which is upon Kings. And that is not only a general image, as they are men, but a special image, and one that is far more visible as they are Kings; yes, the image of that in God for which fear belongs to God—that image is upon the King, the vivid image of his divine power and glory both.

Power first, whether it is power to do good, and therefore fear him—*For with him is mercy, therefore he shall be feared, Psalm* 130:4—or power to do

# THE LIFE OF TAM

Hurt, and therefore fear him, *for he does not bear the sword in vain, Romans 13:4.*

<margin>Institutes, Book 4, Chapter 20.</margin>
And then Glory—the glory of his divine titles, for King and Governor, Lord and Father, Majesty and Sovereignty. Mr. *Calvin* himself confesses, "That they are first and principally God’s titles, and not man's, and that they are so imparted from God to kings, as his deputies and vicegerents, that wherever on earth we meet with them, they ought immediately to affect us with an awful sense of the very divinity itself." Yes, for that very purpose, the glory of his own name is upon them: *I said, you are gods, Psalm 82:6.* I have said it—God himself, it is he who said it; and *I said*, it is his decree and sacred pleasure; he has ordained it shall be so.

And from this ordinance of his, the Scriptures have often expressed it so. *Jacob* of old said it, even of one who was otherwise bad enough, of his lord *Esau*, that he saw God in him: *I saw your face as the face of God, Genesis 33:10.* That is, says the *Chaldee*, God in the prince—God in him as he was the prince. And it is said of *Moses* also: the very scepter he held was God’s, not his own: *The rod of God in his hand, Exodus 17.* And so it is said of *Solomon*: the throne he sat on was the throne of God: *He sat upon the throne of God, 1 Chronicles 29:23.* And so the argument proves invincible: since kings bear both so apparent and so eminent an image of God—the very image of that eminence in God for which God is feared—how can he who does not fear the King, whom he has visibly seen or may see, fear God, who never was, nor is (and I may safely add, who without this other—the fear of the King—never shall or will be) visible to him?

You see the main application of St. *John’s* first argument. And it is just as easy to do the same in the second. Now *this commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should love his brother also.* Is this a good and concluding consequence? Then how much better is this? This commandment we have from him, that he who fears God should fear the King also. And for proof of this, I come back to my text; it is a commandment from him—from God himself principally, though given here by *Solomon’s* pen: *Fear God, my son, and the King.*

And if you require a "new commandment" for it—that is, a commandment in the Gospel, as Christ indeed calls the precept of loving one another *a new commandment, John 13:34*—then I go to the great Apostle for it: *Fear God, honor the King, 1 Peter 2:17.* And then I add that, by this very argument now, the duty of fear is far more clearly proved here than that duty of love is there in St. *John*. For this here is set down *in terms*; you see, we have the places—this of my text and that of St. *Peter*—both of them formal commands, and in plain logical terms, both equally concluding for the fear of God and the King. And yet we do not have, for the love of God and our brother, any place to be found (I speak advisedly) in so express, so distinct, and so mandatory a proposition for those two together in all the Scripture.

But I foresee already what the result of this will be. It is but a hint of court flattery in us, or else all this labor might well be spared. For who denies that the King must be feared? Will not *Bellarmine* or *Junius Brutus* grant that? I know they will; and yet when they have done, I will give them little thanks for it. For how do they do it? *Dolosus ambulat in generalibus* <note>The deceitful man walks in generalities</note>; that is their craft: the treacherous Jesuit in that church, and the factious schismatic in ours. In general terms, indeed, they do not hesitate to loudly profess this doctrine, talking of it in general; and who is half so holy in conscience as they, or so loyal in the duty of fearing the King?

### MATTHEW WREN, D. D.

But yet, bring it at once down to a present instance, and apply it as the occasion shall arise to particular cases and actions, and then you shall find the case is altered with them. Duty and conscience then—forsooth—are against it when they do not like the business. As the Spirit in my text, surely on purpose, has most aptly described them: *Fear God, and the King, and do not associate with those who are seditious*; so we bluntly read it in many of our translations, and it is true, but yet perhaps it is somewhat too coarse for their hypocritical pretenses; they claim to be godly men and good subjects who defy sedition.

Therefore, the original fits them perfectly: *Non cum mutantibus*, or *recedentibus*—do not associate with those who are given to change, nor with those who alter or go backward. And these are the ones now who, when it comes from their general profession to some particular performance, are notable changelings; they alter then, and falter too. They go backward and slily fall away from their profession and from their duty—from the King and from the due fear of him. Indeed, they even alter the text itself in the end and take it backward: that they must fear the King then, but the King must fear them, if they can manage it. And so all at last becomes changed and re-altered with them, from no fear at first to no King at last; they have finished, going from one who does not fear to one who is not to be feared.

And when that is once brought about, I can tell them what will be next also. For they will not stop there either, but will still fall back as far as the text allows: from no King to no God, and from no fear of the one to no fear of the other, to no fear at all of anyone. *Moses* plainly tells them so: *Non contra nos, sed contra Jehovam*—when the *Israelites* murmured against him and *Aaron*, *Exodus 16:8: Your murmurings are not against us, but against the Lord.* And the Lord himself said it just as plainly to *Samuel*: *Non te, sed me*—when they insisted on having another king in his stead. *1 Samuel 8:7: They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me.* And so, *non regem, sed Deum*—not the king, but God—must I say to these who now, by not fearing the King as they should, do as much as they can to dethrone him again. It is not the King but God whom they principally fail; for there is not the least contempt of majesty that is not more than a trace of profanation, and every step of disloyalty is a high degree toward atheism.

And in how high a degree this danger of atheism ranges nowadays, this text of mine, in my view, clearly demonstrates. It showed us before that the fear of the Lord requires the worship of him, and that the due worship of him requires so much beauty and reverence that all our rude and careless demeanor before him—all negligent and perfunctory performance of our religion, or slight and unlawful expressions in it as if in God's presence—are the foulest scorn and abasement possible. In true interpretation, this is no less a denial of his divinity than is rash and unadvised blasphemy.

It shows us now that, next after himself, our God provides for Kings as for himself. He places his eminent image upon them, sets them in his own stead, and establishes only one rule of conscience for the fear of them both—both himself and them. In a word, he values those whom he sets over us so highly that for us now not to be completely right toward them is to be extremely wrong toward God; to fail the one is to be false to the other; to defraud the one is to defy the other.

Consider now a man of understanding among the very heathen—for I still aim at that, to prove it from the evidence of reason itself—and let him see, first, that although these duties of fearing God and the King are imposed upon us not so much by any written law as by an inner law, by the rule of reason and the divine law of conscience, yet many

of the great professors of this religion, those who take it upon themselves above others to be this God’s greatest sons and servants, and to have the best consciences by far, yet for all this, they still stumble and doubt the performance of such a reasonable and appropriate worship to their God. And as for their King, they not only remain in great suspense, but also fiercely dispute whether (despite his closeness to God) he can rightfully be invested with such a divine privilege. Lastly, in this absurd course, they have purposely conditioned their thoughts and forged their consciences to it, so that now they consider it a severe wrong even to be told what is right. If any man dares to be so true to God and the King as to show them the duty of better devotion, they immediately stain him with the mark of dangerous superstition; if he shows better allegiance, they severely brand him with the slander of ambitious flattery. By all means, they consider those who care least about formalities in worshipping God to be the godliest men and the best Christians; but they consider those who most resist the King and refuse to obey him to be the best subjects—or, as the term currently goes in their own currency, "good patriots."

And now let this pagan but say what he thinks of a God who must be treated this way, either in himself or in his deputies, and what difference he can find through reason between such a religion as they have made of it and his own—I will not say his own religion, for even the heathens in their abominations behave more conscientiously—but between such a religion and a complete fable?

And if this is not a logical conclusion, go blame *St. Paul*, who taught me this kind of argument, and that in a matter of religion too, though of much less importance. *For the whole Church*, he says, *when they come together merely to speak in unknown tongues, he cannot tolerate it. And why? Because it is so inconsistent with reason, a confusion so unnatural, that if a heathen man should come in, might he not well consider it a mad religion? Shall he not justly say that they are all out of their wits?* 1 Cor. 14:23.

And how much more then, I say? If a heathen man comes among our "religious" ones and finds such a hideous and strange inconsistency: our profession is indeed a duty of fear and holy worship toward God, and a duty of fear and sacred obedience toward kings; toward both, it is a joint duty—not from policy, or reason, or nature alone (though every one of these laws strongly enforces it), but also from conscience, divine law, and the very principles of religion. Yet, despite this, our whole practice toward God is a careless and irreverent, arbitrary and whimsical, crude and disrespectful sloppiness of his worship; and toward kings, it is a contemptuous and faithless, quarrelsome and graceless, complaining and spiritless reducing of the honors due to them. Might he not well take it for a mad, fabricated religion? Shall he not justly say, *Non est Deus* <note>There is no God</note>; that a God on such contradictory and pitiful terms cannot be a God?

Therefore, my heart's desire and humble prayer to God is that he would open our eyes (as we should be Christians of mature understanding) to see this. We are ready enough, based on the first part of the text concerning the fear of God, to charge our neighbors around us with the danger of idolatry in their manner of divine worship; we should likewise make it a matter of conscience to clear ourselves, in this part of the text concerning the fear of the King, from a crime no less than idolatry in our manner of deliberate refusals. For the Spirit of God, we see, is explicit about it in 1 Samuel 15:23: *that to obey is better than sacrifice*—a better sign of our religion and far more acceptable to God. To be disobedient and restless—*Nolle acquiescere* <note>To be unwilling to submit</note>, as the text says there—to be whining, making excuses, and resisting...

->*Sub conditione filii.*<-
<note>"Under the condition of a son."</note>

I am sure it is a perfect and unhesitating obedience to the powers above us that must cause our days to be good and long in the land, or else God himself misplaced it when he made that—as St. *Paul* also purposely observes—the fifth commandment with such a promise. A promise that every one of us desires to have? And yet generally how many, as though they did not believe God in it, or thought to have it whether God wills it or not, do never regard God’s direction to take his way for it? The promise of long life and welfare is bound strictly to it.

And I am just as sure it is such an obedience that the Spirit aims at here, or else he would never have spoken to us in the dearest language of love, as to sons: *Fear God, my son, and the King*. For that is as much as to say, unless indeed you do not care to be my sons—unless you will be bastards and not sons, slaves and rebels and anything but sons—you will fear God and the King alike; not God alone, but therefore the King also: God for himself, and the King for himself, and the King for God, esteeming God and the King both as your fathers, and accounting yourselves as sons to both—not as servants only out of necessity, nor as friends alone out of mere courtesy, but as sons out of entire duty.

Yes, as one son altogether; "my son," says God here to all—one and all, for none is excused; all as one, for none is excluded—to show us that it must be a joint and mutual consent of all in one. One in the inclination of our heart and affections; therefore, *Fili mi* <note>"My son" (singular)</note>, he says, and not *Filii mei* <note>"My sons" (plural)</note>, "my son" as of one, not "my sons" as of many. One in the tenor of the duty performed; therefore not twice *Time* <note>Latin: "Fear" (imperative)</note>, not two fears—one for God and another for the King—"fear God" and "fear the King"—but once only for both: *Fear God and the King*. And lastly, one in the very ground of the religion; and therefore *Fili mi*, not *Fili noster* <note>"Our son"</note>—that is, son to the King because he is a son to God, and in no other way than as God’s son is he the King’s son—but so, all as one son. And one son all, to both of them as to one; even another sacred mystery of numbers in our religion (besides that of the blessed Trinity and Unity) thus divinely expressed here in this short text: *Fear God, my son, and the King*.

And I may best conclude this sacred conjunction of all parties in the name of God, exhorting every one of us who rejoices in this title of being God’s son to remember, *first*, that *Time Deum* <note>"Fear God"</note> stands here before *Fili mi*; the duty is enforced before the privilege will be allowed. We are apt to forget ourselves, God knows, and because of *Filius* <note>"Son"</note> in the pride of our privilege, we often neglect *Time* <note>"Fear"</note> and have small or no regard for our duty. But *Time fili* <note>"Fear, son"</note>—that is God’s method and order here; it is that relation to him which makes him retain the name of Father to us, and without a due fear of him, no matter how we flatter ourselves regarding our election or predestination, we have no true sonship with him.

Secondly, as a trial of that—whether our *Time Deum* be right or not—here is another coupled with it, *Et regem* <note>"And the King"</note>, to prove ourselves by: *Fear God and the King*. That is, fear God in the King, fear God by the King, send our...

<meta>This page continues Matthew Wren's discourse on Proverbs 24:21, focusing on the necessary synthesis of religious devotion and political allegiance as two sides of the same spiritual coin.</meta>

<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>

Fear of the King of Heaven by our fear of kings on earth; *Fili mi* <note>"My son"</note> is out of place, unless it stands exactly in the middle between *Deum & regem* <note>"God and the king"</note>; to presume we fear God, and yet to go no further—to have no conscience about fearing him who is in God’s stead, or to fear him no further than the lash of his laws will reach us—that does not come from *Filius* <note>"a son"</note>, and it is but a lame and base fear, partly slavish, partly hypocritical, falling far short of both God’s due and a son’s duty.

Much less shall we find any place for *Time regem* <note>"Fear the king"</note> alone, while leaving *Deum* <note>"God"</note> quite out, beginning the text there, at the fear of the king, but with no fear of God at all; or, if any, yet it is heartless and worthless, existing only for fear of the king. No, without *Deum*, you see, the text never has a *Time* <note>"fear"</note> here for *Regem*, no right fear of the king, if God is not first feared. He who fears God only for fear of the king and his laws, in truth, makes the king his god; and he who fears the king more than God, in his heart wishes there were neither king nor God.

So that in the conclusion, these two—our *Time Deum*, which is our religion, and our *Time regem*, which is our allegiance—they are sure and perfect proofs of each other. Look at whatever is pretended for the king: it is fraud, not fear; craft, not allegiance; plain <term>brokage</term> and not obedience, unless it first issues from the throne of heaven, springs from true devotion, and is founded upon religion. Again, look at whatever is professed for God—as where do we not have swarms now of great "professors" <note>Those who profess faith or piety</note>?—yet it is not fear but faction, not devotion but hypocrisy, not religion but abomination, unless it also falls down before the throne upon earth, serves as the life of spotless allegiance, and the animating soul of all civil obedience.

The text implies no less, and God enjoins no less, and I can charge the consciences of all who hear me this day with nothing less than *Time Deum, fili mi, et regem*: *Fear God, my son, and the king*; God and the king, both together, show a due fear of them both, but yet both in that order. Thus, by approving ourselves respectively to God and the king, as sons to both—genuine sons—here in the life of grace, our fear at last may be changed into joy, and our devotion into fulfillment; and we may be made not sons alone, but kings also with God, in the life of glory, by the merits of the Son of God, the King of eternal glory, Jesus Christ our Savior. *Amen.*

## CHRISTOPHER WREN, D.D.

### DEAN *of* W I N D S O R.

---

<margin>Account of Dean Wren.</margin>
<margin>Fasti Oxon. p. 836.</margin>
DOCTOR *Christopher Wren*, Dean of *Windsor*, younger brother of *Matthew*, Bishop of *Ely*, was born in the year 1589, and educated at St. *John's* College in *Oxford*; where in 1620, he took his degree of Bachelor of Divinity; became domestic chaplain to Dr. *Lancelot Andrewes*, Bishop of *Winchester*, and by him was preferred to the Rectory of *Knoyle Magna* <note>Now known as East Knoyle</note> in the county of *Wiltshire*. In 1628, he was appointed Chaplain in Ordinary to King *Charles* the First; in 1630, was created Doctor of Divinity at *Cambridge*, (<term>scil. ex ultroneâ & abundanti academiæ gratiâ absens evectus</term> <note>namely, promoted in his absence by the voluntary and abundant grace of the university</note>); in 1635, by his Majesty's special appointment, he succeeded his brother *Matthew*, upon his advancement to the See of *Norwich*, in the Deaneries of *Windsor* and *Wolverhampton*, and the office of Registrar of the most noble Order of the Garter; and in 1638, was presented to the rich Rectory of *Haseley* in *Oxfordshire*.

The royal Chapel of St. *George* at *Windsor*, and its treasury, having been plundered by the rebels in the Great Rebellion, and the register books and all the ancient records of the Order of the *Garter*—together with the jewels, plate, furniture, *etc.*—carried away and delivered to the trustees appointed by the Long Parliament for the sale of the King's goods, the Dean, through great application, expense, and long attendance on the trustees at their meetings in *Somerset House*, and by the favor of their chairman, Ma-

Major Wither’s, performed, at length, a memorable piece of service to the Order, and recovered out of their hands, *first*, the two old registers, styled the *Black* and the *Blue*; and some time after retrieved the *Red* also, with other books and papers relating to the statutes and annals. All these were carefully concealed and preserved by him until the time of his death in 1658, and afterwards by his son until the time of the Restoration, when they were presented by him to the Sovereign and ordered into the custody of the new Registrar, Dr. *Brune Ryves*, Dean of *Windsor*; for which he gave this receipt:

> “I do acknowledge that I have received from Mr. *Christopher Wren*,

> “in the year 1660. *Brune Ryves.*”

But the Dean failed in achieving the same success in his best endeavors to preserve the *George* and *Garter* of the great *Gustavus Adolphus*, *King of Sweden*. These jewels, containing four hundred ninety-eight diamonds, great and small, were returned after his death by a solemn embassy (pursuant to the statutes of the Order) and, by the Sovereign’s command (24 *May, Anno* 14 *Charles* I), committed to the custody of the Dean and Chapter of *Windsor* to be laid up in the treasury,

<margin>
Ashmole's *History of the Garter*, p. 203 and 641.
</margin>

> “for a perpetual memorial of that renowned
> “King, who died in the field of battle wearing some of those jewels, to
> “the great honor of the Order, and as a true martial prince and companion
> “thereof.”

The Dean, to prevent the irretrievable loss of such valuable ensigns by the plunder of the rebels in the year 1642, took extraordinary care, at the risk of his life, to bury them under the floor of the treasury; he deposited a note in the hands of a worthy person, indicating where they might be found in case of his death.

<margin>
Ibid. p. 204 and 641.
</margin>

In this place they remained securely until about the beginning of *March* 1645, when, being discovered by *Cornelius Holland*, a regicide, and taken from there by Colonel *Ven*, a regicide and then-governor of the castle, and afterwards delivered to Colonel *Whitchcott** (who succeeded him in that government), they were at length fetched away by *John Hunt*, treasurer to the trustees appointed by the Long Parliament for the sale of his Majesty’s goods, and sold by them to *Thomas Beauchamp*, their then-clerk.

<margin>
From the papers of Christopher Wren, Dean of Windsor.
</margin>

Among other remarkable goods and monuments plundered from the Royal Chapel of St. *George* at *Windsor* and the treasury in 1642 were:

I. All the rich plate made by *Van Vianen* the *Nuremburger*, valued with the workmanship and triple gilding at twelve shillings the ounce, and estimated in total at above three thousand pounds.
II. Two fair double-gilt chalices with covers.
III. Two fair double-gilt flagons.
IV. A basin, gilt, for the bread at great Communions.
V. The coat of mail of steel, gilt, of King *Edward* IV, in which (as recorded) he had personally fought eight battles, covered with crimson velvet and bearing the royal armorial ensigns, richly embroidered with pearl and gold and many rubies; this was the only monument which hung over his tomb, without any inscription.

<margin>
Ashmole's *History of the Garter*, Ch. 4. Sect. 2. p. 149.
</margin>

Steel gilt, set to enclose it from the North aisle, carved excellently well in ecclesiastical style.

Over this arch hung the King’s coat of mail, gilded, covered over with crimson velvet, and featuring the arms of *France* and *England* quarterly, richly embroidered with pearl and gold, interwoven with various rubies. This trophy of honor had hung safely over his grave ever since his funeral, but was plundered from there by Captain *Fogg* on the 23rd day of *October*, in the year 1642. On that day, he also robbed the chapel treasury of all the rich plate dedicated to the use of the altar. However, having found an exact measurement and size of each part of it, as well as of his banner—both of which were previously recorded by Sir *William Le Neve*, former Clarencieux King of Arms and a precise observer of everything curious regarding heraldry or ceremony—we think it proper to transmit the details to posterity in this manner:

> "The coat of arms was two feet seven inches deep, and two feet wide 
> "at the bottom.
> "Above (the maunches <note>heraldic sleeves</note> being extended) it was three feet six inches wide, 
> "of which the length of each maunch was one foot.
> "The width of the upper part of the coat, excluding the maunches, was one 
> "foot and a half.
> "The width of each maunch was one foot and eight inches.
> "The arms were embroidered upon velvet, lined with satin, and better 
> "crafted than what is typically made nowadays.
> "The banner, which also hung over his grave, was made of taffeta, and 
> "featured the quarterly arms of *France* and *England* painted upon it: it was 
> "three feet four inches wide, besides a fringe about an inch broad, and 
> "five feet four inches deep, besides the fringe."

VI. The hangings that went across the center of the choir, twelve feet deep, made of crimson velvet and gold.
VII. Thirteen rich copes, embroidered and crafted in gold.
VIII. Two rich copes of gold wire.
IX. A large carpet of gold wire for the communion table.
X. The blue velvet robe of *Gustavus Adolphus*, King of *Sweden*, worn with a train and embroidered with a Garter, pearls, and gold, which was brought back by an ambassador, along with the jewels, after his death.
XI. The great brass basin, or font for christenings, given by the founder, King *Edward* III, etc.

<margin>* Named one of the King’s judges, but would not act at the trial.</margin>
On *October* 25, 1642, one Captain *Fogg*, pretending to have a warrant from the King, demanded the keys to the treasury at *Windsor* in the presence of Colonel *Manwaring**, with threats that if they were denied by the Dean and Prebendaries, he would pull down the chapel around their ears. Not finding the three key-keepers, he caused a blacksmith to make strong iron bars and used them to force open two doors and break down the stone jambs, carrying out of the treasury all the rich plate as specified above. This had been first seized by Sir *John Seton* and restored, but was afterwards taken away by the aforementioned *Fogg*, *Manwaring*, and *Venn*.

It appears that on the 28th of *March* preceding the plunder of the royal chapel, treasury, and memorials of the Garter, His Majesty had been pleased to appoint the celebration of the Grand Feast of St. *George* to be held at *York* in the following *April*; and the proper summons were issued ac-

In consequence of the general summons of *March* 28, 1642, to celebrate
the grand Feast of St. *George* at the city of *York*, several of the Knights-Com-
panions, who were members of the House of Lords in the Long Parliament, gave
notice of it to the House of Lords; whereupon they immediately made the
following order.

WHEREAS the Lord Chamberlain of his Majesty's household, and
some other Lords of Parliament, Knights of the Garter, have been
summoned to give their attendance, and travel to the city of *York*, for the
celebration of St. *George's* feast; who, having informed this House of the sum-
mons aforesaid, it is ordered by the Lords in Parliament, that they attend the
weighty affairs of the kingdom, discussed in Parliament, to which they are
obliged by his Majesty's writ, and the law of the land.

->*John Browne, Clerk of Parliament.*<-

Whereupon every one of the said Knights-companions, before the days
appointed by the postponement for holding the feast, sent their letters
of excuse to the Deputy-chancellor, in which they declared their desire and
readiness to attend in obedience to the said summons; nevertheless, they pleaded
the aforementioned order as the ground for their staying at *London*, and therefore de-
sired him to obtain for them the Sovereign's gracious letters of dispensation:
but when the said letters were individually presented in Chapter, held before
*Vespers* <note>Evening prayers</note> on the eve of the said feast, the Sovereign would not at present either
admit or reject their excuses, but referred the consideration of them until the next Chapter,
to be held by postponement.

<margin>
Ibid.
Echard's History of England, Vol. II. p. 651.
</margin>
The petitioning Lords for the dispensation, were the Earls of *Pembroke*
and *Montgomery*, *Salisbury*, *Dorset*, *Holland*, *Berks*, and *Northumberland*, who
did not follow the King, but sat in the Long Parliament: and after the Com-
mons had taken it upon themselves to abolish the House of Peers, but yet conde-
scended that the Peers should have the privilege to be elected as Knights or Bur-
gesses in Parliament; two of the above-mentioned Lords, with the old Earl
of *Pembroke*, and the Earl of *Salisbury*, and the Lord *Howard* of *Escrick*,
soon after took the benefit of this concession.

The sacrilege and plundering committed on the chapel and treasury, was fol-
lowed by the plundering in the Deanery-house, of all the Dean's belongings; although

At that time he was under a formal protection of the Committee of Lords and Commons for the Safety of the Kingdom, as it was called; and it appeared by an Order of Parliament, upon information of this violence to the Dean and many other inhabitants of *Windsor*, "That both houses denied giving any commission or warrant to the dragoons or troopers, sent by their order to secure the castle, for such unjust proceedings of plundering and pillaging; and declared that restitution should be made to the several owners and offenders punished," which was never done. All that the Dean was able to recover was a harpsichord, valued at about £10, which, having been seized with his other goods by Colonel *Venn*, the governor, was carried to *London* and returned after six years.

The Dean had the honor to receive from the King at *Oxford* a very ample protection for himself, his servants, and estate, in a most gracious manner, although through the hostility of the times it was of little effect, namely:

Charles R.

<margin>
Ashmole of the Garter, p. 251.
</margin>
> Whereas by the ancient constitution and laws of our most noble Order of the Garter, the Register of our said Order is to have his person and estate secured from violence and injury, so that he or his ministers may live securely under our perpetual protection and safeguard; and as often as he shall be harassed, either personally or regarding anything that belongs to him, he is to receive our protection and the assistance of the companions of our Order, according to equity and right. These are therefore to will and command all men, of whatever status they may be, not to trouble or harass Doctor *Christopher Wren*, Dean of *Windsor* and Register of our most noble Order of the Garter, or any of his ministers whomsoever, or anything that belongs to him whatsoever; but to suffer his person, servants, and estate to be in quiet, security, and peace, without any injury or violence to be offered by any to him or his, as they, or every one of them, shall answer to the contrary at their peril.
> 
> Given at our court at *Oxford*, under the signet of our Order, the 12th day of December, in the 19th year of our reign.

From the papers of Dean C. W.

### *Some further particulars observable in the plundering of the Deanery house at Windsor.*

<margin>
* Namely, of the Lords.
</margin>
THE closet called the Registry of the Order of the Garter (within Dean *Wren's* house in the Castle of *Windsor*) had been locked up and sealed by order of the Long Parliament and committed to the safeguard of Colonel *Venn*, the governor of the castle; but at the plundering of the house, this closet also was broken open (contrary to the parliamentary order <note>Namely, of the Lords.</note>) and the following goods, among others, were taken away:

A large case or cabinet of eleven drawers, containing writings and records concerning the Order of the Garter and other things of value.

Another large iron-bound cabinet, with partitions and boxes, gilded and filleted, with special records and papers inside.

A large chest filled with books; among them *Caster's Institutions to the Romish Emissaries*, with Dr. *Wren's Discovery of Their Subtle Practices*, a manuscript undertaken by command and almost finished.

<meta>catchword: A large</meta>

Colonel *Venn*, mentioned before, seized and kept in his possession all the Dean’s plate when he was driven from *Windsor* (which by order of Parliament* should have been restored). The *Elector* often expressed great satisfaction with this convenient retirement from *Whitehall* (where the Parliament had allowed him a lodging) and the opportunity of conversing with the Dean and some other learned friends who used to visit there.

Here the Prince lived in a very private way, with only two gentlemen of his retinue, a secretary, and one who waited in the bedchamber, along with a few junior servants. He dined at a little table by himself; the others dined with the Dean and his family.

### N U M B. I.

<margin>Collections of some importance, from the papers of Dr. C. Wren.</margin>
August 6, 1620. **Dr. Christopher Wren, B.D.**, was admitted as a domestic chaplain to Lord Lancelot Andrewes, Bishop of Winchester, after a sermon delivered this day before him in the chapel of Windsor Palace, on the south bank of the Thames.

<margin>Namely, Matthew.</margin>
After this, he and his eldest brother followed the prelate to Farnham Castle, where the King and the entire royal court were received by the bishop for three days, with most sumptuous preparations and expenses of more than 3,000 *pounds*. **Well done.**

**Dr. Christopher Wren**, of *Windsor*, was well-skilled in all branches of Mathematics; and there are still extant some marginal notes, written by him in Sir *Henry Wotton’s* Elements of Architecture (*London*, 1624, Quarto), which show his knowledge of that art. In those notes, among many other things, he refers to the contrivance of a very strong roof made by him at *Knoyle*, where he was Rector, the figure of which is subjoined there (*Page* 79). But there is one thing mentioned by him as his invention, which I shall transcribe here in his own words.

> “For directing the 
> “current of a river to a great length in a small space, I invented the 
> “Serpentine; a form admirably conveying the current in circular, and yet 
> “contrary motions, upon one and the same level, with walks and 
> “retreats between, for the benefit of all purposes, either for gardening, 
> “planting, banqueting, or airy delights, and the multiplying of infinite 
> “fish in a small area of ground, without any sense of their being 
> “restrained. In brief, it is to reduce a current of a mile’s length into the 
> “compass of an orchard. *Page* 112.”

(This book is now in the *possession* of *Mr. Elias Ferris*.)

### N U M B. II.

<margin>See Notes, MS. regarding the *Cosmography* of Peter Heylyn, Book I, p. 285.</margin>
*A very memorable attestation of Dr.* CHRISTOPHER WREN, *Dean of Windsor and Registrar of the most noble Order of the Garter, concerning the Royal Title of Defender of the Faith.*

POPE Leo X conferred on King *Henry* VIII (in the year 1521) the title of *Defender of the Faith*; it was afterwards made hereditary by Act of Parliament to his heirs and successors. And yet, “That King *Henry* VII “had the same title formerly, appears by the Register of the Order of the “Garter, in the Black Book (so called from the color of its cover, p. 187), “now in my hands by virtue of my office. This I showed to King *Charles* I, which he “received with much joy; nothing pleased him more than that the right “of that title was fixed in the Crown long before the Pope’s pretended “donation.” To all this I make attestation for all posterity, *with this my own handwriting. So I testify, Christopher Wren, Registrar and Secretary of the most honorable order.* <note>I transcribed this from the original manuscript of my grandfather of pious memory, C. W., in the year of our Lord 1733.</note>

<margin>P. 187.</margin>
*The aforementioned citation, in the register—namely, the Black Book—is as follows:*
<note>Henry VII</note> because he excelled his contemporaries in virtues, was by the unanimous voice of all Christendom then esteemed the *principal defender of the Church and of the Faith*; the bright title of which prerogative his most illustrious heir most deservedly received and adorned, so that what the father had excellently begun, the son most perfectly finished.

[*King Henry VII*], because he excelled his contemporaries in virtues, was by the unanimous voice of all Christendom then esteemed the *principal defender of the Church and of the Faith*; the bright title of which prerogative his most illustrious heir most deservedly received and adorned, so that what his father had thus excellently begun, he, his son, most absolutely finished. <note>Anstis of the Garter, Volume II, Page 266.</note>

*Humphry* of *Lancaster*, Duke of *Gloucester*, fourth son of King *Henry* IV and uncle to King *Henry* VI, was created Duke of *Gloucester* by his brother King *Henry* V in the year 1414, and surnamed the *Good*. Upon his marriage with *Jacoba*, daughter and heir of *William*, Duke of *Bavaria*, he used these titles: *Humphry*, by the Grace of God, Son, Brother, and Uncle to Kings, Duke of *Gloucester*, Earl of *Hainault*, *Holland*, *Zealand*, and *Pembroke*, Lord of *Friesland*, Great Chamberlain of the Kingdom of *England*; *Protector and Defender of the said Kingdom and Church of England*. <note>Sandford’s Genealogical History of the Kings of England, etc., Book IV, Chapter 7, Page 316.</note>

# NUMBER III.

## A Memorandum of Dean <term>WREN</term>’s, relating to the ancient Arms of the French Kings.

<margin>
Notes from the manuscript on Heylyn’s Cosmography, Book I, p. 205.
</margin>
THE ancient French heralds say that the armorial ensigns of the Kings of France, in the year of Christ 484, were <note>three toads</note> *Tres Crapauds*. The first change of the coat of arms was Azure, *fretted* and *semé* [strewn] with *fleurs-de-lis Or* [gold], first changed by King *Edward III* and thus placed into his Great Seal in the 20th year of his reign, after his conquest of France, thirty-four years before *Charles VI* came to the throne. In the east window of the church of *Great Haseley*, *Oxfordshire*, where I was rector in the year 1639, the coat of arms of France stood as described above, *fretted* and *semé* with *fleurs-de-lis*, placed there—together with his own coat near it—by the Lord *Barentine*, a Knight of *Rhodes* and a great benefactor to that church. He was a man of great valor and possessed much land in *France* as well as *England*. His tomb, on the northeast side of the chancel, shows he was of a gigantic stature; and his statue, made of one entire stone which I dug out of a heap of rubbish there, makes it appear he was (no less than) seven feet tall.

### *Some further memorable notes.*

<margin>
The same, Book I, p. 285.
</margin>
The victorious King *Edward III* was the founder of the most noble Order of the Garter, into which (by several kings, his successors) were created nine emperors, fifty-five kings, and four hundred princes, the last of whom was Prince Palatine *Rupert*.

<margin>
The same, Book I, p. 285. Greyfriars Abbey.
</margin>
The wicked and tyrannical prince King *Richard III* being slain at *Bosworth*, his body was requested by the nuns at *Leicester* and buried in their chapel there. At the dissolution of that abbey, the place of his burial happened to fall within the boundaries of a citizen’s garden; it was later purchased by Mr. *Robert Herrick* (at one time the mayor of *Leicester*) and was covered by him with a handsome stone pillar, three feet high, with this inscription: “Here lies the body of *Richard III*, once King of *England*.” He showed this to me <note>Christopher Wren</note> while walking in the garden in the year 1612.

## *Testimonial regarding the wonderful oak in the New Forest in Hampshire, by Dr. <term>CHRISTOPHER WREN</term>.*

King *James I* could not be induced to believe the account of the oak in the *New Forest* until Bishop *Andrewes* <note>of Winchester</note>, in whose diocese the tree grew, caused one of his chaplains—a man of known integrity—to provide a true report of it. This he did: for on Christmas Eve, he gathered about 100 cuttings with the leaves newly opened, which he stuck in clay at the bottom of long, white boxes and sent them by post to the court. There they deservedly raised not only admiration but silenced the mouth of disbelief and contradiction forever.

I was an eyewitness to this and distributed many of them to the great persons of both sexes at court, and to other ecclesiastical persons. But in the recent troublesome times, a devilish fellow (of a disposition like *Herostratus*) having hacked it around the root, struck his final blow upon his own leg, from which he died, along with the old wondrous tree. However, it is now sprouting up again and may renew its ancient age, unless some such malicious accident hinders or prevents it; from which the example of that former villain

### Observation of blood flowing from a murdered and submerged man in the presence of the culprit. From the papers of the Reverend Christopher Wren, Doctor of Divinity.

It is certain that when a person has been secretly drowned, the blood leaps up at the approach of the murderer; this is from a story very well known throughout the county of Oxford. At Ricot (in the parish of Haseley, the care of which was formerly entrusted to me) belonging to the Barons Norreys; an elderly park-keeper was lured into the park at night by his nephew. Since he arrived before the appointed time, he lay down under an oak and was overcome by sleep. When he was found, the nephew approached (hoping for the inheritance intended for him after the old man's death) and crushed his skull. He dragged him into a deep ditch and submerged him with a huge stone hung from his neck. There the corpse lay hidden for about five weeks, to the astonishment of the lord and the whole neighborhood as to what had become of the old man. After that time, haymakers working along the edges of the ditch saw such huge swarms of flies that they were driven to investigate such a great marvel. Finally, the corpse was seen, at first obscurely, then pulled out with much labor. They pulled out the body, putrid and barely holding together, and recognized it. But no mortal could guess who the killer was. That he had been murdered and thrown there with great force was indicated by the stone hung from his neck, which completely removed all doubt of suicide.

Therefore, to detect so atrocious a crime, by the very impulse of Him who wills that vengeance belong to Himself, Lord Norreys ordered the putrid body—which had been preserved from the worst stench by being in the water—to be displayed on the following Sunday in the cemetery near the church gate, so that it might be observed by the eyes and almost the touch of those leaving. Only that wicked nephew, conscious of such a great deed, tried to withdraw himself as if he could not bear the sight of his dearest uncle, being seemingly overwhelmed with great grief. But Lord Norreys, suspecting the old man had been taken by the deed of the one to whom the profit of the inheritance would fall, pushed the reluctant man more urgently to approach and touch the hand of the dead man (which many had done voluntarily). At that touch (miraculous to say!), the eyes in the corpse were seen to open and move openly, as if by the finger of God, and blood flowing from the nostrils so terrified the assassin that he collapsed to the ground and confessed the crime he had secretly committed, but which was revealed by the most just judgment of God. For this, he was first brought before a judge, then the executioner, and paid the penalties worthy of such a crime on the gallows. I have thought this fit to be remembered and signed with my own hand. And so I testify.

-> CHRISTOPHER WREN, Rector of the aforementioned church. <-

From the original manuscript.
