### NUMBER V.

->Christopher Wren, only son of the Reverend Christopher Wren,<-
->Dean of Windsor, was born.<-

**O**N Friday, October 20th, a little before eight in the evening, in the year 1632. Solar cycle 17, Lunar cycle 18, dominical letter B. The 3rd year after Leap Year. In which year occurred the *Physical Conjunction* of the Sun and Mercury; which, at the suggestion of Kepler, Gassendus observed in Paris.

Here, in passing, should be noted the opinion of the same Reverend Christopher Wren regarding these words— "In the year of Christ 812, Helvicus places a solar eclipse; but I do not know if it
" should have been called an eclipse: historians of those times say a certain spot was
" observed in the sun for 7 days; others say 9; some say, with little mathematical
" skill, that it was a *Physical Conjunction* of Mercury in the sun. But astronomers 
" rightly hiss at this, for whom it is certain that the motion of Mercury is so swift and 
" volatile that it is impossible for the sun to be joined with Mercury for so many days. 
" Nevertheless, some have recently been found, among whom is Alstedius, who—besides 
" writing that this happened in the year 813, in solar cycle 10 and lunar cycle 16, by a 
" <term>prochronism</term> of one whole year—now 800 years after the event, 
" divines that this prodigy undoubtedly signified the darkening of the Gospel under the 
" Roman Pontiffs. This, being said with more zeal than knowledge, I think should be 
" passed over rather than refuted. Let our mathematicians who have the leisure see 
" whether that spot should be reduced to an evaluation as to whether it was not some 
" larger sunspot; such as they observe today daily passing through the solar body, 
" many of them, being unequal in quantity and shape. Let them see, furthermore, 
" whether those spots should be considered comets, which as long as they remain 
" within the sun's disk (from which it is known all comets come) appear black and 
" opaque; but when they have proceeded further from the sun, they show a rare 
" and transparent light, becoming more vanishing day by day." [From MS notes on Helvicus's Chronology, p. 116 & 166, 167.]

<margin>From MS notes on Helvicus's Chronology, p. 182.</margin> But a prognosis of the true conjunction of the Sun and Mercury, by the same reverend and learned man, was disclosed in this manner: "The *Physical Conjunction* of the Sun and Mercury will occur on October 24th, in the year of Christ 1651. But it will not be visible to us except at its very end, if perhaps the dawn shows a clear sun. Mercury will enter onto the disk of the sun at one and a half seconds past [midnight] in the morning, and will pass through it a little before 8:00 AM."

At this place should be added the observation of the same most learned man regarding the following paragraph of Helvicus's Chronology, on page 182, letter E, namely: "An eclipse of the earth, fearsome to those on the moon, in the 19th degree (which is commonly believed to be a clearly horrendous and terrible eclipse of the Sun) in the 19th degree of Leo. August 1st, Old Style, in the year 1654, a little before noon; fatal to Rome; if only eclipses were to be numbered among the 
" prophets; for they are neither accustomed to predict nor to proclaim anything; nor 
" are they of greater omen than the constant motion of the heavens. Any amateur, <margin>A reply against the terror of eclipses.</margin>
" from natural principles, can predict their meeting at any most remote moments of 
" time. We all know what causes they have; what effects they will have, no one"

> "...no mortal can foreknow; no one but a madman dares to prophesy. They fear the signs of heaven for themselves who, conscious of their crimes, cannot help but shudder at the threats of an angry heaven; but those for whom heaven is their homeland are commanded not to fear.
> Is it not madness to shudder more at the brief darkness of a covered sun than at the constant eight, twelve, or sixteen-hour night in which we are often enveloped? Is there not a far greater harm to be feared from the sun being absent every day for so many continuous hours—if harm it be, since it is not only constant but also natural—than is justly to be feared from the same sun being present but veiled for a few moments? The shadow of the moon never extends to a measure of a hundred miles on the earth; and so, it never stays, but is carried around most swiftly by continuous motion. But the earth itself, by its own shadow, keeps us constantly enveloped for many hours. Also, thick clouds frequently take away the entire ground from the earth, and that for many days; not often without many a terrifying downpour of storms, to be feared indeed when it is felt, and still to be lamented after it has receded. Therefore, the darkening of the earth is not to be feared or grieved for so much from the passing celestial bodies as from the darkness of the earth itself. These things which they call eclipses were the terrors of the heathens, with which sly scoundrels mocked darkened minds, while in the meantime they robbed the purses of the astonished."

## NUMBER VI.

->From the papers of Mr. **CHRISTOPHER WREN**, Dean of Windsor.<-

**I**N the year 1628, the most serene King promoted Dr. Matthew Wren to the deanery of the royal chapel of Windsor, in the place of Dr. Henry Beaumont, deceased, who, not long ago—specifically in the year 1622—had been promoted to that seat through the resignation of Mr. Marc' Antonio de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato; concerning which man, being notable, we shall add a few things.

Marc' Antonio de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato, deserting the Roman Pontiff, went to the King of England; a man truly learned and most well-instructed in every kind of erudition; but he was also pot-bellied and headstrong; and I could not easily say whether he was more greedy for food and wine, or for money. After he had exhausted the very large revenues in the deanery of Windsor and the hospital called the Savoy, and fearing he could not be sufficiently satisfied in England—a truly insatiable whirlpool—he was enticed by the tricks of Gondomar, the Spanish ambassador. Promising himself that everything would go according to his wishes with the Pope (once a companion of his youthful studies), he returned to Rome. There, he was first accused of perfidy against the Roman see, then made guilty of attempted schism against it. He first underwent a sentence of imprisonment in the year 1622. Afterward, his corpse was burned in the year 1624—having died either of weariness or tortures in prison, though many assert he was burned alive—certainly by no active or passive martyrdom. Rome is so tenacious of injuries; nor does she forget for a very long time a slight against her majesty, which she desires to be second only to heaven, if not shared with heaven.

In relation to a person so extraordinary, this further account may be added.

Marc' Antonio de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato, arriving in England in 1617, both preached and wrote well against the Church of Rome, and extolled the Protestant religion, being a man of rare parts and general learning; in regard to which, he came to be made Dean of Windsor and Master of the Savoy, preferments of dignity and value which he enjoyed for some years, though in all other respects he was voluptuous, haughty, rapacious, and

*Marcus Antonius de Dominis*, Archbishop of Spalato, upon his arrival in *England*, had been Archbishop of that see in *Dalmatia* for fourteen years, under the State of *Venice*; and, pretending conscience, he renounced the errors of the Church of *Rome* and conformed to the Church of *England* about a year before he arrived here. He said the *Romish* Church was *mystical Babylon*, the *Pope* a *Nimrod*, a tyrant, *schismatic*, *heretic*, and even *Antichrist* himself. It seems he had a grudge against Pope *Paul V* for making him pay five hundred crowns a year out of his bishopric to a suffragan, and in a fury he left *Italy*. Coming to *England*, he was received by King *James* with as much favor as if he had been a real convert. He soon found out the King's weakness, and by flattering him for his learning and knowledge in divinity, obtained several rich presents and profitable appointments; his Majesty sending him a fine basin and bowl of silver, the Archbishop received it with this compliment:
> *Misit mihi rex Magnae Britanniae, &c. The King of Great Britain has sent me a silver basin to wash from me the filth of the Roman Church, and a silver cup to remind me to drink the purity of the Gospel.*

He was soon after made Dean of *Windsor*, with a good parsonage annexed to it, and Master of the *Savoy*. Gondomar, the *Spanish Envoy*, taking offense at a joke the Archbishop made about him, told King *James* he was still a Papist in his heart, and that he would prove it. To accomplish this, he wrote to his master, the King of *Spain*, to request de *Dominis*'s pardon from the Pope, with a promise of advancement and a cardinal’s hat if he would sign a recantation of what he had said and written against the Catholic Church. De *Dominis* readily embraced the proposal and signed the recantation, which was presented to him by *Gondomar*, who carried it immediately to the King. His Majesty ordered the matter to be kept secret, de *Dominis* being at that very instant a persistent petitioner for the Archbishopric of *York*, which was thought to be vacant by the supposed death of *Matthews*. When his Majesty denied him this, having been convinced of his falsehood, de *Dominis* requested leave to depart the kingdom and was commanded to do so within twenty days, and never to return. This message startled de *Dominis*, who expected to be entreated to stay in *England*; and when he found the King was in earnest, he used all the influence he could to be permitted to stay. But all being in vain, he took ship with Count *Swartzenbourg*, the Imperial Ambassador, and returned to *Flanders*, from where he went to *Rome*, where he lived on a

### NUMBER VII.

#### Certain highly curious collections concerning the ceremonies and pageantry of the election and inauguration of the most serene Prince Charles, son of Charles, into the Order of the Garter. From the papers of Dean CHRISTOPHER WREN.

In the year of our Lord 1638, on May 19th, the companions <note>the Knights of the Garter</note>, having been previously notified of the proclamation of the feast according to custom, traveled to Windsor in obedience to the Sovereign, to celebrate the feast called Saint George’s on the following day.

To increase the pageantry, the most serene Queen, the young Duke of York, and the Duchess of Chevreuse, a visitor from France, had gathered.

On May 20th, sacred to the Holy and Undivided Trinity, the Sovereign observed the morning in the palace of the castle with the greatest devotion, listening most attentively to the sermon.

At three o'clock that day, he and eight companions, descending into the Chapter House, put on the insignia of the Order; once dressed, they stood before the Sovereign.

*After the scrutiny was finished with the sacred rites, and having taken off their robes in the chapter house, the Sovereign ascended with the companions into the castle.*

*May 21. With the Sovereign surrounded by the said companions dressed in their cloaks, all the officers of the order attended him in a private chamber.*

*And now, with the council reconvened, the most serene Queen Mary and the Duchess of Chevreuse were permitted to sit while the solemnities of the election were performed for the first-born Charles, Prince of Great Britain.*

*Before all things, the companions asked two senior members of the order (namely the Earl of Pembroke and the Earl of Arundel) to present the prince, in the name of the rest, to the Sovereign, to be first initiated with the title and rites of a knight bachelor <note>equitis bacchalaurei</note>, as the laws command.*

*For that is the first degree of all military dignity among the British; the basis, as it were, of all honors in England; so much so that it is not lawful for anyone of the British nation—no matter how much they may otherwise excel in blood or the excellence of their virtues—to be admitted into the most honorable society, unless this first degree of military honor has made them fit and capable.*

*Therefore first, in the solemn custom, the prince, kneeling on his knees, was created a knight bachelor <note>eques auratus</note> by the Sovereign.*

*And for the increase of honor, four men were called out from the nobles, whom the Sovereign might raise up under similar auspices, in the hope of greater favor.*

*The first of these, the Earl of Essex, attended by Sir Frederick Hamilton and Sir Robert Honywood, knights, knelt before the throne of the Sovereign to be created.*

*The Earl of St. Albans followed him, accompanied on the right by Sir Roger Palmer, Knight of the Bath; and on the left by Sir Henry Mildmay, Master of the King's Jewels. Then the Earl of Elgin proceeded, whose attendants were Sir John Meldrum and Sir John Withrington.*

*In the fourth place, the Lord Viscount Grandison went between Sir John Harper and Sir John Lucas.*

*When these ceremonies were completed, the Vice-Chancellor, bowing low, presented the previous day's scrutiny <note>voting results</note> to the Sovereign; after reading it, the Sovereign admitted the prince of youth Charles—now eight years old, but far more advanced in virtues than in age—into the noble order. He commanded his election to be announced by his mandate given to the King of Arms, the form of which was as follows in the English language.*

> “Our most dear and entirely beloved son, having to our great comfort seen and considered the maturity of your youth, and conceived joyful and great hopes for your manly virtues—in which we are assured you will grow to your own honor, in prowess, wisdom, justice, and all princely endowments—and that the emulation of *chivalry* will in your tender years provoke and encourage you to pursue the glory of heroic actions befitting your royal birth and our care and education: *We, with the companions of our most noble Order of the Garter*, assembled in chapter held this present day at our castle of *Windsor*, have elected and chosen you as one of the companions of our *Order*. *At this moment, the scribe humbly requested instruction from the Sovereign, asking whether he should read the exact same form of the oath for binding the prince as all the others being admitted into the order performed.*

*“Propose the very same one,” he [the King] said, “in the customary words”; and so it was done.*

*Therefore, as he approached the Sovereign's throne with due reverence, the majestic Father received him with great affection; and immediately he bound his left leg with the garter, sparkling with the brilliance of diamonds, while the Chancellor repeated this formula:*

*To the glory of Almighty God, and for your honor and renown, bind your leg with this noble garter, wearing it as a sign and memory of the most illustrious order, never to be forgotten or omitted; by which you are warned that you should have the strength and the will to stand firm in a just war—which is the only kind you shall enter—to act bravely, and to be completely victorious.*

Once the Prince was received in this manner, all his fellow companions congratulated him one by one.

The fees for the Heralds were doubled, by the overflowing grace of the Sovereign; this was because the *most excellent prince* had first been admitted into the order of knights bachelor, and then into the most honorable society of fellow companions, with the ceremonies repeated according to the laws of the order.

The feeling of such great and spontaneous generosity gave the Vice-Chancellor an opportunity to implore further favor from the Sovereign: that the wives of the fellow companions might be permitted on feast days to wear a jeweled garter on their left arms and to use a blue mantle, *as was the ancient custom*. However, without consulting the Queen, the Sovereign decided that nothing should be determined, nor should this favor be granted, unless it were according to the expressed wishes of the noble ladies.

The Collar with the image of Saint George, the Garter, and the other ornaments of the order—which had been worn by the most illustrious Gustavus Adolphus, the unconquered King of the Swedes, during his life, and returned by an honorary legate after his death—were ordered by the Sovereign's decree to be stored in the treasury at *Windsor* under safe custody, in perpetual memory of that most glorious king and fellow companion.

And now, as the morning of May 22nd dawned, the Sovereign proceeded from the council to morning prayers with the princes. He performed offerings combined with prayers, which the excellent prince completed with even more eminent devotion than the others: namely, two vessels made of chased silver, triple-gilded, whose singular workmanship surpassed the material itself. Weighing 387 ounces and valued at 235 pounds, he dedicated them to God at the altar while kneeling, using these words:

> “To You, and to Your perpetual service, I offer a part of Your goodness, Lord God Almighty.”

The most reverend prelate, after saying the usual blessing, set apart the offered vessels for the eternal service of God.

After the assembly, two of the senior fellow companions left their stalls and led the prince—who was dressed only in a scarlet silk tunic and girded with a sword, with the officers preceding him as is custom—to the stall that sits below the Sovereign’s on the right. There he stood until he had taken the solemn oath mentioned above, which the other companions are usually bound by, read from the book of the order by the scribe, namely:

> *I, Charles, being named and elected as one of the eminent knights of this most illustrious military order, promise, and by the holy Gospels of God which I touch, I here clearly swear that I will inviolably observe all the statutes of this order and the articles contained in them, as long as they are not contrary to divine or national laws, so far as they pertain to me. So help me God and His holy Gospels.*

In the native language, it is as follows:

> “I, Charles, being chosen to be one of the honorable Company of this most
> “noble Order of the Garter, do promise and swear by the holy Evange-
> “lists, touched by me here, to inviolably observe all the Statutes of the said
> “Order, or any Articles contained in them; the same being agreeable and not
> “repugnant to the Laws of Almighty God and the Laws of this Realm, as
> “far forth as belongs and pertains to me. So help me God and His
> “holy Word.”

Authorized by this oath, the two said earls immediately adorned him with the blue robe and the honorary mantle, while the Chancellor spoke the customary formula, namely:

> *Receive this mantle of heavenly color, as a sign of this most illustrious order, and for the increase of your honor, marked, as you see, with the red shield of the Lord’s cross—*

...so that, protected always by His virtue and vigor, you may pass safely through your enemies, prevail over them everywhere, and finally, through most noble merits after this remarkable service of the present time, reach eternal and truly triumphal joys.

*Thus in English:*

> "Receive this Robe of heavenly color (the livery of this most excellent
> Order) for the increase of your honor, ennobled with the shield and
> red cross of our Lord, by whose power you may safely pierce the troops
> of your enemies and be ever victorious over them; and being
> glorious in notable and heroic actions in this temporal warfare, you may
> obtain eternal and triumphant joy."

Among the other insignia for which this order is famous, the collar is worn most conspicuously. The collar is of pure gold and is composed of a continuous series of small garters surrounding the united roses of England, connected to each other by elegant links. To this is usually hung a small image of Saint George slaying the dragon, which lies on its back yet fiercely threatens both the horse and the rider; this image, skillfully crafted from many large diamonds, shines no less for its art than for its value.

The Sovereign's neck was encircled with this, while the Chancellor repeated the short prayer mentioned above, *namely:*

> "Wear this Collar about your neck, etc.," changing only the word "Ribbon" for "Collar."

Then a cap of black velvet, encircled by a diamond chain and decorated with a white plume, was placed upon him.

Shining at last with so many and such heroic ornaments, and more shining himself in virtues, he ascended the stall (the first on the right from the Sovereign).

Meanwhile, the number of companions was increased by the unexpected arrival of the Duke of Lennox and the Earl of Kellie.

Furthermore, it is worth remembering that to increase the solemnity, the most venerable prelates gathered here: William, Archbishop of Canterbury; William of London, the High Treasurer of England; Matthew of Ely, Dean of the Royal Chapel; and other excellent men, besides the royal chaplains and the singing ministers of the royal choir; as well as many others of the clergy. All of these men sang the litany in procession until they had passed through the entire chapel and the area intended for the cemetery, dressed partly in white, partly in linen stoles (as our canons are accustomed by rule), and finally partly in embroidered stoles interwoven with gold. The most honorable brotherhood of companions followed this holy procession, and the best part of them were the two Charleses—the son as Prince and the father as Sovereign.

In these processions, the most august King himself, as Sovereign, proceeded under a portable canopy or awning made of velvet, supported by four silver columns. Its upper surface was occupied by the royal insignia interwoven with gold and gems; the other surface was illustrated by the emblem of the Holy Spirit in the form of a descending dove.

Twenty sons of noblemen also attended the Sovereign, partly to carry the said canopy and partly to carry the long train of his robe.

As the most serene Queen watched all these people from the windows of the chamber which hangs over the southeast corner of the chapel, not without an honorary salute to those passing by, she was seized with great delight.

For who would wonder that the august mother of such a child was struck as if astonished at the sight of such amazing royal character in an eight-year-old son? Especially when among the most experienced fellow companions there were few then who fulfilled the laborious duties of those three days with such exact observance, such sweet grace, and such untiring patience to the very end; I call as witnesses the weeping eyes of the spectators, breaking out—

...unequal to such great joys, which were also supported by that spontaneous profession made to the Prince by that heroic old man, the Earl of Arundel:
> *"Today, most excellent Prince, you have caused a blush of shame to spread over us all; for while we were nearly fainting, your stupendous endurance, your invincible constancy while we were sluggish, and your devout piety and observance while we were yawning, are a reproach to us."*

Following the solemnity of the sacred rites and processions to the castle palace, royal banquets succeeded, furnished with every magnificent preparation. Finally, the usual veneration shown to the Sovereign by his fellow knights in the middle of St. George’s Hall brought a conclusion to these; as they rose for the washing of hands, a solemn farewell was also returned by the Sovereign.

It must not be omitted that in the south aisle of St. George’s Chapel, the Register <note>The "Scriba" or Register of the Order was Christopher Wren the elder.</note> had seen to the placement of a diptych; in the center of its face appeared a huge laurel, surrounding the imperial shield of the Sovereign. The laurel itself flourished with thirteen pairs of both leaves and glittering berries on either side, breaking out in the same order as the stalls on each side of the chapel are usually assigned to the fellow knights who are currently living.

This very large votive tablet, skillfully and neatly drawn and crafted, had the following inscription attached:

## Additions,
->From the same man's papers.<-
->Worthy of cedar and marble.<-

In the year of our Lord 1637, on October 2, eleven fellow knights, having venerated the Sovereign at the royal castle of Windsor, began their council.

Silver vessels, triple-gilt and of truly masterful craftsmanship, weighing 1,320 ounces, provided by the piety of the Sovereign and the fellow knights for the use of the Windsor chapel, were ordered by the Sovereign to be offered the next day by the donors. Once offered, they were to be dedicated to the eternal service of God, the best and greatest, by the most reverend prelate of the order.

->From the chapter house, they go to evening prayer.<-

Then, after the sacred rites were finished, a royal supper followed in St. George’s Hall.

On October 3, the Sovereign and the fellow knights repeated the solemnities, beginning with the sacred rites in the chapel; they walked through it, led by the choir dressed in the most precious dalmatics, singing the litany.

And now, when the liturgy had reached the offertory, the most reverend Walter, Bishop of Winchester, prelate of the most noble order, standing before the middle of the altar, spoke certain selected passages from the Old Testament regarding the dedication of Solomon’s temple and its gifts, while the Sovereign and the princes prepared themselves for the offering. The first of these was taken from Exodus 35:4, the second from the same, verse 21, and the third from Saint Matthew 2:11.

As if invited by these, the Sovereign descended from his throne. With three acts of adoration performed in between, worshiping the one God in the middle of the choir, he fell on his knees at the highest steps of the enclosure. Then, he most humbly offered to God a very large basin (of 210 ounces), brought from the nearby table by the hands of the robed canons, using these words, composed in our own language:

> “A small part of your goodness toward us, Almighty God, I offer to be
> “consecrated to you and your service.”

The prelate received the offering and placed it conspicuously upon the altar.

Then further, following this example of the most august King, the fellow knights each offered their own vessel, similar in form and words in every respect.

Nor should it be kept silent that each knight, in addition, cast gold and silver coins (as has always been the custom of those offerings) into another basin held out by a canon. After these were all placed properly upon the table of God, the prelate, laying his hand on them individually as if on God's behalf, used these words in the common tongue:

> “Lord God, heavenly Father, we your most humble servants earnestly beseech you,
> “that you would graciously deign to accept these sacred offerings, presented to
> “you by the hands of the most serene Sovereign and our lord, King Charles, and
> “the most honorable fellow knights who are present here; grant, we pray, and
> “bring it to pass, that whatever has been offered to you today may be preserved
> “from all profane use and remain always consecrated to your service; through
> “Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

## NUMB. VIII.

### Extract from Mr. *Ashmole*, of the *Order of the Garter*.

<margin>P. 497.</margin>
SO THAT it might appear what was given, by whom, and how bestowed towards the furnishing of the altar of the Chapel of St. *George* at *Windsor*, it was appointed that a short historical account of the sacred offerings and gifts should be made and preserved in the Chapter House at *Windsor*.

The book designed for this purpose is now with his *Majesty*, being a large thin folio in vellum, bearing this title:

->Σ Υ Ν  Θ Ε Ω .<-

->*Memoriæ, veritati, virtuti sacrum. Altare liberæ capellæ regiæ Sancti Georgii martyris, infrà castrum regale Windesoriense, amplissimis donariis, Deo optimo maximo per augustissimum supremum, & honoratissimos commilitones nobilissimi ordinis à periscelide dicatis, recenter adauctum, describit humillimus illius ordinis servus & scriba C. Wren, decanus Windesoriensis, Anno Domini 1637.*<-

It contains the orders made in Chapter in 1625, 1630, and 1668, with the commissionary letters issued upon them, together with the names of all the Knights-Companions present at each Chapter.

After these follow the *arms and quarterings*, very fairly limned in metal and color, within a Garter, with a coronet over each suitable to the dignity of the person; and underneath are entered the styles of all the *Knights-Companions* who were of the *Order* in the year 1625, or admitted after, up to the time of making the book; as also the sum which each *Knight* paid to the *Register*. But as to any account of plate provided upon the *Sovereign's* and succeeding Knights-Companions' contributions, there is none, though probably intended to fill up the many blank leaves that followed.

### NUMB. IX.

To the few extracts inserted before from the *Memoirs of the Garter*, compiled by Drs. Matthew and Christopher Wren (in which an idea may be formed of the royal magnificence and eminent piety of King Charles the Martyr), it may be relevant and curious to add the preface of an earlier register and memorial by Dr. Beaumont, the immediate predecessor of Dr. Matthew Wren. This record commences upon the death of King James I and the accession of his only son, Prince Charles, to the imperial throne.

*Charles, the only son and heir of King James of most blessed memory, now deceased, under the highest protection of God and by the ordaining of His divine grace, on the 27th day of March 1625—on the same day and immediately following his father's death—took up the reins of government over his father's kingdoms, as much by his own excellent right as by the greatest applause and joy of all ranks. That this might turn out fortunately for him, to the glory of God, the growth of the Church, and the supreme happiness of the people, as all pray with their most earnest vows; since the prince is so endowed with every virtue and, most importantly, so kindled with zeal for true religion and piety that nothing more can be desired in him, the hope of all most certainly promises them that it will be so.*

*This most certain hope for the excellent rule of such a great king was so deeply fixed in the minds of all that it could not fail to greatly soothe and soften the profound grief felt by everyone for the death of his father, the best of kings throughout the whole world. Indeed, it so filled everyone's hearts with joy that there was a great struggle as to which was greater: the grief for James's departure from the throne or the joy for Charles's accession to it. However, because present blessings and those most certainly hoped to follow are accustomed to bathe the minds of mortals in greater joy than the loss of past things can overwhelm them with grief, the supreme joy felt for Charles’s elevation to the throne finally overcame the grief—though it too was immense—that had invaded the minds of everyone due to James’s death.*

*The most serene King Charles, Sovereign of the most noble Order of the Garter, judged for many reasons that it was not fitting to celebrate the Georgian feast <note>The Feast of St. George</note> this year on the usual days (namely, the 22nd, 23rd, and 24th of April). Primarily, because it would seem most inappropriate for himself or others to be engaged in celebrating feasts before the funeral rites for his father—such a great king—had been piously and duly performed. By a decree made under the seal of the Order, which remains in the hands of Sir George Moore, knight and most worthy Chancellor of this most distinguished Order, he pronounced that the feast should be postponed from those days named above to the 16th, 17th, and 18th of August. He commanded all knights <note>Literally: fellow soldiers</note> of the most illustrious Order, as well as all officers, to be present then to serve His Majesty as was fitting, etc.*

<summary>This page records the 1625 accession of King Charles I following the death of James I, noting the public's transition from mourning to joy. It also details the King's decision to postpone the Feast of St. George until August out of respect for his father's funeral rites.</summary>

## N U M B. X.

### Several items most worthy of note, from the register of the Garter, commonly called the Black Book.

This book was written in the times of King Henry VIII.
*King Henry I, "Beauclerk," established the college of priests at Windsor.*
*The Order named after the garter was devised by King Richard I, but was instituted by Edward III.*
*The French motto is usually worn on one shoulder, on the leg, and sometimes even on the thumb.*
*King Edward III gave the name of the "Blue Garter" to the order.*
*Edward III began St. Stephen’s Chapel at Westminster; King Richard II completed it.*
*King Henry V built the monasteries of Syon and Sheen; he was also the first to wear the imperial crown.*
*The body of King Henry VI, brought to Windsor by Edward IV, was famous for miracles.*
*King Edward IV rebuilt the church at Windsor (originally built by Edward III) on a larger and grander scale; Reginald de Grey, a counselor to King Henry VII, was a great benefactor.*
*The wise and energetic Cardinal Thomas Wolsey, a most favored counselor of the wisest king, predicted in a favorable spirit: "Henry VI began this structure, Henry VII finished it, and Henry VIII shall adorn it." He who gave the power of prophecy to the voice of Balaam <note>A reference to the biblical prophet Balaam</note> granted prophetic virtue to Wolsey's mouth.*
*The history of Saint George of Cappadocia under the tyrant Dacian is asserted by Saint Ambrose; the story of the Dragon and the rescued royal maiden is perhaps apocryphal or allegorical.*
*The heart and a portion of the skull of Saint George are relics at Windsor; the Emperor Sigismund brought the heart when he was admitted into the Order by Henry V.*

### *Of the Works in Mathematics of Sir Christopher Wren.*

Sir CHRISTOPHER WREN, the only son of Dr. *Christopher Wren*, Dean of *Windsor*, was born at *East-Knoyle* in *Wiltshire*, on the 20th day of *October* in the year of our Lord 1632. His mother was *Mary*, daughter and heir of Mr. *Robert [Cox]* of *Fonthill* in the same county.

His first education in *classic* learning was (because of his delicate health) committed to the care of a domestic tutor, the Rev. *William Shepheard*, M.A., except that for some short time before his admission to the university, he was placed under Dr. *Busby* at *Westminster* School.

In the principles of *mathematics*, upon the early appearance of an uncommon genius, he was initiated by Dr. *William Holder*, mentioned before; sometime sub-dean of the *Royal Chapel*; canon-residentiary of *St. Paul’s* and *Ely*, etc. (This gentleman was a great *virtuoso* and a person of many accomplishments, famed for his wonderful skill in making a young gentleman named *Alexander Popham*, who was born deaf and dumb, speak. He wrote an ingenious discourse on the *Elements of Speech* in 1669; had great skill in the theoretical and practical parts of *music*; and published a treatise on the *Natural Grounds and Principles of Harmony* in 1694; and of the

About the same time, he invented a *pneumatic engine*; the description of which, with the diagrams, he thus introduced to his father:

*Permitte mihi obsecro (Reverende Pater) prolusiones meas tuæ semper paternitati vovere; & si arrideant quæ olim in Physicis, De Ortu Fluminum: quæque nuper in Opticis, nova tentavi; solitâ nunc etiam indulgentiâ, Pneumaticum Hoc (quod antè inter otia excogitavi, jamque ad incudem reduxi) excipias rogo.*

He also contrived a peculiar *instrument* for use in *gnomonics*, which he explained in a treatise entitled *Sciotericon Catholicum*: the use and proposed end of which was the solution of this problem, namely: “On a known plane, at a known elevation, to describe such lines with the rapid turning of rundles to certain divisions, as by the shadow of the style may show the equal hours of the day.”

### To his *Most Illustrious Highness* CHARLES, *Prince Elector Palatine of the Rhine*, &c.

*Most Illustrious Prince*,

<margin>Supposed to be Dr. Wilkins.</margin>
<margin>* A planting instrument which, being drawn by a horse over land ready plowed and harrowed, shall plant corn equally without want and without waste.</margin>
<margin>† The Deanery House at *Windsor*, which his Highness occasionally used for retirement and the benefit of the air.</margin>

When, in ancient times, a votive tablet was hung up to some deity or hero, a few small characters, modestly hiding themselves in some shady corner of the piece (as is still the modern custom), were never prohibited from revealing the poor artist and making him somewhat a sharer in the devotion. Indeed, I was almost prompted to such a presumption out of my own zeal for a Prince who is so much a *mercurialium custos virorum* <note>Guardian of scholarly men</note>, but the learned devotee who consecrates these tables to your Highness (being one who allows me to be a most devoted client of his) civilly assisted my affection for your Highness by adding his commands for me to offer this gift. And had not my too indulgent patron—by undeservedly thinking them not unfit for his own presentation (though exceedingly beneath your Highness's acceptance)—robbed me of my humility and taken away the extremely low thoughts I should otherwise have had of them, I must have called the first device but a rustic thing concerning agriculture only\*, and therefore an unrefined art, tending only to the saving of corn, and improper in that glorious, bountiful soil of yours, where every shower of hail must necessarily press from the hills even torrents of wine. The other concept I must have deplored as a late invention, coming impertinently into the world now after the divine *German* art of printing. Of the third paper I cannot say anything too little; it is enough of an understatement to say that they are two mites, two living nothings—no, but painted nothings, the shadow of nothing; and this shadow rarified, even to forty thousand times its former extension. If it presents you with anything in nature, it is but with a pair of atoms. Now, if it be possible for your Highness to force yourself to accept such extreme littlenesses as these, you will therein imitate the Divinity, which shows itself *maxime in minimis* <note>Most greatly in the smallest things</note>, and preserve that devotion toward your Highness which I conceived while still a child, when you were pleased to honor my father’s house with your presence for some weeks†; he, therefore, must eternally retain a sense of being

->*Your Highness’s most humble and*<-
->*most devoted Servant*,<-

->CHRISTOPHER WREN.<-

Regarding his aforementioned tract, titled *Sciotericon*, and other inventions and experiments related to gnomonics <note>the art of constructing sundials</note> made at the age of sixteen, there is a memorable complimentary account from an eminent mathematician of that time, as follows:

> ->Most Distinguished Young Man,<-
>
> I have received your *Sciotericon*, which is most accurately constructed and acts as a faithful interpreter of the sun's path; indeed, I have examined it with the greatest pleasure. Moreover, I am at a loss whether to congratulate the artist's skill or the author's gift more; I admire and cherish both with amazement. In it, the daily rotation of the sun and its annual approach and departure within the solstitial limits are measured; indeed, the very face of the heavens and the varied regions are set out to be contemplated at a single glance. It is an *instrument of instruments*, rejoicing in no other choice than its own, and certainly more infallible than the invention of the magnetic needle; for you subject that foreign, haughty guidance to your own command and, without its aid, reconcile them in true harmony, ordering it (once your hand is removed) to stay fixed to your purpose. Furthermore, your wonders are not confined within the circle of this sundial. In your father's house, specimens of your skill and the remains of refined philosophy—to be preferred above all tapestries—are displayed; and as the occasion arises, in the chambers, in the dining rooms, and through whatever windows the sun sends its rays, you subject them to the rules of gnomonics. Nor is this done by the contrary arrangement of celestial motion (such as is usually directed between an analemma and a clock), but by an emulating projection of the very solar circuit itself (by the benefit of reflected light). So that the sun, brought down from its sphere, exults like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber and like a giant to run his course. How happy you are! You who bring Phoebus himself before our sight. What a harvest do these seeds of a younger age promise? Nor do I wrongly predict that you, having entered the storehouses and the mysteries of that kind of study, were born to advance their delights and to open up lands still unknown on this globe with the key of your investigation; so much do you apply your strength to it. I pray most earnestly that this may turn out fortunately for you. Farewell, jewel of mathematicians, and love me.
>
> On the day of the salutary passion <note>Good Friday</note>, <span style="display:inline-block; width: 100px;"></span> your most observant,
> 10 April 1649. <span style="display:inline-block; width: 135px;"></span> THOMAS AYLESBURY.

<margin>Exists in the possession of the collector.</margin>
At the age of sixteen, he devised and modeled on pasteboard, illustrated with curious astronomical drawings in appropriate colors, a new hypothesis titled *Hypotyposis Prosthaphæreseon Lunæ* <note>A Preliminary Description of the Lunar Equations</note>, in which its cycles according to Tycho Brahe’s calculations are accurately demonstrated by this new hypothesis.

About the same age, he translated into Latin a tract of Mr. *Oughtred’s* *Clavis Mathematica* [a truly golden key], namely the part on *Geometrical Dialling*; which that eminent and learned mathematician published with his other works, inserting this memorable remark in his preface:

Clavis Mathematica
Preface.

> ——— Moreover, that part which teaches the geometric theory of scioteric clocks [sundials], Mr. *Christopher Wren*, a gentleman commoner of Wadham College, translated from the English idiom into Latin. He is a youth of truly admirable genius who, not yet sixteen years old, has enriched astronomy, gnomonics, statics, and mechanics with distinguished inventions; from that time he continues to enrich them; and truly he is one from whom I can expect great things, and not in vain, very soon.

The letter mentioned above to the Reverend Mr. Oughtred was in this form:

<margin>That is, of Mathematics.</margin>
->To the Venerable Author<-
->of the truly **Golden Key**;<-
->The Great Geometer of his Age<-
->(If any has been such since the heroes<-
->Apollonius and Diophantus),<-
->An Eternal Ornament. Greetings.<-

*So appropriately in this age of ours, most distinguished sir, has your <term>Key</term> shone forth from the sphere of the mathematical arts, that even the most skilled have recognized it as a faithful guiding star. And not undeservedly, since now, with you as their leader, they navigate the turbulent and wide ocean of algebra with sure and safe rowing, so that they may gradually discover those remaining parts of mathematics still unknown. But there were certain short-sighted people among the common crowd who blamed this Remarkable Star as if it were obscure and cloudy—just like those smaller sparks in the sky which, although they are truly immense and bright, and do not yield in size to this globe of ours, nor perhaps to the others in the same choir, yet because they lie hidden in the vast abyss of the heavens, they lose their glory by their extreme height and escape all common sight. Most excellently, therefore, looking out for the splendor of your work, you made this most beautiful star more visible (in the second editions) to both our own and the Latin horizons. However, in the Latin hemisphere, it appeared unaccompanied by that torch which so elegantly illustrated the art of <term>horologiography</term> <note>The art of making clocks or sundials</note>. Therefore, so that it might also come forth attached to your <term>Key</term> in a more worthy language (like a pearl hanging from a gem), the most famous Dr. Scarborough ordered me to apply my meager efforts to this matter. He is a man whose friendship is not so foreign to you, nor is the splendor of his genius so unknown to the learned, that I need to describe him as being most skilled in medicine and the deeper secrets of these arts, as well as in almost every kind of refined literature. To his kindness and most open character, I owe no small part of my slight taste for mathematics (if I have any); indeed, I owe my very life to his skill when I recently languished with illness, as if by the "Hand of God." Forgive me, therefore, best of men, that out of obedience to him—which is sacred to me for so many reasons—I might offend your gravity while I attempted to adapt a boy’s style to your writings. Your works do not seek the allurements of words, but shine forth more through their own characteristic brevity—a brevity, I say, so full and packed with meaning to the very tips of the letters. For you have rightly rejected in your <term>Key</term> the reasoning common to mortals but unsuited to mysteries; and by symbols and notes, without a perplexed heap of words, you instill your wonderful concepts into the minds of readers almost at a single glance. This is a difficult method indeed, but all the more divine; for this, it seems to me, is to imitate the heavenly beings, who, not hindered by the delay of human speech, reveal mysteries to one another simply by directing the mind. Religiously, therefore, in this <term>Horologiography</term> of yours, I have tried to render almost word for word (although you perhaps wrote this part somewhat more loosely than was appropriate, since it pertains more to practice). Truly, I feared lest by my ignorance even one point of that science might be lost—a science in which I consider it a great glory to be a sufficiently teachable beginner. I highly desire this: that (though I am still unknown to you) you might number me among your most observant admirers.*

->CHRISTOPHER WREN.<-

# SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.

->*He may be able to recite in order, and bring into use, the propositions and demonstrations of Archimedes and several others of the ancients.*<-

Mr. Christopher Wren was an assistant to the aforementioned Dr. Scarborough in anatomical preparations and experiments, especially concerning the muscles of human bodies, during their studies at Oxford and elsewhere. In particular, he explained, using models made of pasteboard, *the anatomical administration of all the muscles of a human body as they naturally appear during dissection, etc.*, for the use of Dr. Scarborough’s celebrated lectures in the public theater at Surgeons' Hall. According to reliable reports, these models were deposited in that theater and destroyed in the Great Fire of London. This led to the first introduction of geometrical and mechanical speculation into anatomy.

## *The Reformed Zodiac.*

*My mind is moved to sing of the halls of heaven, radiating with manifold light,*
*And the sacred uses of the stars, whatever they may be, which the vain*
*Superstition of an ancient age had foully distorted. You, whom a most pure*

*Who by a single nod force the wandering stars into their patterns,*

*While I sing of your deeds, and while I set to rhythm the vast work*

*With a foolish soul submerged in long darkness,*
*May lift itself to heaven; and while it stands amazed at the flaming lights*
*Of the world, it may give honor to you alone as the author,*
*And conform the various uses of the stars to those of the Sacred Book.*

*Therefore, these ethereal fires shining in the night,*

(The Egyptians and their fickle minds) twisted the inventions of their ancestors into their own trifles, and thrust shameful monsters into heaven. For what ear would not shudder at Pasiphaë joined to a Bull? Or the Thunderer (Jupiter) as a Cow? And the incestuous beds and unspeakable crimes of the gods, and the dishes that would excuse even the tables of Thyestes? <margin>* Namely, Saturn devouring his own sons.</margin> But though a nation ignorant of eternal law and a despiser of the true God, the poets wandered foolishly—is it right that these names should still be preserved for the stars among Christians? Was it fitting for the students of the heavenly homeland to defile their future seat with these stains? Why should we silently allow the heavenly kingdoms to be credited to the honor of anyone other than the True Creator? Since poets used to celebrate the gods and the famous deeds of men under the forms of the stars, why is it not more rightful for us to sing of the noble deeds of God and the miracles of His right hand, dispersed throughout the world? Whenever we look up at the immense hall of starry Olympus, let us adapt the ancient figures of the stars to stories sought from the holy fountain of Scripture.

## Aries ♈.

Here the prince of the Zodiac and the gatekeeper of the year meets me (where the Equator line cuts the oblique zone and warns that the darkness is equal to the light), the leader of the flock, shining with a starry fleece. Because he once carried Phryxus and Phryxus's sister across the sea when they fled the anger and deceit of their stepmother, Jupiter placed him in heaven (so says lying fame). But by what merit was this? Did he owe such great honors to a beast (because it was the carrier of fugitives) that he should raise it to the heavens? Bah, sterile trifles! For what are these ravings worth? But how much better, Christian, looking upon the shining lights of heaven, might you call the one rising with Phoebus during the Easter holidays the **Paschal Lamb** of the Lord?

<margin>Gen. 22:13.</margin>
Just as that Ram was, when the Patriarch was preparing the sacrifice, who offered himself at the altar (as a substitute) in place of Isaac; he is worthy for this reason to grace the bright figures of heaven, because he presented himself as a pledge for Christ and as a type of Christ. He himself (as if still hiding in the Bramble) is barely seen there, where he leads the constellations with eighteen small stars: and, though he is swept headlong toward the western world, he turns his returning eyes toward the rising sun.

## Taurus ♉.

Next to the Wool-bearer (Aries), turned toward the rosy dawn, the bright, kneeling Taurus boasts his stars; whether he be the carrier of Europa to the Cretan shores, or the infamous Bull of your wicked love, Pasiphaë; it is not our part to splatter a sacred song (much less the heavens) with such crimes.

*Or if it is permitted for the crimes of sinning nations to be inscribed in heaven, why should that Golden Calf \* not be rightly recognized here? It was that calf which the rebellious crowd of Israelites once celebrated with foolish honors on the mountains of Horeb (having broken the divine covenant). But now, carried up to heaven (a memorable sign of a treaty-breaking race), it is seen in the center of the celestial sphere, glittering at night with thirty-two stars. Of these, the one that shines most brightly in the right eye is the star of the Egyptian god Remphan †, into whose empty worship the mindless rabble shamefully fell, and for which they deservedly wept in exile on the shores of Babylon. The Hyades appear scattered across the forehead and horns, along with those stars that illuminate the back with a seven-fold lamp; these are the tears of the Israelites, the atonement for so great a crime. Even now they are accustomed to soak the earth with pouring rains when they first accompany the Sun from his moist rising, and they show by this sign from what origin they were born; for this reason, they have been called by the Greeks by a name meaning "rain-bringers" ‡.*

### Gemini ♊.

<margin>|| Genesis 25:21.</margin>
*The constellations of the Twins follow the Bull (where the climbing chariot of the Sun scorches the Libyan sands, and the Colure divides the new summers from the spring). These were (as the fables of ancient poets imagined) the offspring of Leda and the deceits of the Thundering Swan; their piety earned them heaven and ethereal dances as they shared life and death in turn. Specifically, Pollux—recognized as the offspring of Jove and exempt from death—alternately honors his brother, who was born of mortal seed, by sharing his divinity. A noble pair of brothers! Unless the sacred page had mentioned to us Rebecca ||, pregnant with a nobler pair. Of these, Jacob—selected by the Eternal Judge—is better suited to represent Pollux, while Esau corresponds to Castor. They are brothers born of prayer, the discord of a doubting mother. They are heavy burdens, grasping for the birthright in the very act of birth (while the elderly father Isaac and his once-sterile wife were amazed at the womb swelling with a twin fetus). Now they are also seen naked on the starry arena, holding struggling chests in a tight embrace; they vibrate their entwined radiance with eighteen lights.*

### Cancer ♋.

*Am I mistaken? Or has the Sun now reached the arms of the sea-dwelling Cancer, scorching our world with constant heat, and scarcely admitting the reins of night. They say Hercules was pressed by this foot into heaven (for no other merit or origin) because, sent by Juno, it bit his heel with its claws. Surely he would rather have let it perish buried in the earth than be inscribed in heaven, for he had felt it as an enemy while he lived.*

*Will divine poetry allow the shining kingdoms of the heavens to be exposed to such futile trifles? ### Leo ♌.

*Do not wonder that the grim Lion accompanies the flocks, and that the untamed beast has laid aside its ancient furies; recognize that the peaceful heaven, within the various vault of the sphere, repeats its melody and powerful measures, and the stars lead their dances in a harmonic cycle. Yet, not yet quite forgetful of its innate anger, it still breathes fires and glows with a panting chest, especially when Sirius urges it to rage. They say that this lion once fell in the Nemean woods by the blow of Hercules' club; Juno transferred the slain beast to the stars, lighting it with thirty-three flames, besides five smaller ones.*

*Seeking that the harvests may fare well, while the stars of the grain-bearing Virgin watch the retreating axle of Hyperion.* <note>Hyperion is often used to refer to the Sun.</note> *Whether she was Ceres, who looks far across the fruitful fields, favoring the prayers of the eager farmer; or Isis, driven by furies through the whole world, now an Egyptian deity after being a cow; or if instead fair Astraea should claim this seat, leaving the earth, where she shines surrounded by thirty-two stars. <margin>* Judges 11:30, 31, 34.</margin>

A marvelous glory of the female sex—unless you, Mother, you Spouse of God, you that root of the divine vine, the undefiled Virgin Mary, should overshadow the lesser torch with a much greater light. By the breath of the Godhead alone, knowing no man, your holy womb swelled with the savior offspring, and you gave birth to God with your virgin flower uninjured. Let these beautiful stars shine for your praise, and let your name vibrate before them with trembling flames.*

### Libra ♎︎.

*But now in the middle path of the zodiacal circle, Libra, measuring the durations of light with an equal balance, meeting the darkness and the excessive heat with harsh cold, displays twice four and nine stars* <note>Seventeen stars.</note> *. This is the scale of the Virgin Astraea (so the poets say) with which the Virgin was accustomed to judge the deeds of men on earth with the equal weight of the balance. Now, placed at the pole beneath her mistress's feet (where the colure divides the zodiac into equal parts), she separates the borders of autumn from the summer heat. She acknowledges the Etnean god* <note>Vulcan.</note> *, who presides over the Sicilian caves, as her craftsman; for he had forged it from pure gold and placed the Scales among the stars as a noble monument of his smithing labor. Did you, dirty and club-footed, forge the splendid stars? Am I to believe that a part of heaven shines with the smoky embers of the Cyclopes? Let these stars rather record the supreme wisdom of the Creator and the great power of his right hand, which rules the immense world with just governance and governs the night-wandering lights, and gives the sun its own brilliance. It is this power that commands the balanced mass of the earth and the sea to stay suspended in the middle of the air, and holds the vast ocean in a capable palm, and surrounds the spacious halls of heaven with its hands, and hangs the low-lying mountains with equal weight. It bridles the clouds, waters the thirsty fields with the desired rains, and prudently tempers all things in this twofold structure, just as if they were hanging in the perfectly balanced scale of a balance.*

### Scorpio ♏

*What new face does the sky now wear? Or what horrid North wind saddens the declining year and sharpens the air? Truly, Scorpio now slows the golden reins of Phoebus <note>Phoebus is a name for the Sun.</note>, and the exhausted earth can scarcely endure the weakened rays and the fading lights, stained with the cold poison of the lethal sting. A huge monster extends its arms widely and winds the black curves of its tail in a long circuit; it is sprinkled everywhere with twenty-three sparks <note>The twenty-three stars of the constellation Scorpio.</note>. These sparks Jove is said to have placed as a memorable sign of the defeated Orion; for when, boasting of his strength, he mocked all things and despised the animals of the earth, the angry earth set this monster against him, which subdued his proud tongue with its cruel sting—the sting of the urine-born <note>An allusion to the mythical birth of Orion from the hide of an ox upon which Jupiter, Neptune, and Mercury had urinated.</note>. If vain superstition derives empty lessons for men from the stars, this discovery pleases us better as a superior emblem: the Creator of the world inserted this sign into the heavens so that they might learn the hard and difficult approaches to the sky, and the path which leads to the seats above, an journey scarcely penetrable. It leads through monsters of beasts and the horrendous Scorpion, who wounds the veins with the dire sting of its tail and instills sudden poison. Hardly otherwise does the deceitful torturer of dark Avernus <note>Avernus refers to the underworld or Hell; the torturer is Satan.</note> infest the just man and the faithful minister of Christ, seeking everywhere with an insatiable mouth whom he may devour. Go far away, you timid ones, and stay away from this holy seat, you in whose heart fear stands fixed; go far away, you fugitives! But you heroes! You holy phalanx of the pious, blessed in sacred wars and pledged to Christ your master; proceed, great-hearted ones, protected by the faithful shield of salvation and armed with the sword of the holy spirit. Seek the path to heaven through horrid monsters, through steep places, and through the inaccessible; cross the obstacles of the world; finally the time will come when these eternal seats, and a certain rest from labors, shall be granted above the stars. There, neither the hostile weapon nor the wrath of the asp shall trouble holy souls, nor shall there be cause of death, nor fear, nor the madness of Satan. Safely you shall walk upon the dark Scorpion, and you shall trample the burning snakes of Erebus, rejoicing to celebrate the eternal triumphs of Christ, after the high-thundering Judge has descended from the sky, bringing back the victorious signs in his triumphal flesh. Then you shall see death swallowed up; then you shall see Lucifer, shut in his blind prison, striving in vain and foaming with sulfurous fires from the black jaws of Avernus.*

### Sagittarius ♐

*Behold how the Archer, intent on his breathless course, hunts and surveys the starry regions of vast Olympus with his darts, about to send a swift and dire arrow from his threatening string against the monsters of heaven.*

->Extract of a Letter written, as it seems, in the year 1649, when he was 17 years old.<-

->To my Reverend Father, Doctor WREN.<-

Reverend Father,

<margin>After Martial.</margin>
**H**aving been received by the most kind hospitality of my closest friends, I have spent these Easter holidays here; and you may judge with how much delight from this very brief praise of the place: It is a distinguished house (or rather a palace not unworthy of a prince, whether you consider its size, the beauty of its structure, or the splendor of its furnishings) situated almost at the very top of a very high hill. Most pleasant gardens lie around it, filled with countless paths, paved as much with stone as with mountain turf. Nor are there lacking huge fishponds or very tall groves, whose tops—the noisy republics of the rooks—are burdened with the villages of their nests, or rather entire cities. A deer park also lies adjacent, quite large and pleasant. You would certainly say it is a terrestrial paradise outside, but inside, heaven itself (and indeed more truly than the poet said of Caesar's palace, "The house is in heaven, but the master is better"). For why should I not call this most blessed place *Heaven*? In it, ancient piety and religion, driven from the wicked lands, are said to have finally found a refuge; here all the virtues do not merely visit, as they often do elsewhere, but love to dwell. The threefold graces (divine ones, of course) have chosen this place for themselves, as if it were their own Parnassus or evangelical Pindus. Here, finally, holy mothers and virgins spend almost the entire day in the most blessed company of God and the angels, by singing divine songs, offering the most chaste incense of prayers, or by sacred reading, meditation, and conversation. Among so many delights, what would it be but TAUTOLOGY to write that I am doing well? Hardly anything more could certainly be desired for my great happiness, provided that you yourself are well, and give your blessing to

->Your most obedient son,<-

<margin>March 28.</margin>
->CHRISTOPHER WREN.<-

<margin>Anonymous.</margin>
At the age of nineteen, he composed a short algebraic tract relating to the *Julian Period*, which is of great use in chronology. This was *inserted* in the fifth edition of *Helvicus's Historical and Chronological Theater*, following the introduction. Printed at *Oxford*, in the year 1651.

<margin>See the manuscript notes on Helvicus's Chronological Theater by Dean Christopher Wren.</margin>
This highly useful <note>Highly useful</note>, clear, and most appropriate work for chronological matters (in which one is taught to find and extract the year of the Julian period from given cycles), which was attached to the fifth edition of Helvicus, was obtained from the author by the printer only with great difficulty. That excellent young man of nineteen years modestly judged it a sight not quite worthy of Helvicus's *Theater*. Regarding this matter, his Reverend Father recorded this note: "Finally, I encouraged my modestly resisting son to allow that little algebraic tract—most suitable for finding the Julian period from cycles given in history—to be placed at the beginning, as the Oxford press was then at work."

In 1650, he graduated as a Bachelor of Arts at *Wadham College*; in 1653, Master of Arts; and in the same year, he was elected to a fellowship at *All Souls*. In 1657, he was chosen as Professor of Astronomy at *Gresham College* in *London*; and in 1660, Savilian Professor of Astronomy in the University

## *Preamble of a* CHARTER *to incorporate the* Royal Society, <note>from a first essay and rough draft by Mr. Christopher Wren.</note>

### CHARLES, etc.

**W**HEREAS amongst our regal hereditary titles (to which by divine Providence, and the loyalty of our good subjects, we are now happily restored) nothing appears to us more august, or more suitable to our pious disposition, than that of *Father of our Country*, a name of indulgence as well as dominion; wherein we would imitate the benevolence of Heaven, which in the same shower yields thunder and violets, and no sooner shakes the cedars, but dissolving the clouds, drops fatness. We therefore, out of a paternal care of our people, resolve, together with those laws which tend to the good administration of government, and the people's allegiance to us, inseparably to join the supreme law of <term>Salus Populi</term>, that obedience may be manifestly not only the public but private happiness of every subject, and the great concern of his satisfactions and enjoyments in this life. —— The way to so happy a government, we are sensible is in no manner more facilitated than by the promoting of useful arts and sciences, which, upon mature

It describes how the group moved from Oxford to Gresham College in London before being officially established after the Restoration of King Charles II.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the text related to the founding of the Royal Society, providing the rationale and royal justification for its establishment as drafted or supported by Sir Christopher Wren.</meta>

<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

Upon mature inspection, these are found to be the basis of civil communities and free governments, which gather multitudes, by an *Orphean* charm, into cities, and connect them in *companies*; so that, by laying in a stock, as it were, of several arts and methods of industry, the whole body may be supplied by a mutual commerce of each other’s peculiar faculties; and consequently that the various miseries and toils of this frail life may, by as many various expedients ready at hand, be remedied or alleviated; and wealth and plenty diffused in just proportion to every one’s industry—that is, to every one’s deserts.

And there is no question but the same policy that founds a city also nourishes and increases it; since these mentioned allurements to a desire of cohabitation do not only cause the population of a country, but render it more potent and wealthy than a more populous but more barbarous nation; it being the same thing to add more hands, or, by the assistance of art, to facilitate labor and bring it within the power of the few.

Therefore our reason has suggested to us, and our own experience in our travels in foreign kingdoms and states has abundantly confirmed, that we should effectively prosecute the advancement of <term>natural experimental philosophy</term>, especially those parts of it which concern the increase of commerce by the addition of useful inventions tending to the ease, profit, or health of our subjects. This will best be accomplished by a company of ingenious and learned persons, well qualified for this sort of knowledge, who will make it their principal care and study, and be constituted a regular *society* for this purpose, endowed with all proper privileges and immunities.

Not that in this we would withdraw the least ray of our influence from the present established nurseries of good literature and education, founded by the piety of our royal ancestors and others to be the perpetual fountains of religion and laws—that religion and those laws which, as we are obliged to defend, so the holy blood of our martyred father has inseparably endeared to us. Instead, we purpose to make further provision for this branch of knowledge likewise, <term>natural experimental philosophy</term>, which comprehends all that is required toward those intentions we have recited; taking care in the first place for religion, and so next for the riches and ornament of our kingdoms, as we wear an imperial crown in which flowers are alternately intermixed with the *ensigns of Christianity*.

And whereas we are well informed that a competent number of persons of eminent learning, ingenuity, and honor, agreeing in their inclinations and studies toward this employment, have for some time accustomed themselves to meet weekly and orderly to confer about the hidden causes of things—with a design to establish certain and correct uncertain theories in philosophy, and by their labors in the investigation of nature to prove themselves real benefactors to mankind—and that they have already made a considerable progress by various useful and remarkable discoveries, inventions, and experiments in the improvement of <term>mathematics</term>, <term>mechanics</term>, <term>astronomy</term>, <term>navigation</term>, <term>physic</term> <note>At the time, "physic" referred to the art of healing or medicine.</note>, and <term>chemistry</term>; we have determined to grant our royal favor, patronage, and all due encouragement to this illustrious assembly and so beneficial and laudable an enterprise. — Know therefore, etc.

Mr. *Henry Oldenburg*, the first Secretary to the *Royal Society*, with a lack of integrity and a breach of trust, communicated and secretly conveyed to foreign parts, particularly *Germany* and *France*, various inventions and original experiments of the *Author*; which were afterwards unfairly claimed by others as the true inventors and published abroad under other names.

As the first ideas and essays of ingenious minds have their own special weight with fair and discerning *virtuosi*; the following papers are inserted here, appearing to be the original sketch, in an *English* dress, of an *Inauguration Speech* delivered by Mr. *Wren* in *Latin* at *Gresham College* from the *Astronomy Chair* upon his election to that professorship. The oration still exists and may have a place among his more complete works; however, the subjoined extract—containing some particulars omitted in his public speech, as well as several variations from it and some things (perhaps) explanatory of it—is of further use or entertainment to the curious.

### The Speech.

LOOKING with respectful awe on this great and eminent audience—while here, I see some of the more refined geniuses of our age; here, some of our nobles; there many exceptionally learned in the mathematical sciences, and everywhere, those who are more judges than listeners—I cannot help but betray, with youthful blushes, that for which I must apologize. And indeed, I must seriously fear lest I should appear prematurely eager for fame by daring to ascend the Chair of Astronomy and to take up that powerful word of demonstration, *Dico* <note>"I say" or "I declare," a term used by mathematicians to introduce a proof.</note>; with which (while the humble orator only suggests) the authoritative mathematician commands agreement. It would have better suited the bashfulness of my years to have spent more *lustra* <note>Five-year periods.</note> in a *Pythagorean* silence.

I must confess I had never intended anything further than to practice my geometry in private, unless *those*—whom I may account the great ornaments of learning and our nation, whom it is sacred for me to obey, and *who*, with the support of the worthy senators of this honorable *city*, had pushed me into the public arena—had spoken against my laziness and neglect with continual but friendly encouragement. This was so that, according to my slender abilities, I might explain what has been delivered to us by the ancients concerning the motions and appearances of the celestial bodies, and likewise what has been newly discovered by the moderns; for we have no barren age. And now in this place, I could point to *inventors*; *inventors*, a title so venerable of old that it was merit enough to grant men the status of *divinity* and perpetual adoration.

Nor do I need, for such a knowledgeable audience, to relate to what end or to praise *Hercules* (as they say) by troubling you with a tedious praise of astronomy. We shall leave this to the *Dutch* writers, whose swelling title pages proclaim that their books are useful to theologians, philosophers, philologists, mathematicians, grammarians, and who not? It would be trivial to tell you how much astronomy elevates herself above other sciences, since her subject—the beautiful heavens (infinite in extent, pure and subtle, and eternal in matter, glorious in their starry ornaments, of which every one offers various cause for wonder, most rapid yet most regular, most harmonious in their motions, and in everything to a wise observer, awesome and majestic)—precedes either the lowly or the uncertain subjects of other sciences. It would be pedantic to tell you of the affinity of our souls to heaven, or of our upright faces, given to us on purpose for astronomical observation; or to acquaint you that *Plato* recommended it to his statesmen when he says:
> "From such
> disciplines, a certain instrument of the mind is purified and revived, which
> previously had been clouded and blinded by other studies; for by this alone is 
> truth perceived."
Though truly elsewhere he gives us this great truth:
> "Have you noticed that those who are naturally mathematical appear sharper 
> in almost all disciplines? And those who are slower in intellect, if they are 
> trained in this, even if they gain no other benefit, usually become more 
> intelligent than they were before."
I might be too wordy should I give specific examples showing how much the mathematical minds of this age have excelled the ancients (who pierced only to the bark and outside of things) in handling particular inquiries into nature, in clarifying history, and in fixing chronology. For mathematical demonstrations, being built upon the unbreakable foundations of geometry and arithmetic, are the only truths that can sink into the mind of man free of all uncertainty; and all other discourses

<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

disciplines participate more or less in Truth, according to how much their subjects are more or less capable of mathematical demonstration. Therefore, this rather than Logic is the great instrument (*Organon*) of all infallible science; although I will not exclude Logic from being an instrument of reasoning, but rather include it within Geometry. For the technical and most useful part of it, concerning syllogism and the art of reasoning, is merely a geometrical ordering of the *data* through *proportional means* to determine the *question at hand*. It would be endless to run through the whole circle of knowledge and show you in every part the great use of astronomy; even Queen Theology has been much indebted to the trusty service of this handmaid (*ancilla*), in settling sacred history by the help of chronology. Chronology, as it is a part of astronomy, is built chiefly upon the unerring chronicles of the *deeds of the gods and the heavens*—observations of eclipses, great conjunctions, and similar appearances. Without these indexes of time, all sacred and profane history would be but unorganized heaps and labyrinths, where men are at a loss for where to begin or end. But Chronology (a thing too much neglected by the ancients) has given a ground plan (*ichnography*) of this labyrinth, and described times as if on a map, by which we may safely run back through many thousands (*chyliads*) of years, conversing with those of remote ages and there finding new discoveries, just as through navigation we converse with those of distant climates.

Some, perhaps, will frown if I should say that even Holy Scripture itself sometimes requires an astronomical interpreter; who else shall give a good account of the *Hexaemeron* <note>The six days of creation.</note>, or decide the controversy about the backward movement of the shadow upon the sundial of *Ahaz*? This might be done in many ways without a miracle, by the mere construction of the dial; for it is easy to build a sundial with such a style <note>The gnomon or pointer of a sundial.</note> that every day at a certain time, the shadow will seem to return. But what that dial was, we know if we may believe the *Hebrew* writer, who describes it obscurely, yet in such a way that I can easily imagine it to be the same as that used by the *Eastern* nations, which *Vitruvius* tells us *Berossus the Chaldean* brought into *Greece*—*a hemicycle hollowed out of a square, and cut to the inclination, that is, to the elevation of the pole*. The backward movement must therefore be real, either in the sun or the shadow only. But what if it were truly in neither, but caused by a *parhelion* <note>A mock sun or sundog.</note>? The sun returned ten degrees by which it had gone down; might not a *parhelion* suddenly appear at ten degrees distance from the sun, while the sun was just set below the horizon or hidden by a cloud? (For *parhelia* are refractions made in nitrous vapors higher than the clouds.) Thus, the shadow of this *parhelion* would create the appearance as if the sun had started back; it is what *Cadamosto* and other describers of the *East Indies* say happens often on the island of *Sumatra* in the month of *April*; for ten or fifteen degrees the sun seems to start back and then return again to where it otherwise would have appeared. This may be done either by a *parhelion* or a strong refraction through a vapor in an angular form, like a glass prism, passing between the eye and the sun; for if you gently pass a crystal prism before any objects, the objects will appear to jump out of their places. Nor should we fear to diminish a miracle by explaining it; this backward movement of the sun was given as a sign, just as the rainbow was; had the rainbow never appeared since, it would have been considered miraculous.

I might ask the theologian: who shall explain to me how our *Saviour*, who was buried on *Friday* night and rose again before daybreak on *Sunday*, could be said to be three days and three nights in the sepulchre, when his stay there was only one full day and two nights? The world has hitherto avoided this difficulty with a *synecdoche*—by including parts of *Friday* and parts of *Sunday*—but they still lack a third night. Neither does *Grotius*, with
