An interpretation sometimes of any part of a day or night for a whole *nycthemeron* <note>a 24-hour period consisting of one day and one night</note>, in civil law, does not much improve the matter. Here there seems to be a need for an astronomer, who might possibly explain it thus: While there was created by the motion of the sun a day and two nights in the hemisphere of *Judaea*, at the same time in the opposite hemisphere there was created a night and two days; join these together, and you have three days and three nights. For *Christ* suffered not for *Judaea* alone, but for the whole world; and in respect of all the inhabitants of the earth *jointly*, he rested three days and three nights, though in respect of *Judaea*, or any particular horizon, it was but one day and two nights.

Who but the astronomer shall explain to us how many hundred times one of the great luminaries exceeds the other—which yet is but one of some thousands as great as itself, or larger? Who can better magnify the arm that expanded the heavens than he who tells you that *seven thousand* miles will fall short of the diameter of this earth, and yet that this diameter repeated a *thousand* times will not reach the sun; or this distance between the sun and us, repeated a *thousand* times, reach the nearest fixed star? And yet, in all probability, some are infinitely more remote than others. Certainly, just as it is only from the secretaries of princes that true histories of those princes are to be expected, so only he can truly describe the world whose skill in astronomy has given him a right to the glorious title of *Hipparchus*: to be a "participant and interpreter of the councils of nature."

But not to dwell on extending the dominion of astronomy to the *Empyrean* <note>the highest part of heaven</note>; her influence is great over earthly sciences. Among these, should I say that even medicine has its use for astronomy, I might seem to patronize the groundless fancies of that sort of astrological medicasters who do nothing without the favor of their *Archaeus*, and assign one planet or another to every herb or drug—which they suppose invalid unless mystically timed with this or that aspect, ceremoniously numbering the critical days, not considering that neither time nor number has any reality *outside the human intellect*. But, though with contempt for these follies, let me seriously ask the most rational philosophical inquirer into medicine whether those aphorisms in which *Hippocrates* has marshaled diseases under the seasons of the year, the various winds, and the varieties of weather, do not have as much truth in them as the rest. Were they not as diligently collected from the *bronze tables*, from experiments derived in succession from his aged preceptors before him, and from his own unerring industry as the rest? 

But it may be objected that these astrological aphorisms favor much the *Chaldean* and *Syrian* styles, from whom it appears the *Greeks* received much of their art of healing, as they did almost all their other learning. And indeed we find from *Herodotus* that the knowledge of medicine by way of aphorism was proper to the *Babylonians*, who publicly recorded the history of the disease and method of cure for every particular patient that recovered; to these records others resorted in difficult cases involving similar diseases. Since the great learning of these nations was astrology, we may imagine that they made good observations of epidemic diseases from the distempers of the air and from celestial influences—which are now either wholly lost, corrupted, or useless, as they are not suited to our climate. I know not what other subject those medicinal books of the friend and contemporary of *Hippocrates*, *Democritus*, titled <term>ΠΕΡΙ ΑΚΑΙΡΙΩΝ ΚΑΙ ΕΠΙΚΑΙΡΙΩΝ</term> <note>"On unseasonable and seasonable times"</note> and reckoned in the catalogue of his works by *Laertius*, should contain. I am certain that if we dissected animals of the same species during various changes of weather, we would find a great difference in the brain regarding dryness, moisture, and weight, and in the viscera and mass of blood regarding the—

Quantity, and the salt in it; and in the *lymph ducts*, as to their swelling, as I have frequently tested. And if to these we add the experiments of the fermenting of *wines* and other liquors during moist weather; their souring during thunder and dry weather; and adding likewise the history of pests and epidemic diseases, we shall find a great deal of reason to conclude that a true astrology is to be found by the inquiring philosopher. This would be of wonderful use to *medicine*, though the commonly accepted astrology cannot be thought of as anything but extremely unreasonable and ridiculous—as much as any of the many impostures that have been imposed by antiquity upon a credulous world, at least to anyone who has committed himself to demonstration.

So far, in these major disciplines—theology, sacred and profane history, and *medicine*—we have been assisted only a little by astronomy; but if we look into the next class of science, we shall perceive ourselves wholly indebted to her. It is astronomy that enlarged both our understanding and our habitation; she has given refinement, and consequently religion and laws, to the uncivilized world. Anyone who looks at that small portion of the world with which the ancients were content, and sees now how we furrow the great ocean and gather our aromatic harvests from the remotest parts of the globe—enjoying in our own *Europe* whatever *Thule* or *Ethiopia*, or the rising or setting sun can produce—must surely rejoice that so much larger an inheritance has fallen to mankind by the favor of astronomy. It was astronomy alone that in ancient times undertook to guide the creeping ships of the ancients whenever they would venture to leave the land to find a neighboring shore. Though then she was a temperamental guide, often veiling the face of heaven with clouds and cruelly leaving them to the fickle protection of fortune; for the most part, she only tossed them up and down and amused herself with their ruin. But if she deigned to show them one glimpse of a star—even just of *Alcor* <note>a faint star in the Big Dipper</note> or the smallest whitish spot in the heavens—it was enough to pave a way for them homeward through the horror of the waves and night. In this, the influence of heaven is truly perceived, when the influence of one *Cynosura* <note>the North Star</note> can move a thousand ships of freight and render one element [the sea] as habitable and more fruitful than the other [the land], though more hazardous. Thus the ancients everywhere cultivated the Mediterranean waters, but they disguised their fear of venturing into the ocean with religion, lest they should violate the rites of *Thetis* and the water deities.

At last, astronomy took another assistant for herself: *magnetics* [the compass], a kind of terrestrial astronomy. This is an art that tells us the motions of our own star on which we dwell, every fragment of which moves in true sympathy with the whole. It bids us, despite the clouds, to cross the vast ocean and possess every piece of our own star. And now the gates of true science were opened, and the poor philosophers *Anaximander*, *Anaximenes*, *Leucippus*, and *Empedocles* are laughed at for describing the Earth as a pillar, a table, a drum, or tilted by its own nature. In a few months, we shake hands with those on the opposite side of the earth [the *antipodes*] and pity the supposedly heretical bishop for his "unreasonable" airing of the truth; we also pity the pious ignorance of the *Church Fathers*, who believed the flat Earth was fixed upon infinitely long roots. But divine astronomy intended to discover her own yet-hidden glory to man, as well as the glories of the terrestrial globe. For after the prodigious attempt of *Columbus* and—as it appears to me—the even more difficult voyage of *Vasco de Gama* (who previously pursued the weak beginnings of *Hanno* the *Carthaginian* and twice scoured through the *Torrid Zone* in rounding the *Cape*), first finding it habitable, discovering the errors of the ancients about *Africa*, and first opening a way to the

Indies by sea. By these and succeeding voyages performed by the circumnavigators of our nation, the Earth was concluded to be truly global and equally habitable all around. This gave occasion for *Copernicus* to speculate why this body of Earth, of such a shape so suitable for motion, might not move among other celestial bodies. It seemed probable to him in its consequences and suited to explain the appearances <note>A phrase referring to "saving the phenomena," or providing a mathematical model that matches observed data</note>; and finding this idea also among ancient opinions, he resolved on this occasion to restore astronomy. And now the learned begin to grow heated; the schools <note>The traditional university systems of the time</note> ring with this dispute. All the mathematicians admire the hypothesis for saving nature a great deal of labor and the expense of so many "intelligences" <note>In older cosmology, spiritual beings thought to move the celestial spheres</note> for every orb and epicycle. Yet the apparent absurdity of a moving Earth makes the philosophers despise it, though some of them, captivated by the paradox, begin to observe nature and dare to suppose some old opinions are false. And now began the first happy appearance of liberty for philosophy, which had been oppressed by the tyranny of the Greek and Roman authorities.

Among the honorable defenders of this liberty, I must include *Gilbert*, who, having found an admirable correspondence between his *Terella* <note>A "little Earth" or small spherical magnet used for experiments</note> and the great magnet of the Earth, thought to determine this great question by this means, and spent his studies and estate upon this inquiry; by which, *incidentally*, he found out many admirable magnetic experiments. This man I would have adored, not only as the sole inventor of magnetism—a new science to be added to the bulk of learning—but as the father of the "new philosophy," *Cartesius* <note>René Descartes</note> being merely a builder upon his experiments. This person I should have commended to posterity with a statue, so that the deserved marble of *Harvey* <note>William Harvey, who discovered the circulation of the blood</note> might not stand for future ages without a marble companion of his own profession. He kept correspondence with the *Lincean Academy* at Rome, especially with *Franciscus Sagredus*, one of the participants in the dialogues of *Galileo*, who labored to prove the motion of the Earth negatively by removing objections; but *Gilbert* did so positively. One has given us an exact account of the motion of gravity upon the Earth; the other of the secret and more obscure motion of attraction and magnetic direction in the Earth. I must revere the one for giving occasion to *Kepler* (as he himself confesses) for introducing magnetism into the motions of the heavens, and consequently for building elliptical astronomy; the other for perfecting the great invention of telescopes to confirm this astronomy. So, if one is the *Brutus* of liberty restored to philosophy, certainly the other must be the *Collatinus* <note>Brutus and Collatinus were the first consuls of Rome who established the Republic</note>.

And here I should not only briefly mention that great foreign wit, *Kepler*, the compiler of another new science, *Dioptrics* <note>The study of the refraction of light through lenses</note> (in which, of all mathematics, we can boast that we did not have the Greeks for our masters), but he is even more eminent for being the *Eudoxus* <note>An ancient Greek astronomer who created an early model of planetary motion</note> of this age: the inventor of the elliptical hypothesis. But since he was only the first founder of these *great works*, and because the perfection of both of these is justly to be expected from men of our own nation living today and known to most of this audience, the brilliance of these more recent men makes me cease from a longer praise of *Kepler*. I reserve it for posterity to bestow upon them when it shall be more seasonable to give them an apotheosis among those great inventors I have named.

And indeed, of all the arguments with which the learned of this inquisitive age have busied themselves, the perfection of these two—Dioptrics and elliptical astronomy—seems most worthy of our inquiry. For natural philosophy having of late been organized into a geometrical way of reasoning from visual experiment, so that it might prove a real science of nature and not a hypothesis of what nature might be, the perfection of telescopes, and

Microscopes, by which our senses are so infinitely advanced, seem to be the only way to penetrate into the most hidden parts of nature and to make the most of the creation.

I cannot (most worthy auditors) but be very pleased to introduce Seneca and his prophecy of the new world:

->Venient annis sæcula feris,<-
->Quibus, oceanus vincula rerum<-
->Laxet, & ingens pateat tellus,<-
->Novosque Tiphys detegat orbes,<-

<note>A passage from Seneca’s Medea predicting a time when the ocean will reveal new worlds and Thule will no longer be the edge of the earth.</note>

But I only begin to value the advantages of this age in learning over the previous one when I imagine him continuing his prophecy. I imagine how much the ancient, hardworking explorers would envy us if he had sung to them that a time would come when men would be able to stretch out their eyes, as snails do, and extend them to fifty feet in length. By this means, they would be able to discover *two thousand* times as many stars as we can and find the Milky Way to be composed of myriads of them. Every nebulous star would appear as if it were the firmament of some other world at an incomprehensible distance, buried in the vast abyss of the intermundious vacuum <note>The space between worlds</note>. They would see the planets like our *Earth*, unevenly spotted with hills and valleys. They would see *Saturn*, a true *Proteus* <note>A shape-shifting sea god in Greek mythology, used here to describe the planet's changing appearance</note>, changing more admirably than our *Moon* through the various turnings and shadows of its several bodies, and accompanied, besides, by a *moon* of its own. They would find *Jupiter* to be an oval *Earth* whose night is enlightened by four different *moons* moving at various speeds and creating a multitude of eclipses. They would see *Mars*, *Venus*, and *Mercury* wax and wane. And they would have a view of the *Moon* herself as if they were close by, discovering the heights and shapes of the mountains, the depths of round and uniform valleys, the shadows of the mountains, and the figure of the shores. They would be able to draw pictures of her with more accuracy than we can our own globe. In this, they would repay the *Moon* for her own labors; for she, to help us discover our longitudes by eclipsing the *Sun*, has painted the countries upon our globe with the point of her conical shadow as if with a pencil. After all this, if he should have told them how the very fountain of light is variegated with its *faculae* and *maculae* <note>Bright spots and dark spots (sunspots)</note>, moving around in regular motions, wouldn't any of the astronomers of his time have traded their whole lives for a few windy days (when *solar spots* principally appear) or a few clear nights of our *century*?

But I have lost myself in this subject, which is as endless as the universe itself. The mere contemplation of the *phases* of the celestial bodies is so large a field of philosophy that a true description of the body of *Saturn* alone would be enough for the lifetime of one astronomer. How much more so are their various motions, which I will not discourse upon now, but reserve as the ongoing subject of my future lectures in this place. This is a place where the magnificence of our illustrious founder, *Gresham*, has adorned this opulent city with the profession of the sciences in his own house. By a rare example, he left the *Muses* to be his heirs and successors here forever. They seem to be fond of the place, having preserved it in high esteem by furnishing it until now with men of most eminent abilities, especially in the mathematical sciences. Among them, the names of *Gunter*, *Brerewood*, *Gellibrand*, and *Foster* are fresh in the mouths of all mathematicians.

cians, for the excellent remains they have either left behind them in print or adorned the tables with in reading. Among which, the useful invention of *logarithms*, as it was wholly a *British* art, so here especially it received great additions; and likewise, the whole doctrine of *magnetics*, as it was of *English* birth, so by the professors of *this place* it was augmented by the first invention and observation of the mutation of the magnetic variation; a thing, I confess, as yet crude, yet what may prove of consequence in philosophy, and of so great use, possibly to the navigator, that thereby we may attain the knowledge of *longitudes*, than which, former industry has hardly left anything more glorious to be aimed at in art.

And now since the professorship I am honored with is a benefit I enjoy from this city, I cannot conclude without a good omen to it. I must needs celebrate it as a city particularly favored by the celestial influences—a *Pandora* on which each planet has contributed something. *Saturn* has given it longevity, and to reckon an earlier *era from the founding of the city* than *Rome* itself. *Jupiter* has made it the perpetual seat of kings and of courts of justice, and filled it with inexhaustible wealth. *Mars* has armed it with power. The *Sun* looks most benignly on it, for what city in the world so vastly populous still enjoys so healthy an air and so fertile a soil? *Venus* has given it a pleasant situation, watered by the most pleasant river of *Europe*, and beautified with the external splendor of myriads of fine buildings. *Mercury* has nourished it in mechanical arts and trade to be equal with any city in the world; nor has he forgotten to furnish it abundantly with liberal sciences, among which I must congratulate this city that I find in it so general a relish of mathematics and the *libera philosophia* <note>Free philosophy, referring to experimental or scientific inquiry unrestrained by ancient dogma</note> in such a measure as is hardly to be found in the academies themselves. Lastly, the *Moon*, the lady of the waters, seems amorously to court this place:

> " *And to have cherished this one city more than all others,*
> " *even above Delos.* <note>A paraphrase of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, substituting London for Carthage or Samos</note>

For to what city does she invite the ocean so far within land as here? Communicating by the *Thames* whatever the banks of the *Amazon* or the *Indus* can produce, and at the reflux warming the frigid zones with our cloth; and sometimes carrying and returning safe those hulls that have encompassed the whole globe. And now since navigation brings with it both wealth, splendor, politeness, and learning, what greater happiness can I wish to the *Londoners*? Than that they may continually deserve to be deemed, as formerly, the great navigators of the world; that they always may be what the *Tyrians* first and then the *Rhodians* were called, "*The Masters of the Sea*"; and that *London* may be an *Alexandria*, the established residence of mathematical arts.

<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

"A Consideration of Justice: For in looking through the *Registers* of the Society, I perceived that many excellent things, whose first *invention* should be attributed to him, were casually omitted: This moves me to do him justice on his own, and to give this separate account of his efforts in promoting the design of the *Royal Society*, during the short time in which he has had the opportunity of attending it.
<margin>Laws of Motion.</margin>
"The first instance I shall mention, to which he may lay a unique claim, is the *Doctrine of Motion*, which is the most significant of all others for establishing the first *Principles of Philosophy* by geometrical demonstration. This *Descartes* had begun before, having taken up some experiments of this kind based on conjecture, and made them the first foundation of his whole *System of Nature*. But since some of his conclusions seemed very questionable, because they were only derived from the rough trials of balls meeting one another at *Tennis* and *Billiards*, Dr. *Wren* produced before the Society an *instrument* to represent the effects of all sorts of *impulses* made between two hard spherical bodies—whether of equal or different size and speed, following or meeting each other, or one moving and the other at rest. From these varieties arose many unexpected effects; of all these, he demonstrated the true *theories*, after they had been confirmed by many hundreds of experiments using that *instrument*. These he proposed as the principles of all *demonstrations in natural philosophy*. Nor can it seem strange that these *elements* should be of such universal use, if we consider that *generation, corruption, alteration*, and all the changes of *nature* are nothing else but the *effects* arising from the meeting of small bodies of different shapes, sizes, and speeds."

### NEWTON’S *Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy*
### THE LAWS OF MOTION.
#### SCHOLIUM.
<margin>2nd Edition. Cambridge 1713. p. 19.</margin>
So far I have presented the principles received by mathematicians and confirmed by many experiments. Through the first two laws and the first two corollaries, Galileo discovered that the descent of heavy bodies is in the duplicate ratio of the time, and that the motion of projectiles follows a parabola, consistent with experience, except for how those motions are slightly slowed by the resistance of the air. From these same laws and corollaries depend the demonstrations concerning the periods of oscillating pendulums, supported by the daily experience of clocks. From these same principles and the third law, Sir Christopher Wren, John Wallis, D.D., and Christiaan Huygens—the leading geometers of this age—separately discovered the rules for the collisions and reflections of two bodies. They communicated these to the Royal Society at nearly the same time, agreeing entirely with one another regarding these laws; Wallis published the discovery first, followed by Wren and Huygens. However, the truth was also proven by Wren before the Royal Society through the experiment of pendulums, which the famous Mariotte later saw fit to explain in an entire book.

“account of *Epidemic Diseases*, of blasts, mildews, and other accidents belonging to grain, cattle, fish, fowl, and insects. And because the difficulty of a constant *observation* of the *air*, by night and day, seemed insurmountable, he therefore devised a *clock* \* to be attached to a weathercock, which moved a rundle covered with paper, upon which the clock moved a black lead pencil, so that the observer, by the traces of the pencil on the paper, might certainly conclude what winds had blown in his absence for a twelve-hour space. In a similar manner, he contrived a *thermometer* to be its own *register*. And because the usual *thermometers* were not found to give a true measure of the expansion of the *air*, because the accidental weight of the liquid, as it lay higher or lower in the glass, weighed unequally on the *air* and gave it a further contraction or extension, over and above that which was produced by heat and cold; therefore he invented a *circular thermometer*, in which the liquid causes no error, but remains always at one height, moving the whole *instrument* like a wheel on its *axis*.

[In an improvement of his invention of the *weather-wheel* (the only true way to measure expansions of the *air*), he contrived the *instrument* to be more firmly made by causing the circular *pipes* (which cannot be truly blown in glass) to be formed of brass by those who make trumpets and sackbutts, who wire-draw their pipes through a hole to equalize them, and then filling them with melted lead, turn them into whatever curves they please. The inside of the pipe he varnished with *China varnish* to preserve it from the quicksilver, and the glass was fixed to it with varnish, which is the best cement in the world; for in this way the *Chinese* fix glass and mother-of-pearl in their works.]

To his invention of the *weather clock*, other motions were afterwards added by Mr. *Robert Hooke*, Professor of Geometry in *Gresham College*.

It has six or seven motions: first, a *pendulum clock*, which runs with seventy-five pounds of weight and moves the greatest part of the work. With this, there is a *barometer*, a *thermometer*, a *rain-measure* (such as is described next), and a *weathercock*, which is served by a piece of wheel-work analogous to a *way-wiser* <note>an odometer or distance recorder</note>; and a *hygroscope*. Each of these has its own *register*, and the *weathercock* has two: one for the directions and the other for the *strength* of the wind. All of these work upon paper unrolling from a *roller* which the *clock* also turns.

Mr. *Hooke’s* proposal for augmenting the *weather clock* was first offered by him to the Royal Society in the year 1664, based upon the description of one made by Sir *Christopher Wren*. [*Waller’s Life of Hooke*, page 11.]

" He devised many subtle ways for the easier finding the gravity of the

" Among the new discoveries of the *pendulum*, these are to be attribut-

“ He has made constant observations of *Saturn*; and a theory of that planet, truly answering all observations, before the printed discourse of *Huygens* <note>Hugenius</note> on that subject appeared. By a thirty-six foot glass <note>telescope</note>, he drew many exact pictures of *Saturn*, not only of its *ansae* <note>the "handles" or protruding parts of the rings as seen through early telescopes</note>, but its *spots*; and attained a theory of its *rotation*, and the various *inclination* of its *body*. He also drew the *spots* of *Mars*. He mapped the motions of *Jupiter’s satellites*, and *Saturn’s moon*; and not only drew pictures of the *Moon* as *Hevelius* had done, but gave more exact surveys and maps of it, and discovered exactly its various *inclinations*, and therein *Hevelius’s* errors; he caused a needle to be made of forty inches, in order to discover the *annual motion* of *variation* in it.
“ He has attempted to make a true *selenography* <note>lunar geography</note> by measurement; the world having nothing yet but pictures, rather than surveys or maps of the *Moon*. He has stated the theory of the *Moon’s libration* <note>the perceived oscillating motion of the Moon</note>, as far as his observations could carry him. He has composed a *lunar globe*, representing not only the spots and various degrees of whiteness upon the surface, but the hills, eminences, and cavities, molded in solid work. The globe, thus fashioned into a true model of the *Moon*, as you turn it to the light, represents all the monthly phases, with the variety of appearances that happen from the shadow of the mountains and valleys.

## Second Letter from Sir Robert Moray to Dr. WREN, etc.

*My worthy Friend,*

Since my last, I told the King you had finished your lunar globe and desired to know his further commands; and he commanded me to let you know he would have you bring it here to him. I also have to tell you that, in compliance with your desire to be eased of the further task of drawing the figures of small insects by the help of the microscope, we have moved his Majesty to lay his commands on another, one *Vander Diver*; and we have also persuaded Mr. *Hooke* to undertake the same thing. This is all the trouble you shall now have from, my worthy friend,

->*Your real humble servant,*<-

*Whitehall, 13 August, 1661.*

->R. MORAY.<-

<margin>[Character of Sir R. Moray. See Bp. Burnet, Echard, etc.]</margin>
*N. B. Sir Robert Moray*, one of his Majesty’s Privy Council in *Scotland*, was an excellent mathematician and well-versed in natural philosophy and chemistry. He was among the first who modeled, instituted, and promoted the *Royal Society*, and was elected its second president after Lord *Brouncker*. He was universally beloved and esteemed; he was of such great piety that, in the midst of armies and courts, he spent many hours a day in devotion. He had an evenness of temper that nothing could alter and was in practice a *Stoic*. He possessed a superiority of genius and comprehension beyond most men. He had a most widespread love for all mankind and delighted in every occasion of doing good, which he managed with great discretion and zeal. — A character so similar in all points to that of Sir *Christopher Wren* naturally produced a most friendly and unbreakable attachment to each other. He died suddenly at *Whitehall* and, being particularly in the King’s favor, was buried at his Majesty’s own expense in *Westminster Abbey* in the year 1673.

### Extract from the Preface of Mr. Hooke’s Micrographia.

<margin>London 1665.</margin>
<margin>* Bishop of Chester.</margin>
By the advice of that excellent man, Dr. *Wilkins*\* , I first set upon this enterprise <note>*Micrographia, or Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by the Help of Magnifying Glasses*</note>; yet I still approached it with much reluctance because I was to follow the footsteps of so eminent a person as Dr. *Wren*, who was the first to attempt anything of this nature. His original drawings now serve as one of the ornaments of that great collection of rarities in the King’s closet. The honor which his first beginnings of this kind have received—to be admitted into the most famous place in the world—did not encourage me so much as the risk of following after Dr. *Wren* frightened me. For of him I must affirm that, since the time of *Archimedes*, there has scarcely ever met in one man, in such great perfection, such a mechanical hand and so philosophical a mind.

<margin>Dr. Sprat’s Hist. of the Royal Society. p. 364.</margin>
> “He has made maps of the *Pleiades* and other *telescopic stars*, and proposed methods to determine the great doubt of the Earth’s motion or rest by the small stars near the pole to be seen in large *telescopes*.
<margin>\* In the Museum of the Royal Society. Dr. Grew, p. 364.</margin>
“In order to *navigation*, he has carefully pursued many magnetic *experiments*, of which this is one of the noblest and most fruitful for speculation. A large \* *terella* <note>a spherical loadstone</note>, about four and a half inches in diameter, is placed in the middle of a plain board with a hole into which the *terella* is half immersed, until it is like a globe with the poles on the *horizon*. This is set together with 32 needles upon the margin of the table, by which the different orientation of the needle to the various points of the *terella* may be observed. Then the plane is dusted over with steel filings evenly from a sieve. By magnetic power, the dust is immediately formed into furrows that bend like a sort of *helix*, proceeding, as it were, out of one pole and returning into the other; and the whole plane is thus shaped like the circles of a *planisphere*.
“As it is a question among the problems of navigation—one very much worth resolving—to what mechanical powers sailing (especially against the wind) was reducible, he showed it to be a wedge. He demonstrated how a transient force upon an oblique plane would cause the motion of the plane against the first mover, and he made an † instrument that mechanically produced the same effect and showed the reason for sailing into all winds.
<margin>† In the Museum of the Royal Society, Dr. Grew, p. 364.</margin>

" He contrived a unique *instrument* to draw *perspective* with. He has started

" He was the first *inventor* of drawing *pictures* by *microscopical glasses.*
" He has found out perpetual, or at least long-lived *lamps,* and *registers* of
" *furnaces,* and the like, for keeping a perpetual *temperature* in order to va-
" rious *uses*; such as hatching of *eggs, insects, the production* of *plants, chemical*
" *preparations,* imitating *nature* in producing *fossils* and *minerals,*
" keeping the *motion of watches* equal for the sake of *longitudes* and *astrono-*
" *mical uses,* and infinite other advantages.
He made it no small part of his business to have a fire frequently going
in the laboratory for choice *experiments* in *chemistry,* well knowing that
many parts of *philosophy* are not to be pierced far into without this help;
and little can be done in the business of *trades* without it. *Mechanical phi-*
losophy only teaches us what probably may be done in *nature* by the *mo-*
tion and *shapes* of the little *particles of things,* but *chemistry* helps to de-
termine what is actually done by the *motions* of those invisible *parts* of *li-*
quors, *spirits,* and *fumes*; and oftentimes gives *light* enough to contradict
mechanical *hypotheses* that otherwise seem well-grounded. Thus, in the
*body* of a *man,* if we consider it only mechanically, we may indeed learn
the *structure* and *action* of the organic *parts,* but without *chemistry,* we
shall be at a loss to know what *blood, spirits,* and *humors* are; from
the due *temperature* of which (as of the *spring* in the *barrel wheel*) the *mo-*
tions of all the *parts* depend. With various new and useful *experiments* in
this *art,* he had frequent opportunities of entertaining his *Royal Highness*

In the year 1658, he first found a *straight line* equal to a *cycloid* and its parts. This is clearly shown on his behalf by the Right Honorable and learned Lord Viscount *Brouncker*, Chancellor to her Majesty and President of the *Royal Society*, and the Reverend and learned *Dr. John Wallis*.

The upright southern declining *dial* over *All Souls College Chapel* is a neat piece of work, so curiously contrived by *Sir Christopher Wren* that, though it stands high, yet by the help of two *half-rays* and one *whole one* for every hour, one may see the time to a minute; the *minutes* are depicted on the sides of the *rays*—fifteen on each side—and divided into *groups of five* by a different *character* from the rest.

He invented the art of *double writing*—that is, of making two separate pens on two separate pieces of paper write the same sequence of letters with as near as possible the same beauty and ease found in common writing—by an instrument called the *diplographical instrument*.

### *To the King, on his Happy Return.*

<margin>
*Applied to King Charles II after his Restoration.*
</margin>
> *Diffluxit en gemino quam prodiga sepia ductu,*
> *Ut cadat in titulos, Carole magne, tuos.*
> *Marte, ac consilio nam te bis scribere magnum,*
> *Unica si nequeat dextera, dupla valet.*

### *Uses of the Diplographical Instrument.*

*First*, that by the help of this instrument alone, every ordinary penman may at all times be quickly equipped to write two separate copies of any deeds and evidence, from the shortest to the longest length of lines, in the very same amount of time and with as much ease and beauty—without any dividing or ruling—as he could have finished only one without the help of the instrument.

*Secondly*, that by thus diminishing the tedious labor of transcribing the larger types of deeds, indentures, conveyances, charters, and all other duplicates, the works of the pen (which are countless each year across so many different types and offices) are not only shortened, but the penmen themselves are both relieved and compensated by an honest gain with half the usual toil.

*Thirdly*, in both copies drawn this way, there will be such an exact likeness in the same number and order of lines, and even of words, letters, and punctuation in all parts of both copies, that once they are separated, one shall hardly discern any difference between them, except for what is merely accidental, such as spots or marks in the parchment.

*Fourthly*, this instrument will undoubtedly prevent the mischievous craft of corruption, forgery, and the counterfeiting of signatures and seals; or, if any such foul practice is attempted, it will effectively and clearly reveal it. For what use is it to counterfeit a seal or the hand that signs unless a duplicate could be made in every line, letter, and dot, exactly like the twin copy? This is impossible without the help of the same instrument. Therefore, it may be so beneficial for all intents and purposes of the *state*, in matters of the greatest consequence, that public acts be written by this instrument for testimony and assurance for all time.

<margin>† Oliver Cromwell.</margin>
->SIR,<-

THE account you gave me in your last letter—that a double-writing instrument has lately been claimed in *London* by several people as a production of their own and disclosed to many—has given me the occasion to place into your hands that double-writing instrument, which I certainly have more right to dispose of than any recent pretender. You yourself, Sir, as I remember, were among the other *Ingeniosi* <note>talented or scholarly men</note> who were judges of its effect about three years ago, at the same time it was accidentally commanded to be shown to the then great, and now greatest † person in the nation. I confess my thoughts then were to allow it to be made public, and friends urged me to it, perceiving it not as a mere curiosity, but as something of excellent and very general use. Moreover, to copy out in every detail the exact resemblance, or rather the very identity of the two copies—as if one should imagine such a piece of magic that could make the same thing really two, or as if one saw the same thing double through drunken eyes—is what might be thought almost impossible for the hand of man. But business drew me suddenly away from *London* and from the opportunity of publishing it; content that I had at least shared it with the ingenious few, I willingly left it. And indeed, as the thing always appeared to me as an obvious (though useful) invention, I was easily led to neglect it all this while by the intervention of studies and designs that I much more esteemed; among which, this took up so little space that I am beholden to the person who, by claiming it as his own, has reminded me of it again. I accuse no one of plagiarism, because having shown it to few, I think it would be more trouble for any knowledgeable person to seek it out from others than to reinvent it. Therefore, had it been thought of by any other person around the time I showed it, I would have readily imagined (because of the obviousness of the experiment) that it might as easily have had two fathers as produce a twin copy. But I am inclined to believe, based on good information, that those who now boast of it received it from someone who, having fully seen and carefully examined the author’s (as it is easy to remember, being of no complicated design), described it accurately to his friend and assisted him in making it; and the very glorying in

He designed a compass needle that would work in a coach, being useful for knowing the direction and path when used with the *waywiser* <note>An odometer or instrument for measuring distance traveled.</note>, as well as a pleasant diversion for the traveler, who might thus, so to speak, sail by land. *The machine* is built in this way: In a glass sphere two inches in diameter and half-filled with water, cause a heavy, short, broad needle attached to a chart to float, supported by the chart, both being varnished. Instead of a cap and pin, let the perforated needle rotate around a small wire or horsehair stretched like a vertical axis within the glass sphere. The bottom of the sphere is weighted with lead, and a simulated horizon is cemented to it; let it move in circles like a compass. Then, let a hemispherical bowl, containing the sphere in its gimbals, be hung on springs in this way: Suppose a base upon which three stiff brass springs are set upright; from the ends of these springs, strings are stretched to form an equilateral triangle, the middle of whose sides pass through three small loops on the rim of the bowl. Hanging from the strings, the bowl represents a circle inscribed within a triangle. From the center of the base, a coiled spring (worm-spring) rises, fastened by a string to the bottom of the bowl, pulling it down slightly and acting against the other three springs. These springs will simultaneously absorb much of both the vertical and side-to-side jolts; the gimbals will stop oscillations, and any remaining vibrations will be absorbed by the water and calmed by the chart. For as we see, a wooden plate floating in a bucket prevents water from spilling during transport; likewise, the *Chinese* have their compasses floating in water instead of using gimbal rings. Lastly, the entire bottom of the base is to be covered in bristles like a brush, slightly slanted, which will cushion it like a hundred springs. It should be placed in the middle of the floor of the carriage, where, by opening a window, one may also see the waywiser on the perch <note>The main beam or frame of the carriage undercarriage.</note>.

<margin>Dr. Grew's Museum of the Royal Society, p. 260.</margin>
The *Way-Wiser* <note>An odometer for a carriage.</note> for a coach, contrived by Sir *Christopher Wren* and given by Bishop *Wilkins* to the *Royal Society*, is very manageable. It has five indexes pointing to as many different measures, namely: perches, furlongs, miles, tens of miles, and hundreds of miles; and it is turned by as many wheels. It is made to work in a coach in this way: in the middle of the *axletree* is cut a little box to receive the *Way-Wiser*, from which the *axletree* is made hollow to the end. In this hollow lies a rod, separate from the *axletree* and fastened at one end to the *nave* <note>The central hub of a wheel.</note> of the *wheel*, and so turns round with it. With a *worm* <note>A worm gear.</note> it has at the other end, it simultaneously turns the *perch* wheel of the *Way-Wiser*, which then turns all the rest. Yet by this measure, one yard will sometimes be lost in a hundred yards.

<margin>In the Museum of the Royal Society, Dr. Grew, p. 371.</margin>
He contrived a box-hive, given to the *Royal Society* by Sir *Robert Moray*; the description of which was first published by Mr. *Hartlib* in the year 1652. Since then, it was published by Mr. *Moses Rusden*. It was designed to keep the bees warmer and safer, but especially to prevent their swarming and to better propagate them into colonies.

<margin>In the Museum of the Royal Society.</margin>
He exhibited a great variety of *sciographical, scenographical, dioptrical*, and *catoptrical* experiments, which, when executed with good painting and *geometrical truth* in the *profile*, would deceive the eye with surprising effects. Such, for instance, was the catoptric paint given to the *Royal Society* by Bishop *Wilkins*; on one side the paint appears as if it were altogether crude and irregular, so that nothing can be made of it; but a metallic cylinder being placed perpendicularly upon a certain point of the table, the rays strike it in such a way and are reflected from there to the eye as to represent a variety of curious works in landscape and figures, etc.

### *Extract from the Collection of Philosophical Experiments of Dr.* HOOK, *and others, published by the Rev. Mr.* DERHAM, *London, 1726. p. 1.*

#### *Of the Invention of the Barometer, in the Year 1659.*

<margin>* Mr. Derham.</margin>
In one of Dr. *Hooke's* papers I find this remark, namely: the instrument for finding the different pressure of the air upon the parts of the earth below was first observed by the honorable Mr. *Boyle*, who, upon the suggestion of Sir *Christopher Wren*, erected a tube of glass filled with mercury (as is now usually done in common barometers). This was done in order to find out whether the pressure of the moon, according to the *Cartesian hypothesis*, did affect the air. Instead of finding the fluctuation which might cause the phenomena of the tides, he discovered the variation of its pressure to proceed from different causes and at different times from what that *hypothesis* would have predicted. That property of the air (as far as it appears) was never discovered until that time, etc.

To this I shall add another remark. I find in the minutes of the *Royal Society, Feb.* 20, 1678-9: Upon a discourse of some experiments to be made with the barometer on *the Monument*, it was asked how this experiment of the different pressure of the atmosphere first came to be thought of? And it was related that it was first proposed by Sir *Christopher Wren* in order to examine Monsieur *Descartes's hypothesis*—whether the passing by of the body of the moon did press upon the air, and consequently also upon the body of the water—and that the first trial of it was made at Mr. *Boyle's* chamber in *Oxford*.

The time when these observations were made was about the year 1658 or 1659. At which time, Mr. *Boyle*, having a barometer fixed up for observing the moon's influence upon the waters, happened to discover the use of it in

...in relation to the weather, and to assure himself that it was the gravitation of the atmosphere which kept up the mercury to such a height as the learned abroad, particularly Torricelli, had suspected before.

But although this use of the baroscope is owing to Sir Christopher Wren and Mr. Boyle, yet, to do every man justice, I shall give the history of this excellent instrument from the extracts of a very ingenious friend.

The first inventor of it was Torricelli at Florence, in 1643. From there, Father Mersenne brought it into France the following year, 1644. And Monsieur Pascal, being informed of it by Monsieur Petit the engineer, both tried it in 1646 at Rouen with the same success as it had been tried in Italy. Some time after which, an experiment was made with a tube of forty-six feet, filled with water and also with wine; Monsieur Pascal gave an account of this experiment in a piece printed in 1647, in which year he was informed of Torricelli’s solution to the phenomenon of the weight of the air. He devised, for the examination of it, the famous experiment with two tubes, one within the other, which he mentions in a letter written in November 1647, and finally in 1648. The same Monsieur Pascal made his experiments on the tops and bottoms of hills, buildings, etc. These last experiments Monsieur Descartes laid claim to, affirming that he desired Monsieur Pascal to make them two years before and predicted their success, contrary to Monsieur Pascal’s sentiments.

Monsieur Azout also laid the same claim, but it is most probable that Monsieur Pascal had the best title.

After the Torricellian experiment had been much celebrated in various places, at last Otto de Guerrick, Consul of Magdeburg, was informed of it by Father Valerian at Ratisbon, who claimed it as his own invention; but this was not until the year 1654. After which Guerrick’s experiment (called the Magdeburg experiment) was much talked of.

From this short history of the barometer, not only the inventor and improvers of it appear, but in some measure also its excellent uses: particularly the gravitation of the incumbent atmosphere (one of the noblest philosophical discoveries), the changes of the weather, etc.

->W. DERHAM.<-

In celestial observations we have far exceeded all the ancients, even the *Chaldeans* and *Egyptians* themselves; whose vast plains, high towers, and clear air did not give them as great advantages over us as we have over them by our *glasses*. ...upon me before I was aware, and so I must stay until the Constellation of ♈ [Aries] appears in the Morning, before I can be able to rectify the positions of the telescopic stars, by which I observed the *Comet* to pass; which I hope I may do about a fortnight from now; at which time also I expect to see both the old or first *Comet* with a telescope, and the second or *last Comet* with my eye: for, if their motion is regular, as I see not the least cause to doubt, I hope to be able to map their places among the fixed stars, without erring much more than I am able to see at once with a telescope; and therefore I hope it will be no difficult matter to find either of them, unless the *first* has gone so far as to disappear because of distance, which is indeed the greatest part of my fear: for, if it continues to move in the ways I have imagined, whether we take the supposition of the motion of the Earth and imagine the *Comet* moves in a circle—one side of which touches, or rather goes within the orbit of the Earth on one side, and outside the orbit of *Saturn*, or at least that of *Jupiter* on the other, whose plane is inclined to that of the Ecliptic about 20 *degrees*—or whether we suppose the Earth to stand still and the *Comet* to move in a great circle whose convex side is turned towards the Earth (which, assuming no certain parallax has been observed, may be supposed to be of any size, keeping only the same proportion between its nearest distance from the Earth and the radius or diameter of that circle), it must appear again very near the same place about a fortnight from now. And I am inclined to think the body of the *Comet* is of a constitution that will last much longer than either a month or a year—nay, than an age; and if I can be so lucky as to meet with it again, I hope to trace it to its second appearing. But I weary you with my conjectures; and I do not doubt but that before this, you have perfected the *Theory* of *Comets*, so as to be able to predict much more certainly what we are to expect of these *Comets* in the future; of which, if at your leisure you will please to afford me a word or two, you will much oblige me, *etc.*

<margin>Posthumous Works of Dr. Hooke, p. 104 and 105.</margin>
In one of Mr. *Hook's* Discourses of *Comets*, containing a brief explanation of several opinions of the ancients and some of the moderns regarding the nature of *Comets*; he takes notice of a recent report from *France* of a person, *D. Anthelm*, a *Carthusian* of *Dijon*, pretending to have a true theory of *Comets* and to be able to predict them; which, says he, I think may be much more exactly done than what *Anthelm* has achieved, by the way I have published in my *Cometa*, which was invented by Sir *Christopher Wren*; by which, from any four observations truly made, one may certainly find the line, distance, motion, inclination to the Ecliptic, its place among the fixed stars, the length of its tail, brightness, *etc.* so long as it shall appear to the naked eye; for so long that theory will hold fairly well, *etc.*

All the significant astronomers who have written of *Comets* since *Galileo* conclude them not to be sublunary, but far removed above the moon and ethereal. Such were almost all those who wrote of that great and very bright comet which appeared to the world in the year 1618, and such are those who have written of *Comets* that have appeared since; and more particularly of those two great ones which appeared at the end of 1664 and in the beginning of the year 1665, many of which are comprised in the *Theatrum Cometicum*, printed in 1667.

<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

## NUMB. II.

### To the ROYAL SOCIETY.

Mr. PRESIDENT,

WE begin a new year, and therefore may pause a little, and look back on what we have done, and consider what we may do. It is a great encouragement to us that, by the influence of his sacred Majesty, the prudence and diligence of yourself, and the ingenious performances of the Society, we have so far kept our meetings full and in good reputation at home and abroad, and not without sufficient appearance of doing something considerable; so that we need not now fear lest the world, from all our experiments, should make this one experiment: that there is little use for these inquiries. And I make no question but that the design of so many excellent persons meeting in this Society (besides the present satisfaction that results from the conversation and communication of everyone's thoughts in the investigation of nature) carries along with it, principally, a zeal for proving themselves benefactors to mankind, and for perfecting something for which posterity may be truly obliged to us.

Of effecting this, there seem to be three ways: By advancing, 1. *Knowledge*. 2. *Profit*. 3. *Health* and the conveniences of life.

For the first of these, the improvement of *theories*, we need be least concerned; it is a work that will grow upon us naturally if we are always doing something in experiment. Everyone is more prone to exercise their imagination in building paper theories than they are patient enough to first pile the unsure foundation and hew solid materials out of the *History of Nature*. This is rather our task, and in many things we must be content to plant crab-stocks <note>Wild apple rootstock used for grafting.</note> for posterity to graft on.

The second, I make no question, will be excellently effected by two things now in hand: the carrying on of the *History of Trades*, and the improvement of the *Art of Navigation*; which, being now committed to an excellent hand, cannot but produce something very extraordinary. Besides, there can hardly be anything proposed worth our consideration that will not itself, or some corollary from it, be reducible to this head.

For the third, the *Health of Mankind*, the restorative part is properly the work already of one whole faculty, in which no age or nation affords more learned and inquisitive men than this of ours. Yet I wish we might incorporate with them so far as to have a fire going in the laboratory for choicer experiments in *chemistry*, especially since many parts of philosophy are not to be pierced far into without this help; and little is to be done in the business of trades without it. *Mechanical philosophy* only teaches us what probably may be done in nature by the motion and figures of the little particles of things, but *chemistry* helps to determine what is actually done by the motions of those invisible parts of liquids, spirits, and fumes; and oftentimes gives light enough to contradict mechanical hypotheses that otherwise seem well-grounded. Thus, in the body of a man, if we consider it only mechanically, we may indeed learn the structure and action of the organic parts, but without *chemistry*, we shall be at a loss to know what blood, spirits, and humors are—upon the proper balance of which (as of the spring in the barrel wheel) the motions of all the parts depend.

<sig>I</sig>
<meta>catchword: To</meta>

<summary>Sir Christopher Wren addresses the Royal Society at the start of a new year, outlining three primary goals for their work: advancing knowledge through experimental theories, increasing profit through trade and navigation, and improving human health through chemistry.</summary>
<keywords>Sir Christopher Wren, Royal Society, experimental philosophy, History of Nature, History of Trades, Navigation, Chemistry, Mechanical Philosophy, medical faculty</keywords>

<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

To carry on both together, I could wish we were frequent in the dissections of animals of any sort whatsoever, and that figures be drawn where nature appears anomalous, as she is most often in fishes and insects, especially in the parts that serve for <term>concoction</term> <note>The process of digestion.</note>. And along with this, we may include experiments about generation. The spring should not be lost for observing the progress of hatching eggs, and likewise the sprouting of grain and seeds, which in a rougher proportion gives some light to the generation of animals. Tame rabbits may be kept specifically for dissection, both because they are frequently pregnant and because, lately, some observations have been made from them which seem to contradict those of Dr. Harvey; how true this is will be worth our inquiry.

Besides these, there is another part of physiology <note>The study of natural phenomena and the physical world.</note> which concerns us as closely as the breath of our nostrils, and I know of nothing by which we may more oblige posterity than that which I would now propose. It is not the work of any one person, and therefore fit for a society; nor is it a matter of a little time, though it is of little trouble, and therefore fit to be proposed now at the beginning of the year, and to be carried on along with other matters. The "History of Seasons" is this excellent work I would recommend to you, desired by all modern philosophers, though nobody has yet had the patience to pursue it.

It consists of two parts: 1. A meteorological history. 2. A history of things depending upon the alteration of the air and seasons.

The meteorological parts will be completed by five histories:

1.  A precise diary of the motion of the air—the winds; wherein should be noted not only the <term>rhumb</term> <note>The direction or point of the compass.</note> but the force of the wind, as the seamen have these distinctions, if I mistake not: from a calm they begin with a soft wind; a fresh wind; a stiff gale; a storm; and sometimes a hurricane. These may be noted down by a cipher, such as 1, 2, 3, 4, etc., and the <term>rhumb</term> by letters.
2.  A precise diary of the qualities of the air, as to heat and cold observed by a thermometer, and likewise of the moisture of the air observed by some other instrument.
3.  The refractions should be observed, as well as the rising of dry vapors by the telescope, and the <term>tremulation</term> <note>Shimmering or vibration.</note> of the air.
4.  A diary of the state of the air, such as fair, cloudy, rain, etc.
5.  <margin>Northern lights (*Aurora borealis*).</margin> A register of other accidental meteors, such as figured snows, <term>parhelia</term> <note>Mock suns; originally 'parelii'.</note>, <term>coronae</term>, unusual colors and shapes of clouds (called "fights in the air"), fiery meteors in the night, and falling stars (regarding which I could give directions for finding if anything falls from them upon their extinction).

The second part will be comprised of:

1.  The history of the growth of those annual items used for food, such as fruits and grain. The causes of dearth and plenty and diseases. Especially the "Annals of the Plough" should be kept: how the weather retarded or accelerated seed time, sprouting, flowering, <term>corning</term> <note>The formation of the grain or kernels.</note>, ripening, and harvest; along with the diseases and enemies of that year, such as whether the crop was blighted, mildewed, smutted, choked with this or that weed, eaten by rook-worms, or infected with a little blue mite covering the ear while green—a calamity which I have observed, but which lacks a name. Lastly, the plenty, scarcity, and price of corn <note>General term for cereal grains such as wheat or barley.</note>. We are numerous enough to learn this in every county of England by inquiring or corresponding with those who are a little more curious about country affairs.

<summary>Sir Christopher Wren proposes that the Royal Society undertake a systematic "History of Seasons" to record meteorological data and its effects on agriculture. He also encourages frequent animal dissections and experiments on the generation of life to advance biological knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Royal Society, Christopher Wren, meteorology, agriculture, dissection, Dr. Harvey, biology, weather observation, generation of animals, crop diseases</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Sir Christopher Wren's proposal for a systematic "History of Seasons," focusing on the observation of livestock, agriculture, trade goods, wildlife, and public health.</meta>

<page-num>223</page-num>
<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

2. The state of grass and hay, and consequently of cattle; their plenty, scarcity, diseases, and plagues <note>The original text uses "murrains," referring to infectious diseases in domestic animals.</note>.

3. Wines, which although foreign, make up a large share of our diet, and therefore a record should be given of them; of their quality or defects that year. The same for coffee, tobacco, and similar items of general use.

4. The seasons for fish and fowl are delayed or hastened by weather: foreign birds are observed to arrive in great numbers near the time of their departure at certain coasts of *England*, and there stay for a wind; when it turns in their favor, within a few hours not one is to be seen in the whole country. The seasons for fish depend much upon the seasons for the water-flies and insects that are their food; in two rivers separated by the same meadow, I have known a difference of ten days or more. The seasons of insects are in themselves very significant. The abundance or scarcity of venomous creatures, and of many other similar things, are well worth recording; and all other things found to be either consequences, signs, or omens of weather and seasons.

5. Above all, the physicians of our society should be requested to give us a good account of the epidemic diseases of the year; histories of any new disease that occurs; changes in old ones; differences in the effects of medicine according to the weather and seasons, both internally and in wounds: and to this should be added a proper consideration of the weekly and annual Bills of Mortality in *London*.

Thus, instead of the vanity of prognosticating <note>Predicting the future without a basis in data.</note>, I wish we would have the patience for some years to record past times, which is the certain way of learning how to predict; experiment and reason are the only ways of prophesying natural events. I shall not, therefore, need to urge the utility of this design, since I am confident there is no one here who does not understand what excellent theories and what a multitude of new and clever results will arise from this, leading to profit, health, convenience, pleasure, and the extension of life. And I dare be confident that no other part in the whole extent of *philosophy* will provide us with more delightful or more useful theories, or make us more significant to all *posterity*.

The only thing I fear is that we might lack patience and lose interest in the plan, since in the first few years, it will hardly reach any visible maturity. But as it is a long-term work, it is not difficult, nor will it take up more time than once a year to have an *audit*, wherein everyone shall bring in his account of that part which was assigned to him in this *history*.

The greatest difficulty will be in keeping the *diary* of the *winds* and *air*, because it seems to require constant attention; but this at first may be delegated to four or five men who have *weathercocks* in view near their homes and have diligently determined the orientation of their houses; these may sometimes compare notes, as what escaped the *observations* of one will be recorded by another. The same applies to the *thermometer*.

Some help may be given for the more exact observation of the *wind*, as follows: A *point* being chosen in a convenient *part* of a *window* where the square *vane* of a *weathercock* appears—the closer and higher above the eye, the better—an *ellipsis* <note>An oval shape.</note> may be drawn on the *glass*, and the compass points <note>Originally "rhumbs."</note> within the *ellipsis* so that it may be a *projection* upon the *pane* of the *window* of an imaginary *compass card*, placed horizontally upon the *steeple* whose *center* is the *axis* of the *vane*. Therefore, by observing with only a single glance how the *edge* of the *vane* aligns with these *lines* of the *window*, you have the *wind* direction exactly given to you.

<page-num>224</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

This method has been put into execution with very good effect, along with some other useful additions at *Oxford*.

But because it is important that the changes of winds during the night should not pass unobserved, a weather vane—such as the one at *Whitehall* that shows the direction by an indicator inside a room—may be very necessary for this purpose.

But even this is not yet enough, for many changes may happen while the observer is absent or asleep. I might seem to promise too much should I say that a machine may be built which, even if you visit your chamber only once every half hour in the day, shall tell you how many changes of wind have occurred in your absence (even if there were twenty), at what hour every change happened, and whether the wind was soft, stiff, or forceful. Neither shall the instrument be prone to going out of tune; or if it is, your own hand may rectify it.

Neither shall the thermometer need constant monitoring, for by the same method, it may be made to be its own recorder. There are likewise some errors in the use of the thermometer, which should therefore be used with some caution.

As for the proposed ways of discovering the two other qualities of dryness and moisture in the air, all that I have ever heard of are uncertain. Trials have been made of lute-strings, which move an indicator by their various tensions, but these strings change in their parts, and will not return to the same degrees even in the same air conditions. The beards of oats are even more uncertain.

It is indeed an error to think there are any degrees of dryness, since all dryness is but less or no humidity. And therefore, the degrees of humidity being nothing else but the quantity of moist vapor in the air, it is best measured by collecting the actual moisture of the air in a specific manner, which I shall be ready to demonstrate.

Many other things I might suggest of this nature, which, once the project is begun, I shall most willingly submit, as the occasion arises, to the judgment of the *Society*.

### *Extract from Dr.* **GREW**’s *Musæum Regalis Societatis. P. 284.*

**CRYSTAL**, at least some sorts of it, is the softest, says *Boethius*, of all gems. He should have said of all *transparent* gems, for the *turquoise* is much softer. The most usual figure of *crystal* is *hexagonal*; yet *Terzagi* mentions a rock of square-pointed ones. But it is observable that he says the bed on which they grew seemed to be *gold ore*. If so, it might proceed from some governing principle in the *ore*. For I have heard it noted, as I remember, by *Sir Christopher Wren*, that *grain gold* is often found naturally shaped into *cubes*.

...meanwhile, what to suggest to your Lordship, I cannot guess; the solemnity of the occasion and my solicitude for the honor of the *Society* makes me think nothing proper, nothing remarkable enough. It is not every year that will produce such a master experiment as the *Torricellian* <note>The barometer experiment by Evangelista Torricelli.</note>, and one so fruitful of new experiments as that is; and therefore the *Society* has deservedly spent much time upon that and its offspring. And if you have any notable experiment that may appear to open new light into the principles of philosophy, nothing would better befit the pretensions of the *Society*, though possibly such would be too dry for this purpose, in which there ought to be something of pomp. On the other side, to produce mere tricks and things to raise wonder—such as *Kircher*, *Schott*, and even jugglers abound with—will hardly suit the gravity of the occasion. It must, therefore, be something between both: enlightening in philosophy, and yet whose use and advantage is obvious and requires no lecture; and besides, it may surprise with some unexpected effect and be commendable for the ingenuity of the contrivance. 

Half a dozen experiments thus qualified will be abundantly enough for an hour’s entertainment; and I cannot believe the *Society* can lack them if they look back into their own store. For myself, I must profess freely that I have nothing with me suitable to the idea I have of what ought to be performed before such an assembly. Geometrical problems, and new lines, new bodies, and new methods, however useful, will be but tasteless in a transient show. New theories, or observations, or astronomical instruments—either for observation or for the facilitation of calculations—are valuable only to those experts who have particularly experienced the defects that these things pretend to supply. Sciographical <note>Relating to the art of projecting shadows or sundials.</note> tricks, of which a hundred varieties may be given, are so easy to invent that they are now cheap. Scenographical, catoptrical <note>Relating to mirrors and reflected light.</note>, and dioptrical <note>Relating to the refraction of light through lenses.</note> tricks require excellent painting as well as geometrical truth in the profile, or else they do not deceive the eye. Designs of engines for the ease of labor, or promoting anything in agriculture or the trades—I have occasionally thought upon several, but they are not intelligible without letters and references, and often not without some demonstration. Designs in architecture, etc., and the few chemical experiments I have been acquainted with, will, I fear, be too tedious for an entertainment. Experiments in anatomy, though of the most value for their use, are sordid and unpleasant to anyone but those whose desire for knowledge makes them digest it. 

Experiments for the establishment of natural philosophy are seldom pompous; it is upon billiards and tennis balls, upon the spinning of sticks and tops, upon a vial of water or a wedge of glass, that the great *Descartes* has built the most refined and accurate theories that human wit ever reached. And certainly nature, in the best of her works, is apparent enough in obvious things, were they but carefully observed; and the key that opens treasures is often plain and rusty, but unless it be gilded, it will make no show at court.

If I have been conversant in philosophical things (as I know how idle I have been), it has been principally in these ways which I have recounted to your Lordship, by which your Lordship perceives how useless I am for this service. Yet if your Lordship will still pursue me, I know not what shift to make but to retire back to something I have formerly produced.

I have pleased myself not a little with the play of the "weather-wheel" (the only true way to measure expansions of the air), and I imagine it must certainly give others satisfaction if it were once firmly made. I suppose this may be done if the circular pipes (which cannot be truly blown in glass) were made of brass by those who make trumpets and sackbuts <note>An early form of the trombone.</note> (who wire-draw their pipes through a hole to equalize them, and then, filling them with melted lead, turn them round into whatever curves they please). The inside of the pipe must

...be varnished with China-varnish to preserve it from the quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note>; and the glasses fixed to it with varnish, which I suppose will be the best cement in the world; for thus the *Chinese* fix glass and mother-of-pearl in their works. It would be no unpleasant spectacle to see a man live without fresh air for as long as you please. A description of the vessel for cooling and filtering the air at once, I formerly showed the *Society* and left in Mr. *Boyle’s* hands; I suppose it is worth putting into practice. You will at least learn this much from it: that something else in air is requisite for life besides that it should be cool only and free from the smoky <note>Fuliginous.</note> vapors and moisture it was infected with during exhalation; for all those will, in probability, be deposited during its circulation through the instrument. If nitrous fumes be found requisite (as I suspect), ways may possibly be found to supply those too, by placing some mild chemical spirits that, by fuming, may infuse the air within the vessel.

If an artificial eye were truly and optically <note>Dioptrically.</note> made (which I would have at least as big as a tennis ball), it would represent the picture as nature makes it. The cornea and crystalline lens must be glass; the other humors, water. I once surveyed a horse's eye as exactly as I could, measuring what the spheres of the crystalline lens and cornea were, and what the proportions of the distances of the centers of every sphere were upon the axis. The ways by which I did it are too long to rehearse, but the projection at three times the size Sir *Paul Neile* may possibly find; or if your Lordship thinks it worthwhile, I shall repeat the experiment.

A needle that would function in a coach would be just as useful for knowing the direction and path when joined with the way-wiser <note>An odometer.</note>, as well as a pleasant diversion for the traveler; it would be an acceptable present to His Majesty, who might thus, as it were, sail by land. The construction may be thus: in a glass sphere two inches in diameter, half full of water, cause a short, heavy, broad needle fixed to a chart to swim, being buoyed up by the chart, and both varnished. Instead of a cap and pin, let the perforated needle move about a small wire or horsehair extended like a perpendicular axis in the glass sphere; its nadir being weighted with lead, and a horizon, as it were, cemented to it, let it move in circles <note>Gimbals.</note> like a compass. Then let a hemispherical concave containing the sphere in its circles be hung upon springs in this manner:

Suppose a base upon which are erected perpendicularly three stiff brass springs; from the ends of these springs, strings are strained, forming an equilateral triangle, the middle of whose sides pass through three small loops on the rim of the concave, which therefore, hanging on the strings, represents a circle inscribed in a triangle. From the middle of the base arises a coil spring <note>Worm-spring.</note> fastened by a string to the nadir of the concave, drawing it down a little and acting against the other three springs. These springs, I suppose, will simultaneously absorb much of both the vertical and side-to-side jolts; the circles will absorb oscillations; the remaining agitations will be dissipated in the water and stilled by the chart; for thus we see a platter floating in a bucket keeps the water from spilling during transport; and the *Chinese* have their compass floating in water instead of using gimbals.

Lastly, I would have the entire bottom of the base bristled all around like a brush, somewhat inclined, which is a cheap addition and will ease the movement like a hundred springs. It should be placed in the middle of the floor of the coach, where, by opening a window, you might also see the way-wiser on the perch <note>The wooden frame of a carriage.</note>.

My Lord, if my first designs had been perfect, I would not have troubled your Lordship with so much chatter, but with something performed and done;

# PART I.
## SECTION II.
### Of Anatomy, etc.

Dr. *Wren* assisted Dr. *Willis* in his excellent treatise on the *Anatomy of the Brain*, in the manner which the learned *author* has testified in his *preface* to that *work*, namely:

<margin>Anatomy of the Brain (Cerebri Anatome), London 1664.</margin>
In addition to the help brought by the most skillful hand of this man (Doctor Lower) in dissecting, it is not proper to hide how much I received besides from those most distinguished men, Dr. Thomas Millington, M.D., as well as from Mr. Christopher Wren, LL.D. and Savilian Professor of Astronomy; both of whom frequently attended our dissections and were accustomed to confer on the reasons for the uses of the parts. Furthermore, the former most learned man, to whom I privately proposed my observations and conjectures from day to day, often confirmed me with his support when I was uncertain in mind and less confident in my own opinion. Moreover, that other most distinguished man, Doctor Wren, out of the singular kindness with which he is gifted, did not think it a burden to draw with his most learned hands many figures of the brain and skull, so that the works might be more exact.

<margin>Dr. Plot's Natural History of Oxford, p. 301.</margin>
Dr. *Willis's method* of dissecting the brain (in which he had the assistance of the deservedly famous Sir *Christopher Wren*, Dr. *Millington*, etc.) is new and most natural, and so exact that there is scarcely any part of it that has not received considerable advancements.

Among various new experiments in anatomy which he exhibited at the meetings at *Oxford* were diagrams of several dissected fish, in which the structure of the parts appeared very often irregular and differed much both from beasts and from one another. He observed several very significant things in birds. Some parts of animals he traced more exactly with the help of magnifying glasses <note>Microscopes or lenses.</note>, such as the kidneys, the *plexus* in the brain, etc. He found the nerves to have small veins and arteries in them. He then found that the lymph ducts empty themselves into the receptacle of chyle from all parts, both the bowels and limbs, etc.

<margin>Sprat's History of the Royal Society, p. 317.</margin>
> "He was the first author of the noble anatomical experiment of *injecting liquids into the veins of animals*. This experiment is now commonly known, but it was long ago exhibited at the meetings in Oxford, and from there carried by some Germans and published abroad. By this operation, various creatures were immediately purged, made to vomit, intoxicated, killed, or revived according to the quality of the liquid injected. From this arose many new experiments, and especially that of transfusing blood, which the Society has prosecuted in several instances that will probably end in extraordinary success."

It seems, by the date and a paragraph in a letter to a person of distinction in Ireland*, that he made the first experiment with *infusion* around the year 1656. After the recital of several new experiments in philosophy and anatomy, he proceeds as follows:
> “The most significant experiment I have made lately is this: I injected wine and ale into the blood of a living dog through a vein, in large amounts, until I made him extremely drunk, but soon after he urinated it out. With two ounces of an infusion of *Crocus Metallorum* <note>An antimonial preparation used to induce vomiting.</note> injected this way, the dog immediately began vomiting and continued to vomit until he died. It would take too long to tell you the effects of *opium*, scammony <note>A medicinal resin used as a strong laxative.</note>, and other things which I have tried in this manner. I am continuing to pursue this experiment, which I consider to be of great importance, and something that will shed great light on the theory and practice of medicine <note>Physick: the art or practice of healing; medicine.</note>.”
