## *An Account of the Origin and Early Attempts of a Method to Convey Liquids Directly into the Bloodstream.*

<margin>Philosophical Transactions, No. 7, p. 128, 1665.</margin>
Since some books have recently been published abroad regarding the method of *injecting liquids into veins*—in which the origin of that *invention* seems to be credited to others besides the person to whom it truly belongs—it will surely not be thought inappropriate to say something to assert and preserve the true *inventor's right* beyond any doubt. For this purpose, it is only necessary to state the *time* and the *place* where, and among whom, it was first conceived and tested. Taking all these circumstances together, it is well known that at least six years ago (well before it was heard that anyone else even claimed to have thought of it), the learned and ingenious Dr. *Christopher Wren* proposed a theory at the *University of Oxford*. (He is currently the esteemed *Savilian Professor of Astronomy* there, and many inquisitive people are ready to confirm this account.) He proposed to that noble benefactor of experimental philosophy, Mr. *Robert Boyle*, Dr. *Wilkins*, and other worthy individuals, that he thought he could easily devise a way to convey any liquid directly into the bloodstream—namely, by tying off veins, opening them on the side of the tie closer to the heart, and inserting slender syringes or quills attached to bladders (similar to enema pipes) containing the substance to be injected. This operation was performed on fairly large, lean dogs so that the vessels would be large enough and easily accessible.

Once this proposal was made, Mr. *Boyle* soon ordered an *apparatus* to put it to the *test*. In several experiments on various dogs, *opium* and the infusion of *Crocus Metallorum* were injected into the hind legs of those animals, where the larger blood vessels are easiest to access. The result was that the *opium*, soon circulating to the brain, quickly drugged the dog, though it did not kill him. However, a large dose of *Crocus Metallorum* caused another dog to vomit until he died. All of this is reported more fully and in greater detail by Mr. *Boyle* in his excellent book, *The Usefulness of Experimental Philosophy*, Part 2, Postscript to Essay 2. There it is also mentioned that as the fame of this *invention* and the subsequent trials spread—and particularly coming to the knowledge of a curious foreign ambassador then residing in *London*—he tried it with some *Crocus Metallorum* on a criminal <note>Malefactor: a person who commits a crime.</note> who was one of his lower-ranking servants; the result was that as soon as the—

Since that time, it has been frequently practiced both in *Oxford* and *London*, as well before the *Royal Society* as elsewhere. And particularly that learned physician Dr. *Timothy Clark* has made it part of his work to pursue those experiments with much industry, great accuracy, and significant observations; these were produced by him over two years ago and read before the *Royal Society*, who then asked him, as one of their members, to complete what he had proposed for himself on that subject and then to publish it. The result of this, it is hoped, will soon appear and not prove unwelcome to the curious.

Some of these people, though they may believe that liquids thus injected into veins without preparation and digestion will cause odd commotions in the blood, disturb nature, and cause strange symptoms in the body, yet they have other thoughts about liquids that are prepared from things that have already passed through the digestion of the stomach—for example, the spirit of urine, of hartshorn, of blood, *etc.* And they hope likewise that, besides *medical uses*, they may also serve for *anatomical purposes* by filling the vessels of an animal as full as they can hold in this way, and by greatly distending them, discover new vessels, *etc.* But not to expand upon the uses now, the reader may safely take this narrative as the naked, real matter of fact, by which it is as clear as noonday—both from the time and the undeniable testimony of very many significant persons in that University who can jointly attest to it, as well as from the specific, unquestionable testimony of Mr. *Boyle* and his worthy company, who were the first eyewitnesses of the trials made—that to *Oxford*, and in it to Dr. *Christopher Wren*, this *invention* is due. Consequently, all others who discuss or write about it either derive it from him or came upon the same device several years after him.

### Mr. BOYLE’s *Account of the above-mentioned Invention, and the Experiments thereon.*

To enable you (*Pyrophilus*) to satisfy those inquisitive persons who have heard some, yet only an imperfect, report of a much-publicized experiment that was devised several years ago at *Oxford* and since tried in other places before very illustrious spectators, I am content to take the opportunity afforded me by what was recently mentioned in the previous essay concerning the application of poisons. I wish to inform you that a good while after the writing of that essay, I happened to have some conversation about matters of a similar nature with those excellent mathematicians Dr. *J. Wilkins* and Mr. *Christopher Wren*. During this, the latter of those virtuosi told us that *he thought he could easily contrive a way to convey any liquid poison immediately into the mass of blood.* Since our knowledge of his extraordinary sagacity made us very desirous to try what he proposed, I provided a large dog, on which he performed his experiments in the presence and with the assistance of some eminent physicians and other learned men. His method (which is much better learned by sight than by description) was briefly this: First, to make a small and timely incision over that part of the hind leg where the larger vessels that carry the blood are most easily reached; then to make a ligature upon those vessels, and to apply a certain

...a certain small plate of brass (above half an inch long and about a quarter of an inch broad, with sides bending inward) was shaped almost like a man's thumbnail, but somewhat longer. This plate had four little holes in the sides near the corners so that it could be firmly fastened to the vessel by threads passed through them. In the same little plate, there was also an aperture, or a somewhat large slit, parallel to its sides and almost as long as the plate, so that the vein might be exposed there to the lancet and prevented from shifting aside. This plate being well fastened on, he made a slit along the vein, from the ligature toward the heart, large enough to insert the slender pipe of a syringe. Through this, I had proposed to inject a warm solution of *Opium* in sack [fortified wine], so that the effect of our experiment might be more rapid and obvious. 

Accordingly, our skilled experimenter, having overcome the difficulties caused by the violent struggling of the tortured dog, delivered a small dose of the solution or tincture into the opened vessel. By entering the mass of blood (of which it is difficult to avoid shedding some quantity during the operation), it was quickly carried to the brain and other parts of the body by the circulation. Consequently, we had scarcely untied the dog (whose four feet had to be fastened very strongly to the four corners of the table) before the *Opium* began to show its narcotic quality. Almost as soon as he was on his feet, he began to nod his head and falter and reel in his gait; soon after, he appeared so stupified that bets were offered that his life could not be saved. 

But I, wishing to keep him for further observation, had him whipped up and down a neighboring garden. By being kept awake and in motion, he began to recover after some time. Being led home and carefully tended, he not only recovered but began to grow fat so visibly that it was a cause of wonder. However, I could not observe how he fared for long; for this experiment and other trials made upon him had made him famous, and he was soon after stolen away from me. Subsequent attempts informed us that the plate was not necessary if the fingers were skillfully used to support the vessel to be opened, and that a slender quill fastened to a bladder containing the matter to be injected was somewhat more convenient than a syringe. We also found that, despite this, the experiment would not succeed well unless the dog were quite large and lean, so that the vessels might be large enough and easily accessible.

The *Inventor* of the method later practiced it in the presence of that most learned nobleman, the Marquis of *Dorchester*, and found that a moderate dose of the infusion of *Crocus Metallorum* [an antimonial emetic] did not much affect the dog to which it was given. However, once when he injected a large dose (about two ounces or more), it acted so quickly and violently upon a new dog that within a few hours he vomited up his life and all upon the straw where they had laid him. I later wished that not only some strongly acting drugs, but also their appropriate antidotes (or else powerful liquid cordials) and some alterative medicines, might be injected in plentiful doses. In the case of diuretics, a very ingenious anatomist and physician told me he had tried it with very good success. I likewise proposed that, if it could be done without too much danger or cruelty, trials might be made on some human bodies, especially those of criminals. Some months later, a foreign ambassador—a very inquisitive person residing in *London* at the time—did me the honor of visiting me. He informed me that he had ordered a trial to be made with an infusion of *Crocus Metallorum* upon a lowly servant of his who deserved to have been hanged; but as soon as the injection began to be made, the fellow did (either really or

<margin>*Philosophical Transactions, Number 28. 1667.*</margin>
The *French Journals* in the year 1667 confidently affirmed, as a certainty, that the *French* gave the *English* the first thought or notion of this *experiment*. And why? Because (they say) we are witnesses that a *Benedictine friar*, one *Robert de Gabets*, discussed it at Monsieur *de Montmor's* ten years ago. Surely all honest men will acknowledge that the *certain* way of deciding such controversies as these is a public record, either written or printed, declaring the time and place an *invention* was first proposed, the design of the method to practice it, and the instances of success in its execution. All of this stands in favor of *England*.

Number 7 of the *Transactions* of the *Royal Society* (printed in *December*, *Anno* 1665) informs the world how many years ago Dr. *Christopher Wren* proposed the *experiment of infusion* into veins. This was *hint* enough for the *Royal Society*, some while after, to progress from *infusion* to *transfusion*. For the trial of the latter, they gave orders at their public meeting on May 17, 1665, as may be seen in their *journals*, where it was recorded by the care of their secretaries, who were bound by oath to fidelity. The *trials* proving at that time unsuccessful for want of a proper *apparatus* and a well-designed *method* of operation, the learned physician and expert anatomist Dr. *Lower* since found out such a method. This is not only recorded in the same book but also published in print, Number 20 of the *Transactions*, before which time it had already been practiced by the said doctor in *Oxford*, who was followed by several ingenious men in *London* who successfully practiced it by the public order of the *Royal Society*.

<margin>*Philosophical Transactions, Number 35. 1668.*</margin>
It seems strange that so surprising an *invention* should have been conceived in *France*, as they claim, ten years ago, and remained there so long in the womb until the way of midwiving it into the world was sent there from *London*. To say nothing of the disagreement that seems to exist about the *French* parent of this *fetus*: Monsieur *de Gurye* in his letter attributes it to the Abbot *Bourdelot*, but the author of the *French Journals* attributes it to a *Benedictine friar*.

## Extract of part of a Letter written to Mr. *Oldenburg*, Secretary to the *Royal Society*, by the learned and experienced Dr. *Timothy Clark*, one of his Majesty’s Physicians in Ordinary, concerning the origin of the *injection* into *veins* and the *transfusion* of *blood*.

> Furthermore, since you wish it so, most learned sir, and believe it is appropriate to do so, I will faithfully relate the origin of blood transfusion, at least as it occurred among us. Leaving aside that testimony which you still have in your possession from a trustworthy man and fellow of the Royal Society—namely, that Mr. Potter, a distinguished theologian, thirty years ago, having considered Harvey's theory of circulation, frequently proposed the transfusion of blood to this fellow and other learned men—I, for my part, will report only those things that are certainly known to me regarding this matter. *Wren was the first who conceived of the infusion of various liquids into the bloodstream of living animals and performed it at* Oxford. *At that time, while I was investigating the nature of blood to the best of my ability, he shared what he had done with me. From then on, I prepared myself diligently to perform various experiments of this kind; and among other things I decided to do then, I determined to inject waters, beers of every kind, milk, whey, broths, wines, spirits of wine, and the blood of various animals. In addition to other tubes adapted for various operations, I had some made in such a way that with one end inserted into the artery of one animal and the other into the vein of another, blood could be more easily transfused from one animal to another. To give credit where it is due,* Dr. Henshaw, *also of the Royal Society, had attempted blood transfusion by the same method—either before this or around the same time as I did—but in vain. This was why, when blood transfusion was proposed in the* Royal Society *among other experiments (as is clear enough from its archives), other learned men agreed with me that perhaps nothing was to be hoped for from such an operation; and I myself recounted the difficulties I had encountered while performing this operation. Afterward, the matter was tried again but did not succeed for us, until the most learned and experienced* Dr. Lower *successfully accomplished it at* Oxford *in the year 1666. Once this was done, toward the end of that same year, you yourself made the whole matter public along with the method of the operation. In the following year, we also heard about this operation from* France. *I confess I was filled with joy when I was made certain that French confidence had attempted what our fear or perhaps laziness had scarcely dared to try. You know, most learned man, with how much applause I rose for the famous* Mr. Denis, *who not only most ingeniously undertook the defense of such experiments but also later performed them on humans.*

*But it does not seem to me of such great importance that the learned* Frenchman *should contend so vigorously and spiritedly about the first origin of blood transfusion, or that I should claim its first invention for ourselves. You yourself, if I am not mistaken,* Mr. Oldenburg, *led this* Frenchman *into error. For in your Philosophical Transactions, published in the month of December 1665, where you gave an account of the origin of the infusion of various liquids into veins, you say that at least six years before that time, Dr. Christopher Wren had first of all attempted that infusion.*

*Perhaps no one will doubt that if anyone thought seriously about promoting this experiment and meditated attentively on mixing various things with blood, the mixing of blood from different animals would very easily occur to such a person. Since, therefore, infusion was invented around the year 1659 according to your calculation, and the proposal about blood transfusion is said to have been made in the house of* Mr. Montmor *in the year 1658, either by the famous Abbot* Bourdelot *or by the learned Benedictine* Robert de Gabets *(for the first proposer is not yet agreed upon), anyone could easily be led to the opinion that the first mention of this experiment is at least owed to* France. *But that operation, which you mentioned in those Transactions—namely, the infusion of emetic wine into the bloodstream through the vein of a servant's arm in the house of some foreign ambassador then residing in* London—*was performed in the year 1657 in the house of the* French *envoy,* Mr. de Bordeaux, *in the presence of* Sir Colladon, *a knight and today the ordinary physician to the Queen Mother. Many learned men can testify with me that many such experiments were repeated by us in the same year, some of which were also performed in the house of the illustrious* Marquis of Dorchester.

*It is also worth noting that Dr. Lower’s entire easy method of performing the transfusion was published by you in December 1666, and we did not hear of such an operation from* France *until March of the following year. It seems likely, therefore, unless I am mistaken, that the prize for this invention (if indeed it deserves a prize) is owed to the* English *rather than to the* French.

As for the rest, I would gladly know by what arguments that most learned Roman, Manfredi, judged that this invention was first conceived in Germany. To us, nothing at all has yet occurred that could lead to even the slightest suspicion of that kind. Three or four years ago, a certain Major, a physician of Hamburg, tried to persuade the literary world through some published pamphlets that he had thought of such a thing two years earlier. But undoubtedly that learned man was poorly informed on this matter and publicized his thoughts too hastily. For he says he heard that such an operation—namely, the administering of a cathartic medicine by infusion into a vein—was performed before a certain Palatine prince in Germany; whereas in truth this was performed by me in our royal court before the most high Prince Palatine, Rupert, from where it could afterward have easily been communicated to the Germans. I have narrated the matter faithfully, following the chronological order. — And I boldly assert this: we in England received this invention from no foreigner.

<margin>Philosophical Transactions, Number 37. 1663.</margin>
An *Italian* Philosopher, in a certain tract entitled *Account of the experiments made in England, France, and Italy regarding the transfusion of blood*, printed in *Rome*, undertook to prove that *transfusion* was of greater antiquity, having been known to *Libavius* over fifty years ago. For this, that *Roman* author cited a passage from the said *Libavius* (in *Defense of the synthesis of chemical secrets*, etc., in the year 1615), where *transfusion* is described in these words:

> Let there be a robust, healthy young man, full of spirited blood; and let there stand by a man exhausted of strength, thin, gaunt, and barely drawing breath. Let the master of the art have silver tubes that fit together; let him open the artery of the robust man, insert a tube, and secure it; then let him also open the artery of the sick man and insert a receiving tube. Now let him join the two tubes to each other, and the warm, spirited arterial blood from the healthy man will leap into the sick man, bringing with it the fountain of life and driving away all languor.

The *Observer* here rightly notices that *Libavius* did not propose this operation seriously, but only to mock it, and that he designed it with great danger to both the *recipient* and the *donor* by proposing to open arteries in both. But,

To briefly list some of the first trials performed in *England* and in foreign parts following the publication of Dr. *Wren*’s noble invention of *infusion* (and consequently *transfusion*): it is recorded that in *November* 1667, the experiments of transfusing nine or ten ounces of the arterial blood of a young sheep into a *human* vein in the arm were successfully performed at *Arundel House* by Doctors *Lower* and *King*, in the presence of many distinguished persons; and the account was communicated to the Royal Society.

Monsieur *Denys*, Professor of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy at *Paris*, related in a letter to the publisher of the *Transactions* that they had transferred the blood of four wethers <note>castrated rams</note> into a horse twenty-six years old, and that this horse had received much strength from it and a more than ordinary appetite.

Among other successful transfusions by the same *author* are those of lamb’s blood into dogs—which, several months after the operation, were not only living but were very well, and some of them grew fatter than they were before—and of kid’s blood into a little spaniel bitch twelve years of age,

### Some remarkable experiments of injecting medicated liquors into veins were communicated in a letter from Dantzic, by Dr. FABRICIUS, physician to that city.

Because (said he) we had a great desire to experiment on what would be the effects of the surgery of *injecting* liquors into *human* veins, three fit subjects presenting themselves in our hospital, we thought it good to make the trial upon them. But seeing little ground to hope for a clear operation from any *altering* medicines, we considered the experiment would be more convenient and conspicuous using *laxatives*; which made us *inject* by a siphon about two drams of such a kind of medicine into the *median vein* of the right arm. The *patients* were these: one was a lusty, robust soldier dangerously infected with the *venereal disease*, and suffering grievous protuberances of the bones in his arms. When the purgative liquor was *infused* into him, he complained of great pains in his elbows, and the small valves of his arm swelled so visibly that it was necessary, by a gentle compression of one's fingers, to stroke up that swelling toward the patient's shoulders. Some four hours later, it began to work, not very troublesomely, and so it did the next day; so much so that the man had five good stools after it. Without any other remedies those protuberances were gone, nor are there any traces left of the above-mentioned *disease*. The *two other trials* were made upon the *other sex*. A married woman of thirty-five, and a serving maid of twenty years of age, had both been from their birth very grievously afflicted with epileptic fits, so that there were little hopes left to cure them. They both underwent this operation, and there was *injected* into their veins a *laxative resin*, dissolved in an *anti-epileptic spirit*. The *first* of these had gentle stools some hours after the *injection*, and the next day; the fits recurring now and then, but much milder, have since altogether vanished. As for the other, namely the *maid*, she went to stool four times the same day, and several times the next; but by going into the air, taking cold, and not observing any diet, she died.

The operation had been performed twice with good success; the patient having had a good interval of two months after the first, and all hopes of a longer one after the second, had it not been for the debauches of wine and brandy that he fell into soon after the operation. He was a *Briton* by birth, and the origin of his madness was *love*. <margin>*Philosophical Transactions Number 39.*</margin>
With the accounts of *transfusion of blood*, one other memorable instance among many may be further cited regarding the success of some experiments of *infusing medicines into human veins*, written from *Danzig* to the Honorable *R. Boyle*.

Monsieur *Smith*, physician in ordinary to this city, having been granted liberty to try an experiment upon some persons desperately infected with the *pox* then in the public hospital here, ventured to open a vein and infuse some medicines into the blood. This was tried upon two persons, of whom one recovered and the other died. Yet, being since further encouraged by corresponding with some of the *Royal Society* in *England*, about a month ago, the said physician, together with Monsieur *Scheffeler*, another eminent practitioner in this city, repeated the experiment by infusing *altering medicines* into the veins of the right arms of three persons: one lame with the gout; the other extremely *apoplectic*; and the third reduced to extremity by that odd distemper, the *Plica Polonica*. The success of this—as Monsieur *Hevelius* (who was the only person admitted to be present at the operation) informs me—was that the gouty man found himself quite well the next day, and shortly after went to work, as it was harvest time, and has continued well ever since, leaving the hospital yesterday and declaring himself cured. The *apoplectic* man has not had one *paroxysm*, and the various sores which the *Plica Polonica* had caused are healed; both these persons have been able to work at any time these past three weeks. Dated *August* 18, 1668.

Were it not too lighthearted for the subject, one might be inclined to imagine that the ancient *mythologists* had some notion of the doctrine of *transfusion* and *infusion*, and their wonderful *healing* and *restorative effects*; but not comprehending how it could be possible to attribute them to natural causes, they had recourse to the powers of enchantments and magical arts. Thus *Medea* restored (as it is said) *Aeson*, when he was decrepit with age, to his former vigor of life by exhausting the old blood and infusing medicinal juices and new vital blood into the emptied veins and arteries. She tried the same experiment on an old ram, which became a sucking lamb. These particulars, well adapted to fables, are described by the *Roman poet* with his usual elegance and with this conclusion:

> " *stricto Medea recludit*
> " *Ense senis jugulum; veteremque exire cruorem*
> " *Passa; replet succis: quos postquam combibit Æson*
> " *Aut ore acceptos, aut vulnere; barba, comæque*
> " *Canitie positâ nigrum rapuere colorem :*

### Dr. WREN'S *Operation of cutting out the Spleen of a Dog with Safety, and Method of Cure.*

Mr. Boyle in his *Essays of Experimental Natural Philosophy*, mentions the following experiment of cutting out the *spleen* of a dog with safety. The same experiment was tried by Dr. *Wren*, who has described the whole operation, and given the method of cure, which being deficient in Mr. Boyle's account, is here subjoined to it.

Nor is it a small convenience to the anatomist that he may perform various instructive experiments in the bodies of animals that he dares not venture on in those of men; for instance, that recent noble experiment, which many still do not believe, of taking out the *spleen* of a dog without killing him. We may have occasion elsewhere to show that this experiment may be useful, and we ourselves can witness that it is possible to perform it safely (though I confess many have attempted it unsuccessfully, and it has lately been pronounced impossible in print). And because I have not yet met with any author who claims to relate this experiment (the removal of a dog's *spleen*) as an eyewitness rather than upon the credit of others, I am content to assure you that the skillful dissector Dr. *Joliff* did, at my request last year, take out the *spleen* of a young setter I brought to him. So it might not be claimed that the experiment was performed unfaithfully or favorably, I performed part of it myself and held the *spleen* (which was the largest in proportion to its body I ever saw) in my hand while he cut asunder the vessels reaching to it, so that I might be sure there was not the least part of the *spleen* left unremoved. Yet this puppy, in less than a fortnight, grew not only well but as playful and as lively as before; I need not take pains to make you believe this, since you often saw him at your mother's house, from where he was eventually stolen. And though I remember the famous empiric *Fiorovanti*, in one of his *Italian* books, mentions having been persuaded by the persistence of a lady (whom he calls *Marulla Græca*) much afflicted with splenetic ailments to rid her of her spleen, and adds that she outlived the loss of it many years—yet he who considers the situation of that part and the importance of the vessels belonging to it in human bodies will probably be inclined to think that, though his account may be believed, his recklessness ought not to be imitated.

### The Operation and Method of Cure, by Dr. WREN.

Provide a dog as large as a spaniel, and having tied him in a suitable position on his right side with a cushion under him so that his belly may turn a little upward, first clip away the hair and mark with ink the site for the incision. Draw a line two fingers' breadth below the short ribs across the *abdomen* at right angles to the *musculus rectus*, beginning a finger's breadth short of it and carrying it the length of three fingers' breadth toward the back. Then insert a sharp knife, like a sow-gelder's knife, until you feel you have just pierced through the muscles and *peritoneum*, taking care to avoid the guts. From there, rip upward freely, carrying the point of the knife to the end of the line. Then put in two fingers, and while another person presses down the *abdomen*, draw the *spleen* just out of the wound, taking great care not to pull it too far out because of the risk of disordering the adhering vessels within—the stomach, the caul <note>The omentum</note>, the arteries, and veins. Then either tie the veins and arteries with strong, untwisted thread in three or four places, including the caul, and cut them off close to the parenchyma of the spleen; then, anointing the ends of the vessels and the wound of the caul with balsam or oil of *Hypericum* <note>St. John's Wort</note>, put them back in their places. Alternatively, you may cauterize the vessels and anoint them with the juice of houseleek and plantain beaten with whites of eggs, or else with *Unguento Diacalcitheos* dissolved with vinegar and oil of roses, especially the nerve. Then sew up the wound with the suture called *gastrorrhaphy*, leaving enough room at the lower end for discharge to come out. First anoint the wound with balsam, then take: ℞ *Myrtle and rose oil, 2 oz.; white wax, 1 oz.; barley flour, 1/2 oz.; Armenian bole and Terra Sigillata, 6 drams of each.* Make a large plaster of this to cover the wound and all the muscles around it; bandage his belly

### XXIX.

<margin>
*Philosophical Transactions, Number 43.*
</margin>
Theory concerning the general Laws of Motion; imparted to the Royal Society, December 17, 1668. Though considered by the Author several years before, and verified by many experiments made by himself, and that other excellent mathematician, Mr. *Rooke*, before the said Society, as was attested by many worthy members of that illustrious body.

->*The law of nature concerning the collision of bodies.*<-

*N. B.* As all learned men are concerned in certain historical passages relating to this treatise, and to those communicated to the Royal Society by Dr. *John Wallis*, and Mr. *Christiaan Huygens*, on the same subject; it was thought most proper to publish them in the language of the learned, namely:

<margin>
By Henry Oldenburg, Secretary of the Royal Society.
</margin>
Since in recent months several members of the Royal Society, in a public meeting of the same, more earnestly urged that the very important subject of the Rules of Motion—which had been discussed among them more than once before, but, because many other things intervened, was never, as was fitting, discussed or weighed—should finally be subjected to a rigorous examination and completed; it indeed seemed good to that most illustrious assembly to decree that whichever of its members had applied themselves more than others to investigating the nature of motion should be asked to bring forth their thoughts and discoveries on that matter. At the same time, they were asked to collect and provide those things which had been devised on that subject by those excellent men—namely Galileo, Descartes, Honoratus Fabri, Joachim Jungius, Pierre Borel, and others—to the end that, having consulted and compared the opinions of all in this way, that theory which most closely agreed with observations and experiments (frequently performed with due care and faith) might then be granted its rightful place in the philosophical community.

This call having been issued, members of the said Society were immediately prompted—primarily Christiaan Huygens, John Wallis, and Christopher Wren—to hasten the maturing and preparation of their hypotheses and rules of motion, on the construction of which they had toiled for some time. Thus it happened that this select trio of most distinguished men, after the space of a few weeks, transmitted their theories, elegantly summarized, almost in competition, and sought the opinion of the Royal Society upon them. First of all, Mr. Wallis communicated his principles for estimating motions in a letter dated November 15, 1668, which was delivered and read on the 29th of the same month. Soon after him followed Mr. Christopher Wren, who caused the law of nature concerning the collision of bodies to be publicly presented to the same Society on the 17th of the following December. The Society soon gave orders (the consent of both these authors having been previously obtained) that, for the more convenient communication of these writings and for a more widespread discussion, the whole matter should be sent to the press.

While these things were happening among us, look, a messenger brought us on January 4th following (<note>Old Style</note>) Mr. Huygens’ letters, written on the 5th of the same month (but <note>New Style</note>), containing the first four rules of his writing, *On the motion of bodies from mutual impulse*, along with the demonstrations. I had ready a copy of Wren's theory, and immediately on that same day, thanks to the public messenger, I sent it back to Mr. Huygens in exchange. I delayed opening Huygens' letters (in which I suspected, because of their size and the author's previous promise, such a thing was included) until an opportunity arose to speak with the most noble and wise President of the Royal Society, Lord Viscount Brouncker. This being done, once the rules of both were compared in the aforementioned Society, a wonderful agreement immediately shone out in both; this produced in us a great willingness to commit both these writings to our press. We lacked nothing here on Huygens' part except his consent; without which we judged it by no means right to publish his discovery, especially since he had not given it to us in its entirety at that time. Meanwhile, we were careful to enter his writing into the public records of the Royal Society, and at the same time to return formal thanks to the author on January 11th for that wise communication. This was followed (on February 4th) by a concerned reminder that he should see to it that this theory of his was printed, either in Paris (which was easy to do in the *Journal des Sçavans*, as they call it) or here in London in the *Philosophical Transactions*, or at least that he should permit it. After these letters were sent, a little while later we received a second letter from Huygens, mentioning that Wren’s writing on this subject had been correctly delivered, yet saying nothing at all about preparing an edition of his own writing, either in Paris or London.

From this, I would altogether think it clear that Huygens himself was lacking in hastening that publication; indeed, by procrastinating, he gave the occasion for the praised Mr. **Wren**—who produced an entirely identical theory by the sagacity of his own genius—to rightly come into a share of the glory due to this speculation. It is beyond all doubt that neither of them knew anything of the other's theory before their writings appeared, but each, by the fertility of his own genius, gave birth to this beautiful offspring.

To be sure, Huygens solved those cases of motion that were proposed to him several years ago while he was in London; this is a brilliant argument indeed that he had even then explored the rules by which he performed it with such evidence. But he himself will not claim that he revealed anything of his theory to any of the English; rather, he is bound to admit that he was urged by some of them to communicate it, yet was never, until very recently, persuaded to do so.

These things being offered to truth and justice, we now present the rules of Huygens himself, etc.

*Table of the refraction of rays in a glass medium (assuming the maximum refraction of glass to be 489) calculated according to the most exquisite hypothesis of the English philosopher.*

## A Catalogue, with Vouchers of several of the Works of Sir CHRISTOPHER WREN; in the Method they are recited by Mr. WARD, (in his Account of the Lives of the Professors of Gresham College) exclusive of some Variations and Additions enumerated in the preceding Catalogue and Accounts.

### 1. Horologiographia geometrica.
This was a Latin version of an English treatise. It was written by Mr. Oughtred while Mr. Wren was a gentleman commoner at Wadham College in Oxford, and was afterwards published by Mr. Oughtred at the end of his *Clavis Mathematica* (Mathematical Key). <note>See the preface by G. O. to the Clavis Mathematica.</note>

### 2. *Tractatulus ad periodum Julianam spectans, Chronologiæ summè utilis.*
This short tract, which contains a method to find any particular year required upon being given the cycles, is inserted in the Prolegomena of *Helvicus's Theatrum historicum & chronologicum* (Historical and Chronological Theater), Oxford Edition, 1651, and continued in the later editions. The author's name is not mentioned; but that it was written by Mr. Wren is manifest from a note endorsed on the title page of the book in the hand of his father, the Dean, now in the possession of *Christopher Wren, Esq.* The words are these:
> Denique filio meo modestius renitenti incentivum adhibui, ut tractatulum illum algebraicum; Julianæ periodo (e cyclis in historia datis) expiscandæ accommodatissimum, sudante jam hoc prælo Oxoniensi, præfigi sineret. <note>Finally, I gave an incentive to my son, who was modestly resisting, so that he would allow that little algebraic tract—most suited for investigating the Julian period from the cycles given in history—to be prefixed, as the Oxford press was already at work on this.</note>
By the time in which this tract was first published, it appears that Mr. Wren could not be more than nineteen years of age when he wrote it.

### 3. *Oratio inauguralis habita Londini, in Collegio Greshamensi, per Christophorum Wren, A. M. Astronomiæ professorem electum, Anno 1657, Ætatis suæ 25.*
This inaugural oration is now first published in the *Appendix*, number VIII, from a copy communicated by *Christopher Wren, Esq.* to Dr. Mead, by whom I was favored with it.

### 4. *De recta tangente cycloidem primariam.*
->ΕΥΘΥΣΜΟΣ (Straightening) of the curve line of the primary cycloid demonstrated according to the method of the ancients.<-
->*On the dimensions of contracted and protracted cycloids.*<-
->*On solving the Keplerian problem by the cycloid.*<-
These four tracts, being communicated by him to Dr. Wallis at the beginning of *July* 1658, were afterward published by the Doctor as an appendix to his *tractatus de cycloide* (Treatise on the Cycloid). <note>See J. Wallis, mathematical works, volume I, page 533.</note>

The discourses that follow were written in the year 1612—others as late as 1720; and the whole consists of diverse methods proposed by Sir Christopher for that end, with drawings of several instruments proper for the purpose (engraved on copper plates). These papers are also in the hands of the same gentleman, along with the discourse last mentioned.

This catalogue in Mr. Professor Ward's work, compared and adjusted with the catalogues recounted before, may be deemed the most perfect that currently exists.

Sir *Christopher* has sometimes been heard to reflect sharply on the dishonesty of Mr. *Oldenburg*, who had neglected not only to enter several of his inventions and experiments into the registers of the *Society*, but also sent them to foreign parts, specifically *France* and *Germany*, where they were later published under other names as if they were their own.

<margin>Section XL, p. 311.</margin>
Consequently, Dr. *Sprat*, in his *History of the Royal Society*, took the opportunity—out of simple consideration for justice—to publish a separate account of Wren's endeavors in promoting the goals of the *Royal Society*. This was because, while reviewing the registers, he perceived that many excellent things, whose first invention ought to have been credited to Wren, were casually (or rather, intentionally) omitted.

The problem mentioned earlier as Number XXXII was sent from *France* as a challenge to the *English* mathematicians, with a cash reward promised to the person who could provide a solution. The solution was provided beyond any doubt, and the prize was requested; yet in the end, through some trickery, it was dishonorably withheld.

His generous nature in lending out papers that were never returned, his peculiar modesty, and his disregard for public applause and the methods by which men of the world usually proclaim and support the merits of their own work, prevented the appearance in public under his own name of many useful tracts, and caused him not to carry several discoveries through to perfection.

N. B. Mr. *Henry Oldenburg*, mentioned before (page 118), was chosen as a Fellow and Secretary upon the founding of the *Royal Society*. He collected and published the *Philosophical Transactions*, beginning on March 6, 1664, and continuing until Issue No. 136, dated *June* 25, 1677.

<margin>“It will be appropriate to examine what results from the hypothesis of the motion of the earth, in relation to the fixed stars and to the apparent poles of the earth and the ecliptic.” Cassini’s 2nd Fig.</margin> I send you here some reflections on Monsieur *Cassini’s* remarks on my letter to Dr. *Wallis*, together with an account of the effects of the Earth’s motion in changing the longitudes, latitudes, right ascensions, and declinations of the fixed stars. It is a new subject, and never, as far as I know, handled before. For though Mr. *Cassini* proposes to himself *to examine what will be the result of the hypothesis of the Earth’s motion, with respect to the fixed stars and the apparent poles of the Earth and the ecliptic*, in order to prove that the greatest removal of the Pole Star from the pole is made about the beginning of the foreign *April*, and its nearest approach in *October*; yet he has done it in such a manner as will make it appear to you that, though there is *some truth in the conclusion*, it does not result from his *premises* (as I asserted) or any deep consideration of the *effects* of the Earth’s motions or geometrical argumentation.

His first figure represents mine well enough, and his report of the contents of my letter is fair and candid; but the ground of his error is laid in his second, where, with me, making IODR represent the Earth’s orbit, he raises perpendiculars from every point of it until they intersect the plane EQ (supposedly placed on the surface of the sphere parallel to the plane of the ecliptic), whereby they describe on it the orbit EML, which will therefore be an exact representative of the orbit DOIR. Now, all those who allow the motion of the Earth make it an ellipsis; therefore, that must be an ellipsis too, and the point M in this will represent the sun, or the point S in the original orbit DOIR; though in his 3rd figure, he makes and calls it a circle wherein a movable pole of the ecliptic is carried annually about a fixed one and divides it into twelve signs marked with their proper symbols. Again,

Drawing lines parallel to the Earth’s axis to every point of the original orbit DOIR until they intersect the aforementioned plane EQ, he projects another curve NPQ, which shall also be an ellipsis (but more oblique than the former) and a distinct representative of the Earth’s orbit, the sun’s place in it being at P, in the line SP, drawn from the sun S in the original parallel to the axis.

Yet in his 3rd figure, *he makes and calls it a circle* in which a movable pole of the world revolves annually about a fixed one, and this also he distinguishes with the twelve signs, as he had done the other.

Near this last representative orbit, he plots a star at V, which he says shall be sometimes nearer, and at other times farther off from the pole of the world. He shows no reason why this star’s place may not be plotted with the same respect to the other distinct representative orbit EML and to the original IODR. Let it be done for the first at V and for the original at Y; it appears now that as the Earth makes her annual revolution, she sometimes comes nearest

# SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.

...to it, and moves further from it at others, through all the various orbits; which contributes nothing to his purpose.

<margin>Cassini's 3rd Figure</margin>From these preliminaries, he proceeds and transfers the second representative orbits of his 2nd figure into his 3rd. Making their suns the fixed poles of the ecliptic at P and of the world at A, he positions the Pole Star A on the surface of his sphere by its longitude from the next colure and the complement of its latitude, and thereby finds its place at S in his 3rd figure.

But it appears from what was remarked before that both his circles described around the two fixed poles are distinct representatives of the Earth's orbit (whatever he chooses to call them), and their centers represent the sun's positions in them. He may, and ought therefore, to position the star with the same relationship to Pole A that it has to Pole P; then its position on the surface of his sphere would be at $\varsigma$.

And now, just as in his 2nd figure we had three orbits of the Earth, as many suns, and three positions for one fixed star; so in this third figure, we have two suns, two fixed poles, and two movable poles (of the world and the ecliptic), along with two positions for the star—which is quite an absurdity.

Let those who so fiercely defend Mr. *Cassini’s* conclusion choose whichever pair of his poles they wish to discard; it will be evident that his conclusion vanishes and that (as I affirmed) it does not follow from these premises.

I foresee an evasion that Mr. *Cassini* might make, which I shall keep in mind and answer in its proper place. For now, I shall only remind him that those who understand how all diurnal appearances occur under the hypothesis of the Earth's motion also know how to represent them with lines drawn on its surface, or on a fixed *rete* <note>A net-like structure or grid used in astronomical instruments</note> enclosing it so closely that the Earth only has room to revolve within it (as I have shown in my *Doctrine of the Sphere*, a book printed over twenty years ago, and which I am well assured they are not ignorant of at the *French* Observatory). By using lines designed upon it, I shall endeavor to do what he has proposed (judge for yourself how well he has performed it): that is, to explain the effect of the Earth's motion (or the parallaxes of the annual orbit) in changing the longitudes, latitudes, right ascensions, and distances from the pole of the fixed stars.

Imagine the eye placed at an infinite distance in the plane of the Earth's orbit ABCD; it will be represented by the line AC, its diameter. Let Fig. A. represent the sun's position at the center at E. Again:

Imagine a star placed in the north latitude at *e*. Lines *e*A and *e*C, drawn from the star at *e* to the ends of the diameter A and C, will form the angle AEC, the greatest parallax of the orbit at the star. Extend CA to H; then angle *e*AH is the greatest apparent latitude of the star, and angle *e*CH is the least.

Through *e*, the position of the star, draw the line *ac* parallel to the ecliptic EH, and around *e*, let the orbit of the Earth be described as equal and similar to the original orbit, but positioned oppositely. From the ends of its diameter *ac* to E, draw the lines AE and CE. It is evident to any competent geometrician that angle *a*EC is equal to angle *Ce*A, the greatest parallax of the orbit.

And that instead of supposing the star is fixed at *e* and the Earth moves around it in the orbit ABCD, the Earth may be supposed fixed at E and the star carried around in the representative orbit *abcd*, whose plane is parallel to the plane of the ecliptic.

By this means, the parallaxes and the star's apparent position will be shown to be the same in all respects as if the original orbit had been used.

Therefore, let E represent the center of the Earth, now fixed, and FG a quadrant of a circle of longitude on it. Let the line Ea, drawn from the cen-

If, furthermore, lines are drawn from the center of the Earth E, touching the representative orbit at *d* and *b*, these will intersect the Earth's perimeter at p and $\delta$, and will give the greatest diameter of the curve described on the surface of the Earth by lines proceeding from its center to the infinite points of the representative orbit.

The shortest diameter was found in the preceding paragraph to be $a \gamma$. This curve (because all the points in the orbit *a b c d* are conceived to be in a plane parallel to the ecliptic, and lines drawn from E to every one of them describe a cone) shall be an ellipse, whose diameters are given.

1. Hence it follows that the longest or transverse diameter of every ellipse or curve expressing the parallax of the orbit shall lie parallel to the plane of the ecliptic.

2. The conjugate or shortest diameter is at right angles to it; and the ratio of the longer to the shorter shall be as the radius is to the cosine of the star's latitude.

3. The farther any star is from the Earth or Sun, the smaller these ellipses or parallactic curves shall be; and furthermore,

4. If a star has no latitude, then lying in the plane of the ecliptic, and the Earth moving always in the same plane, its latitude cannot be altered by parallax, but its parallax of longitude will cast it sometimes in antecedence <note>westward motion</note>, and sometimes in consequence <note>eastward motion</note> of its middle place.

5. If a star is conceived also to be at the pole of the ecliptic at i, the parallax of longitude shall cast it always into the same longitude as the Sun, and its latitude shall be always the complement of half the entire parallax of the orbit; so that the star, with the Sun, shall traverse all the signs of the zodiac in the space of one year.

6. From the time of the first quartile <note>quadrature</note> with the Sun, after its emergence from his rays, to the second quartile (while the Earth moves from D by A to B, or the representative point of the star from *d* by *a* to *b*), the star (supposed at H) appears to move always retrograde; from there, by the conjunction to the first quartile star (while the Earth moves from B by C to D, or the star in its representative position from *b* by *c* to *d*), it appears again continually direct. The parallaxes of longitude cease and do not change its true or middle place at the conjunction and opposition to the Sun, being greatest in antecedence at the first quartile, and in consequence at the second.

These are the characteristics of the parallactic curves or ellipses, and the properties of the parallaxes of the orbit at the fixed stars, deduced from this figure; we shall find more in the next Figure B.

In which let $\Upsilon \backsimeq \sigma W$ <note>The symbols for Aries, Libra, Cancer, and Capricorn</note> represent the ecliptic, P its pole, A the pole of the Earth, and $\backsimeq$ E $\Upsilon W$ the equator; conceive a star placed in the first point of Aries ($\Upsilon$), without latitude. The ellipse that expresses its parallax shall have no latitude, and therefore will appear as a straight line; let it be represented by the short straight line $l \Upsilon m$ coinciding with the ecliptic. At the conjunction with the Sun ($\odot$), its primitive or middle place is unaltered; from there, after its emergence from the Sun, it moves in consequence towards m, at which point it arrives when the Sun is in quartile to it. And now it is evident by the figure, that although its latitude is not changed, yet by the parallax of longitude it has gained North declination from the equator equal to half of the entire parallax of longitude $l \Upsilon C$; when afterwards the Sun comes into Cancer ($\sigma$), and the point on which the star appears is $l$, it has there as much South declina-

But if the star has 20, 40, or 60 degrees north latitude, the parallaxes may be expressed by the three small ellipses placed one above another in the line ♈ P; and lines drawn from the pole of the ecliptic P to the designated place of the sun, to be found in them, will show which way the parallax carries the star, in <term>consequence</term> or in <term>antecedence</term>, and in what proportion its distance from the said pole is augmented or diminished by it. However, for the parallax of <term>right ascension</term> and distance from the pole of the globe, that narrow ellipsis placed next to the ecliptic represents the parallactic curve of a star that has 20 degrees north latitude. Let arcs of hour-circles be struck from the pole of the world A to the nearest and farthest points of this ellipsis; they show that the star shall have its greatest declination, or least distance from the pole, a little after its first quartile with the sun (when the sun is in Cancer ♋), and its greatest distance from the pole, or least declination, a little after the second quadrature (when the sun is in Capricorn ♑).

The ingenious reader will consider that although I count the sun's longitude along these curves, the places designated by them show only those points where the star appears because of the parallax of the orbit; and the distances of these points from either of the said poles in the arc of a great circle represent the distance as the parallax makes it appear, augmented or diminished with respect to either of them.

As the latitude of the star increases, the parallaxes of longitude, latitude, right ascension, and declination all increase, as may be easily understood by the sole inspection and consideration of this figure. However, there are too many varieties to be recounted here, except by those who have a great deal of leisure and are desiring to let the world see their excellent abilities in detailing things at length. I leave them to the sagacious reader to collect from the figure, and proceed to show how the appearances of the <term>Pole Star</term> shall be altered by the parallax of the orbit, if it is detectable.

<margin>Fig. C.</margin>
The present longitude of the Pole Star is Gemini (♊) at 24¼ degrees, and its latitude is 66 degrees north. Let PA in Fig. C represent an arc of the <term>solstitial colure</term>, equal to 23½ degrees (the distance between the pole of the world and the ecliptic). Let *Pe* be the line of the Pole Star’s longitude and its distance from the pole of the ecliptic. About *e*, let the parallactic ellipsis *o n q m* be described in such a way that its longer diameter may lie parallel to the ecliptic, and may be in proportion to the shortest as the radius is to the sine of its latitude. It is evident, by bare inspection of the figure, that its greatest distance from the pole of the ecliptic shall then happen when the star appears on *n*; and the sun is in the same longitude with it in the beginning of our June. Its least distance is in December, when their longitudes are opposite, or (to include both in our expression) they shall both happen when the sun, Earth, and star are all in the same plane perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic.

But the nearest approach of the Pole Star to the pole of the globe, and its greatest removal from it, will be distant from these points at about *q* and *o*, as appears by the figure, perhaps not much different from the times when Mr. *Cassini* places them. However, to determine exactly the location of these points on the curve, the resolution of this problem will be required: *A point being given, and an ellipse described on the surface of the sphere, to strike two arcs of great circles through the said point to the ellipse, so that one of them shall be the shortest and the other the longest that can be between them.* There is, then, an oversight committed in my letter to Dr. *Wallis*, where I place the greatest removal of the Pole Star from the pole in June and the nearest approach in December. <meta>This page continues the critique of Giovanni Domenico Cassini's theories on stellar parallax. Although the previous page ended with the partial word "parall...", this page begins with "it not," likely completing a phrase such as "noticed it not" or "found it not."</meta>

it not: it is no very great fault to have committed an oversight when they did not find it for four years' time. We are obliged to Mr. *Cassini* for the discovery of it; yet it appears that he did not understand the *effect* of the parallaxes of the Earth's orbit in changing and varying the distances of the fixed stars from the pole of the globe. He endeavors to represent them with the help of two circles placed around the poles of the ecliptic and the globe, even though the hypothesis neither requires nor admits any such thing, but only one ellipsis—and in many cases a very narrow one (*frustra fit* <note>Latin: "it is done in vain," part of a philosophical principle that simpler explanations are better.</note>).

Mr. *Cassini* may say that just as I move the orbit of the Earth from around the sun and draw it around the star to represent the parallaxes, he may likewise remove my ellipses from around the star and draw a circle or two around the two poles to achieve the same thing. But he should remember that the parallactic curves are ellipses, and not circles; and that not circles, but ellipses alone serve to represent these effects of parallaxes in the hypothesis of the Earth's motion. Furthermore, it has been shown to him that his circles are actually ellipses and representatives of the Earth's orbit, with suns in them, and therefore they are not proper exponents of the parallaxes.

However, I am obliged to him for giving me an opportunity to clear up this subject, which (as far as I know) has not been handled by anyone else until now. Since it is evident that the parallaxes of such stars as are nearest to us and lie in the neighborhood of the equinoctial colure <note>One of the two principal meridians of the celestial sphere.</note> will (if detectable) be perceived by the change of the meridional distances from the pole—observed at six-month intervals when they were at quadrature to the sun, as appears from what I have remarked—I shall return to my collection of night observations to seek those most suitable for discovering any error in the instrument, and afterward those most convenient for showing the parallaxes of the orbit. I shall copy the very first notes of both, faithfully and exactly as they were transcribed from the instrument, and compare them to see what parallax they allow, so that the skillful reader may correct, examine, and compare them himself if he thinks he can do it more accurately than I shall. Something has been done toward this already. Nothing is to be expected from the *French* because their instruments are commonly no more than one-fourth the radius of mine; or if they are equal to mine or larger, as I think one of them is, they are not fixed as they ought to be for this purpose. This makes me wish I had a larger instrument than my current one, and a better wall to fix it on than the one to which I have fitted the large and costly one I made at my own great expense. However, if the good providence of Heaven, which has blessed all my labors so far, gives me health until after the holidays, I hope I may by that time give you a full account of what it has provided.

->S I R,<-
->Your faithful humble servant,<-
->JOHN FLAMSTEAD, M. R.<-

Honored Sir, ->The Observatory, Nov. 19, 1702.<-

### An Account of the Heights of the Welsh Hills, etc.

Honored Sir, July 1, 1696.

To satisfy you that I was not mistaken in the account of the heights of the Welsh hills I gave you, I have examined some letters I received from Mr. *Caswell* in the year 1682, who was employed by Mr. *Adams* in his survey of Wales, wherein he gives me the measurements of them taken with good instruments, made according to my directions.

The *Wreckin* <note>The Wrekin</note> in *Shropshire*, he says, by leveling with a long pole, he found to be 396 yards above the level of the *Severn*. But by a base and altitudes taken by a quadrant with telescope-sights, 30 yards more; 396 + 30 + 40 = 466 yards.

The *Severn* in that place where he measured is 40 yards higher than the sea, and falls 3 yards 3 inches in five miles.

*Stiperstone Clee Hill* <note>Likely referring to the Stiperstones or Clee Hill in Shropshire.</note>, in *Shropshire*, he concludes is 600 yards high.
*Penmenmaur* <note>Penmaenmawr</note> in *Caernarvonshire*, 515 yards.
*Caddorydris* <note>Cader Idris</note> in *Merionethshire*, 970.
*Snowdown* <note>Snowdon</note> in *Caernarvonshire* (270 yards more than *Caddorydris*), = 1240.

*Snowdown* is 27 886/1000 miles distant from *Caddorydris*. He gives me the height of the <term>☿</term> <note>The mercury in a barometer.</note> on the top of *Snowdown* as 25 886/1000 inches, but does not note the time: on *Caddorydris* (July 26, 1682) 26 45/100 inches.

## N U M B. III.

*Extract of a letter from Mr. Sprat (afterwards Bishop of Rochester) to Mr. Wren, Professor of Astronomy at Gresham College, London, in 1658, at which time the college was garrisoned by the rebels and the professors driven out.*

DEAR SIR,

THIS day I went to visit *Gresham College*, but found the place in such a filthy condition, so defiled, and the smells so infernal, that if you should now come to make use of your telescope, it would be like *Dives* looking out of hell into heaven. Of all your colleagues, Dr. *Goddard* remains in possession, which he could never have been able to do had he not previously prepared his nose for camp perfumes by his voyage into *Scotland*, and had he not such excellent restoratives in his cellar. By the violence they have inflicted on the seats of the Muses, the soldiers have made themselves hateful to the entire intellectual world; and even if we ignore their having ruined the nation, we shall never be able to forgive them this crime. And as for what concerns you, they have now proved that their claims to religion were all feigned, since by hindering your lectures, they have committed such a manifest offense against heaven. Yet your many friends here hope you will hereafter compensate for this unfortunate leisure which is granted to you by making those admirable discourses, which you had intended for that place, more public; and that you will imitate *Cicero*, who, being hindered from delivering his oration, *pro Milone*, by the guards of *Pompey’s* soldiers that surrounded his chair, published it afterward more perfectly than all the rest.

### From the abovementioned *Mr. Sprat*, to *Mr. Wren*, on his Translation of *Horace*'s Epistle to *Lollius*.

->MY DEAR FRIEND,<-

I received two of your letters at once, for both of which I very heartily thank you; but you must give me leave to disagree with your opinion in one of them, in which you maintain that *Horace* cannot be well translated; for, by that elegant epistle *to Lollius* which you sent me, you have proven yourself wrong. You have admirably captured his spirit; your verse is rhythmic; your philosophy is very instructive for life; your freedom in translating is enough to make it seem like an *English* original, and yet not so much that the mind of the author is not still faithfully observed. So, even if you have not adorned the "fat jester" (as you most pleasantly call him) with feathers, you have adorned him with jewels, which is a more majestic, though not so flashy, a display. Most other attempts on him (even those of *Ben Jonson* himself) appear to me to have been very unfortunate until now, and his translators have seemed to remember less that he was a friend to *Augustus* than that he was <term>libertino Patre natus</term> <note>born of a freedman father</note>: so crudely and so clumsily have they handled him.

You perfectly agree with my opinion in favoring this poet above others; for, ever since I have had the good fortune to read him as something other than a schoolboy, I have always respected him as one of the most accomplished men of that incomparable age. He was almost the first writer who brought poetry away from the fables of their ridiculous religion and from flattering the beauty of women, to speak of human affairs and to show humanity to itself. The propriety of his structure and creativity is admirable; everything is so justly and temperately stated that even the hypercritical *Matt. Clifford* himself cannot find one word in him to erase. He is so natural that every idea seems to flow from his pen without any mental struggle, and yet he was the slowest and most rigorous of his time; the wit which he shows is exactly right for the subjects which he undertakes, and no more. This I esteem as one of the most certain and noble of perfections,

Moderation of imagination is a thing most commendable and most difficult; it being hard for men of hot and violent minds (such as most commonly great writers have) to stop themselves at full speed and to understand when they have done enough.

He meets, I confess, with some *Tuccas* <note>A reference to a character from Ben Jonson's *Poetaster*, signifying a harsh or ignorant critic.</note> who blame him for his many straightforward and proverbial sentences, and for the roughness of his style. But as for the first, it must be said that if his plain morals are not considered wit in this age, yet they were then—and so great, too, that we have nothing else left to us of all the most ancient and most applauded *Grecians* but some few such sayings, of which we meet many hundreds in *Horace*. And if we consider his style too, we shall find it was very smooth compared to those who wrote before him; for the best judge of poetry in the world gives this judgment of the best of <margin>*Horace, Satires, book 1, satire 4.</margin> the most ancient Romans, *Lucilius*, that he was *durus componere Versus* <note>Latin: "harsh in composing verses."</note>. Nor can his way of writing be called crabbed or harsh, but rather a masculine plainness and a smooth course of verse. If there is any unevenness or ruggedness in it, it is such as that of his own *Rome* was, to which it was not an injury but an advantage that it was built on hills. Nor are all things immediately to be praised because they are smooth, for then perhaps *Quarles* might come into competition with *Cowley*; and if to be oiled were to be harmonious, I do not know why a coach-wheel or a roasting jack does not make good music.

Those who blame him for the equality and familiarity of his style are not worth refuting; let such people remain ignorant, who admire nothing but what is lofty and swelling; those who prefer

# SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.

...fear of it, some have wholly forsaken my acquaintance and rejected my passion; some have fled the kingdom; and some (for all I know) have gone into another world. It is with this murderous instrument that I now come to assault you; and I trust its operation will confirm the opinion of you philosophers: that anything, though ever so innocent, may be a poison if taken in too great a quantity. It shall, I promise you, be as long as the paper will allow me; and to its length, I will also add that it shall be written on a *subject* about which I have heard *you yourself speak many admirable things*, so that you may undergo the torment of reading *your own thoughts* disfigured by my expressions. This, I hope, will be as great a grief to you as it was to that king (whose name I have forgotten) when the *Scythians* sent home his own ambassadors to him with their ears, noses, and lips cut off.

Now then, my dearest friend, you may recollect that we went lately from *Axe-yard* to walk in *St. James’s Park*, and though we did not meet the *incomparable person* whose company we sought, yet he was present enough in our thoughts to lead us to discuss that in which he so much excels: the wit of conversation. *Some part of what you then said, you shall now hear over again*; for though I have a most treacherous memory in other matters, yet my love for *Kit Wren* makes it always faithful in preserving whatever he commits to it.

The wit of discourse, therefore, is as different among the various parts of mankind as the temper of their air and the constitution of their bodies; and so it is to be divided into general and particular. The *general* is that which consists of terms, similitudes, and humors which are received by many nations. This either prevails by conquest—and so the *Roman* language and wit have prevailed over all the countries where they sowed civility by their victories—or else by the situation, authority, and commanding genius of one people over another. Thus the *Greeks* became teachers of the arts of talking to the *ancients*, and the *French* lately to the *moderns*; their tongue and customs have gone further in *Europe* than their present king, however terrible he appears, is likely to carry their armies.

Of this general wit, there are manifest differences to be observed. That of the *Chinese* consists in the skill of writing various characters. That of the *Egyptians* consists in using things themselves, instead of words, for similitudes: in painting a snake with its tail in its mouth to signify the year; a lion for courage; the sun, moon, and stars for a thousand conceits. This is a strange kind of laborious way of expressing their minds; if the orators of our time should use it in their luxuriance of metaphors, they would need Noah's Ark to carry about with them any one of their orations. The *Eastern wit* in all ages has been principally made up of lofty and swelling comparisons, as we may see today in the titles of the *Sophy* <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia.</note> and *Grand Seigneur* <note>The Ottoman Sultan.</note>, which no doubt are some of their noblest fancies; and yet to our understanding, they require the assistance of *Mahomet’s* dove <note>A legendary bird said to have whispered divine revelations into the Prophet's ear.</note> to make sense of them. That of the *Moors* was the same as the *Spanish* at this time. The *Italian*, *French*, *English*, and *Dutch* (if they have any) are somewhat alike, according to their common origin, *Latin*. Of the *Muscovite* or *Tartarian*, I can give but little account; but I assure you, even the *Irish* had a wit of their own, though you will hardly believe it until some of our friends go there; nay, to say more to their advantage, they had this peculiarity: that almost their entire nation was at the same time both poets and saints.

The *particular* wit is that which arises from the frequent meetings of private assemblies. This, too, is capable of infinite divisions; for there is hardly the smallest company in the world that meets together but has its common sayings, figures, characters, and observations, which are great raillery within their proper circle but tasteless to strangers. This is evident in

several counties of *England*. When I was in the *North*, there was a buffoon who was a terrific humorist among the *Yorkshire* gentlemen, and yet scarcely spoke a grain of salt to our *Southern tastes*. This likewise appears in several professions of men. The lawyers will laugh at those jests in the *Temple* which, perhaps, will not move us at *Charing Cross*. And it is likely that *Tom Killigrew* himself would not seem like good company to a table of Benchers. The wit beyond *Fleet Bridge* has another color from that on this side. The very watermen on the *Bankside* have their quips and their repartees, which are not intelligible except upon the *Thames*. But to say no more, this is to be seen in every private family: I had almost gone so far as to say that there is scarcely a husband and wife in the world who do not have a particular way of wit among themselves; but this I will not affirm, because this evil age believes that few married persons are accustomed to delight so much in one another's company as to be merry and witty alone. Now then, having discovered this mighty *Proteus*, which puts on so many various shapes in several places and occasions, let us try to define it. —— The wit of conversation is (to speak magnificently) the greatest art about the smallest things: for to confess a secret, as *Sir William Davenant's* way differs very little from *Frank Bowman's*, and yet the one is the gayest and the other the most insipid; for true pleasant talk and the vainest chatter are not very much distinguished. The subjects of both of them are a thousand little trifles, and the difference lies only in the management. Nor does this meanness of matter

prejudice the art, for then it would follow that your divine works in the *King's Closet* <note>The private collection or study of the King, likely referring to Robert Hooke's "Micrographia" and the microscopic studies favored by the early Royal Society.</note> are the worse because they are the descriptions of a louse, a flea, and a nit. This wit, therefore, is made up of many inexpressible excellencies. It must have a general evenness of humor; it must perfectly observe all the rules of decency to know when enough is said; to forbear cutting remarks about things not to be touched; to abstain from abusing honest and virtuous matters.

It must apply itself to the condition and inclination of the company; it must rather follow than lead; it must not always strain to speak extraordinary things, for that is a constant walking on a tightrope, in which though a man does often well, yet he may have one fall that may chance to break his neck. It must allow everyone their turn of speaking; for it is natural to all to better love the company of those who give them occasions for speaking well, than those who do it themselves. It must mingle stories with arguments, pleasant things with solemn; it must vary the subject often, and not exhaust itself all at once. This, if you will believe *Mr. Cowley*, is a wise quality: for in a copy of verses which you have not yet seen, he says:

> "So the imperial eagle does not stay
> "Until the whole carcass he devours
> "That has fallen into his power,
> "As if his noble hunger understood
> "That it can never lack plenty of food;
> "He only sucks the tasteful blood,
> "And to fresh game flies cheerfully away;
> "To kites and meaner birds he leaves the mangled prey.

This noble eagle-wit, therefore, uses the best and easiest words, is not the first that takes up new ones, nor the last that lays down old ones. But above all, its chief dominion is in forming new meanings and images of things and persons. And this may be so suddenly practiced that I have known, in one afternoon, new idioms, proverbs, and fashions of speech raised which were never thought of before, and yet gave occasion to most

The truth is, it is seldom to be found among men of large, full, and high thoughts; because such minds overlook the small details and fly immediately to general axioms, which may be more useful, yet they do not affect our thoughts with such immediate and familiar delight. But to speak the truth, the perfection of this glorious faculty, without which life would be no life, belongs not so much to men as to the softer sex; for they usually have their heads less disturbed with busy thoughts, their minds are quicker and readier for new impressions, they talk more of circumstantial things, they sit longer together, and (as you used to say is of great concern in our northern and phlegmatic climate) they keep their feet warmer and drier, and go less into the moist and open air. But regarding women being the best speakers, I could give you two undeniable instances: your *Laura* (as I think you call her) and she who was once my *Clelia*. The one speaks with great freedom and spirit, and an abundance of excellent words; the other talks less, but with as much sweetness and nature; from the one nothing can be taken away; to the other nothing ought to be added. But I dare not go further in this description for memory of an old story: that while a painter was drawing a most beautiful lady, he fell desperately in love with her, and it would have cost him his life had not *Alexander* bestowed her upon him! The first part of this tale, I am sure, would be my fortune if I should employ my thoughts longer on such a lovely object; and I am just as certain that I would perish long before I would find an *Alexander* to pity me. To proceed then in my first purpose: wit consists in a proper ordering of things and words for delight. But—stay—now that I look about me, what need have I to go any further? You are, without question, already sufficiently tired, and so my end is obtained; and then it will be useless to speak more on this subject, seeing that the age in which we live runs already so mad after the affairs of wit. All the world are poets at present: the poetical bees are all at work; comedies, tragedies, verses, satires, burlesques, and songs buzz everywhere about our ears; and (to ease my hand a little by changing my pace):
