I Must confess I have some little pique against you ——— therefore I am not much displeased that I have this occasion to tell you some bad news. The Vice-chancellor did yesterday send for me, to inquire where the *Astronomy* Professor was, and the reason of his absence so long after the beginning of the term—I used all the arguments I could for your defense. I told him that *Charles the Second* was King of *England, Scotland, France, and Ireland*; that he was by the late *Act of Parliament* declared absolute monarch in these his dominions; and that it was this mighty Prince who had confined you to *London*. I endeavored to persuade him that the drawing of lines in Sir *Harry Saville's* School was not altogether of so great a concern for the benefit of *Christendom* as the rebuilding of * St. *Paul's*, or the fortifying (a) of *Tangier*: (for I understood those were the great works in which that extraordinary genius of yours was judged necessary to be employed) All this I urged, but after some discourse, he told me that he was not to consider you now as ‡ Dr. *Bayly*, (for in that role he owed you all kindness) but as *Vice-chancellor*, and under that capacity he most terribly told me that he took it very ill you had not all this while given him any account of what hindered you from the discharge of your office. This he bid me tell you, and I do it not very unwillingly, because I see that our friendships are so closely tied together that the same thing which was so great a loss to me (my losing your company all this while here) does also somewhat redound to your disadvantage. And so, my dear Sir, now my spite and spleen are satisfied, I must needs return to my old temper again, and faithfully assure you that I am with the most violent zeal and passion,

->*Your most affectionate and devoted Servant,*<-

This employment he had no inclination to accept (it being then inconsistent with his health) but humbly prayed his Majesty to allow of his excuse and to command his duty in *England*.

### N U M B. IV.

**I**N the year 1665, Mr. *Wren* took a journey to *Paris*, where, at that time, all arts flourished in a higher degree than had ever been known before in *France*; and where there was a general congress of the most celebrated masters in every profession, encouraged by royal munificence and the influence of the great Cardinal *Mazarin*.

How he spent his time in that place will in part appear from a short account he gave by letter to a particular friend; wherein he returns thanks for the recommendation of him to the Earl of *St. Albans*, who during the journey, and ever since, had treated him with all the kindness and indulgence imaginable, and proved his character as one of the best men in the world. He then proceeds to the following particulars: "I have," says he, "busied myself in surveying the most esteemed buildings of *Paris* and the surrounding country; the *Louvre* for a while was my daily object, where no fewer than a thousand hands are constantly employed in the works; some in laying mighty foundations, some in raising the stories, columns, entablatures, etc., with vast stones by great and useful engines; others in carving, inlaying of marbles, plastering, painting, gilding, etc. All of these together make a school of architecture, probably the best in *Europe* at this day. The College of *The Four Nations* is usually admired, but the artist has purposely set it awkwardly, so that he might show his wit in struggling with an inconvenient situation. An Academy of painters, sculptors, architects, and the chief artisans of the *Louvre* meet every first and last Saturday of the month. *Monsieur Colbert*, the Superintendent, comes to the works of the *Louvre* every *Wednesday*, and, if business does not hinder him, *Thursday*. The workmen are paid duly every *Sunday*. *Monsieur Abbé Charles* introduced me to the acquaintance of *Bernini*, who showed me his designs for the *Louvre* and for the King's statue. *Abbé Bruno* keeps the curious rarities of the Duke of *Orleans's* library, which is well filled with excellent intaglios, medals, and books of plants and fowls in miniature. *Abbé Bourdelot* keeps an academy for philosophy at his house every *Monday* afternoon. But I must not think to describe *Paris* and the numerous sights there within the compass of a short letter. The King's houses I could not miss: *Fontainebleau* has a stately wildness and vastness suitable to the desert it stands in. The antique mass of the Castle of *St. Germains* and the hanging gardens are delightfully surprising (I mean to any man of judgment), for the pleasures below vanish away in the breath that is spent in ascending. The palace—or, if you please, the cabinet—of *Versailles* called me twice to view it; the mixtures of brick, stone, blue tile, and gold make it look like a rich livery. Not an inch within is anything but crowded with little curiosities of ornaments. The women, as they create the language and fashions here and meddle with politics and philosophy, so they also sway architectural tastes; works of <term>filigree</term> and little trinkets are in great vogue. But building certainly ought to have the attribute of being eternal, and is therefore the only thing incapable of following new fashions. The masculine furniture of the *Palais Mazarin* pleased me much better, where there is a great and noble collection of antique statues and busts (many of porphyry), good bas-reliefs, excellent pictures by the great masters, fine Arras tapestries, and true mosaics, besides <term>Pierres de Rapport</term> <note>inlaid stonework or pietra dura</note> in compartments and pavements, vases of porcelain painted by *Raphael*, and infinite other rarities; the best of which now furnish the glorious apartment of the *Queen Mother* at the *Louvre*, which I saw many times. After the incomparable villas of *Vaux* and *Maisons*, I shall only name *Ruel*, *Courances*,"

### INTRODUCTION.

AFTER the most dreadful Conflagration of *London*, in the fatal year 1666, Dr. *Christopher Wren* was appointed *Surveyor-General* and *principal Architect* for rebuilding the *whole City*; the Cathedral Church of *St. Paul*; all the parochial churches (fifty-one in number, as enacted by Parliament in place of those that were burned and demolished) with other public structures; and for the layout of the streets. A charge so great and extensive, falling upon a single person, inclined him to take as his assistant Mr. *Robert Hooke*, Professor of Geometry in *Gresham College*, to whom he assigned chiefly the business of measuring, adjusting, and setting out the ground of the private street-houses for the various proprietors; reserving all the public works for his own specific care and direction.

On the 6th of *March*, 1667-8, he received his *Majesty’s Warrant* under the *Privy Seal* (in confirmation of a deputation from Sir *John Denham*, Knight of the *Bath*) to execute the office of *Surveyor-General* of the *Royal Works*. Upon whose death in the same month, his *Majesty* was pleased to

# PART II.

## SECT. I.

->Of *London* in ancient times, and the boundary of the *Roman* colony, discerned by the Surveyor after the Great Fire.<-

**T**o have a right idea of *London* of old, it will be necessary to consider the state of the *Britons* at the time the *Romans* made their first descent on the *island*; and surely we cannot reasonably think them so barbarous, at least in that age (and the accounts before that are too fabulous), as is commonly believed. Their manner of fighting was in chariots, like the ancient heroes of *Greece* in the *Trojan* War, and occasionally on foot, with such order and discipline as much embarrassed the *Roman* legions and put a stop to the progress of the invincible *Caesar*; who could do nothing great nor conquer any part, but, says *Tacitus*, only showed the country to the *Romans*; and, according to *Lucan*, was obliged shamefully to retreat.

->*Territa quaesitis ostendit terga Britannis.*<-

The *Britons* went to sea in vessels covered with hides, for they lacked pitch. They traded chiefly with the *Gauls*, and certainly the principal *emporium*, or town of trade to which the *Gallic* ships resorted, must have been *London*; though situated far up the country, yet it was most commodiously accessible by a noble river among the thickest population; taking its name (according—

Here the *Romans* fixed a civil, or trading colony, in the reign of *Claudius*, which greatly increased under *Nero* by the gathering of merchants and the convenience of commerce, and was inhabited by *Christians* and *Heathens* together.

The extent of the *Roman Colony*, or *Prefecture*, particularly northward, the *Surveyor* had the opportunity to discover by this accident. The parish church of *St. Mary le Bow*, in *Cheapside*, required to be rebuilt after the *Great Fire*: the building had been poor and low, with one corner taken out for a tower, but upon restoring that, the new church could be made square. Upon opening the ground, a foundation was discerned firm enough for the new intended fabric, which (on further inspection, after digging down sufficiently and removing whatever earth or rubbish lay in the way) appeared to be the walls, with the windows also, and the pavement of a temple, or church, of *Roman* workmanship, entirely buried under the level of the present street. Thereupon, he determined to erect his new church over the old; and in order to achieve the necessary regularity and squareness of the new design, he restored the corner; but then another place had to be found for the steeple. The church stood about 40 feet back from the high street, and by purchasing the ground of one private house not yet rebuilt, he was enabled to bring the steeple forward so as to align with the street-houses of *Cheapside*. Here, to his surprise, he dug about 18 feet deep through made ground, and then imagined he had come to the natural soil and hard gravel; but upon full examination, it appeared to be a *Roman Causeway* of rough stone, packed and well-rammed, with *Roman* brick and rubbish at the bottom for a foundation, and all firmly cemented. This *Causeway* was four feet thick [the thickness of the *via Appia*, according as *Mons. Montfaucon* measured it, was about three *Parisian* feet, or three feet two and a half inches *English*.] Underneath this *Causeway* lay the natural clay, over which that part of the city stands, and which descends at least forty feet lower. He concluded then to lay the foundation of the tower upon the very *Roman Causeway*, as it was most proper to bear what he had designed: a weighty and lofty structure.

He was of the opinion, for various reasons, that this *highway* ran along the *north* boundary of the *colony*. The breadth then, *north* and *south*, was from the *causeway* (now *Cheapside*) to the River *Thames*; the extent *east* and *west* was from *Tower Hill* to *Ludgate*; and the principal middle street, or *Praetorian Way*, was *Watling Street*.

The colony was walled next to the *Thames* and had a gate there called *Dowgate*, but anciently *Dour-gate*, which signified the *Water-gate*.

On the north side, beyond the *causeway*, was a great fen, or morass, in those times; which the *Surveyor* discovered more particularly when he had the opportunity to build a new east front to the parish church of *St. Laurence* near *Guildhall*. For the foundation of this, after sinking seven feet, he was obliged to pile twelve feet deeper; and if there was no *causeway* over the bog, there could be no reason for a gate that way.

At length, about the year 1414, all this marshy ground was drained by the industry and expense of *Falconer*, a Lord Mayor, and still retains the name of *Moorfields*, and the gate, *Moorgate*. *London-stone*, as is generally supposed, was a pillar in the manner of the *Milliarium Aureum* at *Rome*, from which the account of their miles began; but the *Surveyor* was of the opinion, by reason of the large foundation, it was rather some more considerable monument in the *Forum*; for in the adjoining ground on the south

On the west side was situated the <term>Prætorian Camp</term>, which was also walled-in to *Ludgate*. Within the <term>Vallum</term> <note>rampart</note> of this camp, near the *Gate*, a stone was dug up after the *Fire* featuring an inscription and the figure of a *Roman* soldier. The *Surveyor* presented this to the Archbishop of *Canterbury*, who sent it to *Oxford*, where it is deposited among the <term>Arundellian Marbles</term>. This is a sepulchral monument dedicated to the memory of *Vivius Marcianus*, a soldier of the Second Legion, styled *Augusta*, by his wife *Januaria Matrina*. The inscription is in this manner:

The soldiers used to be buried <term>in Vallo</term> <note>within the rampart</note>, just as the citizens were buried <term>extra Portas in Pomærio</term> <note>outside the gates in the open space</note>; therefore, it is most probable that the extent of the camp reached to *Ludgate*, following the decline of the hill in that direction. The *Surveyor* gave little credit to the common story that a temple to *Diana* had been here (which some have believed based on the reports of digging up, both formerly and in later years, stag horns, ox heads, boar tusks, etc.), as he met with no such indications in all his searches. However, it was manifest that the north side of this ground had been a great burial place in very ancient times; for upon digging the foundations of the present fabric of St. *Paul's*, he found, in a row below the graves of later ages, the burial places of the *Saxon times*. The *Saxons*, as it appeared, were accustomed to line their graves with chalk-stones, though some more eminent individuals were entombed in coffins made of solid stone. Below these were *British* graves, where ivory and wooden pins (made of a hard wood seemingly like boxwood) were found in abundance, about six inches long. It seems the bodies were only wrapped up and pinned in woolen shrouds, which, having decayed, left the pins entire. In the same row and deeper still, *Roman* urns were intermixed. This was eighteen feet deep or more, and belonged to the colony when *Romans* and *Britons* lived and died together.

The most remarkable *Roman* urns, lamps, <term>lachrymatories</term> <note>vials for tears</note>, and fragments of sacrificial vessels, etc., were found deep in the ground toward the northeast corner of St. *Paul's* Church, near *Cheapside*. These were generally well-made and embossed with various figures and designs, the color of modern red *Portuguese* ware; some were brighter like coral, with a hardness equal to *China* ware and just as well glazed. ## S E C T. II.

### *Proposals for rebuilding the City of London, after the great Fire.*

The manner of building in the City of *London*, practiced in all former ages, was commonly with timber—a material easily procured and at little expense when the country was overburdened with woods. This often subjected the town to great and destructive fires, sometimes to the ruin of the whole, as happened, for instance, in the year 1083 during the reign of *William* the *Conqueror*, the street houses being then made of timber covered with thatch. Notwithstanding these incidents, this style continued until the two fatal years 1665 and 1666; but then the successive calamities of *Plague* and *Fire* gave everyone reason to seriously reflect on the causes of the increase of *both* to that excessive degree: namely, the *closeness* of buildings and combustible materials. Consequently, the desire for the necessary improvement of both, by widening the streets and building with stone and brick, became universal.

Some intelligent persons went further and thought it highly necessary that, in its *Restoration*, the city should rise with beauty—through the straightness and regularity of buildings—and convenience for commerce—through the well-planned arrangement of streets and public places, the opening of wharves, and so on—which the excellent situation, wealth, and grandeur of the *Metropolis* of *England* truly deserved. This was also fitting for the rank she held among all other trading cities of the world, of which, though she was previously one of the richest in estate and dowry, she was unquestionably the least beautiful. *Informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum.* <note>Shapeless, huge, and deprived of light.</note>

Therefore, to achieve a proper reformation, Dr. *Wren* (pursuant to the royal commands) immediately after the *Fire* took an exact survey of the entire area and borders of the *burnt area*, having traced over the great plain of ashes and ruins with much trouble and danger. He designed a plan or model for a new city in which the deformity and inconveniences of the old town were remedied by enlarging the streets and lanes and carrying them as nearly parallel to one another as possible; avoiding all acute angles where compatible with greater convenience; by placing all the parish churches in conspicuous and <term>insular</term> <note>detached/free-standing</note> positions; by forming the most public places into large *piazzas*, the centers of eight-way junctions; by uniting the halls

of the twelve chief Companies, into one regular square annexed to *Guildhall*; by making a commodious *Quay* on the entire *bank* of the *river*, from *Blackfriars* to the *Tower*.

Moreover, in designing the general *plan*, the following particulars were chiefly considered and proposed:

The streets to be of three sizes; the three principal ones leading straight through the City, and one or two cross-streets to be at least 90 feet wide; others 60 feet; and lanes about 30 feet, excluding all narrow dark alleys without thoroughfares, and courts.

The Exchange to stand free in the middle of a piazza, and be, as it were, the nave or center of the town, from which the 60-foot streets, like so many rays, should proceed to all principal parts of the city: the building to be designed after the form of the *Roman Forum*, with double porticos.

Many streets also to radiate toward the Bridge. The streets of the first and second size to be carried on as straight as possible, and to center into four or five piazzas.

The *Quay* or open wharf on the bank of the *Thames* to be spacious and convenient, without any interruptions; with some large *docks* for deeply loaded barges.

The canal to be cut up to *Bridewell*, 120 feet wide, with <term>sasses</term> <note>sluice gates or locks</note> at *Holborn Bridge*, and at the mouth to cleanse it of all filth; and stores for coal on each side.

The churches to be designed according to the best forms for capacity and hearing, adorned with useful porticos, and lofty ornamental towers and steeples, in the larger parishes. All churchyards, gardens, and unnecessary empty spaces; and all trades that use large fires, or produce offensive smells, to be placed out of the town.

The *model* or *plan* formed on these principles, drawn by *Dr. Wren*, was laid before the King and the honorable *House of Commons*; and is thus explained:

From that part of *Fleet Street* which remained unburnt, near *St. Dunstan's Church*, a straight street 90 feet wide crosses the valley, passing by the south side of *Ludgate Prison*, and from there in a direct line ends gracefully in a piazza at *Tower Hill*; but before it descends into the valley where the great sewer (*Fleet Ditch*) now runs, near what was once the middle of *Fleet Street*, it opens into a round piazza, the center of eight ways, where from one position are these views:—First, straight forward quite through the city: Second, angled toward the right hand, to the beginning of the Quay, that runs from *Bridewell Dock* to the *Tower*. Third, angled on the left to *Smithfield*. Fourth, straight on the right, to the *Thames*. Fifth, straight on the left, to *Hatton Street*, and *Clerkenwell*. Sixth, straight backwards, towards *Temple Bar*. Seventh, angled on the right, to the walks of the *Temple*. Eighth, angled on the left, to *Cursitor's Alley*.

Passing forward we cross the valley, once stained with an offensive sewer, now to be beautified with a useful canal, passable by as many bridges as there are streets that cross it.—Leaving *Ludgate Prison* on the left side of the street, (in place of which gate, a triumphal arch was designed for the founder of the new city, *King Charles the Second*.) This great street presently divides into another equally large, which carries the eye and passage to the south front of the *Exchange*, (which we leave for now for a second journey) and before these two streets spreading at acute angles can be clear of one another, they form a triangular piazza, the base of which is filled by the cathedral church of *St. Paul*.

But leaving St. *Paul's* on the left, we proceed as our first way led us toward the *Tower*, the way being adorned all along with parochial churches.

We return again to *Ludgate*, and leaving St. *Paul's* on the right hand, pass the other great branch to the *Royal Exchange*, situated in the place where it was before, but free from surrounding buildings, in the middle of a piazza included between two great streets; the one from *Ludgate* leading to the south front, and another from *Holborn*, over the canal to *Newgate*, and from there straight to the north front of the *Exchange*.

The practicality of this whole scheme, without loss to any man or infringement of any property, was demonstrated at that time, and all material objections were fully weighed and answered. The only—and, as it happened, insurmountable—difficulty remaining was the obstinate aversion of a large part of the citizens to altering their old properties and giving up building their houses again on the old ground and foundations. There was also a distrust in many and an unwillingness to give up their properties, though for a time only, into the hands of public trustees or commissioners, until they might be distributed to them again with more advantage to themselves than was otherwise possible to achieve. For such a method was proposed that, by an equal distribution of ground into buildings, leaving out churchyards, gardens, *etc.* (which were to be removed out of the town), there would have been sufficient room both for the widening of the streets, the placement of the churches, halls, and all public buildings, and to have given every proprietor full satisfaction. Although few proprietors would happen to have been situated again directly upon the very same ground they had possessed before the *Fire*, yet no man would have been pushed any considerable distance from it, but would have been placed at least as conveniently—and sometimes more so—for their own trades than before.

By these means, the opportunity was largely lost to make the new city the most magnificent, as well as the most convenient for health and trade, of any on Earth; and the *Surveyor* being thus confined and cramped in his designs, it required no small labor and skill to model the city in the manner it has since appeared.

In the *Acts* of *Parliament*, 19 and 22 *Car.* II <note>Charles II</note> for the rebuilding of the city of *London*, among other rules and directions consistent with the *Surveyor's* opinion and advice, it is enacted:

> “That there shall be left a Quay,
> “or open wharf, from *London Bridge* to the *Temple*, forty feet broad; and
> “in order to achieve this, all buildings, sheds, *etc.* within forty feet northward
> “of the *Thames* shall, within the eight ensuing months, be taken down and
> “removed; and the buildings to front the said *Quay* shall be of the se-
> “cond or third rate of buildings, observing uniformity as in other
> “streets, *etc.*”

A clause so well calculated for the ornament and advantage of the city should have been punctually observed and executed by the citizens, according to the full extent and virtue of the law.

## SECT. III.

### *Of the ancient cathedral Churches of St. Paul; from the first Age of Christianity, to the last great Fire of London, in* 1666. *And of the Surveyor's Design for repairing the old ruinous Structure, made (by Order of his Majesty, and the Commissioners) upon an accurate Survey, about four Months before the Conflagration.*

<margin>* See the Bishop of Worcester's Origines Britannicae.</margin>
The Christian faith, without doubt, was very early received in *Britain*; and without having recourse to the monkish tale of *Joseph* of *Arimathea* and other legendary fictions, there is authentic testimony of a *Christian Church* planted here by the *Apostles* themselves, and, in particular, very probably by St. *Paul*.

<margin>† Rapin's History of England, Book 1.</margin>
It is very certain this *Apostle*, from his first imprisonment at Rome to his return to *Jerusalem*, had spent eight years in preaching in various places, but more especially in the *western countries*. We know he designed to go to *Spain*, and it is not improbable that his earnestness to convert the *Britons* might have carried him to this *island*.

This opinion may be strengthened by the evidence of *Venutius Fortunatus*, who says the same thing, speaking of the travels of St. *Paul*, in his poem on the life of St. *Martin*.

> *Transit & oceanum, vel quà facit insula portum,*
> *Quasque Britannus habet terras, quasque ultima Thule.*

Every *Christian Church* derived from the *Apostles* had a succession of *Bishops* from them too, and the condition of the *British Church* was so early established that some maintain there were *Bishops* at the Council of *Nice*, assembled in 325. And it is certain that twenty-two years after, *Restitutus*, Bishop of *London*, was one of the three *British Bishops* present at the Council of *Arles*.

<margin>† Du Pin.</margin>
Some *British* prelates were likewise at the Council of *Ariminum*, assembled in 359, and these were of such dignity that they refused the Emperor's allowance, thinking it beneath them not to bear their own expenses.

The first cathedral of this episcopal see of *London* (built in the area where the *Roman Praetorian camp* had been, the site of all the succeeding structures until this time) was demolished under the great and general persecution by *Diocletian*. But although, in pursuance of the strictness of his edicts, the *Christian churches* in all the provinces of the *Roman* government were ordered to be pulled down, yet possibly the *Prefects* might not take the pains, once they had made them unfit for use, to tear up the foundations also. The time of the persecution was short, for under *Constantine*, the Church flourished again; the churches in *Rome* and other parts of the empire were soon rebuilt, and most likely ours was among the first, after the pattern of the *Roman Basilica* of St. *Peter* and St. *Paul* in the *Vatican*, and, as the *Surveyor* conceived, upon the old foundations left by the persecutors; for the *Christians* were zealous and in haste to be settled again.

->The<-

<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

The Church, thus rebuilt under *Constantine*, was afterwards destroyed by the *pagan Saxons* and restored again upon the old foundations when they embraced *Christianity* in the seventh century by *Mellitus*, Bishop of *London*, under *Ethelbert*, King of *Kent*, the first *Saxon* King of the *Christian Faith*.

This Church, together with the whole city, was destroyed by an accidental fire in the year 1083. *Mauritius*, then Bishop of *London*, obtained from the King the old stone of a spacious castle in the neighborhood called the *Palatine Tower*, demolished by the same fire (this *fort* stood at the entrance of the *Fleet River*, as if to defend the little haven, which was then capable of receiving ships). He began the building upon the old foundations, the fourth time that *structure* was built, which after additions at several times to the east and west, continued until the last general conflagration of the city in 1666.

The fabric thus begun by *Mauritius* originally had, as the *Surveyor* believed, a semicircular *presbyterium* or chancel, after the usual *fashion* of the *primitive churches*, and came near the form of a *cross*, short to the east; as he concluded for this reason: a *Choir* in later times was added to give a greater length eastward than at first. This building was apparently of a more modern *Gothic style*, not with *round* (as in the old church) but *sharp-headed arches*; to make way for which, the semicircular *presbyterium* had been taken down. Upon demolishing the ruins after the last *fire* and searching the foundations of this *Choir*, the *Surveyor* discovered nine wells in a row; which, no doubt, had anciently belonged to a street of houses that lay sloping from the high street (then *Watling Street*) to the *Roman Causeway* (now *Cheapside*). This street, which was taken away to make room for the new *Choir*, came so near the old *presbyterium* that the church could not extend further that way at first. He discovered also that there had been a considerable addition and a new front to the west, but in what age is not ascertained.

The reason the *Surveyor* was of the opinion that, though the structure had been ruined several times, the foundations might remain as they were originally laid, was upon his observing that they consisted of nothing but *Kentish rubble-stone*, artfully worked and consolidated with exceedingly hard mortar in the *Roman manner*, much excelling what he found in the superstructure. The outside of the structure was built chiefly with the freestone of the old *Palatine Tower* and freestone supposed to be from the quarries of *Yorkshire*, and in every part it was apparently less skillfully performed and with worse mortar.

<margin>Dugdale's St. Paul's, p. 6.</margin>
<margin>Godwin de Praesul. p. 237. &cc.</margin>
Though there is now no history or record documenting directly the first building of the first new *Choir*, yet it is probable it might have been executed by *Richard*, who was Bishop of *London* in the first year of the reign of King *Richard the First* and had been treasurer to King *Henry the Second*. He is said to have expended a vast sum of money on the buildings of his church, etc.

<margin>Dugdale's St. Paul's, p. 12.</margin>
But the said *Choir* being afterwards not thought beautiful enough, and a resolution taken for an improvement, they began with the *steeple*, which was finished in the year 1221 (5 *Hen.* III), and then, going on with the *Choir*, perfected it in 1240 (24 *Hen.* III) in the form it continued until the last great fire in 1666.

Under the *Choir* was a noble vault, wherein were three ranks of large and massive pillars; this, being made a parish church, was dedicated to *St. Faith*.

Upon the happy *Restoration* of King *Charles* II, it was determined to proceed with the repairs of the old cathedral church, which had been interrupted by the *Great Rebellion*; and Dr. *Wren* was ordered to prepare proper designs

designs for that purpose. His predecessor, Mr. *Inigo Jones*, had (pursuant to a royal commission in 1631, the 7th year of *Charles I*) put the *choir*—which was of a more modern *Gothic style* than the rest of the building, as previously specified—into very good repair. He had proceeded to case a great part of the outside with *Portland stone*; had rebuilt the north and south fronts; and also the west front, with the addition of a very graceful *portico* of the *Corinthian order*, built of large *Portland stone*. The great tower remained to be newly cased inside and out, and the entire interior from the *choir* to the west door was to be newly cased and reformed in some measure.

The vaulting required much repair; for this purpose, it was all well-centered and upheld with supports made of several hundred tall masts.

<margin>*Dugdale's St. Paul's, p. 146, etc.*</margin>
The building was in this state when the Great Rebellion began. "But in 1643, all the materials, etc., assigned for the repairs were seized; the scaffolds were pulled down; and the body of the church was converted into a stable for the soldiers' horses. The beautiful pillars of *Inigo Jones's portico* were shamefully hewn and defaced to support the timberwork of shops for seamstresses and other trades; for these sordid uses, that stately colonnade was completely occupied and defiled. Upon removing the inner scaffolds that supported the arched vaults for their recently intended repair, the entire roof of the south transept tumbled down, and the rest of the roof frequently fell in several places of the church. Thus, the structure remained a woeful spectacle of ruin until the happy Restoration.

"In 1662, the Dean and Chapter took care to prepare the eastern part of the church beyond the old *choir* for divine service, enlarging it by the length of one arch into the *choir*, until the repairs of the remaining part of the old building should be completed."

<margin>*Continuation of Dugdale's St. Paul's, p. 149.*</margin>
"To expedite this general repair, a royal commission was passed in 1663. After this, time was spent in taking down houses and nuisances that had been erected by the recent usurpers at the west end and sides of the church; in clearing the rubbish; inspecting the decay; repairing the *portico*; and providing stone, timber, and all necessary preparations until the beginning of the year 1666. By this time, Dr. *Wren* had finished and adjusted his designs for the entire repair and laid them before the King and the commissioners."

The first business Dr. *Wren* entered upon, before forming designs for the general repairs, was to take an exact plan, elevation <note>orthography</note>, and section based on an accurate survey of the whole structure, down to the inch. In the course of this, he was astonished to find how negligent the original builders had been; they seemed to have used the *Norman* foot, but they did not value exactness. Some spaces between columns were an inch and a half too large, and others as much, or more, too small. Nor were they accurate in their levels. The building consisted largely of old materials which the founder, *Mauritius*, Bishop of *London*, had procured from King *William the First* from the ruins of the *Palatine Tower*; these were small *Yorkshire* freestone, *Kentish* ashlar, and *Kentish* ragstone from *Maidstone*. They made great pillars without any graceful style and thick walls without judgment. They had not yet adopted the *Gothic* pointed arch, as was followed in the *choir* of a later date, but kept to the circular arch. They retained that much of the *Roman* style, but nothing else. They could not have cornices for lack of larger stones; in short, it was a vast but heavy building. Adjoining the south transept was a chapter house in a more elegant *Gothic* style, with a cloister two stories high.

The lofty *Spire* which formerly rose from the great middle stone tower, the *Surveyor* [Wren] observed, was not originally intended to be made of stone, for there were no diagonal arches to reduce it into an octagon; it was therefore finished in timber covered with lead. This was twice set on fire by lightning, and the last time, in 1561, it was totally consumed.

<margin>Camden's *Britannia, 2nd Edition, p. 378.*</margin>
Antiquaries differ in their accounts of its altitude. By *Stow’s* measurements, the stone tower and *spire* were each 260 feet in height, totaling 520 feet. Mr. *Camden’s* dimensions reach 534 feet. *Dugdale* (seemingly on good authority, having taken his account from a brass tablet formerly hung on a pillar in the north part of the *choir*) makes the height of the tower 260 feet and of the spire 274 feet, and yet the whole—namely, both tower and spire—did not exceed 520 feet, as is testified by the tablet (of which there is also a manuscript copy in the public library in *Cambridge*). This is 14 feet shorter than the height of the tower and spire dimensions added together. "This," (says the Right Reverend and learned editor of *Camden's Britannia*) "must indeed have been true had the spire risen from the summit of the battlements; whereas, I suppose, it rose (as the spires of most steeps do) much below them. The battlements here, rising 14 feet above the base of the spire, must account for the difference."

The entire stone tower was standing when the *Surveyor* measured it before the *Fire*, and, consistent with the other accounts, it was 260 feet in height. He found the *base* of the spire was 40 feet; therefore, according to the usual proportion of spires in *Gothic buildings* (which was 4 diameters, or 5 at most), it could rise no higher than 200 feet, making the total altitude not exceed 460 feet to the gilded copper *ball* and *cross*. Upon this, after the first fire by lightning, was added a *weathercock* representing an *eagle*, also of gilded copper.

The proportions of these copper *ornaments* are recorded as follows: the *ball* was 9 feet 1 inch in circumference. The height of the *cross* from the *ball* was 15 feet 6 inches, and its crossbeam was 5 feet 10 inches. The *eagle* from the beak to the tail was 4 feet, and the breadth across the wings was 3 and a half feet.

<margin>May 1.</margin>

These were based upon an accurate survey taken in 1666, which, together with the various respective drawings, were laid before the King and Commissioners some months before the Great *Fire of London*.

<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

“...lacked the Grandeur, which exceeds all minor curiosity; this being the effect of wit only, the other a monument of power, and mighty zeal in our ancestors for public works in those times, when the city had neither a fifth part of the people, nor a tenth part of the wealth it now boasts of.

“I shall presume therefore to enumerate the defects of beauty as well as stability, so that the one may be reconciled with the other in the restoration. And yet I should not propose any matter of mere beauty to be added, except where there is a necessity of rebuilding, and where it will be nearly the same effort to perform it well as poorly.

“First, it is evident by the ruin of the roof, that the work was both poorly designed and poorly built from the beginning: poorly designed, because the architect gave not enough buttressing to counterpoise and resist the weight of the roof from spreading the walls; for, the eye alone will reveal to any man that those pillars, as vast as they are—even eleven feet in diameter—are bent outwards at least six inches from their first position. This being done on both sides, it necessarily follows that the whole roof must first open in large and wide cracks along the walls and windows, and finally drop down between the yielding pillars.

“This bending of the pillars was made easier by their poor construction; for, they are only cased on the outside, and that with small stones, none greater than a man can carry; but inside is nothing but a core of small rubbish-stone and much mortar, which easily crushes and yields to the weight. This outward coat of free-stone is so much torn with age and the neglect of the roof, that there are few stones to be found that are not crumbled and chipped away by the saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate deposits that cause stone decay</note> that is in them—an incurable disease which perpetually throws off whatever coat of plaster is laid on it, and therefore cannot be masked.

“From this I infer that, as the outside of the church was newly faced with stone of a larger size than before, so should the inside be as well. In doing this, it will be as easy to perform it in a good *Roman* manner as to follow the *Gothic* crudeness of the old design; and that, without placing the face of the new work any more than a few inches further out or in than the surface of the old work, or adding to the expense that would arise if it were performed the worse way.

“This also may be safely affirmed, not only by an architect taking his measurements from the rules and examples of the ancients, but by a geometrician (this part being capable of demonstration), that the roof is, and ever was, too heavy for its buttressing. Therefore, any part of the old roof that is newly patched will still only cause further ruin, and the second ruin will follow much sooner than the first, since it is easier to force a thing that is already leaning. It must therefore be either a timber roof plastered (which, in such buildings where a little soaking from weather is not immediately discovered or repaired, will soon decay), or else a thinner and lighter shell of stone, very geometrically proportioned to the strength of the buttressing. The roof may be brick if it is plastered with *stucco*, which is a harder plaster that will not fall off with the drip of a few winters, and which to this day remains firm in many ancient *Roman* buildings.

“The middle part is most defective both in beauty and stability, outside and inside; for the tower leans visibly due to the settling of one of the ancient pillars that supported it. Four new arches were, therefore, in later years incorporated within the old ones, which has narrowed and hindered both the space and the clear thorough view of the nave,

> "The excessive length of buildings is commendable only because it yields a pleasing perspective through the continuous optical reduction of the columns; and if this is cut off by columns set inside the line of the others, the grace that would be acquired by the length is totally lost.
> 
> "Besides this deformity of the tower itself within, there are others near it; for instance, the next intercolumniation <note>The spacing between columns.</note> in the *Navis* or body of the church is much smaller than all the rest. Also, the north and south wings have aisles only on the west side, the others being originally closed off for the Consistory. Lastly, the intercolumniations, or spaces between the pillars of the choir next to the tower, are very unequal. Again, on the outside of the tower, the buttresses that have been built one upon another to secure three corners on the leaning sides (for the fourth lacks a buttress) are so irregular that, ultimately, it must be concluded that the tower from top to bottom, and the adjacent parts, are such a heap of deformities that no judicious architect will think it can be corrected by any expense spent on resurfacing it. Instead, it will still remain unworthy of the rest of the work, weak and tottering; and for these reasons, I suspect, it was previously decided that it should be taken down.
> 
> "I cannot propose a better remedy than to cut off the inner corners of the cross to reduce this middle part into a spacious dome or *rotunda*, with a cupola or hemispherical roof; and upon the cupola (for outward ornament), a lantern with a spire-like top to rise proportionately, though not to that unnecessary height of the former spire of timber and lead which was destroyed by lightning.
> 
> "By this means, the deformities of the unequal intercolumniations will be removed; the church, which is much too narrow for its height, will be made spacious in the middle, which may be a very proper place for a large congregation. The outward appearance of the church will seem to swell in the middle by degrees, from a large base rising into a rotunda bearing a cupola, and then ending in a *lantern*; and this with incomparably more grace from a distance than the lean shaft of a steeple could possibly afford. Nor, if it is managed correctly, will the expense be much more than that of covering the tower and unfinished corners with new stone and rebuilding the old steeple; the lead from that steeple will be sufficient for a *cupola*, and the same quantity of ashlar <note>Square-cut stone.</note> makes the corners outward that would make them inward as they are now. The materials from the old corners of the aisles will serve as filling-stone for the new work.
> 
> "For I would not suggest that the tower be pulled down at first, but that the new work be built around it. This is partly because public expectations must be maintained; for many skeptics would mourn the loss of old *Paul*'s steeple and lose hope if they did not see a promising successor rising in its place. Chiefly, however, it would save a large number of scaffolding poles, as the necessary scaffolds can be fixed between the old and the new work. And when the *tholus* <note>The internal vault or dome.</note> or inward vault is to be laid, the tower—having been taken down to that height—will support the centering of the vault very conveniently and make it easier to place the machines for raising the stones. After everything is finished and settled, the remaining part of the tower may be completely removed from the inside. All of this can only be perfectly understood from the designs."

“ Thieves) You (along with other gentlemen and myself) were named by King *Charles* as commissioners to survey the damages and to report to his *Majesty* in order to ensure a speedy repair; I am sure you will not forget the struggle we had with some who were for patching it up in any way (so that the steeple might stand) instead of a new building, which it completely needed. The great and dreadful *Fire of London*, which began on the 2nd of September in the year 1666, consumed the greatest part of the city. The parish churches were destroyed, and the ancient cathedral of St. *Paul* was miserably shattered and demolished; the roof fell down and, with a mighty force, broke through those vaults called the *undercroft*, etc. The first thing planned after this deplorable *fire* was to prepare some part of the ruined church for a *choir*, where the dean and prebends might hold divine service until the repair of the whole or a new structure could be completed. To this end, upon inspection, it was resolved that part of the main body towards the *west end* might, with the least expense, be made useful for that purpose. Consequently, workmen were assigned to it, and scaffolds were raised to examine the walls and to cut the remainder of the unmelted lead from the high roof and other parts of the church.

In this work—as well as in digging up the melted lead, clearing the rubbish, taking down the remainder of the vaulted roof and walls with the greatest part of the tower steeple, digging up the floors, sorting the stone and carrying it to various places, repairing the Convocation House, and building new offices for the work—no less than two years (namely, the rest of 1666, the whole of 1667, and part of 1668) were spent. Towards the end of these two years, they began casing some of those great and massive pillars that stood between the middle aisle and the side aisles, starting with those below the little north door toward the west. But before the third pillar was perfectly encased, the excessive heat of the fire had left it—along with the remaining pillars and walls, which were all miserably scaled by the flames and shattered—so weak and unsound that upon further inspection, they were found to be completely incapable of any substantial repair. It was therefore fully concluded that, for the sake of a new building, the foundations of the old cathedral, thus ruined, should be totally cleared, and preparations of materials and all necessary things should be made ready for a new structure. This work continued until the last day of *April* 1674.

The state of the old building after the *fire*, the unsuccessful attempts to repair the ruins, and the defects of *Inigo Jones*’s work are further explained in the following transcript of a letter from the Rev. Dr. *William Sancroft*, then Dean of St. *Paul*’s, and afterwards (in 1677) Archbishop of *Canterbury*.

->To my worthy friend Dr. *Christopher Wren*, *Professor of Astronomy*<-
->in *Oxford*, *April* 25, 1668.<-

->S I R,<-

As it was said of old, *Prudentia est quaedam divinatio* <note>Prudence is a kind of divination</note>, so science (at the level you have mastered it) is prophetic too. What you whispered in my ear during your last visit here has now come to pass. Our work at the west end of St. *Paul*’s has fallen about our ears. Your quick eye discerned that the walls and pillars had shifted from their perpendiculars, and I believe you saw other defects too, which are now exposed to every common observer.

About a week ago, while we were at work on the third pillar from the west end on the south side—which we had recased with new stone where it was most defective, almost up to the capital—a great weight falling from the high wall so disabled the vaulting of the side-aisle next to it that it threatened a sudden ruin. This was so visible that the workmen immediately moved away; and the next night the entire pillar fell, carrying the scaffolds and everything else to the very ground.

The second pillar (which you know is larger than the rest) stands now alone, with an enormous weight on the top of it; we cannot hope it will stand long, and yet we dare not venture to take it down.

<margin>
<unclear>I have</unclear>
<unclear>note</unclear>
<unclear>that</unclear>
in 1668, p. 199.
</margin>
This breach has revealed to all who look at it two great defects in *Inigo Jones's* work: one, that his new casing of stone in the upper walls (massive as it is) was not set upon the upright of the pillars, but upon the core of the groins of the vaulting; the other, that there were no key-stones at all to tie it to the old work. All of this being very heavy with the *Roman* ornaments on the top of it, and already having shifted so far outward, cannot possibly stand long. In short, it is the opinion of all men that we can proceed no further at the west end. What we are to do next is our current deliberation, in which you are so absolutely and indispensably necessary to us that we can do nothing and resolve on nothing without you.

It is therefore in my Lord of *Canterbury's* name, and by his order (already, as I suppose, suggested to you by the Dean of *Christ Church*), that we most earnestly desire your presence and assistance with all possible speed.

I know you will think it proper to bring with you those excellent drafts and designs you formerly favored us with; and in the meantime, until we enjoy your company here, consider what to advise that may be for the satisfaction of his *Majesty* and the whole nation—an obligation so great and so public that it must be acknowledged by better hands than those of—

->Your very affectionate friend and servant,<-

->W. SANCROFT.<-

I am therefore commanded to give you an invitation here, in his Grace’s name and the rest of the commissioners, with all speed, so that we may prepare something to be proposed to his *Majesty* (at least the design of such a choir as may be a fitting part of a greater and more magnificent work to follow). ## S E C T I O N IV.

### *Of the new cathedral Church of St. Paul's.*

Preparation for the new structure being thus made, and several designs presented to the King for its form and fashion—which was intended to equal, if not exceed, the splendor and magnificence of the old cathedral when it was in its best state—his *Majesty*, well approving of one of them, commanded a *model* to be made of it in so large and exact a manner that it might remain as a perpetual and unchangeable rule and direction for the conduct of the whole work. And for the more speedy progress in this vast and mighty building, he issued his letters patent under the Great Seal of *England*, dated the 12th day of *November* in the 25th year of his reign, *Anno scilicet* <note>namely, in the year</note> 1673, to several lords spiritual and temporal, and other persons of eminent rank and quality, and *Christopher Wren*, Doctor of Laws, Surveyor General of the Royal Works; authorizing them, or as many of them as are therein appointed and enabled to act, to proceed in that great undertaking and to endeavor to perfect it by such ways and means, and according to such rules and orders, as are mentioned therein. A transcript of the preamble of which commission is inserted here.

> Whereas—Since the issuing of our commission (namely, in the year 1663, the 15th year of the reign of *Charles* II), the late dreadful Fire in *London* has destroyed and consumed the cathedral church of St. Paul to such a degree that no part of the ancient walls or structures can be relied upon with any safety or left standing; so much so, that it has now become absolutely necessary to totally demolish and raze to the ground all the relics of the former building, and in the same place, but upon new foundations, to erect a new church; (in order that it may be done to the glory of God and for the promoting of His divine worship and service to be celebrated there; and so that the same may equal, if not exceed, the splendor and magnificence of the former cathedral church when it was in its best state, and so become much more than formerly the principal ornament of our royal city, to the honor of our government and of this our realm), we have caused several designs for that purpose to be prepared by Dr. *Christopher Wren*, Surveyor General of all our works and buildings, which we have seen, and one of which we more especially approve, and have commanded a *model* of it to be made in so large and exact a man-

Whereas we have been informed that a portion of the tax laid on coals, which by Act of Parliament is appointed and set apart for the rebuilding of the cathedral church of St. Paul, in our capital city of London, does at present amount to a considerable sum, which, though not proportional to the greatness of the work, is notwithstanding sufficient to begin the same; and with all the materials and other assistance which may probably be expected, will put a new choir in great forwardness: and whereas among various designs which have been presented to us, we have particularly chosen one, both because we found it very skillfully designed, proper, and useful, and because it was so arranged that it might be built and finished in sections. We do therefore by these presents signify our royal approval of the said design, annexed here; and do will and require you to proceed immediately according to the said design, beginning with the east end or choir, and completing the same with the present stock of money and such supplies as may probably accumulate, according to the tenor of the commission directed to you; and for so doing this shall be your warrant. Given at our Court at *Whitehall*, the 14th day of *May*, 1675, in the 27th year of our reign.

->By His Majesty's Command,<-

->HENRY COVENTRY.<-

In the management of the former repairs of the old fabric, under the direction of *Inigo Jones*, Surveyor of the Royal Works, no other fund was advanced toward defraying the expense but the voluntary contributions of pious and charitable people. These came in so slowly, in proportion to the greatness of the work, that—notwithstanding royal generosity and the considerable sums of money brought from time to time into the Chamber of *London* from private benefactions—the zeal of Archbishop *Laud* for the honor of God and the Church of *England* (promoting it by his own example and exciting others to liberal donations for the restoration of such a significant monument of our ancestors' piety, it being the principal ornament of the realm) was such that the celebrated architect was not able to execute even a third of what was necessary.

Before such time, therefore, as a tax on sea-coal <note>Coal brought to London by sea, usually from Newcastle</note> had been granted by Parliament for the building of the church (which duty did not commence until the first of *May* 1670), it seemed pointless in any new designs to propose an edifice too large and costly to be brought to a successful and timely completion.

Upon this consideration, the *Surveyor* was at first directed to design a fabric of moderate size, but of good proportion: a convenient choir, with a vestibule and porticoes, and a dome conspicuous above the houses. A long body with aisles was thought unsuitable, as our religion does not use processions.

THE LIFE OF

It was to be vaulted underneath for burials, so that the pavement above might be preserved. A model in wood was made of this church which, though not as large, would have been beautiful and very fit for our way of worship. It was also a convenient auditory (for the sermons traditionally held outdoors from a stone pulpit in the churchyard were now to be brought into the church), and by the help of the vestibule, it was capable of any grand ceremony. It had porticoes on the outside, which might prevent disturbance within. This was applauded by persons of good judgment as containing all that was necessary for the church of a metropolis; it had a beautiful shape and an expense that might reasonably have been managed. However, being designed in the *Roman style*, it was not as well understood and liked by others, who thought it strayed too much from the old *Gothic* form of cathedral churches, which they had been used to seeing and admiring in this country. Others observed it was not stately enough, and contended that for the honor of the nation and the City of *London*, it ought not to be exceeded in magnificence by any church in *Europe*.

<margin>
(a) The model of *Bramante*'s first design of St. *Peter*'s Church is preserved with great care in the *Vatican Palace*.
</margin>
After this, in order to find what might satisfy everyone, the *Surveyor* drew several sketches merely for the sake of discussion; and observing that most people were for grandeur, he endeavored to gratify the taste of the *connoisseurs* and critics with something colossal and beautiful, with an antique and well-studied design conformable to the best style of *Greek* and *Roman* architecture. Some persons of distinction, skilled in antiquity and architecture, expressed themselves much pleased with the design and wished to see it in a model. The *Surveyor* complied with their desires as well as his own and made a very intricate large model in wood, accurately crafted and carved with all its proper ornaments, consisting of a single order, the *Corinthian* only (like St. *Peter*'s in *Rome*). This model was for many years kept in the Office of the Works at St. *Paul*'s in a shed built for that purpose; from there, after the finishing of the new building, it was deposited (together with the other models, and particularly one for the high altar, to consist of rich spiraled marble columns, etc., in a manner similar to that of St. *Peter*'s at *Rome*) over the Morning Prayer Chapel on the north side. There, it is to be hoped, such public care will be taken that it may be preserved and, if damaged, repaired, as an eminent and costly achievement and a monument, among the many others, of the skill of the greatest geometrician and architect of his time. [The original designs drawn on a large scale for the King's use still exist.] (a)

This much is specified, upon recollection, that the *Surveyor* in private conversation always seemed to set a higher value on this design than any he had made before or since, as it was worked on with more study and success; and (had he not been overruled by those whom it was his duty to obey) it was what he would have executed with more cheerfulness and satisfaction to himself than the later design.

But as yet nothing could be fully resolved upon; the *Chapter* and some others of the clergy thought the model was not enough of a "cathedral fashion"—to give a specific instance, the Choir was designed to be circular, etc. In the meantime, the money granted by Parliament from the coal tax began to come in; something had to be done in order to make a beginning without more delay. The *Surveyor* then turned his thoughts to a "cathedral form" (as they called it), but so refined as to reconcile, as nearly as possible, the *Gothic* to a better style of architecture, with a *cupola* and above that, instead of a lantern, a lofty spire and large porticoes.

<margin>1 May 1675.</margin> King Charles approved those designs, and so that there might be no further interruption, the *Warrant*, as previously recited, was issued under the Privy Seal for beginning the works. From that time, the <term>Surveyor</term> resolved to make no more models or publicly expose his drawings, which (as he had found by experience) only wasted time and frequently subjected his business to incompetent judges. By these means, at last, the scheme of the present mighty <term>structure</term> (different in some manner from the former, and preferable in his <term>Majesty's</term> own judgment, upon second thoughts) was no sooner concluded on and ordered, than it was begun by his <term>Surveyor</term> with vigor in the year 1675. And the King was pleased to allow him the liberty, in the prosecution of his work, to make some variations—rather ornamental than essential—as he should see fit from time to time, and to leave the whole to his own management.

### SECTION V.
Of the taking down of the vast ruins of the old cathedral, and of the foundations of the old and new structure.

THE pulling down of the walls, which were about 80 feet high and 5 feet thick, was a great and troublesome task; the men stood above and worked them down with pickaxes, while laborers below moved away the materials that fell and dispersed them into heaps. The lack of room made this method slow and dangerous, and some men lost their lives; the heaps grew

grew steep and large; and yet this had to be done before the masons could begin to lay the foundations.

The city, having streets to pave anew, bought most of the stone called *Kentish-rag* from the rubbish, which provided some room to dig and to lay foundations; yet this was not easy to perform with any exactness except by this method.

The *Surveyor* placed scaffolds high enough to extend his lines over the heaps that lay in the way, and then, using perpendiculars, set out the places below from the lines drawn with care upon the level plan of the scaffold.

Thus he proceeded, gaining more room every day until he came to the middle tower that bore the steeple. Since the remains of the tower were nearly 200 feet high, the laborers were afraid to work above; thereupon, he decided to facilitate this work by the use of gunpowder.

He dug a hole about four feet wide down by the side of the northwest pillar of the tower, the four pillars of which were each about 14 feet in diameter. When he had dug to the foundation, he then, with crowbars and tools made for the purpose, worked a hole two feet square level into the center of the pillar. There he placed a small pine box containing eighteen pounds of powder and no more; a cane was fixed to the box with a quick-match (as gunners call it) within the cane, which reached from the box to the ground above, and along the ground a train of powder was laid with a match. After the mine was carefully closed up again with stone and mortar to the top of the ground, he then observed the effect of the blast.

This small quantity of powder not only lifted up the whole angle of the tower, along with two great arches that rested upon it, but also two adjoining arches of the aisles and everything above them. It seemed to do this somewhat leisurely, cracking the walls to the top and visibly lifting the whole weight about nine inches, which, suddenly jumping down, made a great heap of ruin in that place without scattering. It was half a minute before the fallen heap opened in two or three places and emitted some smoke. By this description, the incredible force of powder may be observed: only 18 pounds of it lifted up above 3,000 tons and saved the work of 1,000 laborers.

The fall of such a great weight from a height of 200 feet gave a concussion to the ground that the inhabitants nearby mistook for an earthquake.

Encouraged by this success, he intended to proceed in this way; but being obliged to go out of town in the *King's* service, he left the management of another mine that had been started to the care of his next officer. This officer, who was too wise in his own conceit, put in a greater quantity of powder and neither went low enough nor sufficiently reinforced the mouth of the mine. Although it had the desired effect, one stone was shot out to the opposite side of the churchyard, through an open window, and into a room of a private house where some women were sitting at work, though no harm was done. This accident frightened the neighbors to such a degree that he was urged to use no more powder and was also directed to stop by his superiors; although with due caution it might have been executed without any hazard and saved much time and money.

He then turned his thoughts to another method to gain time, prevent much expense, and avoid endangering men's lives: making an experiment with that ancient engine of war, the *battering ram*.

He took a strong mast about 40 feet long, arming the larger end with a great iron spike reinforced with bars along the mast and ferrules. This mast was hung at two points from a single ring with strong tackle, and so suspended level to a triangle-prop, such as they weigh great guns with. Thirty men, fifteen on a side, vibrated this machine back and forth and beat against the wall in one place the whole day; they believed it was of little pur-

<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

Seeing no immediate effect, he told them not to despair but to proceed another day. On the second day, the wall was perceived to tremble at the top, and in a few hours, it fell. The reason to be given for it may be this: it is not by any immediate violence that the *Ram* is able to overturn a wall of such bulk and solidity, but by vibrating incessantly with equally spaced pulses, it creates a small internal motion through all the imperceptible parts of the wall. By degrees, it loosens the bond of the mortar and moves every stone from its bed; and though the movement is not the hundredth part of an inch at every blow, yet this motion, once begun, has more and more effect until at length the wall is quite loose and falls. He made good use of this machine in knocking down all the lofty ruins, and he was pleased that he had recovered this notable engine, which was of such great service to the *Ancients* in the besieging of towns—though heavy guns have now put them out of use, as they are more efficient and require fewer men to manage.

It has been observed before (*Section* I) that the graves of several ages and fashions in *strata*, or layers of earth one above another—particularly on the north side of *St. Paul's*—clearly showed great antiquity from the *British* and *Roman* times, by which means the ground had been raised. However, upon searching for the natural ground below these graves, the *Surveyor* observed that the foundation of the old church stood upon a layer of very close and hard pot-earth, and he concluded that the same ground which had borne such a heavy building might reasonably be trusted again. Nevertheless, he had the curiosity to search further, and accordingly dug wells in several places. He discerned this hard pot-earth to be about six feet thick or more on the north side of the churchyard, but it grew thinner and thinner towards the south, until on the decline of the hill it was scarcely four feet. Still he searched lower and found nothing but dry sand, sometimes mixed unequally but loose, so that it would run through the fingers. He continued until he came to water and sand mixed with periwinkles and other seashells; these were at about the level of the low-water mark. He continued boring until he came to hard beach, and still under that, until he came to the natural hard clay which lies under the city, the countryside, and the *Thames* as well, far and wide.

From these shells, it was evident the sea had been where the hill now is, on which *St. Paul's* stands.

The *Surveyor* was of the opinion that the entire country between *Camberwell Hill* and the *Hills of Essex* might have been a great *estuary* or *bay* of the sea, and much wider near the mouth of the *Thames*. This created a large plain of sand at low water, through which the river found its way; but at low water, as often as it happened in summer weather when the sun dried the surface of the sand and a strong wind happened at the same time before the flood tide came in, the sands would blow with the wind and raise heaps, and in time large and lofty sand-hills. For this is how sand-hills are raised upon the opposite coasts of *Flanders* and *Holland*. The sands, upon such a combination of sunshine and wind, drive in visible clouds; this might be the effect of many ages before recorded history, and yet without needing to refer to the Great Flood.

This massive, broad sand (now good meadow) was restrained by large banks still remaining, which reduced the river into its channel—a great work of which no history gives an account. The *Britons* were too primitive to attempt it; the *Saxons* were too busy with continual wars; he concluded, therefore, it was a *Roman work*. One small breach in his time cost £17,000 to restore.

The sand-hill at *St. Paul's* in the time of the *Roman colony* was about 12 feet lower than it is now; the finer sand, which blew more easily with the wind, lay uppermost, and the hard coat of pot-earth might have been made this way. For pot-earth dissolved in water and viewed through a microscope is nothing but impalpably fine sand, which will turn to glass in a fire; and of this earth upon the place,

<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

In this place were those urns, sacrificial vessels, and other pottery-ware made, which (as noted before) were found here in great abundance, especially towards the northeast of the ground.

In the progress of the work on the foundations, the *Surveyor* met with one unexpected difficulty. He began to lay the foundations from the west end and had proceeded successfully through the *dome* to the east end, where the brick-earth bottom was still very good; but as he went on to the northeast corner, which was the last part and where nothing was expected to cause an interruption, he fell, while executing the design, into a pit where all the pot-earth had been robbed by the potters of ancient times. Here were discovered quantities of urns, broken vessels, and pottery-ware of various sorts and shapes. There was no occasion to examine how far this pit extended northward. No ox-skulls, horns of stags, or tusks of boars were found to corroborate the accounts of *Stow*, *Camden*, and others, nor were there any foundations further eastward. If there was formerly any temple to *Diana*, he supposed it might have been within the walls of the colony, and further to the south. It was no small frustration to fall into this pit at the very end. He needed only six or seven feet to complete the design, and this pit fell exactly in the northeast angle. He knew very well that under the layer of pot-earth, there was no other good ground to be found until he reached the low-water mark of the *Thames*, at least forty feet lower. His craftsmen proposed that he use piles, which he refused; for, although piles may last forever when they are always in water (otherwise *London Bridge* would fall), if they are driven through dry sand—even if it is sometimes moist—they will rot. His endeavor was to build for eternity. He therefore sank a pit about eighteen feet square, shoring up the sand with timber, until he came forty feet lower into water and sea-shells, where there was a firm sea-beach. This confirmed what was previously asserted: that the sea had been, in ages past, where *St. Paul's* now stands. He bored through this beach until he came to the original clay. Being then satisfied, he began a square pier of solid, good masonry from the beach, ten feet square, until he came within fifteen feet of the present ground; then he built a short arch underground to the former foundation, which had been interrupted by the unfortunate accident of the pit. Thus, this northeast corner of the choir stands very firm and, no doubt, will continue to stand. This narrative may be of use to others, advising them not to trust piles unless they are always and in all parts wet; for almost all sorts of timber under water will prove everlasting, but when alternately wet and dry, they will soon perish. The same cannot be said of iron, for that will decay under water; but this has been observed: in taking out cramps from stonework at least four hundred years old, which were so bedded in mortar that all air was perfectly excluded, the iron appeared as fresh as if from the forge. Therefore, in the cramping of stones, no iron should lie within nine inches of the air, if possible; for the air is the solvent that consumes all materials whatever. When there is a necessity to use iron for want of stones large enough, care is to be taken to sufficiently exclude the air from it. To mention another caution of use to craftsmen: regarding some cornices with large projections, even though the upper joints are as closely fitted as good workmen can make them, the water from melting snow will still dribble through and stain the cornice. The *Surveyor* avoided this inconvenience in this way: he ordered the masons to work the stone next to the joint so as to leave an eighth of an inch rising on each side, so that the water might fall off sooner than soak into the joint. He also observed this in the paving of the upper portico of the principal front of *St. Paul's*, and furthermore, the joints there are filled with lead; the same was done wherever he was obliged to cover surfaces with stone only.

(the south side of *St. Paul's* was one) should be forty feet wide, but the old foundations narrowed the street toward the east end to under 30 feet.

Secondly, the churchyard on the north side was wide, and afforded room that way to give the new building a more free and graceful appearance.

Thirdly, to have built on the old foundations would have confined the *Surveyor* too much to the old plan and form; the ruinous walls were not to be trusted again in any part, nor would old and new work firmly unite or stand together without cracking.

Since it was found advisable, therefore, to change the foundations, he took the advantage of more room northward and laid the middle line of the new work inclining more toward the northeast than it was before, which was not exactly east and west. Neither did the old front of the cathedral face directly toward *Ludgate*, as it does not at present, which was not practical to change without purchasing and tearing down a great number of houses and obtaining the aid of Parliament. This, though much wished for, he was not able to achieve; the commissioners for rebuilding the city had, in the first place, marked and staked out all the streets, and the Parliament confirmed their report before anything had been fully determined about the design for the new building. The property owners, with much eagerness and haste, had begun to build accordingly; incredible progress had been made in a very short time; many large and handsome houses were erected; and every foot of ground in that trading and populous part of the town was highly valued.

# S E C T. VI.

## *Answers to Objections; and some Account of the new Building.*

**I**n order to satisfy those persons who are charmed with the grandeur of the *Vatican* Church of *St. Peter* in *Rome*, with its stately colonnades and spacious area in front, and who think no structure of this sort is to be esteemed truly noble and majestic unless it arises to or nearly approaches that magnificence; it must be considered that at *St. Paul's* the *Surveyor* lacked room and had little hope of procuring more than he found, for the reasons mentioned above. When all the adjacent ground and newly built streets were in private possession under various titles—which, on account of their good situation for trade in the greatest and richest city in all *Europe*, were valued at a very high rate—proper and necessary ground for both the grandeur and graceful approach to all parts of the building could only be had by a special act of Parliament. This would have been needed to oblige the numerous proprietors to part with their estates upon fair terms and to apply a part of the fund from coal taxes or otherwise to that particular purpose; which, unfortunately, was never obtained. For this reason, no more space was left, especially before the west front and to the northwest, though great sums of money were expended even with the assistance of Parliament to purchase houses and to gain what present room there is.

Some have inquired why the *Surveyor* chose to use two orders, rather than one *single order* with an attic story, as at *St. Peter's* in *Rome*. It is most certain his intention and desires from the beginning were to have followed that example, had all things succeeded to his wish. This appears in all his first designs, and in particular by the *great model* mentioned earlier.

*Bramante* knew the quarries of *Tivoli* * would yield blocks large enough for his columns at *St. Peter’s*, of nine feet in diameter, but then he was at a loss to find stones for his cornices; and this was the reason that obliged him to diminish the proportions of the proper members of his cornice. At *St. Paul’s*, the *Surveyor* was cautious not to exceed columns of four feet, which had been tried by *Inigo Jones* in his portico; the quarries of the Isle of *Portland* would just afford stone for that proportion, but not readily, for the artisans were forced sometimes to wait some months for one necessary stone to be raised for their purpose, and the further the quarrymen pierced into the rock, the quarry produced fewer stones than near the sea. All the most eminent masons of *England* were of the opinion that stones of the largest <term>scantlings</term> (dimensions) were to be found there, or nowhere. An inquiry was made after all the good stone that *England* afforded. Next to *Portland*, *Rock-abbey* stone and some others in *Yorkshire* seemed the best and most durable; but large stone for the *St. Paul’s* works was not easily to be had even there.

For these reasons, the *Surveyor* decided upon *Portland stone*, and also to use two orders, and by that means to keep the just proportions of his cornices; otherwise, he must have fallen short of the height of the building, which now exerts itself over all the country, as well as the city, as it did of old, when that structure, though rude, was lofty and majestic.
