At the *Vatican Church*, *Bramante* was ambitious to exceed the ancient *Greek* and *Roman* temples, which generally were built from the noble marble quarries of the islands of the *Archipelago* and *Egypt*, where stones were to be had of the largest size architects could have occasion to use; and although by necessity he failed in the due proportions of the proper members of his cornice, because the *Tivoli* stone would not hold out for the purpose; yet (as far as we can find) he succeeded in the † diameter of his columns, for the largest of the antique pillars that remain (supposed to have been part of the frontispiece of *Nero’s* Golden House, and brought from there by *Vespasian* to the *Temple of Peace*, and now standing before the temple of *Santa Maria Major*) is less in ‡ diameter than those at *St. Peter’s*. The glory, however, of the *Roman* pillar must be acknowledged in this wonderful particular: that it consists of only one solid || stone of *Parian* marble, of the *Corinthian* order.

A query has been made as to why all the pilasters of the outside were doubled? They are of the same use as buttresses, and they provide space for large windows between them, which is necessary in our darker weather. As also for the good regularity of the arcades within and the roof, they will appear proper to those who consider the whole design together.

<margin>
§ See the plan in the architecture of Sebastiano Serlio.
</margin>
Again, why were the columns of the west portico doubled? This, no doubt, is not according to the usual fashion of the *ancients* in their ordinary temples, which, for the most part, were small; but it was followed in their <term>colossi</term>, or greater works. For instance, in the portico of the § *Temple of Peace*, the most magnificent in old *Rome*, the columns were very properly and necessarily doubled to make wider openings, after the manner of the middle openings in the porticoes of the *Greek* temples, to accommodate five doors at unequal distances: namely, three near together, which lead into the great middle <term>nave</term>, or body of the temple, and one to each side aisle, at greater distances. (*a*) *Bramante* used double columns without scruple, as did *Michael Angelo* inside and outside the cupola of *St. Peter’s* in the *Vatican*. The same is done in the portico of the church of *Santa Maria Major* in *Rome*, and also in other public and private buildings by the most celebrated architects; to in-

<margin>* Palaces of Rome by Pietro Ferrerio.</margin>
instance among others, in the *facade of the Palace of Messrs. Caffarelli alla Valle,* built by *Raphael Urbin* in the year 1515; which contains 26 paired columns in front. The *French* architects have practiced the same to good effect, especially in the beautiful facade of the *Louvre*. It is to be observed in the portico of *St. Paul's*, two columns are brought closer together to create larger inter-columns alternately, to give a proper space for three doors. The ancients, particularly the *Greeks*, in their temples, generally made the middle inter-column wider than the rest; and as they shifted the columns of the portico for a better approach to one door, so at *St. Paul's*, for the same reason—where there are three doors (the two side-doors for daily use, and the middle for solemnities)—the columns are widened to make a more open and commodious access to each. This results gracefully by placing the pillars alternately, <term>Eustyle</term> (well-spaced) and <term>Pycnostyle</term> (tightly-spaced). *Hermogenes*, who first contrived the <term>Pseudodipteron</term> (a temple with a single row of columns but the space of two) by taking away a whole range of columns to enlarge the portico, went further than his masters dared before him, yet is commended by *Vitruvius* for this very thing because it was useful. The *Romans*, after the *Greek* examples, not only widened the middle openings in the colonnades before their temples, but followed the same manner in arcades also: thus in the *Colosseum*, or Amphitheatre of *Vespasian* in *Rome*, of the eighty arches, four which lead principally to the *arena*, were made wider than all the rest. They generally took such liberties, well knowing that the orders were to be adapted to their proper use, and not the design too servilely to the orders; of which a hundred examples may be given. Those who duly examine by measure the best remains of the *Greek* or *Roman* structures, whether temples, pillars, arches, or theatres, will soon discern that even among these there is no certain general agreement; for it is manifest the ancient architects took great liberties in their capitals and members of cornices to show their own inventions, even where their design did not oblige them. But where it did oblige them to a rational variation, while still keeping a good symmetry, they are surely to be commended, and in like cases to be followed. We now most esteem the learning of the *Augustan Age*, yet, no question, there were many different styles in oratory, and perhaps some as good as *Cicero's*. This is not said as any inducement to masons, or every novice who can draw lines, to fall into crude *Gothic* inventions far from the good examples of the ancients, any more than to encourage a barbarous style in *Latin*; and yet surely we cannot but with *Erasmus* laugh at him who dared not use one word that he could not find in *Tully* (Cicero).

To proceed in examining what has been further objected, particularly why the architrave within is cut off by the arch. In this, the *Surveyor* always insisted that he had the ancients on his side; in the *Templum Pacis*, and in all the great halls of the baths, and in all the great structures of three aisles, this was done, and for this reason: in those wide inter-columns, the architrave is not supposed to lie from one great column to another, but from the column to the wall of the aisle, so the end of it will only appear upon the pillar of the inside of the great <term>Navis</term> (nave). *Vitruvius* tells us that architecture took its beginning from wooden porticoes; suppose therefore a portico of three aisles in wood, or at least with the roof of timber, the architraves must join the pillars of the aisles, and not be in range with the inside pillars, but cross to that line; so nothing will appear upon the pillars of the nave but the ends of the architraves. If it be said that in the *Templum Pacis* the cornice is cut off as well as the architrave, the answer is plain: there is not the same reason to cut off the cornice of the arches at *St. Paul's*, which do not rise so high; for a cornice may be carried within, even without pillars (provided the proportion of its due height is kept), much more so with pillars.

The *Surveyor* followed the *Templum Pacis* as near as our measurements would admit, having but three arcades in each of the bodies East and West, as there;

...but where there are no arcades, and next to the dome, he has continued the whole entablature.

In one thing he seems to have varied from the ancients: he has incorporated smaller pilasters with the larger ones, both of the same *Corinthian* order. It is true that the imposts of old upon which the arches rested had a particular capital in the *Doric* style, and not the same capital as the pillar, as can be seen in the surviving triumphal arches and theaters. But above all things, they were careful that this capital of the impost should not have more sally or projection than to lie upon the great pillar or pilaster. This was easily done on the outside of buildings, where there was enough room to advance the pilaster until it could receive the impost moldings to lie against its side; but inside *St. Paul's*, it would have narrowed the great nave and made the breaks of the cornice above too heavy. Whether *Bramante* was aware of this in *St. Peter's* may be questioned, at least until after he had laid the bases of the great pilasters; for he has chopped off the cornice moldings of the imposts to give way for the pilaster to break through them, which is ungraceful and without authority or good reason. Whatever veneration we may have for this great man, surely in this it must be admitted that he has confessed an oversight. If anyone thinks it improper to incorporate large and small pillars together, as is done in the aisles at *St. Paul's*, let him consider the *Basilica* of the *Colonia Julia* at *Fanum*, which is the only piece *Vitruvius* acknowledges himself to be the author of. He will easily perceive that small pillars must be incorporated into the large ones to support the galleries, and he will find that the whole frieze is used by *Vitruvius* to provide light.

*Bramante* has no hesitation about incorporating pilasters throughout his entire exterior of *St. Peter's*. The *Surveyor* at *St. Paul's* chose to make the little pilasters of the same order as the large ones in the aisles because the opposite wall is beautified with the same smaller order; for the aisle along the whole length of the church is itself a long and graceful portico, without being interrupted by the legs of the dome.

In giving the entablature to this order, the *Surveyor* has taken the liberty to leave out certain members, as the ancients did in the interior of porticoes. The architrave is essential in all works, but in interiors, they often chose to leave out the frieze and cornice as well, except for some of the lower members which they added to the architrave so that it would not appear too meager. By this liberty (in which he was authorized by the best ancient porticoes), he could fit most of the members of the entablature of the smaller order within the projection of the large pilaster, without abruptly chopping off the members of an impost. If anyone still says the small pillars should not have been of the same order, let them examine the *Templum Pacis* <note>The Temple of Peace in Rome, now known as the Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine.</note>. They will find a small colonnade continued through every arch, and that of the *Corinthian* order, as appears by some small *Corinthian* capitals still adhering to the great structure.

This temple, being an example of a three-aisled building, is certainly the best and most authentic pattern for a cathedral church, which must by custom have three aisles and be vaulted. Though it may not always be necessary to vault with diagonal-cross vaults, as the *Templum Pacis* and the halls of the *Roman* baths are, the *Romans* used hemispherical vaulting also in some places. The *Surveyor* chose these as being demonstrably much lighter than the others; so the entire vault of *St. Paul's* consists of 24 cupolas cut into semicircles with segments to join the great arches in one direction, and which are cut across the other way with elliptical cylinders to let in the upper lights of the nave. But in the aisles, the smaller cupolas are cut in semicircular sections in both directions; together they create a graceful geometrical form, distinguished by circular wreaths, which is the horizontal section of the cupola. For the hemisphere may be cut in all sorts of ways into circular sections; and the arches and wreaths...

Wreaths being of stone carved, the spandrels between are of sound brick covered with *stucco* of cockle-shell lime, which becomes as hard as *Portland* stone; and which, having large planes between the stone ribs, are capable of further ornaments of painting, if required. Besides these 24 cupolas, there is a half-cupola at the east, and the great cupola of 112 feet diameter, in the middle of the crossing of the great aisles. In this, the *Surveyor* has imitated the *Pantheon*, or *Rotunda* in *Rome*, excepting only that the upper order is there only suggested, not projecting as at St. *Paul's* out of the wall, but only distinguished by different colored marbles. The *Pantheon* is no higher within than its diameter; St. *Peter's* is two diameters; this appears too high, the other too low. The *Surveyor* at St. *Paul's* took a middle proportion, which shows a concave every way; and it is very bright due to the windows of the upper order, which strike down the light through the great colonnade that encircles the dome without, and serves for the abutment of the dome, which is brick of two bricks thick, but as it rises every five feet high, has a course of excellent brick 18 inches long, banding through the whole thickness. <note>(a) The bricks in the ruins of the Roman wall, and multangular tower at *York*, are about seventeen inches of *English* measure long, and about eleven inches broad, and two and a half inches thick, measured by the ingenious Mr. *Lister*, and communicated to the *Royal Society*, 1683. [Phil. Trans. No. 149.]</note> The concave was built upon a centering; which was judged necessary to keep the work even and true, though a cupola might be built without a centering; but this is noteworthy: that the centering was laid without any upright supports from below to support it; and as it was both centering and scaffolding, it remained for the use of the painter. Every story of this scaffolding being circular, and the ends of all the horizontal poles meeting as so many rings, and truly crafted, it supported itself. This machine was an original of its kind, and will be a useful project for similar work for an architect hereafter; for since he must have scaffolds for the inside ornaments, the same thus contrived will also serve for the builders, and bear all the weight until the cupola is completed, and that without any upright supports. It was necessary to give a greater height than the cupola would gracefully allow within, though it is considerably above the roof of the church; yet the old church having had before a very lofty spire of timber and lead, the world expected that the new work should not in this respect fall short of the old (though that was but a spit, and this a mountain). He was therefore obliged to comply with the whim of the age (though not with ancient example, as neither did *Bramante*) and to raise another structure over the first cupola; and this was a cone of brick, so built as to support a stone lantern of an elegant figure, and ending in ornaments of copper gilt.

As the whole church above the vaults is covered with a substantial oaken roof and lead (for no other covering is so durable in our climate), so he covered and hid out of sight the brick cone with another cupola of timber and lead; and between this and the cone are easy stairs that ascend to the lantern.

He took no care to make little lucarne windows in the leaden cupola, as are done at St. *Peter's*, because he had otherwise provided for enough light to the stairs from the lantern above, and round the pedestal of the same, which are not seen below; so that he only ribbed the outward cupola, which he thought less *Gothic* than to stick it full of such little lights in three stories, one above the other (as is executed in the cupola of St. *Peter's* at *Rome*), which could not be mended without difficulty, and if neglected would soon damage the timbers.

The inside of the whole cupola is painted and richly decorated by an eminent *English* artist, Sir *James Thornhill*, containing, in eight compartments, the history of St. *Paul*. In the crown of the vault, as in the Pan-

<margin>(a) The judgment of the *Surveyor* was originally, instead of painting in the manner it is now performed, to have beautified the inside of the *cupola* with the more durable ornament of *mosaic work*, as is nobly executed in the *cupola* of *St. Peter's* in *Rome*, which strikes the eye of the beholder with a most magnificent and splendid appearance, and which remains without the least defect, as does the building itself. For this purpose, he had projected to procure four of the most eminent *artists* in that profession from *Italy*; but as this art was a great novelty in *England* and not generally understood, it did not receive the encouragement it deserved. It was imagined also that the expense would prove too great and the time for execution very long; but although these and all other objections were fully answered, this excellent design was pursued no further.

The painting and gilding of the architecture of the east end of the church over the communion table was intended only to serve the present occasion, until such time as materials could have been procured for a magnificent design for an *altar*. This design consisted of four wreathed pillars of the richest *Greek marbles*, supporting a hemispherical canopy with appropriate decorations of *architecture* and *sculpture*, for which the respective drawings and a model were prepared.

Information and particular descriptions of certain blocks of marble were once sent to the *Right Reverend Dr. Compton*, Bishop of *London*, from a *Levantine merchant* in *Holland* and communicated to the *Surveyor*; but unluckily, the colors and dimensions did not answer his purpose. So the matter rested in expectation of a better opportunity; otherwise, this curious and stately design would probably have been finished at the same time as the main building.</margin>
theon, is a circular opening, by which not only the lantern transmits light, but the inside ornaments of the painted and gilded cone display a new and agreeable scene (a).

Although the dome needs no abutment, yet for greater caution, it is hooped with iron in this manner: a channel is cut into the band of *Portland stone*, in which is laid a double chain of iron strongly linked together every ten feet, and the whole channel is filled up with lead.

Among all the works of the ancients, we find no cupolas raised above the necessary weight of the hemisphere. However, as is seen particularly in the *dome* of *Florence* and the great church of *Venice*, later designs were raised higher. The *Saracens* greatly favored this style, in imitation of the first most eminent pattern given by *Justinian* in his *Temple of Sancta Sophia* at *Constantinople*. *Bramante* would not fall short of those examples, nor could the *Surveyor* do otherwise than gratify the general taste of the age, which had been so used to steeples that these round designs were hardly noticed unless they reached a remarkable height.

Thus *St. Paul's* is lofty enough to be seen at sea to the east and at *Windsor* to the west; but our air, being frequently hazy, prevents those distant views except when the sun shines after a shower of rain has washed away the clouds of sea-coal smoke that hang over the city from so many thousand fires kindled every morning—besides glass-houses, brew-houses, and foundries, each of which emits more black smoke than twenty houses.

In the beginning of the new works of *St. Paul's*, an incident occurred that was noted by some people as a memorable omen. When the *Surveyor* in person marked out the dimensions of the great dome on site and fixed upon the center, a common laborer was ordered to bring a flat stone from the heaps of rubbish (whatever should first come to hand) to be laid as a mark and direction for the masons. The stone that was immediately brought and laid down for that purpose happened to be a piece of a gravestone, with nothing remaining of the inscription but this single word in large capitals:

->**RESURGAM**<-

The first stone of this *basilica* was laid in the year 1675, and the works were carried on with such care and industry that by the year 1685, the walls of the choir and side aisles were finished, along with the circular north and south porticoes, and the great pillars of the dome were brought to the same height. It pleased God in His mercy to bless the *Surveyor* with health and length of days, and to enable him to complete the whole structure in the year 1710, to the glory of His most holy name and the promotion of His divine worship.

...the principal ornament of the imperial seat of this realm. <margin>*Such majesty befits a God.* Ovid's Fasti, Book 1.</margin>

The highest or last stone on the top of the lantern was laid by the hands of the Surveyor's son, *Christopher Wren*, acting as a deputy for his father, in the presence of that excellent craftsman Mr. *Strong*, his son, and other *Free and Accepted Masons*, who were chiefly employed in the execution of the work.

Thus was this mighty building, the second greatest church in *Europe*, begun and finished within the span of thirty-five years by one architect, and under one Bishop of *London*, Dr. *Henry Compton*. The cost was supported mainly by a small and manageable tax on sea-coal brought to the Port of *London*; whereas the Church of *St. Peter* in *Rome* (the only edifice that can compete with it) continued under construction for 145 years, carried on by no fewer than twelve architects in succession. It was assisted by the policy and interests of the *Roman See*, the easy acquisition of marble, and attended by the best artists in the world in sculpture, statuary, painting, and *mosaic-work* during the reigns of nineteen Popes, as may be seen in the following view.

“The grand Cathedral of St. *Paul's* (says an ingenious Writer) is undoubtedly one of the most magnificent modern Buildings in *Europe*; all the Parts of which it is composed are superlatively beautiful and noble; the North and South Fronts in particular are very perfect Pieces of Architecture, nor should the East go without due Applause. ## SECTION VII.

Another distinguished work, in a different style of architecture, was the repair of the ancient Abbey Church of St. Peter in *Westminster*. This was conducted by the *Surveyor* until the time of his death, over a period of 25 years, with as much diligence as the portion of the coal duty granted by Parliament for that purpose would allow. A specific account of this will be best understood from his own words, in the following memorial to the Bishop of *Rochester* in the year 1713.

> “When I had the honor to attend your Lordship to congratulate you on your episcopal dignity, and to pay the respect that particularly concerned me as the person employed in the chief direction of the works and repairs of the Collegiate Church of St. Peter in *Westminster*, you were pleased to give me this timely advice: that I should consider my advanced age; and as I had already made significant progress in the repair of that ancient and dilapidated structure, you thought it very necessary for the public service that I should leave a memorial of what I had done, and what my thoughts were for carrying on the works in the future.

In order to describe what I have already done, I should first give a state of the fabric as I found it; which, being the work of 500 years or more, through several ages and kings' reigns, it will come in my way to consider the modes of building in those times, and what light records may afford us; such as I am at present able to collect, give me leave to discourse upon a little.

That a Temple of *Apollo* was here on *Thorney Island* (the place anciently so called, where the church now stands) and ruined by an earthquake in the reign of the Emperor *Antoninus Pius*, I cannot readily agree. The *Romans* did not used, even in their colonies, to build so slightly; the ruins of more ancient times show their works to this day; the least fragment of a cornice or capital would demonstrate their handiwork. Earthquakes do not break stones to pieces, nor would the *Picts* take that trouble; but I imagine the monks—finding the *Londoners* claiming to have a Temple of *Diana* where *St. Paul's* now stands (horns of stags, tusks of boars, etc., having been dug up there in former times, and it is said also in later years)—would not be left behind in antiquity. But I must assert that, having changed all the foundations of Old *Paul's*, and on that occasion rummaged all the ground thereabouts, and being very desirous to find some footsteps of such a temple, I could not discover any, and therefore can give no more credit to *Diana* than to *Apollo*.

To pass over the fabulous account that King *Lucius* first founded a little church here in *A.D.* 170, out of the ruins of the Temple of *Apollo*, destroyed by an earthquake a little before; it is recorded with better authority that *Sebert*, King of the *East Saxons*, built a monastery and church here in 605, which, being destroyed by the *Danes*, was about 360 years later repaired by the pious King *Edgar*. This, it is probable, was a strong, good building after the mode of that age, not much altered from the *Roman*. We have some examples of this ancient *Saxon* manner, which was with piers or round pillars, much stronger than *Tuscan*, with round-headed arches and windows; such was *Winchester* Cathedral of old; and such at this day is the Royal Chapel in the *White Tower* of *London*; the Chapel of *St. Cross*; the Chapel of *Christ Church* in *Oxford*, formerly an old monastery; and various others I need not name, built before the *Conquest*; and such was the old part of *St. Paul's* built in King *Rufus's* time.

King *Edward the Confessor* repaired, if not wholly rebuilt, this abbey church of King *Edgar*; of which a description was published by Mr. *Camden* in 1606, from an ancient manuscript, in these words: " *Principalis area do-*
" *mus, altissimis erecta fornicibus quadrato opere, parique commissura circum-*
" *volvitur; ambitus autem ipsius ædis duplici lapidum arcu ex utroque latere*
" *hinc inde fortiter solidata operis compage clauditur. Porrò crux templi quæ*
" *medium canentium domino chorum ambiret, & sui gemina hinc inde susten-*
" *tatione mediæ turris celsum apicem fulciret, humili primùm & robusto fornice*
" *simpliciter surgit; deinde cochleis multipliciter ex arte ascendentibus plurimis*
" *intumescit; deinceps vero simplici muro usque ad tectum ligneum plumbo di-*
" *ligenter vestitum pervenit.*"

> " choir in the middle, and the better to support the lofty tower, rose with a
> " plainer and lower vaulting; which tower then spreading with artificial wind-

<page-num>297</page-num>
<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

“Winding stairs were continued with plain walls to its timber roof, which was well covered with lead.”

These ancient buildings were without buttresses, having only thicker walls; the windows were very narrow and latticed, for King *Alfred* is praised for the later invention of lanterns to protect the lamps in churches.

In the time of King *Henry* the Third, the fashion began of building chapels behind the altar to the *Blessed Virgin*. What this chapel specifically was is not now to be discovered; I suppose its foundations are under the steps of King *Henry* the Seventh's Chapel, and this work, probably semicircular (as four more were later added outside the aisles), was also intended for his own burial. Some of his own relations lie there now, just below those steps, and may be supposed to have been within his chapel. He laid the first stone of this in the year *1220*, and took down the greatest part of St. *Edward*'s Church to rebuild it according to the style that came into fashion after the Holy War.

This we now call the *Gothic* manner of architecture (so the *Italians* named whatever was not in the *Roman Style*), though the *Goths* were destroyers rather than builders; I think it should, with more reason, be called the *Saracen Style*. For those people lacked neither arts nor learning; and after we in the West had lost both, we borrowed from them again, out of their *Arabic* books, what they had translated with great diligence from the *Greeks*.

They were zealots in their religion, and wherever they conquered (which they did with amazing rapidity), they erected mosques and *caravanserais* in haste, which obliged them to adopt a different way of building. For they built their mosques round, disliking the *Christian form* of a cross; the old quarries from which the ancients took their large blocks of marble for whole columns and architraves were neglected, as they thought both were unnecessary. Their transport was by camels, therefore their buildings were designed for small stones and columns of their own invention, consisting of many pieces; and their arches were pointed without keystones, which they thought were too heavy.

The reasons were the same in our northern climates, which abound in freestone but lack marble.

The *Crusade* gave us an idea of this form, after which King *Henry* built his church, though not according to a well-considered plan at first; for I think the chapels outside the aisles were an afterthought, as the remaining buttresses between the chapels would be useless if they had been built at the same time. And the King, having opened the east end for St. *Mary*'s Chapel, decided to create more chapels for burial; this was very acceptable to the monks after they obtained a license from *Rome* to bury people inside churches, a custom not used before.

The King's intention was certainly to complete only the cross-aisle to the westward, for up to that point it is in a different style from the rest of the building further west, which was built after his time, as the pillars and spandrels of the arches show.

I am inclined to think the King did not live to complete his intention, nor to reach four inter-columns west of the tower; the walls of this part were probably built in his time, but the vaulting now covering the choir, though it is more adorned and gilded, was done without proper care in the masonry and is the most poorly executed of all the work done previously. This stone vault was finished 23 years after his death, in the reign of King *Edward* the First, so that the old verse is not strictly accurate:

> *Tertius Henricus est templi conditor hujus.* <note>Henry III is the founder of this temple.</note>

But alas! it was now likely to have been all spoiled; the Abbots wanted a cloister, but hesitated, I suppose, at moving some venerable corpses laid between the outside buttresses; then came a bold but ignorant architect who undertook to build the cloister so that the buttresses should be outside the cloister, spanning over it, as may be seen in the cross-section.

This was a dangerous attempt. It is by due consideration of static principles and the right balancing of the weights of the abutments to the arches that good architecture depends; and the abutments ought to have equal gravity on both sides. Although this was done to satisfy the whims of the monks, yet the architect should have considered that new works carried very high, especially upon a newer foundation, would shrink; as a result, the walls above the windows were forced out ten inches, and the ribs broken. I could not discern that this failure was so bad until the scaffold over the choir was raised to give a close view of it; and then I was amazed to find it had not completely fallen. This is now repaired with all care, and I dare promise it shall be much stronger and more secure than the first builders ever left it.

After what had been done by King *Henry* the Third and his successor, it is said the work was carried further by the Abbots and Monks toward the west; and I also notice the contiguous cloister was built in the manner begun by King *Henry* the Third, with buttresses spanning over the cloister. They were forced to proceed in this way because of how it had been started, though, by error, it could not be corrected until it was carried beyond the cloister. But then they proceeded with regular buttresses matching the north side, until they came to the west front. This west vault was proceeded with much better care and skill, and was a work of many years during the reigns of the three succeeding *Edwards* and King *Richard* the Second. I suppose there was a great pause or slackness in the work until the *Lancastrian* line came in; for then, in the very first bay of this work, I find the Rose of *Lancaster* in the vaulting and the keystones.

In the tumultuous and bloody wars between the two houses of *York* and *Lancaster*, little was done to the Abbey except by the zeal of the Abbots, who drove the work on as well as they were able—though slowly—to the west end, which was never completely finished.

When King *Henry* the Eighth dissolved the monastery, the cloister was finished, along with other things for the convenience of the Abbey.

The *Consistory* (no contemptible fabric) was, I think, completed in the time of King *Edward* the First; and, in order to join it to the church, the east side of the cloister was taken out of the west side of the cross-aisle of the church (by ill advice), for it might have otherwise been done by a more decent arrangement. But it may be that the King was to be obeyed, who founded this octagonal fabric. The Abbot lent it to the King for the use of the House of Commons, upon the condition that the Crown should repair it, which—though it is now used for records—has lately been done.

The *Saracen* mode of building seen in the East soon spread over *Europe*, and particularly in *France*; we were inclined to imitate the fashions of that nation in all ages, even when we were at enmity with it. Nothing was thought magnificent that was not excessively high, with the "flutter" of arch-buttresses—as we call the sloping arches that balance the higher vaulting of the nave. The *Romans* always concealed their abutments, whereas the *Normans* thought them ornamental. I have observed that these are the first things that cause the ruin of cathedrals, being so much exposed to the air and weather. The coping, which cannot protect them, fails first; and if they give way, the vault must spread. Pinnacles are of no use and provide as little ornament. The pride of a very high roof raised above a reasonable pitch does not lead to durability,

for the lead is apt to slip; but we are tied to this unwise form, and must be contented with original faults in the first design. But that which is most to be lamented is the unhappy choice of the materials: the stone is decayed four inches deep and falls off perpetually in great scales. I find that after the Conquest, all our artists were brought from *Normandy*; they loved to work in their own *Caen stone*, which is more beautiful than durable. This was found expensive to bring here, so they thought *Reigate stone* in *Surrey* the nearest like their own, being a stone that would saw and work like wood, but is not durable, as is manifest; and they used this for the ashlar of the whole fabric, which is now disfigured in the highest degree. This stone takes in water, which, being frozen, scales off, whereas good stone gathers a crust and defends itself, as many of our *English* free-stones do. And though we also have the best oak timber in the world, yet these senseless artificers in *Westminster Hall* and other places would use chestnut from *Normandy*; that timber is not natural to *England*; it works finely but decays sooner than oak. The roof in the Abbey is oak, but mixed with chestnut and crafted in a poor *Norman* style that does not secure it from stretching and damaging the walls, and the water from the gutters is poorly carried off. All this is said to better represent to your Lordship, in the next place, what has been done and what still remains to be carried on, as time and money are allowed to make a substantial and durable repair.

First, in the repair of the stone-work, what is done shows itself: beginning from the East window, we have cut out all the ragged ashlar and faced it with a better stone from *Oxfordshire*, brought down the river from the quarries about *Burford*. We have amended and secured the buttresses in the cloister garden for the most part, and we proceed to finish that side; the chapels on the South side are done, as are most of the arch-buttresses all along as we proceeded. We have not done much on the North side for these reasons: the houses on the North side are so close that there is no room left for the raising of scaffolds and ladders, nor for passage to bring materials. Besides, the tenants, taking every inch up to the very walls of the church to be included in their leases—this ground being already too narrow—have divided it into the backyards of houses, with wash-houses, chimneys, privies, and cellars. The vaults of these, if unwisely dug against the base of a buttress, may inevitably ruin the vaults of the chapels (and indeed I perceive such mischief is already done by the opening of the vaults of the octagonal chapel on that side); and unless effectual means be taken to prevent all nuisances of this sort, the works cannot proceed, and if finished, may soon be destroyed. I need say no more, nor will I presume to dictate, not doubting but proper means will be taken to preserve this noble structure from such nuisances as directly lead to its demolition.

And now, in further pursuance of your Lordship’s directions, I shall clearly set down what yet remains to finish the necessary repairs for ages to come. And then, in the second place (since the first intentions of the founders were never brought to a conclusion), I shall present my thoughts and designs in order to a proper completing of what is left imperfect, hoping we may obtain for this the continuance of the Parliamentary assistance.

I have yet said nothing of King *Henry* the Seventh’s Chapel, a delicate, intricate work performed with tender *Caen stone*; though lately built by comparison, it is so eaten up by our weather that it begs for some compassion, which I hope the sovereign power will take, as it is the royal burial place.

I begin, as I said, to set down what is necessary for completing the repairs, though part thereof at present I can only guess at, because I cannot yet come at the North side to make a full discovery of the defects there, but I hope to

...find it rather better than the south side; for it is the fluctuations of heat and cold, drought and moisture, that rot all materials more than the constant extremes of any of these conditions. This is evident in timber, which, if always underground and wet, never decays; otherwise *Venice* and *Amsterdam* would fall. It is the same in lead-work, for the north side of a steep roof is usually much less decayed than the south; and the same is commonly seen in stonework. Besides, the buttresses here are more substantial than those of the south side, which I complained earlier were indiscreetly altered for the sake of the cloister; and I find some improvements have been made about eighty years ago, but not well. On the whole matter, I may say that of the necessary repairs to the outward stonework, one-third is already completed. The most dangerous part of the vaulting over the choir, currently being worked on, will be finished in a few months, but the roof over it cannot be opened until summer. The repairs to the stonework, along with all the chapels, flying buttresses, windows, and moldings of the north side, are yet to be done, except for part of the north transept aisle. A great part of the expense will be in the north front and the great rose window there, which, being very ruinous, was patched up for the time being to prevent further ruin several years ago, before I was involved, but must now be replaced entirely; I have prepared a proper design for it. The timber of the roof of the nave and the transept is repaired and secured with lead, as are the chapels; but the whole roof and aisles from the tower westward, requiring the lead and pipes to be recast, still need to be mended, along with all the woodwork, as has already been done east of the tower. The chapels on the north side must have their roofs repaired once we can see how to reach them, after the removal of one small house.

And now, having given a summary account of what will complete the mere repairs, let me add what I wish might be done to give a proper appearance to those parts which were left abruptly unfinished by the last builders when the monastery was dissolved by King *Henry* the Eighth. The west front is very necessary to be finished because the two towers are not of equal height and are too low for the bells, which hang so much lower than the roof that they are not heard as far as they should be. The great west window is also too weak, and the gable end of the roof over it consists only of painted weatherboards.

The original intention was plainly to have had a steeple, the beginnings of which appear on the corners of the transept crossing, but it was stopped before it rose as high as the ridge of the roof; and the vault of the choir under it is only lath and plaster, now rotten, and must be attended to.

Lest it should be doubted whether the four pillars below are able to bear a steeple, because they seem a little swayed inward, I have considered how they may be unquestionably secured so as to support the greatest weight that need be placed upon them, and this in a manner that will add to their shape and beauty.

It is clear to the eye that the four innermost pillars of the crossing are bent inward considerably and seem to tend toward ruin, and the arches of the second level above are also cracked. I shall demonstrate how this has happened and how it is to be secured.

I believe the architect knew very well that the four pillars at the intersection of the transept and nave would not prove to be a sufficient buttress to stand against the pressure of so many arches unless they were much larger than the other piers; but that could not be done without cluttering the main part of the church. But though these angular pillars could not be made larger, they could be made heavier to stand against the pressure of the se-

several rows of arches, which might prove equivalent, as may appear in this way:

Let A B C be an arch resting at C against an immovable wall K M, but at A upon a pillar A D, which is so small as to be unable to provide a sufficient buttress <note>archaic: butment</note> to the pressure of the arch A B. What is then to be done? I cannot add F G to it to make it a buttress, but I build up E so high that, by the addition of weight, I establish it as firmly as if I had attached F G to it to make it a buttress. There is no need to ask how much weight E must be, since it cannot be too much, provided A D is sufficient to bear the weight placed upon it. This is the reason why, in all Gothic structures <note>archaic: fabricks</note> of this form, the architects were accustomed to build towers or steeples in the middle, not only for ornament, but to stabilize the middle pillars

against the thrust of the several rows of arches, which exert force against them from every direction. The architect understood this well enough; but knowing that it might require time to provide such a buttress as the tower for his arches, which was to be done last, and fearing there might be a failure in the meantime, he wisely considered that if he tied these arches every way with iron (specifically those next to the middle of the cross), this might serve the purpose until he built the tower to make everything secure—which has not been done to this day. These iron ties, which were hooked from pillar to pillar, have been stolen away; this is the reason for the four pillars being bent inward and the walls above being cracked. But nothing can be repaired until the pillars are first restored, which I have considered how to perform and have represented in a model. This must be done first; otherwise, adding weight upon that which is already crooked and weak <note>archaic: infirm</note> will only make it more so. But once the pillars are well-secured from further distortion, it will be necessary to strengthen everything by adding more weight upon them—that is, by building a tower according to the original intention of the architect. This was indeed begun, as appears by the work, but left off before it rose to the ridge of the roof. In my opinion, the tower should be continued to at least as much in height above the roof as it is in breadth; and if a spire is added to it, it will give a proper grace to the whole building and the west end of the city, which seems to need it.

I have made a design, which will not be very expensive but light, and still in the Gothic form, and of a style with the rest of the structure, which I would strictly adhere to throughout the whole intention: to deviate from the old form would be to run into a disagreeable mixture, which no person of a good taste could relish.

I have varied a little from the usual form, in giving twelve sides to the spire instead of eight, for reasons to be discerned upon the model.

The angles of pyramids in the Gothic architecture were usually enriched with the flower the botanists call *Calceolus*, which is a proper form to help workmen to ascend on the outside to amend any defects, without raising large scaffolds upon every slight occasion; I have done the same, being of such good use, as well as an agreeable ornament.

The next thing to be considered is to finish what was left undone at the West-front.

It is evident, as was observed before, the two West towers were left imperfect, and have continued so since the dissolution of the monastery—one much higher than the other, though still too low for bells, which are stifled by the height of the roof above them; they ought certainly to be carried to an equal height, one story above the ridge of the roof, still continuing the Gothic manner in the stonework and tracery.

Something must be done to strengthen the West window, which is unstable <note>archaic: crazy</note>; the pediment is only boarded, but ought undoubtedly to be of stone. I have given such a design as I conceive may be suitable for this part: the *Jerusalem Chamber* is built against it, and the access from *Tothill Street* is not very graceful.

The principal entrance is from *King Street*, and I believe always will continue so; but at present, there is little encouragement to begin to make this North-front magnificent in the manner I have designed, while it is so much encumbered with private tenements, which obscure and smoke the building <note>archaic: fabrick</note>, not without danger of setting it on fire.

The great North window had been formerly in danger of ruin, but was upheld and stopped up, for the present, with plaster. It will be most necessary to rebuild this with *Portland stone*, to answer the South rose window, which was well rebuilt about forty years ago; the staircases at the corners must be newly ashlar-faced, and pyramids set upon them conformable to the old—

This, probably at first a *pagan* custom, continued to the Reformation and could hardly be swept away then. Though the church was now dedicated to the memory of the great apostle *St. Paul*, yet they seemed willing not to forget the goddess *Diana*, to whom (we are told) an ancient temple was erected in this very place; and that in the time of *Mellitus*, the first bishop of *London*, *Ethelbert*, King of *Kent*, built a church to the honor of *St. Paul* where a Temple of *Diana* stood before, as an ancient manuscript in the *Cotton* Library tells us. <margin>*Ibid. 299.*</margin> *London sacrifices to Diana, suburban Thorney (Thorney* is now *Westminster*) burns incense to Apollo.

*Mr. Camden* thinks it not improbable that there was anciently a Temple of *Diana* where *St. Paul's* Church now stands, based on the great number of ox heads that were found there while digging up the churchyard in the reign of *King Edward I*; these were looked upon as *pagan* sacrifices, and in this opinion he is followed by his learned editor, as well as by *Mr. Samms*, *Mr. Howel*, and others. Particularly, the ingenious *Dr. Woodward* acquaints us that he has in his collection tusks of boars, horns of oxen, and of stags, as well as representations of deer and even of *Diana* herself upon the sacrificing vessels dug up near *St. Paul's* Church, and likewise a small image of that goddess found not far off. Now it appears from ancient writers that not only stags, but oxen and swine also, were sacrificed to *Diana*.

There is extant an earthenware lamp, which was procured from the above-mentioned *Mr. Kemp* and is supposed to have been dug up among the other lamps and antiquities at *St. Paul's*; on it is embossed the figure of *Diana* in a hunting posture, in the same manner as she is represented on the ancient Greek coins of *Ephesus*, and conformable to an antique marble statue in the gallery of the King of *France* at *Versailles*. This lamp, like the other mentioned before, is of very poor workmanship; on the reverse, in the center, are some letters—probably the potter's name, as was usual—but so poorly executed as to be hardly legible.

...partly from the damages of time and weather, especially the lofty spire, which had been much shaken and cracked by a tempest and lightning storm, required the skill and direction of the *Surveyor* for a speedy repair. To achieve this, the defects of the steeple necessarily claimed first consideration, because it could not collapse alone without bringing down the roof and vaults of the church with it. He therefore took special care to strengthen and effectively secure it by bracing it with iron bands forged by anchor-smiths—men accustomed to large-scale work for ships. These were so judiciously placed and skillfully executed that the structure remains demonstrably stronger than when it was first built.

He had performed an accurate survey of the entire structure of this ancient cathedral in 1669, at the request of his excellent friend Dr. *Seth Ward*, Bishop of that See. In his report to the Bishop and the Dean and Chapter, after listing the fundamental errors, defects, and current decay, he provided his advice and full instructions for the necessary repairs, restoration, and maintenance to prevent further decline, diagnosing the "diseases" of the building and suggesting the "cures." As this church is justly esteemed one of the best examples of *Gothic building*, a short architectural account of it, taken from the first part of the *Surveyor's* report, may interest the curious as a further taste of that style of architecture.

> "The shape of the church is a cross, at the intersection of which stands a tower and spire of stone, as high from the foundation as the whole length of the *nave*, or body of the church; and it is founded only upon the four pillars and arches of the intersection. Between the steeple and the east end is another crossing of the *nave*, which lacks its aisles on the west side only; all other sides of the main body and the crosses are supported on pillars with aisles attached, and buttressed outside the aisles, from which rise bows or flying buttresses to the walls of the *nave*, which are concealed within the timber roof of the aisles. The roof is almost as sharp as an equilateral triangle, made of small timber after the ancient manner without principal rafters; but the wall-plates are double and tied together with couples over forty feet long. The whole church is vaulted with chalk between arches and cross-springers only, after the older manner, without bosses and tracery, except under the tower, where the springers divide and represent a wider sort of tracery; and this appears to me to have been a later work, done by some other hand than that of the first architect, whose judgment I must justly commend for many things beyond what I find in various *Gothic* structures of later date, which, though more elaborate with delicate and small details, yet lack the natural beauty that arises from the proportion of the original dimensions. For here the breadth to the height of the *nave*, and both to the shape of the aisles, bear a good proportion. The pillars and the intercolumniations (or spaces between pillar and pillar) are well suited to the height of the arches; the moldings are decently mixed with large planes without an affectation of filling every corner with ornaments, which, unless they are admirably good, glut the eye as much as too much 'division' <note>In music, 'division' refers to a rapid melodic ornamentation or the breaking of long notes into shorter ones.</note> gluts the ears in music. The windows are not made too large, nor is the light obstructed by many mullions and transoms of tracery-work, which was the bad fashion of the next following age. Our artist knew better—that nothing could add beauty to light; he trusted to a stately and rich simplicity that his marble shafts gave to his work. I cannot call them pillars because they are so small and slender and generally bear nothing, but are only added for ornament to the outside of the great pillars and decently fastened with brass."

<sig>i i</sig>
<meta>catchword: " the</meta>

> "Despite this praise for the architect, there are some original errors for which I must blame him; the discovery of these will shed light on the cause of the current decay.
"First, I must fault him because, building on a low and marshy soil, he did not take sufficient care of the foundation, especially under the pillars. A foundation that will support a wall will not support a pillar, for pillars push themselves into the earth and force open the solid ground if the foundation beneath them is not wide. Furthermore, if it is not made of hard stone, it will be ground down and crushed like things bruised in a mortar if the weight is great.
"A second fault was the failure to raise the floor of the church above the risk of floods; many adequate foundations have failed after the earth has been too drenched with unusual floods. Besides, it is unsightly to descend into a building.
"The third fault is in the balance of the building: generally, the substructures are too slender for the weight above.
"The pillars appear small enough, yet they look much greater than they actually are; the shafts of marble that surround them seem to fill the pillars out to a proportionate size, but in reality, they support little or no weight. Some of those that are under pressure break and split; if those ornaments were removed, the pillar would then appear too small for its burden. However, this is nowhere as extreme as under the steeple, which, being four hundred feet high, is supported by four pillars not much larger than the pillars in the aisles. Therefore, for fear of overburdening them, for forty feet above the interior of the tower, the *Navis* is constructed with a slender, hollow design of pillars and arches. It lacks any buttresses, and the spire itself is only seven inches thick, although its height is over one hundred and fifty feet. This design of pillars and arches within the tower leads me to believe that the architect placed his first timber floor forty feet higher than the vault below (which, as I mentioned, was added later). Without doubt, he intended a belfry above (as indicated by the spaces left in the walls for timber and the fastening of bell frames) and so would have finished with only the tower, without a spire.
"And if this addition of a spire was an afterthought, the artist is more excusable for having omitted buttresses from the tower. His ingenuity is commendable for fixing this defect by bracing the walls together with many large iron bands inside and out, joined together with great diligence and precision. Besides those that are visible, I have reason to believe that various other braces are hidden within the thickness of the walls. These are so essential to the stability of the work that if they were broken, the spire would push the tower walls outward, and it would not stand for a minute. But this method of tying walls together with iron, instead of making them of such a substance and form that they naturally balance themselves upon their supports, is against the rules of good architecture. This is not only because iron is susceptible to rust, but also because it is unreliable, having inconsistent qualities in the metal; some pieces in the same bar are three times stronger than others, yet all appear sound. I shall not blame our artist for those errors that were generally the mistakes of builders in that age; yet it will not be out of place to discuss those that seem to affect us and cause some of the weaknesses in our buildings.
"Almost all cathedrals in the Gothic style are weak and defective in the balance of the aisle vaults. As for the vault of the *Navis*, both sides are equally supported and propped up against spreading by the flying buttresses, which rise from the outer walls of the aisles. However, as for the vaults of the aisles, they are supported on the outside by

These surveys, and other occasional inspections of the most famous cathedral churches and chapels in *England* and foreign parts, led the *Surveyor* to make some inquiry into the rise and progress of this *Gothic style*. He observed no small amount of art, ingenuity, and geometrical skill in the design and execution of a few, but found an affectation of height and grandeur, though without regularity and good proportion, in most of them. He wished to consider how the old *Greek* and *Roman* style of building, with its various regular proportions of columns, entablatures, etc., came to be so much altered and almost universally abandoned within a few centuries.

He was of the opinion (as has been mentioned in another place) that what we now commonly call the *Gothic* ought properly and truly to be named *Saracenic architecture refined by Christians*. This style first began in the East after the fall of the *Greek Empire* due to the immense success of those people who followed *Muhammad's* doctrine, who, out of zeal for their religion, built mosques, caravansaries, and tombs wherever they went.

They designed these in a round form because they would not imitate the Christian shape of a cross, nor the ancient *Greek* manner, which they thought to be idolatrous; for that reason, all sculpture became offensive to them.

They then adopted a new style of their own invention, though better sense might have been expected, considering the *Arabians* did not lack geometers in that age, nor did the *Moors*, who translated many of the most useful ancient *Greek* books. As they spread their religion with great diligence, they also built mosques in haste in all their conquered cities. The quarries of great marble, which had supplied the vanished nations of *Syria*, *Egypt*, and all the East for columns, architraves, and great stones, were now abandoned. The *Saracens* were therefore forced to adapt their architecture to such materials, whether marble or freestone, as every country readily provided. They thought columns and heavy cornices were unnecessary and could be omitted; and, preferring the round form for mosques, they built cupolas in some instances with enough grace. The Crusades gave the Christians who had been there an idea of *Saracen* works, which they later imitated in the West; and they refined upon it every day as they proceeded in building churches. The *Italians* (among whom there were still some *Greek* refugees), along with the *French*, *Germans*, and *Flemings*, joined into a fraternity of architects. Obtaining papal bulls for their encouragement and special privileges, they called themselves Freemasons and traveled from one nation to another as they found churches to be built (for very many were being built everywhere in those ages, through piety or competition). Their government was orderly, and where they settled

Near the building project at hand, they created a camp of huts. A surveyor governed as chief; every tenth man was called a warden and oversaw the other nine. The gentlemen of the neighborhood, either out of charity or as a commutation of penance, provided the materials and transport. Those who have seen the exact accounts in the records of the costs of the structures of some of our cathedrals nearly four hundred years old cannot help but have great respect for their economy and admire how quickly they erected such lofty buildings. Indeed, they thought great height was the greatest magnificence; few stones were used except those that a man might carry up a ladder on his back from scaffold to scaffold, though they had pulleys and spoked wheels when needed. But having rejected cornices, they had no need for large machines; stone upon stone was easily piled up to great heights. Therefore, the pride of their works lay in pinnacles and steeples. In this, they essentially differed from the *Roman way*, where all moldings were laid horizontally, which created the best perspective. The *Gothic way*, on the contrary, carried all its moldings perpendicularly, so that once the groundwork was settled, they had nothing else to do but spire everything upward as high as they could. Thus, they made their pillars from a bundle of small *toruses*, which they divided into more when they reached the roof; and these *toruses* split into many small ones, and crossing one another, gave rise to the *tracery-work* (as they called it), of which this society were the inventors. They used the sharp-headed arch, which could be built with little centering, required lighter keystones and less abutment, and yet could support another row of double arches rising from the keystone; by diversifying these, they erected eminent structures, such as the steeples of *Vienna*, *Strasburg*, and many others. They favored steeples, though the *Saracens* themselves mostly used cupolas. The Church of *St. Mark* in *Venice* is built after the *Saracen manner*. Glass began to be used in windows, and a great part of the exterior ornamentation of churches consisted of the tracery-work used to arrange the window mullions for the better installation of the glass. Thus the work required fewer materials, and the craftsmanship was for the most part performed using *flat-moulds*, in which the wardens could easily instruct hundreds of artisans. It must be admitted that this was an ingenious simplification of work suited to these northern climates; and I must also own that works of the same height and magnificence in the *Roman way* would be much more expensive than in the *Gothic* manner when managed with judgment. But, as all styles do when once the old rational methods are despised, it turned at last into unbounded fancies; this tracery led to too much mincing of the stone into open battlements and spindly pinnacles, and small carvings without regard for the proportion of distance. Thus, the essential rules of good perspective and durability were forgotten. But about two hundred years ago, when ingenious men began to reform the *Roman* language to the purity they assigned and fixed to the time of *Augustus* and that century, architects also—ashamed of the modern barbarity of building—began to carefully examine the ruins of *Ancient Rome* and *Italy*, to search into the orders and proportions, and to establish them by inviolable rules. Thus, to their labor and industry, we owe in a great degree the restoration of architecture.

The ingenious Mr. *Evelyn*, in his *Account of Architecture*, makes a general and judicious comparison of the ancient and modern styles, with reference to some of the particular works of *Inigo Jones* and the *Surveyor*. In a few words, this gives a correct idea of the majestic symmetry of the one and the absurd system of the other.

<margin>Account of Architecture, p. 9.</margin>
> "The ancient *Greek* and *Roman architecture* satisfy all the perfections required in a faultless and accomplished building; such as were for so many ages so renowned and respected by the universal agreement of the civilized world,"

<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

" World, and would doubtless have still existed, and made good their
" claim, and what is recorded of them; had not the *Goths*, *Vandals*, and
" other barbarous nations, overturned and demolished them, together with
" that glorious empire, where those stately and magnificent monuments stood;
" introducing in their stead, a certain fanciful and unrestrained manner of
" building, which we have since called *Modern* or *Gothic*. Masses of
" heavy, dark, gloomy, and monastic buildings, without any just propor-
" tion, use, or beauty, compared with the truly ancient; so that when we
" meet with the greatest industry and expensive carving, full of fretwork and
" pitiful imagery—sparing neither pains nor cost—a judicious spec-
" tator is rather distracted or quite confounded, than touched with that ad-
" miration which results from the true and just symmetry, regular propor-
" tion, union, and arrangement; and from the great and noble manner in
" which the august and glorious structures of the ancients are executed.

It was after the invasion and swarms of those ferocious people from the
North; the *Moors* and *Arabs* from the South and East, overrunning the
civilized world; that wherever they fixed themselves, they soon began to
corrupt this noble and useful art; when instead of those beautiful orders,
so majestic and proper for their placements, becoming variety, and other or-
namental accessories; they set up those slender and misshapen pillars, or rather
bundles of staves and other inconsistent props, to support overhanging weights
and heavy arched roofs, without entablature; and though not without
great industry (as *M. D'Aviler* well observes) nor altogether devoid of showy
sculpture and common, cluttered carvings; it is such as overwhelms the eye, rather than grati-
fies and pleases it with any reasonable satisfaction: For proof of this (without
traveling far abroad) I dare appeal to any man of judgment, and
who has the least taste for order and magnificence; if after he has looked
a while upon King *Henry* the VIIth's Chapel at *Westminster*, gazed on its
sharp angles, overhangs, narrow windows, defective statues, lace-work, and other cut-
work and crinkle-crankle; and shall then turn his eyes on the Banqueting
House built at *Whitehall* by *Inigo Jones*, after the ancient manner; or on what
his Majesty’s *Surveyor*, Sir *Christopher Wren*, has developed at *St. Paul's*, and
consider what a glorious object the cupola, porticoes, colonnades, and other
parts present to the beholder, or compare the schools and library at *Oxford*
with the theater there; or what he has built at *Trinity College*, in *Cambridge*,
and since all these, at *Greenwich* and other places; by which time our
home-traveler will begin to have a just idea of ancient and modern
architecture: I say, let him well consider and compare them judiciously, with-
out partiality and prejudice; and then pronounce which of the two manners
strikes the understanding as well as the eye with the more majesty and solemn
greatness; though in so much a plainer and simpler dress, conforming to the re-
spective orders and entablature; and accordingly determine to whom the
preference is due: Not as we said, that there is not something of solid, and
oddly ingenious too, after a fashion: but then the universal and unreasonable thick-
ness of the walls, clumsy buttresses, towers, sharp-pointed arches, doors,
and other openings without proportion: nonsensical insertions of various
marbles pointlessly placed; turrets and pinnacles thick set with monkeys
and chimeras, and an abundance of cluttered work and other incongruities scatter
and break the sightlines, and so confound the eye that one cannot
consider it with any steadiness, or know where to begin or end; taking away from that noble
air and grandeur, that bold and graceful manner, which the ancients had so well and
judiciously established: but, in this fashion have they and their followers
ever since filled not *Europe* alone, but *Asia* and *Africa* besides, with moun-
tains of stone—vast and gigantic buildings indeed, but not worthy the name
of architecture, etc.

<meta>catchword: SECTION</meta>

<summary>This text contrasts the "Gothic" style of architecture, characterized by its cluttered, disproportionate, and "monkish" qualities, with the classical "ancient" style revived by Inigo Jones and Christopher Wren. The author argues that the classical style achieves a superior majesty through symmetry and order, whereas Gothic structures are merely "mountains of stone."</summary>

## SECT. IX.

*A Catalogue, short Description, and general Dimensions, of Fifty-one parochial Churches of the City of London, erected according to the Designs, and under the Care and Conduct, of Sir Christopher Wren, in place of those which were burned and demolished by the great Fire in the Year 1666, together with other Churches built, and repaired; and public buildings.*

---

<margin>New View of London, 1708.</margin>
I. **ALLHALLOWS** *Bread-street* Church, in the Ward of *Bread-street* within the Walls of *London*, was rebuilt and finished in 1684, and the steeple in 1697. It is a pleasant church of the *Tuscan* Order; the length is 72, breadth 35, and height 30 feet. The steeple (like the church) is of stone, built square, of the *Doric* Order, and well adorned; the key-stones over the windows are carved heads, and between each is a large festoon; its height is about 86 feet.

II. *Allhallows the Great*, situated on the south side of *Thames-street*, in the Ward of *Dowgate*, within the Walls of *London*, was re-erected and finished in 1683, of the *Tuscan* Order, supported and adorned with pillars and <term>membrettos</term> of that order, and strongly built of stone. Its length is about 87 feet, breadth 60, height 33, with a square stone tower, 86 feet high.

III. *Allhallows Lombard-street* Church, situated on the north side of that street, in the Ward of *Langbourn*, was rebuilt and finished in 1694. In the church is only one pillar, which, as well as the pilasters, are of the *Tuscan* Order; the length is 84 feet, breadth 52, height about 30; the height of the tower is about 85, built square.

IV. *St. Alban Wood-street* Church, situated on the east side of *Great Wood-street*, in the Ward of *Cripplegate*, was rebuilt and finished in 1685; the building both of the outside and inside is *Gothic*, as it was before the fire, in length about 66, breadth 59, height 33 feet; the tower is of stone, built square, with *Gothic* pinnacles; its height is 85 ½ feet, or 92 feet to the top of the pinnacles.

V. The Church of *St. Anne and Agnes*, situated on the north side of *St. Anne's-lane*, within *Aldersgate*, was re-erected and finished in 1680, and beautified in 1703; it is very pleasant and ornamental, though small; 53 feet square, and about 35 feet high; and the tower to the top of the turret is about 84 feet. The roof is supported by four handsome *Corinthian* pillars, which are positioned in a geometrical square from each other; its ornament consists of four arches of fretwork, with flowers, fruit, leaves, cherubim, etc. At the four angles, the roof is lower and consists of four quadrangles, within each of which is a circle formed by a circumference of very rich fretwork.

VI. *St. Andrew's Wardrobe* Church, situated on the east side of *Puddle-dock-hill*, in the Ward of *Castle-Baynard*, was re-edified and finished in 1692, built of brick, but finished or rendered over in imitation of stone; the facias and corners are stone, with very good rustic quoins. VII. *St. Andrew's Holborn* Church, situated on the south side of *Holborn Hill*, in the Ward of *Farringdon* Without the Walls of *London*, but within the Liberty, was rebuilt and finished in 1687, beautiful and spacious; the columns that support the roof, adorned with fretwork, are of the *Corinthian* Order; the walls are of stone; the length is 105, breadth 63, and height 43 feet; the altitude of the tower, or square steeple, is 110 feet; it has four large windows fronting E. W. N. and S. adorned with pilasters, architrave, frieze, cornice, pediments, and is of the *Doric* Order; finished in 1704.

VIII. *St. Anthony's*, alias *St. Antholin's* Church, situated at the west end of *Watling Street*, in *Cordwainer Street* Ward, was re-erected and finished in 1682; built of stone, the outside is of the *Tuscan* Order, but the roof within (which is an elliptical cupola adorned with fretwork of festoons, with four porthole windows) is supported by eight pillars of the *Composite* Order; the length is about 66, breadth 54, and height within 44 feet: It has a neat spire steeple, with an altitude of 154 feet.

IX. *St. Augustin's* neat little church, situated on the north side of *Watling Street*, near *St. Paul's* Cathedral, was finished in 1683, and the steeple in 1695; the church and steeple are of stone, the latter being a tower with acroteria, a cupola, a lantern adorned with vases, and a spire whose lower part is of a parabolic form. The roof is camerated <note>vaulted or arched</note>, divided into panels, adorned with fretwork, and supported with pillars of the *Ionic* Order; the length of the church is about 51, breadth 45, and height 30 feet; and that of the steeple 145 feet.

X. *St. Benedict* (commonly called *St. Bennet*) *Gracechurch*, situated on the east side of *Gracechurch Street*, in the Ward of *Bridge Within* (meaning within the walls of *London*), was rebuilt and finished in 1685; its length within is about 60, breadth 30, height 32; and the steeple is 149 feet.

XI. *St. Bennet's Paul's Wharf* Church, situated on the north side of *Thames Street*, in the Ward of *Castle Baynard*, was rebuilt in 1683 of brick and stone, ornamented on the outside with festoons carved in stone around the building; the quadrangular roof within is supported by four pillars and pilasters of the *Corinthian* Order, with their architrave, frieze, and cantilever cornice; the length within is 54, breadth 50, height 36 feet; the steeple (which is of brick and stone, like the church) consists of a tower, dome, and turret, the altitude being about 118 feet.

XII. *St. Benedict's* (commonly called *St. Bennet*) *Fink Church*, situated on the north side of *Threadneedle Street*, in the Ward of *Broad Street*, was built in 1673 of stone, and is a fine piece of architecture; the body of the church within is a complete ellipsis (a very commodious form for the auditory <note>the congregation</note>), and the roof is an elliptical cupola (at the center of which is a turret glazed all around) environed with a cantilever cornice, and supported by six columns of the *Composite* Order; between each of these is a spacious arch, and six large light windows with strong mullions and transoms: The length (or greater diameter) of the church is 63, the breadth (or lesser diameter) 48, the altitude 49 feet. XIII. *St. Bartholomew's Exchange* (or the *Little*) Church, situated on the east side of *Bartholomew Lane*, and near the *Royal Exchange*, in the Ward of *Broad Street*, was rebuilt in 1679; it is a strong building, the roof flat, adorned with fretwork, and supported with columns of the *Tuscan* Order, and large arches. Here are three fine door-cases, on the north, south, and west sides of the church, whose pilasters, entablature, and pediments are of the *Corinthian* Order, adorned with cherubs, shields, festoons, etc.; that towards the south being more particularly spacious and fine. The length is 78 feet, breadth 60, height 41; and that of the square tower, about 90 feet.

XIV. *St. Bridget*, alias *St. Bride's* Church, situated on the south side of *Fleet Street*, in the Ward of *Farringdon*, outside the walls of *London*, but within the Liberty of the city, was rebuilt with great beauty and strength in 1680, and further adorned in 1699; the roof is elevated on pillars and arches, with entablatures of the *Tuscan* Order; the length is 111 feet, breadth 57, height 41 feet. The altitude of the steeple is 234 feet; it consists of a tower and lofty spire of stone, adorned with pilasters and entablature of the *Corinthian* Order, arched pediments, urns, etc., and spiry arcades, of a most elegant effect.

XV. *Christ-church*, situated on the north side of *Newgate Street*, was rebuilt in 1687; the fabric is of stone, spacious and beautiful, with buttresses on the outside, and adorned with acroteria, pineapples, pediments, etc. The spire was finished in 1704, which is likewise of stone, adorned with vases, etc. The roof of the nave of the church is camerated <note>vaulted or arched</note>, and those of the two side-aisles are flat; the first supported by ten pillars of the *Composite* Order, the others by as many pilasters of the same order; the length is 114 feet, breadth 81, height 38; the altitude of the steeple (which consists of a tower and spire) is about 153 feet.

XVI. *St. Christopher's* Church, situated on the north side of *Threadneedle Street*, in the Ward of *Broad Street*, was not totally destroyed by the Great Fire (the walls partly escaping the flames) and had probably fared better had it not been filled with paper. It was repaired soon after the *Fire* in 1671, and afterwards beautified in 1696. All the old part left by the *Fire* is *Gothic*, but the pillars within are *Tuscan*; the length is 60 feet, breadth 52, height 40 feet; altitude of the tower about 80 feet.

<margin>*Inscribed on a stone of white marble on the north side of the chancel.*</margin>
XVII. *St. Clement Danes* Church, situated on the north side of the *Strand*, a little westward of *Temple Bar*, in the Liberty of *Westminster*, "being greatly decayed, was taken down in the year 1680, and rebuilt and finished in 1682, etc. Sir *Christopher Wren*, his Majesty's Surveyor, freely and generously bestowing his great care and skill towards the contriving and building of it, etc." The fabric is of stone, strong and beautiful, of the *Corinthian* Order, with a tower, and the late addition thereon of an ornamental <margin>*by Mr. Gibbs.*</margin> steeple. The east ends both of the church and chancel are elliptical. The roof is camerated <note>vaulted or arched</note>, supported with *Corinthian* columns, and enriched with fretwork. On the south, fronting the *Strand*, is a circular portico of six *Ionic* pillars. The length is 96 feet, breadth 63, height 48; altitude of the tower about 116 feet.
