XVIII. *St. Clement's Eastcheap* Church, situated on the east side of *St. Clement's Lane*, near Great *Eastcheap*, in the Ward of *Candlewick Street*, was rebuilt of brick and stone in 1686, in the *Composite* order, having a tower, a flat roof, and pilasters around the *inside* of the church. The ceiling is adorned with a spacious circle, whose periphery is intricate fretwork. The length is 64 feet, the breadth 40, the height 34; and that of the tower is 88 feet.

XIX. *St. Dionis Backchurch*, situated on the west side of *Lime Street*, in the Ward of *Langbourn*, was rebuilt in 1674; and the steeple in 1684. The building is chiefly of stone; the tower and the pillars within are strong; but part of the walls are of brick *finished over*. The said pillars and the pilasters that strengthen the walls within and support the roof are of the *Ionic* order, as is also the end fronting *Lime Street*. The length is 66 feet, the breadth 59, the height 34; and that of the tower and turret is 90 feet.

XX. *St. Dunstan in the East* is situated midway between *Tower Street* to the north and *Thames Street* to the south, in *Tower Street* Ward. The church was only repaired and newly beautified, but the steeple was erected as it now appears in 1698. The windows and steeple are of a modern *Gothic* style, but the pillars and arches within are *Tuscan*. The height of the steeple—consisting of a stone tower and spire, at each corner of which tower are four neat smaller spires, and a fifth or principal one erected on four *Gothic* arches—is 75 feet.

XXI. *St. Edmund the King*, situated on the north side of *Lombard Street*, in *Langbourn* Ward, is well built of stone and of the *Tuscan* order. The roof is flat, and there are no pillars within to support it. The length is 69 feet, the breadth 39, the height 33; and that of the tower is about 90 feet. The church was rebuilt in 1690.

XXII. *St. George Botolph Lane* Church, situated on the west side of *Botolph Lane*, in the Ward of *Billingsgate*, was rebuilt of stone in 1674. The roof over the two side aisles is flat, but that over the nave is vaulted and supported by columns of the *Composite* order. The outside of the east end is adorned with a stone cornice and pediment, and enriched with a cherub and festoons; the roof has fretted arches and an entablature above the columns. The length is 54 feet, the breadth 36, the height 36; and that of the steeple is about 84 feet.

XXIII. *St. James Garlick Hill* Church, situated on the east side of that *hill*, near *Thames Street*, in the Ward of *Vintry*, was rebuilt in 1683 of stone, with handsome outer door-cases of the *Corinthian* order. The roof within is flat and supported by twelve columns, besides pilasters, of the *Ionic* order. The length is 75 feet, the breadth 45, the height 40 feet; and that of the steeple (which is a tower with a rail and baluster above the cornice) is about 90 feet.

XXIV. *St. James, Westminster*, Church, situated on the north side of *Jermyn Street*, fronting toward *St. James's Square*, within the Liberty of the City of *Westminster*, was erected at the expense and credit of *Henry Jermyn*, Earl of *St. Albans*, and of the inhabitants, owners, and occupiers of the houses and lands in this precinct; and with the authority of an Act of Parliament passed in the third year of *James* II, constituting this church parochial. The walls are of brick, with rustic quoins, fasciae, doors, and windows of stone. The roof is arched, supported by pillars of the *Corinthian* order; and the door-cases are of the *Ionic* order. XXVII. *St. Margaret Lothbury Church*, situated on the north side of *Lothbury*, in the Ward of *Coleman Street*, was rebuilt and finished in 1690, of stone; with a steeple consisting of a spacious tower, on which is a small dome, and on that a spire. XXXI. *St. Mary-at-Hill Church*, situated on the west side of the street called *St. Mary Hill*, in the Ward of *Billingsgate*, was rebuilt in 1672. The front facing the *Hill* is stone; the rest of the walls are stone covered with a plaster finish; the tower is also of stone. The inside of the roof over the middle aisle is slightly arched, in the middle of which is a handsome cupola. The roofs of the side aisles are flat and at their lowest at the four corners, supported by four columns. At each end of the church are two pilasters, of no specific <term>order</term>, but a hybrid type composed partly of the <term>Doric</term> and <term>Corinthian</term>. The roof of the cupola is adorned with cherubim, arches, and leaves, and the rest of the church ceiling with quadrangular figures, all of <term>fret-work</term>; under which is a <term>cantilever</term> cornice. The length is 96 feet, the breadth 60, the height to the ceiling of the roof 26, and to the center of the cupola 38 feet; and that of the steeple, consisting of a tower and turret, is about 96 feet.

XXXII. *St. Mary Aldermary Church*, situated on the east side of *Bow Lane*, in the Ward of *Cordwainer*, was rebuilt by a private donation before the public fund was established by Parliament from the tax on coals for rebuilding the churches demolished by the *Fire*. The lower part of the tower was repaired by the <term>Surveyor</term> <note>Sir Christopher Wren</note>, and the upper part was newly built in 1711. The height to the peak of the pinnacles is 135 feet.

XXXIII. *St. Mary Magdalen, Old Fish Street Church*, situated on the north side of *Little Knightrider Street*, in the Ward of *Castle Baynard*, was rebuilt in the year 1685, mostly of stone, with a rail and balustrade around the outside. There are three aisles and a handsome stone tower. The length is 60 feet, the breadth 48, the height 30 feet; and that of the tower

XXXIV. *St. Mary Somerset Church*, situated on the north side of *Thames Street*, in the Ward of *Queenhithe*, was rebuilt in 1695 of stone, including the tower. There are two aisles, with a flat roof adorned with a cornice; and between the windows with <term>fret-work</term> of cherubim, etc. The length is 83 feet, the breadth 36, the height 30 feet; and that of the tower, to the top of the highest pinnacles, is 120 feet.

XXXV. *St. Mary-le-Bow*, situated on the south side of *Cheapside*, in the Ward of *Cordwainer*. This church was rebuilt and finished in 1673 upon the walls of a very ancient church from the early period of the *Roman colony*, which, due to the rising of the ground in succeeding ages, was entirely buried under the level of the present street of *Cheapside*. It is built of brick and stone; the walls are covered with a plaster finish; the roof is arched and supported by ten <term>Corinthian</term> columns; there are three aisles, besides the cross-aisle at the west end. The model follows that of the <term>Templum Pacis</term> <note>The Temple of Peace in Rome</note>.

But the principal ornament of this church is the steeple, erected near the northwest corner and joined to the church by a lobby, which is founded upon an old Roman causeway lying about 18 feet below the level of the street. It is considered by discerning artists to be an admirable piece of architecture, unparalleled by the steeple of any parish church in *Europe*. It was designed by the incomparable Sir *Christopher Wren*, begun in 1671, and finished in 1680. It is built of Portland stone, consisting of a tower and spire. The tower is square; on its north side is a door and beautiful door-case; the piers and arch are of the <term>Tuscan</term> order, and it is adorned with two columns and an <term>entablature</term> of the <term>Doric</term>

On the <term>cornice</term> of this last order stand <term>cartouches</term>, upon which is erected an <term>obelisk</term> of considerable height, and at its vertex a spacious ball; and above that (serving as a weathercock) is the figure of a dragon made of gilt brass, about ten feet long; in its expanded wings is figured a cross (the supporter of the armorial ensigns of the City of *London*). The dimensions of the church within are: length 65½ feet, breadth 63, height 38; and that of the famous steeple is 225 feet.

XXXVI. *St. Mary Woolnoth* Church, situated on the south side of *Lombard Street*, was repaired in 1677. The sides, the roof, and part of the ends having been damaged by the *Great Fire*, the steeple was old and needed rebuilding, which, along with the whole church, is now very substantially completed by the ingenious and skillful architect Mr. *Nicholas Hawksmoor*; who formerly was, and continued for many years to be, a domestic clerk to the Surveyor, and was afterwards employed under him in the *royal and other public works*.

XXXVII. *St. Mary Aldermanbury* Church, situated near the middle of *Aldermanbury*, in the Ward of *Cripplegate*, was rebuilt in 1677 of stone, with the steeple consisting of a tower and turret. The roof within is vaulted and supported by twelve columns of the <term>*Composite* order</term>. At the east end is a large <term>cornice</term> and <term>pediment</term>; also two large <term>cartouches</term> and carved stone pineapples; the inside of the roof is adorned with arches of <term>fretwork</term>, and the said columns with an <term>entablature</term>; the <term>cornice</term> is *cantilever*. The length is 72 feet, breadth 45, height 38 feet; and the steeple is about 90 feet.

XXXVIII. *St. Matthew Friday Street* Church, situated on the west side of *Friday Street*, near *Cheapside*, in the Ward of *Farringdon*, was rebuilt in 1685. The walls and tower are made of brick; the windows and door-cases are stone, as is the entire front facing *Friday Street*. The length is 60 feet, the breadth 33, and the height 31; the tower is 74 feet high.

XXXIX. *St. Michael Basinghall* (also known as *Bassishaw*) Church, situated on the west side of *Basinghall Street*, in the Ward of *Bassishaw*, was rebuilt and finished in 1679. The walls are brick and the tower is stone. It has three aisles, and the openings on each side are similar to those on the opposite side in number and style. It features pillars of the <term>Corinthian order</term>. The roof is <term>camerated</term> <note>arched or vaulted</note> and divided into quadrangular panels of <term>crocket-work</term> <note>ornamental carvings</note>. It also has a <term>cantilever cornice</term>, <term>frieze</term>, etc., enriched with foliage, etc. The length is 70 feet, the breadth 50, and the height 42 feet; the tower is 75 feet high.

XL. *St. Michael Royal* Church, on the east side of *College Hill*, in the Ward of *Vintry*, was rebuilt in 1694. The walls are stone, with some brick at the east end. It has a flat, square roof adorned with <term>fret</term> and <term>crocket-work</term>. The length is 86 feet, the breadth 48, and the height 40; the tower is about 90 feet high.

XLI. *St. Michael Queenhithe* Church, on the southwest corner of *Little Trinity Lane*, in *Thames Street*, in the Ward of *Queenhithe*, was rebuilt in 1677. The walls are stone and there are three aisles. The roof is square and flat, with the decoration of a quadrangle bounded by <term>fret-work</term>. The length is 71 feet, the breadth 40, and the height 39; the steeple, consisting of a tower and spire, is 135 feet high.

XLII. *St. Michael Wood Street* Church, on the west side of *Great Wood Street*, in the Ward of *Cripplegate*, was rebuilt of stone in 1675. The roof is flat and adorned with <term>fret</term> and <term>crocket-work</term>, and the walls feature arches and <term>imposts</term>. The front facing *Wood Street* has stone <term>pilasters</term>, an <term>entablature</term>, and a pitched <term>pediment</term> of the <term>Ionic order</term>. The interior length is 63 feet, the breadth 42, and the height 31 feet; the tower is 90 feet high.

XLIII. *St. Michael Crooked Lane* Church, on the east side of *St. Michael’s Lane*, in the Ward of *Candlewick Street*, was rebuilt of stone in 1688. The length is 78 feet, the breadth 46, and the height 32 feet; the tower, to the top of the pinnacles, is about 100 feet high.

XLIV. *St. Michael Cornhill* Church, on the south side of *Cornhill*, in the Ward of *Cornhill*, was demolished by the Great Fire (except for the tower) and rebuilt in 1672, mostly of stone. It has three aisles. The roof is <term>camerated</term> <note>arched</note>, having <term>groins</term> and <term>imposts</term> covered with lead, and is supported by <term>Tuscan columns</term>. The length is 87 feet, the breadth 60, and the height 35 feet; the tower, to the top of the small pinnacles at the corners, is 130 feet high.

L. *St. Sepulchre’s* Church, on the north side of *Snow Hill*, in the Ward of *Farringdon Without*, was almost demolished by the Great Fire (except for part of the wall and steeple) and was rebuilt in 1670. The roof over the nave is <term>camerated</term> <note>arched or vaulted</note>, though it appears flat; it is lower by about 8 feet over the side aisles, which are supported by twelve strong stone columns of the <term>Tuscan order</term>. The length (excluding the passage or ambulatory at the west end) is 126 feet, the breadth (excluding the chapel on the north side) is 58, the height of the roof over the middle aisle is 35; and the tower and spires are about 140 feet high.

LI. *St. Stephen’s Coleman Street* was rebuilt in 1676, chiefly of stone, with two aisles. The roof is flat, without pillars to support it. On the outside, the front of the east end is adorned with a cornice and circular pediment between two pineapples, etc. The length is 75, breadth 35, height 44; and the tower, besides the turret, is 65 feet high.

LIII. *St. Swithin’s* Church, on the north side of *Cannon Street*, near *London Stone*, in the Ward of *Walbrook*, was rebuilt in 1679 of stone, including the tower; the roof is supported with half-columns of the *Composite* order. Here are three aisles; and the whole is convenient and pleasant, though small. The length is 61 feet from north to south, from east to west 42 feet, height 40 feet; and the tower and spire are 150 feet high.

LIV. *St. Vedast*, also known as *Foster* Church, on the east side of *Foster Lane*, in the Ward of *Farringdon*, was rebuilt in 1697 of stone, with three aisles; the roof is flat, supported on the south side with *Tuscan* columns, and adorned with an elliptical figure within a parallelogram, surrounded with curious fretwork, etc. The length is 69 feet, breadth 51 feet, height 36 feet; and the tower is about 90 feet high.

In the ninth year of the reign of *Queen Anne*, 1708, an Act of Parliament was passed to erect *fifty* new additional *parish* churches in the cities of *London* and *Westminster*. The *Surveyor* <note>Sir Christopher Wren</note>, being appointed one of the commissioners for carrying on the works, attended that service with all the diligence his other offices would permit; and preparatory to that, took the opportunity to share his thoughts to this effect in a letter to a friend on that commission.

SINCE Providence, in great mercy, has extended my life to the finishing of the cathedral church of *St. Paul* and the parochial churches of *London*, in place of those destroyed by the *Fire* (all of which were executed during the labors of my employment in the service of the Crown, from that time to the current happy reign); and being now appointed one of the commissioners for building, according to the recent *Act*, *fifty* more churches in *London* and *Westminster*; I shall venture to briefly communicate my opinions, after long experience; and without further ceremony present for better judgment what currently occurs to me, in a brief overview of this whole affair; not doubting but that the debates of the worthy commissioners may hereafter give me occasion to change or add to these observations.

1. First, I believe the churches should be built, not where vacant land may be purchased cheapest at the edges of the suburbs, but among the more numerous inhabitants for the convenience of the wealthier residents, even though the site of them should cost more; the wealthier inhabitants contribute most to future repairs, the ministers and officers of the church, and the expenses of the parish.

<sig>4</sig>
<meta>catchword: 2.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Sir Christopher Wren's letter concerning the Act of Parliament for building fifty new churches, transitioning from a list of rebuilt churches to his specific recommendations for urban planning and church construction.</meta>

<page-num>319</page-num>
<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

2. I could wish that all burials in churches might be forbidden, which is not only unhealthy, but ensures that the floors can never be kept even, nor the pews upright. And if the churchyard is closely packed around the church, this is also inconvenient; because the ground being continually raised by the graves, it eventually causes a descent by steps down into the church, which makes it damp and the walls green with mold, as is clearly evident in all old churches.

3. It will be asked, where then shall the burials take place? I answer, in cemeteries situated in the outskirts of the town; and since it has become the fashion of the age to solemnize funerals with a train of coaches (even where the deceased are of moderate means), though the cemeteries might be half a mile or more distant from the church, the cost need be little or no more than usual. The service may be performed first in the church; but for the poor, and those who must be buried at the parish expense, a public hearse with two wheels and one horse may be kept at small expense, with the usual bearers to lead the horse and take out the corpse at the grave. A piece of ground of two acres in the fields can be purchased for much less than two roods <note>A rood is a unit of area equal to one-quarter of an acre.</note> among the buildings. This being enclosed with a strong brick wall, and having a walk around it and two cross-walks decently planted with yew trees, the four quarters may serve four parishes. There, the dead would not need to be disturbed at the whim of the sexton, nor piled four or five upon one another, nor have their bones thrown out to make room. In these places, beautiful monuments may be erected; but even so, the dimensions should be regulated by an architect and not left to the fancy of every mason; for otherwise the rich, with large marble tombs, would crowd out the poor. A pyramid, a good bust, or a statue on a proper pedestal will take up little room in the quarters, and would be more appropriate than figures lying on marble beds. The walls will hold escutcheons and memorials for the dead, and the area will provide good air and walks for the living. It may be considered further that if the cemeteries are thus placed in the fields, they will limit the excessive growth of the city with a graceful border, which is currently encircled by scavengers' dung-heaps.

4. As to the situation of the churches, I would propose they be brought as forward as possible into the larger and more open streets, not in obscure lanes, nor where coaches will be much obstructed in passage. Nor should we, I think, too strictly observe an East or West orientation in the position, unless it happens to fit properly. Such fronts as happen to lie most open to view should be adorned with porticos, both for beauty and convenience; these, together with handsome spires or lanterns rising in good proportion above the neighboring houses (of which I have given several examples in the City of different forms), may be sufficient ornament to the town without great expense for decorating the outward walls of the churches, in which simplicity and durability ought principally, if not wholly, to be studied. When a parish is divided, I suppose it may be thought sufficient if the mother-church has a tower large enough for a good ring of bells, and the other churches have smaller towers for two or three bells; because great towers and lofty steeples sometimes account for more than half the cost of the church.

5. I shall mention something regarding the materials for public buildings. It is true that the massive demand for the hasty construction of thousands of houses at once after the Fire of *London*, and the frauds of those who built on a large scale, have so debased the value of materials that good bricks are not to be had now without higher prices than formerly; and indeed, if rightly made, they deserve those prices. But brick-makers spoil the earth in the mixing and hasty burning until the bricks will hardly support weight; though the earth around *London*, if rightly managed, will yield as good brick as the *Roman* bricks (which I have often found in the old ruins of the city) and will endure in our air beyond

He critiques the poor quality of contemporary brick-making compared to Roman standards following the Great Fire of London.</summary>

any stone our island provides; which, unless the quarries lie near the sea, are too expensive for general use: the best is *Portland* or *Roche Abbey* stone; but even these are not without their faults. The next material is the lime; chalk-lime is the usual practice, which, well mixed with good sand, is not bad, though much inferior to hard stone-lime. The vaulting of *St. Paul's* is a rendering as hard as stone; it is composed of cockle-shell lime well beaten with sand; the more labor in the beating, the better and stronger the mortar. I shall say nothing of marble (though *England*, *Scotland*, and *Ireland* provide good marble of beautiful colors), but this will prove too costly for our purpose, except for altarpieces. In windows and doors, *Portland* stone may be used with good bricks and stone quoins. As for roofs, good oak is certainly the best, because it will withstand some negligence: the churchwardens' care may be lacking in quickly repairing leaks; they usually whitewash the church and record their names, but neglect to preserve the roof over their heads. It must be admitted that because the roof is more out of sight, it is even more neglected. Next to oak is good yellow deal, which is a long and light timber that makes excellent work at first; but if neglected, it will quickly perish—especially if gutters (which is a common fault in builders) are made to run upon the principal rafters, the ruin may be sudden. Our naval demand for oak and the wars in the North Sea make timber at present excessively expensive. I suppose before long we must have recourse to the *West Indies*, where most excellent timber may be had for the cutting and fetching. Our tiles are poorly made and our slate is not good; lead is certainly the best and lightest covering, and being of our own growth and manufacture, and lasting—if properly laid—for many hundred years, it is without question the most preferable; though I will not deny that an excellent tile could be made to be very durable; our artisans are not yet trained in it, and it is not a quick process to instruct them.

6. The capacity and dimensions of the new churches may be determined by a calculation. It is, I believe, fairly certain that the number of inhabitants for whom these churches are intended is five times as many as those in the City who were burnt out; there are probably more than 400,000 adults who should come to church, for whom these fifty churches are to be provided (besides some chapels already built, though too small to be made parish churches). Now, if the churches could hold 2,000 each, it would still fall very short of the necessary supply. The churches, therefore, must be large; but still, in our Reformed religion, it seems pointless to make a parish church larger than one in which all who are present can both hear and see. The *Romanists*, indeed, may build larger churches; it is enough for them if they hear the murmur of the Mass and see the elevation of the Host, but ours are to be designed for auditories <note>Spaces specifically designed for an audience to hear clearly.</note>. I can hardly think it practical to make a single room so spacious, with pews and galleries, as to hold more than 2,000 persons, and have everyone hear the service, and both hear distinctly and see the preacher. I endeavored to achieve this in building the parish church of *St. James's, Westminster*, which I believe is the most spacious church with these qualities that has yet been built; and yet, at a formal occasion when the church was very crowded, I could not see from a gallery that 2,000 were present. In this church I mention, though it is very broad and the central nave is vaulted, there are no walls of a second order, nor lanterns, nor buttresses, but the entire roof rests upon the pillars, as do the galleries; I think it may be found beautiful and convenient, and as such, the cheapest of any design I could invent.

7. Concerning the placement of the pulpit, I shall observe: A moderate voice may be heard 50 feet in front of the preacher, 30 feet on each side, and 20 feet behind the pulpit—and even then, only if the pronunciation is distinct and even, without dropping the voice at the last word of the sentence, which is commonly empha-

emphatic, and if obscured, it spoils the whole sense. A *French* man is heard further than an *English* preacher because he raises his voice and does not lower his last words; I mention this as an insufferable fault in the pronunciation of some of our otherwise excellent preachers, which schoolmasters might correct in the young as a faulty pronunciation, and not as the *Roman* orators spoke. For the principal verb is in Latin usually the last word; and if that is lost, what becomes of the sentence?

8. Based on what I have said, it may be considered reasonable that the new church should be at least 60 feet wide and 90 feet long, besides a chancel at one end and the belfry and portico at the other. These proportions may be varied; but to build more room than that in which every person may conveniently hear and see is to create noise and confusion. A church should not be so filled with pews that the poor do not have enough room to stand and sit in the aisles, for to them equally is the Gospel preached. It were to be wished there were no pews, but benches; but there is no stopping the tide of profit and the advantage of pew-keepers, especially since the minister is chiefly supported by pews in the <term>chapels of ease</term>. It is evident these fifty churches are not enough for the present inhabitants, and the town will continually grow; but it is to be hoped that hereafter more may be added as the wisdom of the government shall think fit, and therefore the parishes should be so divided as to leave room for subdivisions, or at least for <term>chapels of ease</term>.

I cannot overlook mentioning the difficulties that may be found in obtaining the ground suitable for the sites of the churches among the buildings, and the cemeteries on the borders outside the town; and therefore I shall recount the method that was taken for purchasing ground on the north side of *St. Paul's* Cathedral, where in some places the houses were only eleven feet distant from the structure, exposing it to the continual danger of fires. There were seventeen houses, all contiguous and held in leasehold from the Bishop, the Dean alone, the Dean and Chapter, or the petty canons, with various undertenants. First we treated with the superior landlords, who, being perpetual bodies, were to be compensated in kind with rents of the like value for them and their successors; but the tenants in possession were compensated for a valuable consideration. To find what this amounted to, we learned by diligent inquiry what the inheritance of houses in that quarter were usually valued at: we found this was fifteen years' purchase at the most, and the value of each lease was easily determined in a scheme proportional to this, referring to a map. These rates, which we resolved not to deviate from, were offered to each person; and to cut off much debate, which one might imagine everyone would engage in, they were assured that we followed one uniform method which could not be abandoned. We found two or three reasonable men who agreed to these terms; immediately we paid them and took down their houses. Others who resisted at first, finding themselves amidst dust and rubbish and realizing that ready money was better, as the case stood, than to continue paying rent, repairs, and parish duties, easily gave in. The whole ground at last was cleared, all concerned were satisfied, and their legal documents were surrendered. The greatest debate was about their expenses for fitting up their new houses for their particular trades: for this we allowed one year's purchase and gave leave to remove all their wainscoting, reserving only the materials of the building itself. This was fortunately finished without a court or jury, although in our present case, we may perhaps sometimes find it necessary to have recourse to Parliament.

In the year 1671, the *Surveyor* began the building of the great fluted column of *Portland* stone, and of the *Doric* order (commonly called the *Monument* of *London*, in memory of the burning and rebuilding of the city) and finished it in 1677. The artisans were obliged to wait sometimes for stones of

It greatly exceeds in *height* the pillars at *Rome* of the Emperors *Trajan* and *Antoninus*, those stately remains of *Roman* grandeur; or that of *Theodosius* at *Constantinople*. In forming this *colossal* column, the *Surveyor* took the liberty to exceed the received proportion of the Order by one module, or semi-diameter. In place of the brass urn on the top (which is not skillfully performed and was set up contrary to his opinion), a *colossal* statue in gilded brass of King *Charles the Second* was originally intended, as the founder of the new city, in the manner of the *Roman* pillars which terminated with the statues of their *Caesars*. Alternatively, a figure of a woman crowned with turrets, holding a sword and a <term>cap of maintenance</term>, with other symbols of the city’s grandeur and rebuilding, was considered. The altitude from the pavement is 202 feet; the diameter of the shaft (or body) of the column is 15 feet; the ground bounded by the plinth, or lowest part of the pedestal, is 28 feet square; and the pedestal is 40 feet in height. Inside is a large staircase of black marble, containing 345 steps, 10 1/2 inches broad with six-inch risers. Over the capital is an iron balcony surrounding a *cippus* or *meta* 32 feet high, supporting a blazing urn of gilded brass. Prior to this, the *Surveyor* (as it appears by an original drawing) had made a design for a pillar of somewhat smaller proportions, namely 14 feet in diameter and using a unique design; for as the *Romans* expressed history through *relief* on the pedestals and around the shafts of their columns, so this *monument* of the fire and the resurrection of the city of *London* was represented by a pillar in flames. The flames, blazing from the loopholes of the shaft (which were to provide light to the stairs within), were depicted in gilded brass-work; and on the top was a phoenix rising from her ashes, also of gilded brass.

<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

*Charles II, by the Grace of God, King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, in the eighteenth year of his reign, and most of the peers of England—after nearly the entire City was consumed by fire and restored in a more grand manner within the space of three years, and built not as before of wood or mud, but partly of brick and partly of marble buildings, and so adorned with works that it seems to have risen much more beautiful from its ruins; the city boundaries having also been increased to an immense size—placed this monument here, where the first flame of such a great disaster broke out, for the eternal memory of both events.*
->They placed this Monument.<-
*Let the present and future ages learn, so that no similar disaster may occur, to appease the Deity with timely prayers; and let them recognize with a grateful mind the generosity of the King and the peers, by whose liberality, besides decoration, even greater security has been added to the city.*

> *O how much the city owes to you, AUGUSTUS,*
> *So many temples being born, so many reborn,*
> *So many spectacles? ——* MARTIAL.

As Augustus said of Rome, "I found it built of brick, and left it of marble," so the rebuilder of London might as properly say, "I found it of mud and wood, and left it of brick and stone."

*Injury has often made room for greater fortune: many things have fallen so that they might rise higher and even greater. Timagenes, an enemy to the prosperity of the city, used to say that fires in Rome were his only sorrow because he knew that better things would be rebuilt than had burned.*
[*Seneca, Epistle 92.*]

*The entire Column of the Emperor Antoninus, in Rome, is 230 Roman palms high. The diameter of the shaft contains 16 palms and 4 inches.*

*The entire Column of the Emperor Trajan, in Rome, from its base to the top of the statue of Saint Peter, is 193.5 Roman palms high; its diameter near the base encompasses 16.5 inches; so that this diameter contains as many inches as the whole structure is known to be palms high.*
*N. B. A Roman architectural palm contains 9 English inches.*
*The column called the Historical, in Constantinople, belonging to either the Emperor Theodosius or Arcadius, is 147 feet high, according to the calculation of Petrus Gyllius.*

The Custom House for the Port of London, situated on the south side of Thames Street, was erected in 1668, adorned with an upper and lower order of architecture. In the lower order are stone columns and an entablature of the <term>Tuscan Order</term>; in the upper are pilasters, an entablature, and five pediments of the <term>Ionic Order</term>. The west end is elevated on columns, forming a piazza. The length of this building is 189 feet; its breadth in the middle part is 27 feet, and at the west end, etc., it is 60 feet.

The frontispiece of the <term>Middle Temple</term>, facing Fleet Street, was erected in the year 1684, of stone and brick. The base is a rustic arcade of stone, supporting four pilasters, an entablature, and a triangular pediment of the <term>Ionic Order</term>, and the rest is made of rubbed brick.

## SECTION X.

### A Catalog and Short Description of the Surveyor's Designs of Buildings in the Service of the Crown.

I. General Plan of the location, with the plan and architectural drawing of the royal palace at the City of *Winchester* (the *Venta Belgarum* of the *Romans*, a military station and the seat of the *West Saxon Kings*.)
This palace was begun by the commands of King *Charles II* (*March* 23, 1683) and carried out with such speed that the greatest part was roofed and finished, as to the exterior shell, before the King's death in *February* 1684-5. It extends 326 feet to the west and 216 feet to the south.

King *Charles II*, taking a liking to the location of *Winchester* because of the excellence of the countryside for all kinds of rural sports, commissioned Sir *Christopher Wren*, that great architect (who had the honor of designing *St. Paul's Church* in *London*, laying the first stone, and living to see it finished), to create a plan for a royal palace where the old castle stood; and King *Charles* was so fond of it and promoted it with such diligence that the entire shell of the palace was roofed and nearly finished when that prince died. It will be the finest palace in *England* when finished, and inferior to few abroad. It faces the city to the *east* with a noble courtyard between two wings. There is a chapel on the left for the King, and another on the right for the Queen; and behind the chapels are two courts, finely adorned with piazzas, to give light to the inward rooms. There was to be a terrace around it, as at *Windsor*, and the ground laid out for a garden, very spacious, with a park marked out of eight miles circumference, and that park to open into a forest of twenty miles circumference, without either hedge or ditch. The King designed also a street from the area to the *East*, in a direct line, by an easy descent, to the great door of the cathedral.

Queen *Anne* came once to see *Winchester*, where she stayed seventeen days, and designed to have finished it as a jointure house for her consort Prince *George* of *Denmark*; but an expensive war, and the Prince’s death before her, prevented it. Whether his Majesty, or the Prince, when they please to make a circuit through their dominions, may not think it worth while to finish so noble a structure, time will discover.

Bishop *Morley*, who had been an exile with King *Charles*, and was made Bishop of this See after the Restoration, seeing his Majesty designing to make *Winchester* a royal residence, thought himself obliged to keep pace with the King; and therefore pulled down a great part of the old episcopal palace, and, under the direction of the same architect, Sir *Christopher Wren*, began a new one; but he dying about the same time as the King, his palace stood still with the King’s. However, he had completed one wing in his lifetime, and left money for finishing the rest; but Bishop *Mew*, his successor, seeing no probability of a court at *Winchester*, never minded it. Sir *Jonathan Trelawny* succeeding Bishop *Mew*, in Queen *Anne*’s time, called for the money left by Bishop *Morley*, and finished it. It is a very handsome palace, *in the modern style*.

III. Design of the *Mausoleum*, which was erected in *Westminster Abbey* at the funeral services of Queen *Mary* II, March 5, 1694/5.

IV. *Plans*, *Elevations*, and *Views* of *Chelsea College*. This noble hospital was founded, and nearly finished, by King *Charles* II; continued by King *James* II; and completed and furnished with all sorts of necessities and conveniences for the comfortable maintenance of maimed and retired soldiers by King *William* and Queen *Mary*. The industry and conduct of the *Surveyor* and Sir *Stephen Fox*, jointly, in the erection and settlement of this building are worthy of remembrance: Sir *Stephen Fox*, a Lord of the *Treasury*, took care for the due payment of the works, while the *Surveyor* vigorously prosecuted his part in the buildings; and lastly, he prescribed the statutes and the whole economy of the house, which for cleanliness, health, and convenience is deservedly esteemed one of the best regulated in *Europe*, well suiting, in every particular, the pious design and munificence of its royal founders.

V. *Designs* of the royal *hospital* at *Greenwich* for disabled and retired seamen, begun in 1699. The *Surveyor* was among the first who petitioned their Majesties King *William* and Queen *Mary* to convert the site and buildings of their *royal palace* to this most charitable use; which was also industriously promoted by Lord *Somers*, Mr. *Evelyn*, Mr. *Bridgman* (Secretary of the *Admiralty*), and Mr. *Lowndes* (Secretary of the *Treasury*). This extensive charity was not only intended for the relief and support of veteran seamen and those who had been wounded or disabled in the service, but also for the relief and maintenance of the widows and the education of the orphans of those whose husbands and parents had been killed in the defense of the nation at sea. <page-num>328</page-num>

# SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.

This project was so timely adjusted for the encouragement and improvement of that other most important branch of the national defense, the naval *arms* of *Great Britain*. After the grant had passed the *great seal*, and an ample *commission* was appointed with powers to conduct and regulate all affairs relating to the building of the *hospital*, and the *surveyor* was nominated as a *director* and chief *architect* of this great undertaking, he cheerfully engaged in the work for free (*gratis*). He designed the new *fabric* to be extensive, durable, and magnificent, in conformity with the graceful *pavilion* which had been erected there by King *Charles* the *Second* and originally intended for his own palace. He contributed his time, labor, and skill, and prosecuted the works for several years with all the speed that circumstances would allow, without any salary, profit, or reward (a good example which, it is to be hoped, has since been followed); preferring in *this*, as in every other passage of his life, public service over any private advantage of his own through the acquisition of wealth, for which he always had a great contempt.

->*Extracts from the Account of the Buildings of Greenwich Hospital, published by the deputy-surveyor Mr.* Hawksmoor, *in the year* 1728, *for the perusal of the Parliament.*<-

HER Majesty Queen *Mary*, the foundress of the Marine Hospital, enjoined Sir *Christopher Wren* to build the fabric with great magnificence and order; and being ever solicitous for the completion of the design, she had several times honored *Greenwich* with her personal inspections of the building erected by King *Charles* II as part of his palace, and likewise of the one built by Mr. *Inigo Jones*, called the Queen's House, etc. Upon these viewings, she was unwilling to demolish either building, as was proposed by some. This led to the preservation of an approach from the *Thames* directly up to the Queen's House, 115 feet wide, out of the grant that was made to the hospital, so that her Majesty might have access to that house by water as well as by land; and she retained a desire to add four pavilions to that palace, according to *Inigo Jones’s* design, so that she might make that little palace complete as a royal villa for her own retirement, or as a place from which ambassadors or public ministers might make their entry into *London*.

Her Majesty's absolute determination to preserve the wing built by her uncle King *Charles* II, and to keep the Queen's House and the approach to it for the reasons stated above, naturally led to the arrangement of the buildings as they are now placed and situated.

The principal front of this great building lies open to the *Thames*; from there, we enter into the middle of the Royal Court, nearly 300 feet square, lying open to the north, and bordered on the west by the Court of King *Charles* II, and on the east by the equal Court of Queen *Anne*; and on the south, the Great Hall and Chapel.

The Court of Queen *Anne* contains the great range or wing next to the Royal Court, as mentioned, and holds 140 men. To the east of this Court of Queen *Anne* is another range of building, which contains 66 persons, etc.

The Great Pavilion next to the *Thames* contains four very commodious apartments for officers.

The Great Pavilion at the south end of Queen *Anne’s* Court contains lodgings for officers, and some suitable rooms for the care of widows and children.

The Court of King *Charles* II contains the great wing on the west of the Royal Court mentioned above, built by that Prince as part of his own intended palace. It is a noble structure, having in the middle a tetrastyle portico with arcades;

<sig>4</sig>

<vocab>Sir Christopher Wren, Greenwich Hospital, Mr. Hawksmoor, Queen Mary, King Charles II, Inigo Jones, Queen's House, Thames, architecture, naval defense</vocab>

<summary>Sir Christopher Wren designed Greenwich Hospital without a salary, prioritizing public service and the improvement of Britain's naval defense. The site's layout was carefully planned to preserve existing structures like King Charles II's wing and the Queen's House at the request of Queen Mary.</summary>

...cades; the walls are rusticated, all in Portland stone; the windows artfully decorated and proportioned; the order is *Corinthian*; the body of the building is crowned with an entablature of that order; and the two extremes in two great pavilions (all in the same style) rising with an *Attic* order above the other part, forming two eminent towers.

This wing, together with the base-wing to the west of the Court of King Charles II, contains 206 persons, etc.

The great pavilion toward the *Thames*, closing the north side of this court, contains four apartments for officers and other conveniences.

The great pavilion on the south end of this court contains several lodgings for officers, the great kitchen, and the rooms belonging to it.

The wing to the west, which was built for offices for immediate service, contains chambers for servants and other uses of the household. This is called the base-wing of King *Charles* II.

Keeping the central lines of the whole plan that runs through the royal court and the esplanade in the park, the next buildings we come to lie on the south side of the royal court, and are, first:

The colonnade, having a portico on the right and left sides of *Doric* pillars 20 feet high, is crowned with an entablature and balustrade of *Portland* stone; each of these porticos is 430 feet in length, and both together are sustained by 300 pillars and pilasters.

These porticos are intended for passage from the hall and chapel to the wards and dormitories, and to protect the men from the inclemency of the weather and give them air at any time without inconveniencing them; this is very useful where a number of people are to inhabit one college.

On the west side of this colonnade is built the Court of King *William*, containing the great hall, vestibule, and cupola. The drum of the cupola is a peristyle of double pillars of the *Composite* order, and divided at the corners with groups of pillars; the *Attic* is a circle without breaks, covered with a dome and small lantern.

Underneath is a smaller hall, a room for the guard, and a common meeting place for the house. On the west side of this court is a large dormitory and various lodgings. This wing will contain 200 persons.

On the south side of King *William’s* Court is another large dormitory with several rooms. This wing will contain 320 persons.

On the east of the colonnade is the Court of Queen *Mary*, which contains the royal chapel, with the vestibule and cupola, and a large dormitory to the south, like that of King *William*, holding 320 persons, and a dormitory on the east side of this court to hold 100 persons. Besides the grandeur, regularity, and beauty of this public building, the spacious accommodations, the wards and chambers, can entertain 1,352 men, excluding officers, servants, and rooms for public use.

There was once only this exception: some gentlemen thought the base-wing of offices was too inferior for the rest of the building, and desired that a proposal might be made to alter it to the style and dignity of King *Charles’s* front; this was done and shown to the persons then in power. This led to the doubling of the great north pavilion, making it as large as it is now, with the flag tower at the center, which completed the strength and beauty of the north front of this royal hospital toward the *Thames*.

# VII. Design of the Marble Altar-piece, with the original ornaments and statues, erected in King James the Second’s Chapel at Whitehall, which was saved from the fire and given by Queen Anne to the collegiate Church of St. Peter in Westminster.

->*Preface to the following account (in Section XI) of the design for the tomb of King Charles the First.*<-

---

<margin>
Echard’s Hist. of England, Vol. II. p. 649.
</margin>
<margin>
Vol. III. p. 200.
</margin>
It has been questioned and wondered at by many why a specific monument was not erected at *Windsor* for King *Charles* the *First* after the restoration of his son; especially when the Parliament was well inclined to have given a large sum for that grateful purpose. This has caused several conjectures and reflections; and hints have been given as if the royal body had never been deposited there, or else had been afterwards removed by the Regicides; and Lord *Clarendon* himself speaks cautiously and suspiciously of this matter, as if he believed the body could not be found. But to dispel all such imaginings, we shall here insert a memorandum, or certificate, sent by Mr. *John Sewell*, Registrar at *Windsor*.—*Anno* 1696, *September* 21. The same vault in which King *Charles* the *First* was buried was opened to lay in a stillborn child of the then Princess of *Denmark*, now our gracious *Queen*. On the King’s coffin, the velvet pall was strong and sound, and there was around the coffin a leaden band with this inscription cut through it: KING CHARLES, 1648. *Queen Jane’s* coffin was whole and entire; but that of King *Henry* the *Eighth* was collapsed at the breast, and the lead and wood consumed by the heat of the gums he was embalmed with; and when I laid my hand on it, it was run together and hard, and had no foul smell. As a further memorandum relating to the King’s burial, he says that when the body of King *Charles* the *First* lay in the *Dean’s Hall*, the Duke of *Richmond* had the coffin opened and was satisfied that it was the King’s body. Several people who were alive and then present have declared they knew this to be true, such as Mr. *Randue* of *Windsor* and others; so that he thinks Lord *Clarendon* was misled in that matter, and that King *Charles* the *Second* never sent to inquire after the body, since it was well known to the inhabitants of the castle and town that it was in that vault. To this may be added that Mr. *Fishborne*, a gentleman of *Windsor* and a relation of Sir *Christopher Wren’s*, was among those who were present at the burial of the King. He went into the vault and brought away a fragment of King *Henry’s* pall; he observed the vault was so narrow that it was quite difficult to fit the King’s coffin in alongside the others.

## SECTION XI.

### *A Catalog and Short Account of Designs, in Pursuance of Royal Commands, for Buildings Which Have Not Yet Been Executed.*

#### I. A General Plan, <term>Orthography</term> <note>an elevation drawing</note>, and Section, with the Statues and Ornaments, Designed for the Tomb of King Charles I.

<margin>Echard’s History of England, Vol. III. page 441.</margin>
King Charles II was pleased to order the Surveyor to design a mausoleum, or tomb, for his father, the Royal Martyr, after the House of Commons had voted, upon the motion of Lord O’Brian, on (a) January 30, 1677-8 (the House having been in session during part of that day):
> “The sum of seventy thousand pounds for a solemn funeral of his late Majesty King Charles I, and to erect a monument for the said prince of glorious memory; the said sum to be raised by a two-month tax, to begin at the expiration of the current (b) tax for building ships.”

The form of this structure (as appears by the Surveyor’s original drawings, which were laid before the King) is a rotunda with a beautiful dome and lantern; a circular colonnade on the outside, of the Corinthian order, resembling the Temple of Vesta. The decorations on the outside and within are designed to be costly and magnificent; to give examples from only a few items taken from the first estimate, and particularly of the interior, namely:
> “Eight bases of black marble for the great pillars under the dome, at £30 each. Eight shafts of rich marble from single stones, 28 feet long and 3 1/2 feet in diameter, to be brought from the Levant, valued at £400 each. Eight capitals of gilded brass-work for the above-named pillars, at £250 each. 3,520 feet of incrustation with various marbles in the lower order of pilasters within the niches. Entablatures of white marble. In the spandrels over the niches, inlaid marbles. 1,606 square feet of mosaic work in the tops of the niches. 4,620 square feet of the best fresco painting in the cupola. Ten life-sized figures, cast in brass and gilded, at £400 each. Seven genii, or cherubim, of gilded brass,

---

(a) Note: The historian mistakes the day; the vote passed on the 29th, as is seen in Dr. Sprat’s sermon before the House of Commons, at St. Margaret’s, Westminster, January 30, 1677-8.
<margin>London, printed for Henry Brome, at the Gun in St. Paul’s Churchyard, 1678. Page 4.</margin>
The beautiful paragraph runs thus:
> “I confess I might—and permit me to say it—I intended to have complained that the present age had not made that use of him [King Charles] which it ought: neither his enemies for their repentance and amendment, nor even his friends for his praise and honor. But, blessed be God, I am fortunately forestalled in one part of the complaint; I have nothing now to wish, but that his enemies would perform their duty to him as well as it must be acknowledged you [the House of Commons], his friends, have done yours, by that much-desired, long-expected *yesterday’s vote*; in which you have given a resurrection to his memory by planning magnificent rites for his sacred ashes. So that now, for the future, an Englishman abroad will be able to mention the name of King Charles I without blushing; and his heroic worth will be handed down to posterity as it always deserved to be, not only freed from calumny or obscurity, but in all things most illustrious; in all things to be commended; in most things to be imitated; in some things scarcely imitable, and only to be admired.”

After divine service, the House sat (as appears by the Order of Thanks): Wednesday, January 30, 1677-8. Ordered, that the thanks of this House be returned to Dr. Sprat for his sermon preached this day before the House at St. Margaret’s, Westminster, and that he be requested to print it, etc.

The *monument*, designed in this way, was approved by the King and determined to be erected at *Windsor* Castle, at the east end of *St. George’s* Chapel, in the place where a small *Gothic* building raised by Cardinal *Wolsey* now stands, called the *Tomb-house*. In the middle of it, he intended to erect a grand monument for King *Henry* the Eighth and had almost finished it before he died. But this was demolished in *April* 1646 by order of the Long Parliament; and the statues and figures provided to adorn it, being all made of gilded copper and exceedingly enriched \*, were taken from there.

<margin>
\* Jane Seymour, his third wife.
</margin>
“King *Charles* the First, of ever blessed and glorious memory, intended to enlarge this place and make it suitable and capable of holding not only his own royal body, but also the bodies of his successors, the Kings of *England*, had not bad times followed; times which, with much difficulty, afforded him only an obscure grave near the first <term>haut-pace</term> <note>a raised floor or dais</note> in the choir of the chapel, his head lying opposite the eleventh stall on the *Sovereign’s side*, and in the same vault where the bodies of King *Henry* the Eighth and his \* *Queen Jane* still remain.” [*Echard’s History of England*, Vol. II. p. 649. *Athenæ Oxon.* p. 528.]

The *Tomb-house*, which had been long neglected and was in a ruinous state, was therefore proposed to be demolished, and the ground was judged to be a most proper location for the new *mausoleum*. After some time, the King returned the drawings and estimates to the *Surveyor*, with orders to keep them until they were called for again. But, in conclusion, the entire design for the *funeral* and *tomb*, due to the incidents of the times or motives unknown to the public, was laid aside.

Upon *his Majesty’s death*, King *James II* ordered the old structure to be immediately repaired and the ceiling to be painted by Signior *Verrio*, as it remains today, with the intention, it is said, of converting the room into a chapter house for the use of the *Order of the Garter*.

<margin>
\* By the eminent craftsman Mr. Gibbons.
</margin>
In the *Surveyor’s* original designs (which still exist) for the *mausoleum*, there are three grand niches (besides the one the portal at the entrance breaks into) rising from the pavement to the entablature of the large columns inside. Whether it was intended by these that the three royal coffins, upon finishing the *tomb*, were to be moved there and proper monumental statues and ornaments placed in the respective niches, or whether the two niches were to be reserved for other royal monuments, is uncertain. In the middle niche facing the entrance, the *King’s monument* was designed in this manner: Four statues, emblems of heroic virtues, standing on a square base or plinth and pressing down prostrate figures representing Rebellion, Heresy, Hypocrisy, Envy, etc., support a large shield. On this shield is a statue of the *royal martyr* in modern armor; over his head is a group of cherubim bearing a crown, palm branches, and other devices. There are two drafts of this sculptural design, \* one adapted for brass-work and the other for marble, to be used as most approved.

In the year 1674, at which time the Surveyor was rebuilding some parts of the *Tower of London*, it happened that the bones of King *Edward* the Fourth’s children (those two innocent princes, King *Edward* the Fifth, and his brother, *Richard* Duke of *York*, the one thirteen, the other eleven years of age, most barbarously murdered there, in their bed, by their unnatural uncle, the usurper *Richard* the Third) were, after 191 years, found about 10 feet deep in the ground, in a wooden chest, as the workmen were removing the stairs which led from the royal lodgings into the chapel of the *White Tower*. The circumstances of this discovery being fully represented to the King by the Surveyor, Sir *Thomas Chicheley*, then Master of the Ordnance, and other persons of worth and credit who were eyewitnesses to the whole search, the following warrant from the Lord Chamberlain of his *Majesty’s Household* was directed to the *Surveyor*; in pursuance of which, he designed an elegant urn of white marble on a pedestal, with an *inscription*; all of which, being approved by *his Majesty*, was erected in the east wall of the north aisle of King *Henry* the Seventh’s Chapel.

Sir *Christopher Wren* was one of the commissioners who, at the suggestion of Sir *Jonas Moore*, Surveyor General of the Ordnance, had been appointed by His Majesty to find a proper location for erecting a Royal Observatory. He proposed *Greenwich*, which was approved; and on *August* 10, 1675, the foundation of the building was laid. When finished under the supervision of Sir *Jonas*, with the advice and assistance of Sir *Christopher*, it was furnished with the best instruments for making astronomical observations, and the celebrated Mr. *John Flamsteed* was appointed His Majesty's first professor there (a).

## SECTION XII.

### A Catalogue and Account of Building Designs in the University of Oxford and Cambridge.

#### Plan and Elevations of the Theatre of Oxford, and Scheme of the Roof.

This Theatre, a work of admirable contrivance and magnificence, was the first public performance of the Surveyor in architecture. It would have been executed in a greater and better style, with a view to the ancient *Roman grandeur* discernible in the *Theatre of Marcellus at Rome*, but he was obliged to put a stop to the bolder strokes of his pencil and confine the expense within the limits of a private purse. What (among other beautiful and distinguished parts of this structure) has been esteemed very remarkable is the geometric flat roof, which Dr. *P—t* <note>Dr. Robert Plot</note> has particularly *described in his Natural History of Oxfordshire* as follows:

<margin>* Natural History of Oxfordshire, Chapter 9.</margin>
> “It was an excellent device, whoever first contrived it, of making flat floors or roofs of short pieces of *timber* continued to a great breadth, without either *arch* or *pillar* to support them, but sustained only by the *side walls* and their own *texture*; for by this means, the defect of long *timber* or the mistakes of workmen are often supplied and rectified without any prejudice to the *building*. Of this sort of work we have an example in the *Schools*, in the floor of the uppermost room of the *tower*. There is also a diagram of such work in the *Architecture* of *Sebastian Serlio*. But 
<margin>* Lib. 1 de Geometry, Chapter 1.</margin>
> * Dr. *Wallis* was the first that demonstrated the reason for this work and has given various forms of it, beside the aforementioned, in his book *De Motu*, from which are taken the 
<margin>See Table 13, Dr. Plot.</margin>
> * *diagrams, Table* . Figure 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Upon the first two of these depend the last three, and all others of the kind whatever, whether made up of *quadrates* or oblong *parallelograms* (of which there are some other *forms* in the previously cited book *De Motu*, besides that marked Figure 3, consisting of great and small *quadrates*), or *triangles alone*, as Figure 4, or mixed with *hexagons*, as Figure 5.”

<margin>Dr. Grew’s Museum of the Royal Society, Page 362.</margin>
A model of a geometric *flat floor*, contrived by the aforementioned Dr. *Wallis* and given to the Museum of the Royal Society, is obvious to the eye in its design. The outsides represent the walls of the building on which the flat floor or roof is to be laid. The beams next adjoining to the sides have one end lodged on those walls; the other end is sustained by another beam lying across, both ends of which are, in like manner, sustained by other cross beams; and those again by others, until they reach the other walls. So that no one of them can fall unless the walls fail or the beams break, all mutually sustaining each other without any pillar or prop to support them besides the outer walls.

<margin>Dr. Plot, as above.</margin>
> “But of all the *flat floors* having no pillars to support them, and whose *main beams* are made of various pieces of *timber*, the most admirable is that of the *Theatre of Oxford*, from side wall to side wall, 80 feet across one way and 70 the other; whose *lockages* <note>interlocking joints</note> being so quite different from any mentioned before, and in many other *particulars* perhaps not to be paralleled in the world, I have taken care to represent an exact *draft* of it.”

(a) Dr. *Gilbert Sheldon*, educated at the University of *Oxford*, became Warden of *All-Souls*, and having been Chaplain to King *Charles* I, and having experienced many difficulties, was, after the *Restoration*, made first, Bishop of *London*, and lastly Archbishop of *Canterbury*; which See he held with great honor and reputation for over 14 years, until he died at seventy-nine years of age, in the year 1677. Besides his learning and piety, he is particularly distinguished by his munificent benefactions, in which no man more readily signalized himself; and especially he immortalized his name in that glorious work the *Theatre* of *Oxford*, which cost him more than sixteen thousand pounds; besides the gift of two thousand pounds, to buy lands worth £100 per year to keep it in repair. We are assured from his relations, that from the time of his being Bishop of *London*, to that of his death, it appeared in his book of accounts, that upon public, pious, and charitable uses, he had bestowed about *sixty-six thousand pounds*.

On the 9th of *July*, 1669, the new Theatre was opened with great solemnity, followed by a most splendid *Act*, the likes of which had not been equaled in the memory of man. The munificent founder honored the architect, on this first essay of his skill, with the gift of a golden cup; and by his statutes, appointed him, jointly with the Vice-chancellor, as perpetual curator of the fabric.

> "We *William Townesend* of *Oxford*, mason, and *Jeremiah Franklin* and *Thomas Speakman* of the same, carpenters, do hereby certify that by the command of the Reverend *Robert Shippen*, Doctor of Divinity and Vice-chancellor of the University of *Oxford*, we did, on the date written here, survey and strictly examine the entire fabric of the Theatre in the said University. We find that all of it is in perfect repair and good order; the walls nowhere appear to be in the least defective. The roof, which had formerly sagged or sunk in the middle by about eleven inches—caused by the shrinking of some of the timber and the great weight of books formerly stored upon it—appears to us to be in as good a condition as it was over twenty years ago when a similar examination was made. And we do further certify that the entire fabric of the said Theatre is, in our opinion, likely to remain and continue in such good repair and condition for one hundred or two hundred years to come. In testimony of which, we have signed our names this eighth day of *March, in the year of our Lord* 1720.

> ->*Thomas Speakman.*<-

N.B. This certificate, from builders of the highest reputation in *Oxford*, was prompted by a groundless rumor at that time that the building was in need of repair.

<margin>Dr. Grew's Description of the Museum of the Royal Society, Page 361.</margin>
A model of a geometrical flat floor, designed by Dr. *J. Wallis*, was given to the *Royal Society* by Bishop *Wilkins*; the following account of which, by the author, is an abstract of that which he has published in his book *De Motu*, Chapter vi, Proposition 10, Figure 243.

I first, says the doctor, designed and sketched it in the year 1644, at *Queen's College* in *Cambridge*. When afterwards I was made Professor of Geometry at *Oxford*, about the year 1650, I had it framed of small pieces of *timber*, prepared by a *joiner*, and put together by myself.

This I showed soon after to various people in *Oxford*, and particularly to Dr. *Wilkins*, then Warden of *Wadham College*. After the King's Restoration, I had another one made; and in the year 1660, presented it to his Majesty, who was well pleased with it and had it placed in his closet.

Regarding the model first mentioned, I read two public *lectures* at *Oxford*; one in the year 1652, concerning its construction; the other in the year 1653, concerning the calculation of what weight every joint of it sustains, whereby it might be better judged how far it may be safely practiced. The greatest weight placed on any one joint does not amount to ten times the weight of one beam; and the greatest weight borne by one beam does not amount to seventeen times its own weight. And even this is not laid all on the same part, but distributed to several parts of it.

A third *lecture*, much to the same purpose, I read in May 1669, in the same place, before the Grand Duke of *Tuscany*.

The design is obvious to the eye. The outsides represent the walls of the building on which this flat floor or roof is to be laid. The beams next adjoining to the sides have one end lodged on those walls; the other end is sustained by another beam lying across; both ends of which are in like manner sustained by other crossbeams; and those again by others, until they reach the other walls. So no one of them can fall unless the walls fail or the beams break; all mutually sustaining each other without any pillar or prop to support them besides the outer walls.

The models I had made, and that of the Royal Society in imitation of them, are in width about four times as much as the length of the longest beam; but they may be continued, at pleasure, to a further width as shall be thought fit; with this caution, that the further the work is continued, the greater weight will be placed on every joint, especially near the middle. And though in this model no one beam is loaded with as much as seventeen times its own weight, yet if the work is continued to a greater width, the proportional weight will be thereby increased. Therefore it must be limited according to the strength of the *timber*, which must be able to bear more or fewer times its own weight.

<margin>See the figures.</margin>
I do not know if it has yet been put into practice in more than four pieces in this form. Such is one of the floors in the *Tower* of the public schools at *Oxford*: the width of which, compared to the length of the beams, is as three to two. But it may doubtless be continued much further, especially in such a roof that is not intended to bear much more than its own weight.

<sig>2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Thus,</meta>

<summary>Dr. John Wallis describes his invention and modeling of a "geometrical flat floor," a self-supporting structural system for roofs and floors that requires no internal pillars. He details its mathematical properties, weight distribution, and its presentation to the Royal Society and King Charles II.</summary>

<keywords>Dr. John Wallis, geometrical flat floor, architecture, structural engineering, Royal Society, Bishop Wilkins, Oxford University, timber framing, weight distribution, Sebastiano Serlio</keywords>

--- Page 355 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of architectural framing and structural geometry, moving from the theoretical model to practical applications and commemorative verse.</meta>

<page-num>339</page-num>
<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNIGHT.</header>

Thus, for instance, a *bowling green* of nearly an acre of ground may be covered with a frame of long, slender pieces, without any other support than on the sides, for vines or other similar *plants* to grow upon, so as to shade the whole area.

*Note here* that since the ends of the various pieces are to lie upon those that cross them near their middle, it will be necessary at every *joint* to notch both pieces halfway, or nearly so, so that one may be let into the other and the whole structure reduced to a *flat surface*. But whether such a piece, so notched, ends flush with the piece on which it lies or extends somewhat beyond it, does not matter. And although the former may seem more elegant, the latter, perhaps, may be more practical for use.

Each piece, as I said, must be notched halfway, or nearly so. For, since those beams—especially those of considerable length—will bow a little under the weight, if this notch is somewhat less than halfway (which would cause the whole structure to rise slightly in the *middle* if it did not bow), the bowing will reduce it to a *flat surface*.

*Note also* that a frame designed this way needs neither *nail* nor *pin*, as the various pieces fasten as well as support one another. Yet, if it is to bear a weight much greater than its own, it will be useful to fasten each *joint* with *pins* and, if necessary, to strengthen it with *iron plates* or reinforce it with other pieces of *timber* fastened with *iron bolts*. This compensates for the weakness caused by the notches at the *joints*, which will make the entire frame exceedingly strong.

### II.

*But no eloquence, no decorative arrangement*
*of sounding words,*
*will equal the inexpressible texture of the vast beams,*
*nor express their solid harmony.*
*See how, suspended in the sublime air, the flat expanse*
*is stretched out, supporting the ridges of heavy lead,*
*and the mountain heavy with its teeming peak!*
*O how firm a trust binds the loving trees,*
*once accustomed to being wooed by sweet murmurs*
*and sweet nods:*
*joined in a stable marriage, no force shall tear them apart,*
*nor shall fierce ages cause a divorce.*
*Behold with what great effort the daring machine*
*leaves the walls abandoned on this side and that,*
*and continually strikes a playful fear into those beneath,*
*though they are ever safe and secure!*
*It no more fears a fall, secure in its menacing planisphere,*
*than the firm chamber of the vaulted sky fears*
*the ruin of its eternal arch.*
*The genius of the powerful architect commands*
*such stable vastness to exist,*
*than which nothing is more solid or wider,*
*which sustains the ethereal mass with Herculean strength,*
*and, ignoring the prison of the old small spheres,*
*extends the boundaries of the majestic heaven far and wide.*

### III.

*Alas! Wren has long raised up divine Mathematics,*
*which were too soiled even by learned dust,*
*rising into the heights,*
*and gave them new light among the stars,*
*to be envied by the stars themselves.*
*There, a spectator in the starry Amphitheatre,*
*he saw the splendid battles of wild beasts,*
*and funeral pyres flashing from angry throats and eyes.*
*There, in the painted scenes of serene nights,*
*he saw the planets, the foreknowing mimes of heaven,*
*playing out human fates,*
*now with smiles on a comic face to come—*

## CONCLUSION

DURING the time of the *Surveyor's* employment in the service of the *public* and of the *Crown*, by virtue of Letters Patent consistent with the pleasure of six crowned heads under the Great Seals of King *Charles* the second, King *James* the second, King *William* and Queen *Mary*, Queen *Anne*, and King *George* the first (besides the ordinary duties of his office in the survey and care of the repairs and new buildings of all the royal palaces), he began and completed the cathedral church of *St. Paul*, the second greatest structure in *Europe*; fifty-one parish churches; the great *column* called the *Monument*, and other public edifices of *London*; the two royal palaces of *Hampton Court* and *Winchester*; the royal hospitals of *Chelsea* and *Greenwich*; the North Front and other repairs of *Westminster Abbey* from the year 1698 to the time of his death in 1723; the Theatre of *Oxford*; the Theatre Royal in *Drury Lane*; the *Duke's* Theatre in *Salisbury Court*, which was taken down some time ago; the magnificent library of *Trinity College* in *Cambridge*; the elegant chapel of *Emmanuel College* there; with many other buildings of less note and private estates.

<margin>London, 1706. Dedication to Sir Christopher Wren.</margin>
> "That I take the boldness (says the learned and ingenious *John Evelyn, Esq.*) to adorn this little work [*Account of Architects and Architecture*] with the name of the *Master of the Works* (whose patronage alone can give it reputation), I have no excuse for but an ambition of publicly declaring the great esteem I have ever had for his virtues and accomplishments; not only in the art of *building*, but throughout all the learned *cycle* of the most useful knowledge and more obscure sciences, as well as the polite and shining ones. All of which is so justly attributed to him that he needs no panegyric or other *history* to immortalize them than the *greatest city of the universe*, which he has rebuilt and beautified, and is still improving; witness the *churches*, the royal *courts*, stately *halls*, *magazines* <note>Storehouses or armories</note>, *palaces*, and other public *structures*; besides what he has built of great and magnificent in both the *universities*, at *Chelsea*, and in the *country*; and he is now advancing the Royal Marine Hospital at *Greenwich*, etc. All of them are so many trophies of his skill and industry, and conducted with such success that if the whole *art of building* were lost, it might be recovered and found again in *St. Paul's*, the historical *pillar*, and those other *monuments* of his happy *talent* and extraordinary *genius*."

All these works form such a body of civil *architecture* that they will appear rather as the production of a whole *century* than the life and industry of one man, for which no parallel instance can be given.

<margin>In the ninth year of King William.</margin>
In an Act of Parliament in the *ninth year* of the reign of King *William*, for the *completing and adorning the cathedral church of St. Paul, London*, a clause was inserted *to suspend a moiety <note>A half portion</note> of the Surveyor's salary until the said church should be finished; thereby to better encourage him to finish the same with the utmost diligence and expedition*.

It was at that time a common notion and misreport that the *Surveyor* received a large annual salary for *that building*, and, consequently, it was his in-

interest to delay the finishing of the building, for the sake of continuing this supposed pay; which, it seems, caused that *Clause*.

The Surveyor's salary for building *St. Paul's*, from the foundation to its *finishing* (as appears from the public accounts), was no more than £200 per year. This, in truth, was his own choice, but what the *rest of the Commissioners*, at the commencement of the works, judged unreasonably small, considering the extensive responsibility; the effort and skill in the design; in preparing drawings, models, and instructions for the craftsmen in their several stations and assignments; in almost daily overseeing and directing in person; in making estimates and contracts; and in examining and adjusting all bills and accounts, etc. Nevertheless, he was content with this small allowance and did not seek any additional profit, always preferring public service to any private gain.

<margin>*The ninth year of Queen Anne's reign.*</margin>
Upon the completion of this great building, a clause was passed in the *Act* of Parliament in the ninth year of the *reign of Queen Anne* declaring the *church finished*, to empower the Commissioners to pay the *Surveyor* the *arrears* of this half of his salary.

His allowance for building all the parochial churches of the City of London was about £100 *per year*, and the same for the repairs of *Westminster Abbey*.

In the year 1685, Sir *Christopher Wren* was elected and returned as a Burgess for the borough of *Plympton* in the county of *Devon*, and served in that Parliament which began at *Westminster* on May 29, in the 1st year of the reign of *James* II, 1685.

In the Parliament which met at *Westminster* on January 22, 1689, he was elected and returned as a Burgess for the borough of *New Windsor*, in the county of *Berks*, by the *inhabitants paying scot and lot* <note>A form of municipal taxation</note>; but, upon a petition, the resolution of 
<margin>August 6.</margin>
the House was that the right of election belonged to the mayor, bailiffs, and *select number of burgesses only*.

In the year 1690, in the 2nd year of the reign of *William and Mary*, he was elected and returned for the *same borough* by the mayor, bailiffs, and select number of burgesses
<margin>May 17.</margin>
*only*. On the report of the merits of this election, the question being put, "That the House agree with the Committee, that the right of election is in the mayor, bailiffs, and select number of burgesses only," it passed in the negative—namely, *Yeas* 138, *Noes* 144.

In the year 1700, he was elected and returned as a Burgess for the borough of *Wemouth and Melcombe Regis*, in the county of *Dorset*, and served in that Parliament which began at *Westminster* on February 10, in the 12th year of the reign of *William* III.

<margin>*The fourth year of King George I.*</margin>
In the year 1718, Sir *Christopher Wren*'s patent for the *Office of Surveyor of the Royal Works* was superseded, in the *eighty-sixth year of his age*, and after more than fifty years spent in a continuous, active, and laborious service to the Crown and public; at which time his merit and labors were not remembered by some.

<margin>At Hampton Court.</margin>
He then retreated to a country retirement, saying only with the Stoic, —*Nunc me jubet fortuna expeditius philosophari* <note>"Now fortune commands me to philosophize more freely."</note>. In this retreat, free from worldly affairs, he passed the greatest part of the *last five years* of his life in contemplation and studies, and principally in the consolation of the *Holy Scriptures*; cheerful in solitude, and as well pleased to die in the shade as in the light.
