Dr. *Isaac Barrow*, in his oration at *Gresham* College in the year 1662, gives him this most extraordinary character:—"It is most certainly established that, just as no one ever showed earlier promise, so no one ever brought forth more mature fruits; once a prodigy as a boy, now a miracle as a man, indeed a genius among men; and so that I do not seem to lie, it will suffice to have named the most ingenious and excellent Christopher Wren" (a).

Part of his thoughts for the discovery of the longitude at sea, and a review of some former tracts in *astronomy* and *mathematics*, shared in the employment of those hours he could spare from meditations and research in *Holy Scripture* during his last retirement. At that time, it appeared that though time had enfeebled his limbs (which was his chief ailment), yet it had little influence on the vigor of his mind, which continued with a vivacity rarely found at that age until within a few days of his death. Not until then could the continued aim of his whole life cease: to be (in his own words) *a benefactor to the human race*; for his great humanity appeared to the last in benevolence and kindness, free from all bitterness in behavior or appearance.

After a short illness, it was the will of the omnipotent Author and Dispenser of all beings to release him from this mortal state and to invest him with immortality on the 25th day of *February*, in the year of grace 1723, and in the *ninety-first* year of his age.

->*Thus Nestor well completed his fate, and had*<-
->*added to forty-five years, another forty-five.*<-
->Ovid. *Tristia* Book 4.<-

*It is pleasant to be with oneself as long as possible, when one has made oneself worthy of enjoying one's own company.*
->Seneca, Letter 59.<-

<margin>Dr. Sprat, *History of the Royal Society*, on Mr. Lawrence Rooke.</margin>
As to his bodily constitution, it was naturally delicate rather than strong, especially in his youth, when he seemed consumptive. And yet, by a judicious regularity and temperance (having acquired good knowledge in medicine), he continued healthy, with little intermission, even to this extreme old age. Furthermore, it is observable that he was happily endowed with such an evenness of temper, a steady tranquility of mind, and Christian fortitude, that no injurious incidents or anxieties of human life could ever ruffle or discompose him; in practice, he was a *Stoic*. Such was *Seneca's* good man: *Certain of judgment, unshaken, fearless; whom some force may move, but none disturbs; whom fortune, when she has hurled at him the most harmful weapon she has with the greatest force, stings but does not wound—and this happens rarely.* [Ep. 45.] *Such is the mind of the wise man, like the state of the world above the moon; it is always serene there.* [Ep. 60.] In a word (as was said on another occasion by an elegant writer): "His knowledge had a right influence on the temper of his mind, which had all the humility, graceful modesty, goodness, calmness, strength, and sincerity of a sound and unaffected philosopher. <margin>*Aubrey's Miscellany, Chapter 5, Page 52, from the mouth of Christopher Wren.*</margin>
<margin>*Fought September 3.*</margin>
*Sir Christopher Wren*, while at his father’s house in 1651 at *Knoyle, Wiltshire*, dreamed that he saw a battle in a great marketplace which he did not recognize, where some were fleeing and others pursuing; and among those who fled, he saw a kinsman of his who had gone into *Scotland* to join the King's army. They had heard in the countryside that the King had come into *England*, but they could not tell whereabouts he was. The next night, his kinsman came to his father's house at *Knoyle* and was the first to bring the news of the battle at *Worcester*.

When *Sir Christopher Wren* was at *Paris* around 1665, he was taken ill and feverish, passed very little urine, and had a pain in his kidneys. He sent for a physician, who advised him to be bled, thinking he had a *pleurisy*; but since bleeding greatly disagreed with his constitution, he chose to defer it a day longer. That night, he dreamed that he was in a place where palm trees grew (supposing it to be *Egypt*) and that a woman in a romantic dress handed him dates. The next day he sent for dates, which cured him of the pain in his kidneys.

<margin>*Aubrey's Miscellany, Chapter 5.*</margin>
As a parallel to this: "While the plague was raging in the army of the Emperor *Charlemagne*, he dreamed that a decoction of the root of the <term>Dwarf-thistle</term> [a mountain plant, since called the <term>Caroline-thistle</term>] would cure that disease." See *Gerard's* Herbal, which tells us this. Note: He says the army was thus delivered from the plague, but does not mention the dream, page 1158.

*Pliny (Natural History, Book 25, Chapter 2) tells a story of this kind.*

> " *Nuper cujusdam militantis in prætorio mater vidit in quiete, ut radicem syl-*

> " *parte: Casu accidit, ut milite à morsu canis incipiente aquas expavescere,*
> " *superveniret epistola orantis ut pareret religioni: Servatusque est ex insperato;*

<note>Recently, the mother of a certain soldier in the praetorian guard saw in a dream that she should send her son the root of a wild rose (which they call <term>Cynorrhodon</term>), which had pleased her with its appearance the day before in a thicket, for him to drink. The event took place in Lusitania, the part of Spain closest to us. It happened by chance that while the soldier was beginning to fear water [rabies] from a dog bite, a letter arrived from his mother begging him to obey the religious vision. He was saved unexpectedly, and afterward, so was anyone else who attempted a similar remedy.</note>

*Nestor* of *Athens* was not only in his profession the greatest man of that age, but had given more proofs of it than any other man ever did; yet for want of that natural freedom and audacity which is necessary in dealings with men, his personal modesty overthrew all his public actions. *Nestor* was in those days a skillful architect, and in a manner the inventor of the use of *mechanical powers*, which he brought to so great perfection that he knew to an atom what foundation could bear such a superstructure: And they record of him that he was so prodigiously exact that, for the sake of experiment, he built an edifice of great beauty and seeming strength, but so contrived as to bear only its own weight, and not to admit the addition of the least particle. This building was beheld with much admiration by all the *virtuosi* of that time, but fell down with no other pressure than the settling of a *Wren* upon the top of it: Yet *Nestor’s* modesty was such that his art and skill were soon disregarded for want of that manner with which men of the world support and assert the merits of their own performances. Soon after this instance of his art, *Athens* was, by the treachery of its enemies, burnt to the ground. This gave *Nestor* the greatest occasion that ever a builder had to render his name immortal and his person venerable: For all the new city rose according to his arrangement, and all the monuments of the glories and distresses of that people were erected by that sole artist; indeed, all their temples, as well as houses, were the effects of his study and labor; insomuch that it was said by an old sage, surely *Nestor* will now be famous, for the habitations of the gods, as well as men, are built by his contrivance. But this bashful quality still put a damp upon his great knowledge, which has as fatal an effect upon men’s reputations as poverty; for, as it was said, <margin>Ecclesiastes, chapter 9, verse 15.</margin> *The poor man by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man:* So here we find, the modest man built the city, and the modest man’s skill was unknown. But surely posterity is obliged to allow him that praise after his death which he industriously declined while he was living.

# APPENDIX.

## Of ARCHITECTURE; and Observations on *Antique* Temples, etc.

->[*From some rough drafts, imperfect.*]<-

### TRACT I.

Architecture has its political use; public buildings being the ornament of a country, it establishes a nation, draws people and commerce, and makes people love their native country, which passion is the origin of all great actions in a commonwealth. The emulation among the cities of *Greece* was the true cause of their greatness. The obstinate valor of the *Jews*, occasioned by the love of their Temple, was a cement that held that people together for many ages through infinite changes. The care for public decency and convenience was a major cause of the establishment of the *Low Countries* and of many cities in the world. Modern *Rome* still subsists by the ruins and imitation of the old, as does *Jerusalem* by the Temple of the Sepulchre and other remains of *Helena's* zeal.

Architecture aims at eternity; and therefore the only thing incapable of modes and fashions is its principles, the *Orders*.

The *Orders* are not only *Roman* and *Greek*, but *Phoenician*, *Hebrew*, and *Assyrian*; therefore, being founded upon the experience of all ages, promoted by the vast treasures of all the great monarchs and the skill of the greatest artists and geometricians—everyone emulating each other—and because experiments in this kind are greatly expensive and errors are uncorrectable, this is the reason that the principles of architecture are now the study of antiquity rather than of fancy.

Beauty, firmness, and convenience are the principles; the first two depend upon geometrical reasons of *optics* and *statics*; the third alone creates variety.

There are natural causes of beauty. Beauty is a harmony of objects, producing pleasure through the eye. There are two causes of beauty: natural and customary. Natural beauty comes from *geometry*, consisting in uniformity (that is, equality) and proportion. Customary beauty is produced by the familiarity of our senses with those objects which are usually pleasing to us for other reasons, just as familiarity or a particular inclination breeds a love for things not in themselves lovely. Here lies the great source of errors; here the architect's judgment is tested; but the true test is always natural or geometrical beauty.

Geometrical figures are naturally more beautiful than other irregular ones; in this, all agree as if to a law of nature. Of geometrical figures, the square and the circle are most beautiful; next, the parallelogram and the oval. Straight lines are more beautiful than curved; next to straight lines, equal and geometrical flexures; an object elevated in the middle is more beautiful than one that is depressed.

<meta>catchword: Position</meta>

<page-num>352</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF</header>

Position is necessary for perfecting beauty. There are only two beautiful positions of straight lines: perpendicular and horizontal. This comes from nature and consequently necessity, since no position other than upright is firm. Oblique positions are a discord to the eye unless they are balanced in pairs, as in the sides of an <term>equicrural</term> <note>An isosceles triangle; one with two sides of equal length.</note> triangle. Therefore, Gothic buttresses are all unattractive and were avoided by the ancients; almost no roofs except spherical ones were raised to be visible, except in the front where the lines correspond. In spherical shapes, the ribs correspond in all positions. Cones and multi-angular prisms lack neither beauty nor firmness, but they are not ancient.

Views contrary to beauty are deformity (which is a defect of uniformity) and plainness (which is an excess of uniformity); variety creates the middle ground.

A variety of uniformities creates complete beauty. Uniformities are best balanced like rhymes in poetry: alternately, or sometimes with more variety, as in stanzas.

In things to be seen all at once, too much variety creates confusion, which is another vice of beauty. In things that are not seen at once and have no relation to one another, great variety is commendable, provided this variety does not transgress the rules of optics and geometry.

An architect ought to be wary of novelties in which whim blinds the judgment; he should consider his judges to be both those who will live five centuries after him and those of his own time. That which is commendable now for its novelty will not be a new invention to posterity, when his works have been often imitated and it is unknown which was the original; but the glory of that which is good in itself is eternal.

The architect ought, above all things, to be well-skilled in perspective; for everything that appears well in the <term>orthography</term> <note>An elevation drawing showing the building's dimensions without perspective.</note> may not be good in the model, especially where there are many angles and projections. Furthermore, everything that is good in a model may not be so when built, because a model is seen from different vantage points and distances than the eye sees the building. However, this will hold universally true: whatever is good in perspective, and remains so in all the principal views—whether direct or oblique—will be just as good on a large scale, if only this caution is observed: that regard be had for the distance of the eye at the principal stations.

Things seen near at hand may have many small members, be well-furnished with ornaments, and may lie flatter; on the contrary, all this care is ridiculous at great distances. There, bulky members and full projections casting sharp shadows are commendable. Small ornaments at too great a distance serve only to confuse the symmetry and take away the luster of the object by darkening it with many little shadows.

There are different reasons for objects whose chief view is from the front and for those whose chief view is from the side.

Fronts ought to be elevated in the middle, not at the corners, because the middle is the place of greatest dignity and first arrests the eye; they should also project forward in the middle rather than being hollow. For these reasons, pavilions at the corners are worthless, because they create both faults: a hollow and a depressed front. Where hollows and solids are mixed, the hollow is to be in the middle; for hollows are either niches, windows, or doors. The first require the middle to give the statue dignity; the second, so that the view from within may be direct; the third, so that the <term>visto</term> <note>A vista or view, often through a long, narrow passage.</note> may be straight. The ancients elevated the middle with a <term>tympan</term> <note>A tympanum; the triangular space forming the center of a pediment.</note> and statue, or a dome. Triumphal arches, which now seem flat, were elevated by the magnificent figure of the victor in his chariot with four horses abreast and other accompanying statues. No sort of pinnacle is worthy enough to appear in the air except a statue. Pyramids are Gothic; pots are modern French. Chimneys ought to be hidden; if not,

still not to be well adorned. No roof can have enough dignity to appear above a cornice, except for the circular one; in private buildings, it is excusable. The ancients preferred flatness. In buildings where the view is sideways, as in streets, it is absolutely required that the composition be square, intercolumniations equal, projections not great, the cornices unbroken, and everything straight, equal, and uniform. Breaks in the cornice, projections of the upright members, variety, inequality in the parts, and various heights of the roof serve only to confound the perspective and make it deformed, while the breaches and projections are cast one upon another and obscure all symmetry. In this sort of building, there seems to be no proportion of length to height; for a portico is the more beautiful the longer it is *in infinitum*. On the contrary, fronts require a proportion of breadth to height; it is indecent for a building to be more than three times higher than its breadth, and just as bad for it to be more than three times as broad as it is high. From this rule, I except obelisks, pyramids, and columns—such as *Trajan’s, etc.*—which seem more like single things than compositions. I also except long porticoes, even when seen directly, where the eye, wandering over the same members infinitely repeated and not easily finding the bounds, makes no comparison of them with the height.

* Vitruvius has led us the true way to find out the origins of the Orders. When men first lived together in civil commerce, there was a necessity for forums and public meeting places. In cold countries, people were obliged to shut out the air, the cold, and the rain; but in hot countries, where civilization first began, they desired to exclude only the sun and admit as much air as possible for coolness and health. This naturally brought in the use of porticoes, or roofs for shade set upon pillars. A walk of trees is more beautiful than the most artificial portico; but since trees were not easily preserved in marketplaces, they made the more durable shade of porticoes. In these, we see they imitated nature: most trees in their prime—that are not saplings or <term>dotards</term> <note>Decaying trees; specifically those that have lost their tops or large branches due to age.</note>—closely follow the proportions of *Doric* pillars in the length of their <term>bole</term> <note>The trunk of a tree.</note> before they divide into branches. I think this is a more natural comparison than that of the body of a man, in which there is little resemblance to a cylindrical body. The first pillars were the actual trunks of trees, turned or cut into prisms of many sides. A little curiosity would lead one to place the *torus* at the top; and the conjecture is not wrong to say it was originally a band of iron used to keep the cracks caused by the sun from opening under the weight above. To keep the weather from penetrating those cracks, it was necessary to cover it with the <term>plinth</term> <note>The square slab at the base of a column or the top of a capital.</note>, or square board. The architrave joined all the pillars lengthwise, while the <term>couples</term> <note>Rafters or beams used in pairs to support a roof.</note> joined them crosswise. I suppose now that the ends of the couples might be hollowed away, as in this diagram. * * * * * [The rest is missing.]

### TRACT II.

Modern authors who have written on architecture generally seem to have little more in view than to set down the proportions of columns, architraves, and cornices in the several orders, categorized as *Doric, Ionic, Corinthian,* and *Composite*. Finding these proportions in the ancient buildings of the *Greeks* and *Romans* (though they were used more arbitrarily than these authors care to acknowledge), they have reduced them into rules that are too strict and pedantic, not to be transgressed without the crime of barbarity. In reality, these were merely the modes and fashions of the ages in which they were used; but because they were found in the great structures (the ruins of which we now admire), we think ourselves strictly obliged

still follow the Fashion, though we can never attain the Grandeur of those Works.

Those who first labored in the Restoration of Architecture, about three centuries ago, studied principally what they found in *Rome*, above-ground, in the ruins of the theaters, baths, temples, and triumphal arches; (for among the *Greeks* little was then remaining) and in these there appeared great differences; however, they criticized them, and endeavored to reconcile them, as well as they could, with one another, and with what they could meet with in the *Italian* cities: and it is to be considered, that what they found standing was built, for the most part, after the Age of *Augustus*, particularly the arches, amphitheaters, baths, etc. The *Doric* Order they chiefly understood by examining the Theater of *Marcellus*; the *Ionic*, from the Temple of *Fortuna Virilis*; the *Corinthian*, from the Pantheon of *Agrippa*; the *Composite*, from the triumphal Arch of *Titus*, etc. I have seen among the collections of *Inigo Jones*, a pocketbook of *Pyrrho Ligorio's*, (an excellent sculptor and architect, employed by Pope *Paul* the Third in the building of the Vatican Church of *St. Peter* in *Rome*, about the year 1540) wherein he seemed to have made it his business, out of the antique fragments, to have drawn the many different capitals, moldings of cornices, and ornaments of *friezes*, etc., purposely to judge the great liberties of the ancient architects, most of whom had their education in *Greece*.

In further proof of this, we now have a very remarkable account from an eminent and learned critic in architecture, namely:

<margin>*History of Amphitheatres, by C. Maffei, London Edition, 1730.*</margin>
> “The first story of the *Coliseum* at *Rome* is said to be *Doric*, and yet the
> “*frieze* of it is not plain and smooth. The third story is *Corinthian*, but
> “without carving or ornaments, except in the capitals. The fourth story is
> “*Composite*, but with *Corinthian* capitals, and like those of the third order;
> “the *corbels* in the *frieze* showing them to be of the *Composite* order. The pillars
> “of the four orders, one above the other, do not diminish in dimension, ac-
> “cording to rule, but are all of a thickness; and the void of the arches, the
> “parts, ornaments, and measures in the different stories, do not have that diver-
> “sity of proportion which is believed to be essential to different orders. By
> “the example of this amphitheater, (the noblest remain of ancient magni-
> “ficence) as well as by many others, it is evident that in the rules of the
> “proportions and different members, etc. of the orders, there was no cer-
> “tain, perpetual, and universal law, but the same orders, measures, and man-
> “ners differed, according to the various kinds of buildings, the judgment of
> “the architect, and the different circumstances of things.”

<margin>*Epistle 87.*</margin>
But although architecture contains many excellent parts besides the ranging of pillars, yet curiosity may lead us to consider where this affectation originally arose, so as to judge nothing beautiful but what was adorned with columns, even where there was no real use for them; as when half-columns are stuck upon the walls of temples or *basilicas*; and where they are hung on, as it were, upon the outside of triumphal arches, where they cannot be supposed to be of any use, but merely for ornament; as *Seneca* observed in the *Roman* baths: *Quantum columnarum est nihil sustinentium, sed in ornamentum positarum, impensæ causâ!* <note>How many columns there are supporting nothing, but placed for ornament, for the sake of expense!</note> It will be to the purpose, therefore, to examine where this affectation of a mode that has continued now for at least 3,000 years proceeded from, and more so, because it may lead us to the grounds of architecture, and by what steps this habit of colonnades came into practice in all ages.

The first temples were, in all probability, in ruder times, only little *cellae* to enclose the idol within, with no other light than a large door to reveal it to the people when the priest saw proper, and when he went in alone to offer incense, the people paying their adorations outside; for all

Sacrifices were performed in the open air, before the front of the temple; but in southern climates, a grove was necessary not only to shade the devout, but, through the darkness of the place, to strike some terror and contemplation in those who approached. Therefore, trees being always an adjunct to the *cellæ*, the Israelites were commanded to destroy not only the idols, but to cut down the groves which surrounded them. But as trees decay over time, or grow unevenly (even if initially planted in good order), or perhaps lack sufficient room, when temples were moved into cities, similar walkways were represented by stone pillars supporting the more durable shade of a roof instead of an arbor of spreading boughs. And still, in the ornaments of stonework, foliage—or a type of work composed of leaves—was imitated (as well as the materials would allow) in the capitals, friezes, and moldings, which remains to this day.

This, I am inclined to think, was the true origin of colonnades surrounding the temples in single or double aisles.

People could not assemble and converse except under shade in hot countries; therefore, the *forum* of every city was also at first planted with rows of trees—

> ->*Lucus in urbe fuit mediâ, laetissimus umbrâ.*<-

These avenues were later, as cities grew wealthier, remodeled into porticoes of marble; but it is probable that at first the columns were set no closer together than the trees had been, and that both architraves and roofs were made of timber, because the spacing between columns would certainly have been too large to have had stone architraves. But architects in later ages, being ambitious to build everything in stone and to load the architraves with heavy stone cornices, were forced to bring the pillars closer together. From this arose the differences between the *Eustyle*, *Systyle*, *Diastyle*, and *Pycnostyle* arrangements of columns, by which *Vitruvius* and his followers tried to make a systematic science of their art, forming fixed rules based on the diameters of their columns for the spacing between them, and the proportions of the architrave, cornice, and all the components of which they are composed.

However, it should be noted that the diameters of columns were thicker at first—even though timber architraves did not require a more substantial pillar, as seen in the *Tuscan Order*—because in the groves, ancient trees of large growth (and antiquity always carries veneration with it) were held in the highest esteem. So at first, columns were six diameters in height; when the imitation of groves was forgotten, the height was increased to seven diameters; then to eight; then to nine, as in the *Ionic Order*; then, finally, to ten, as in the *Corinthian* and *Italic Orders*. And in this, the architects had good reason, given the great expense of raising and carving columns; slenderer columns gave them more opportunity to show their skill in carving and decorating their works in the capitals and moldings. Thus the *Corinthian Order* became the most delicate of all, and although the column was slenderer, it bore a greater weight of entablature than the more ancient *Orders*.

When the old sculptors in *Greece*, such as *Phidias*, *Praxiteles*, and their disciples, began to be celebrated for their art, and the people grew fond of their works, it is no wonder (for *honos alit artes*) that they settled upon the *Corinthian* capital, which has not been improved upon in any age since then, even though the *French* king, *Louis XIV*, offered rewards to any artists who could discover a *Gallic Order*. Therefore *Callimachus*, the ancient architect and inventor (according to *Vitruvius*’s story of the nurse and the basket), must still retain the

honor of it; for neither will the fleur-de-lis of the *French*, nor the palms of *Villalpandus*, in his imaginary scheme of the Temple of *Solomon*, come up to the grace of the old form of the *Corinthian* capital.

It seems very unaccountable that the majority of our recent architects focus so much upon this ornamental aspect and so slightly pass over the geometrical, which is the most essential part of architecture. For instance, can an arch stand without sufficient <term>abutment</term>? If the abutment is more than enough, it is a useless expense of materials; if too little, it will fall; and the same is true for any vaulting. And yet no author has given a true and universal rule for this, nor has considered all the various forms of arches.

The rule given by authors for the abutment of arches is this: [See Figure I.] Let ABC be the arch, of which B is a third part; extend the line BC, and make CD equal to CB, and draw the perpendicular CDF; this determines the abutment GF (as they say), but why? For if you add to the bottom, such as KL, the arch then must certainly press more upon the higher part than the lower; or if some additional weight is added above the arch, that must still press more than before this was added. So this rule (even if it were built upon any sure geometrical theorem, which it is not) is neither true nor universal; and what is true will be shown to be only determinable by the doctrine of finding the centers of gravity in the parts of the proposed design. In demonstrating this, I will not trouble the reader with intricate geometrical speculations or calculations, but use easy inductions; supposing he has read *Archimedes*, or the modern mathematicians who have specifically treated the subject of centers of gravity; or at least, that he will trust those who have established all the principles of this science by unquestionable demonstration; so it will not be necessary to delve into the basics.

<margin>Fig. II.</margin>
Let a stone be cut in this form: FB a parallelogram, CD a semicircle added, AB a perpendicular, M the center of gravity of FB, and N of ACD. Now, if N is equal in weight to M on each side of the perpendicular AB, it is certain the whole stone will stand immovable upon the base at B, although it is but half an arch; add a similar stone on the opposite side until the ends meet in an entire arch, and thus the whole will stand as well as the halves. If anything is added outside M, that changes nothing except that it is a useless expense; but if anything is added above N, that alters the center of gravity, which therefore must be accounted for by adding more weight to M; and the same may be shown in all kinds of vaulting. So it appears that the design, where there are arcades, must be regulated by the science of statics, or the discovery of the centers of gravity, and the proper balancing of all parts to weigh equally; without which, a fine design will fail and prove abortive. Hence I conclude that all designs must, in the first place, be brought to this test or be rejected. I have examined some celebrated works, such as the *Pantheon*, and judge there is more abutment than necessary, though it is flat and low; but I suppose the architect ensured it should stand against earthquakes, as indeed it has, and will. The great structure of *St. Peter's*, if it had been built as *Bramante* had designed it, would have been as durable; but the abutment of the cupola was not placed with judgment. However, since it was reinforced with iron hoops, it is safe at present and, barring an earthquake, will be for ages to come. Iron, in any case, is a good precaution; but the architect should balance his work as if it were not necessary.

The Freemasons were not very concerned about this because they used buttresses on the outside of the wall, which they extended as far as they guessed would be sufficient; and they had yet a further help by loading the buttress with a pinnacle, to the height of which they were not restricted. The *Romans* never used buttresses on the outside, but rather inside, though they cut off a part of the arch, but not of the vaulting that depended on the arch, as it appears

<summary>Wren argues that architectural stability relies on the geometric principles of statics and centers of gravity rather than ornament or arbitrary rules. He critiques the structural designs of the Pantheon and St. Peter's, comparing Roman techniques with those of the Freemasons.</summary>

It seems very unaccountable that the majority of our recent architects focus so much upon this ornamental aspect and so slightly pass over the geometrical, which is the most essential part of architecture. <header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

...appears in the aisles of *Diocletian's* Baths, and in some respect also in the *Templum Pacis* [Temple of Peace],

<margin>Fig. V.</margin>
The different forms of vaulting are necessary to be considered, either as they were used by the ancients or the moderns, whether *Freemasons* or *Saracens*. The *Romans*, though they sometimes used a hemisphere where the room was round—or half-hemispheres, as in the *exedrae* of the baths, or the tribunes of temples and *basilicae*—yet generally they used a plain cylindrical vaulting where the walls were parallel, or cross-vaulting where two cylinders intersect in diagonals, as in the *Templum Pacis* and in all the theaters in the passages under the steps. The moderns, whose arches were not circular but made of sections of circles, commonly used another sort where the spandrels, resting upon the pillars, sprang out in every direction as their arch rose. It is not easy to give a geometrical definition except by calling it a circular inverted cone (A) resting upon its apex (B); the middle (C) they filled up with tracery work, for which this method gave them great opportunity for various variations, which I need not insist on.

Another way—which I cannot find used by the ancients, but rather in the later Eastern Empire, as appears at *St. Sophia*, and by that example in all the mosques and cloisters of the *dervishes*, and everywhere at present in the *East*—and of all others the most geometrical, is composed of hemispheres and their sections only. Since a sphere may be cut in all manner of ways and still result in circles, it may be accommodated to lie upon all positions of the pillars.

<margin>Fig. III.</margin>
<margin>Fig. IV.</margin>
Let E be a cupola or hemisphere resting upon four pillars A, B, C, and D, from which arise the four arches to which the sections (being semicircles) must join on all sides, whether A B is equal to B C or not. If you cut the hemisphere horizontally again, the section will be an entire circle touching the keys of the arches; G, H, K, and L will be spandrels resting upon the pillars, yet they are still parts of the hemisphere. If the horizontal circle is removed, you may build an upright wall upon that circle which may support another cupola above, as is done at *St. Sophia*, *St. Peter's*, and at all the churches in *Rome*. I do not doubt that those at *Constantinople* inherited it from the *Greeks* before them; it is so natural and is still found in the present Seraglio, which was the episcopal palace of old; the imperial palace, whose ruins still appear, being farther eastward. Now, because I have for good reasons followed this method in the vaulting of the church of *St. Paul's*, I think it proper to show that it is the lightest manner and requires less buttressing than cross-vaulting, as well as being of an agreeable view; at the same time, I shall show how the centers of gravity are to be computed. To show that it requires less buttressing than diagonal cross-vaulting, I will compare them both together, without any complex demonstration, as follows:

It is evident that the spandrels, or the weight of the diagonal cross-arches where two cylindrical vaults meet, must be an inverted pyramid whose base is a parallelogram with two straight sides and two circular ones; wherever it is cut horizontally, it will be cut into similar parallelograms. Now, in the other Eastern way of vaulting by hemispheres, the spandrels are the solids that remain when a hemisphere is taken out of a half-cube; each of these also must be a sort of inverted pyramid whose bases and sides are circular, and wherever it is cut horizontally, it is cut into pieces of circles.

What these are that provide the buttressing of arcades in the various forms of arches may be geometrically determined; for example, in the *Roman* way of cross-arches.

But none of these vaultings are thought necessary in buildings to be filled up to the crowns of the vaultings, but only so high as to give abutment to the arches above the pillars, which architects have determined, by practice, to be a third part of the height of the arch. It seems necessary to consider the proper abutment of cylindrical or straight vaultings upon parallel walls, or two pillars only of some breadth. ## TRACT III.

The Tyrian order was the first manner, which, in *Greece*, was refined into the *Doric* order, after the first temple of that order was built at *Argos*: but if we consider well the *Doric* order, we manifestly may trace the same to be but an imitation in stone of what was usually done in timber, in the long porticoes they used to build in cities, by which they endured the heat of the day and conversed together: the roofs of those porticoes were framed in this manner.

First, they laid the timber, called the *architrave*, to join the pillars in a row; upon these they laid the beams that joined the opposite rows, then upon these they raised the rafters, which *Vitruvius* calls *capreoli*, which, meeting in a triangle, made the roof cast off weather; the rafters were fastened by two tenons into the very ends of the beams, by sawing aslant into the ends of them, not as we do with mortises. Upon the architrave they placed a plank, the better to join the ends of these architraves together upon the pillars; then the pins (improperly called *guttae*) driven upwards would not only fix the *capreoli* to the beams but prevent them from sliding upon the architraves, and gauge the opposite architraves together to keep a straight range in the long porticoes:

And thus may be discerned the reason for the triglyphs and for the whole *Doric* order; and these long porticoes were the general method of building cities in hot climates.

<margin>See *Monsieur Desgodetz*.</margin>
<margin>* The *Roman palm* is nine *inches* by *English* measure.</margin>
When *Alexander* had determined to build *Alexandria* and had settled on the location, he left his architect *Dinocrates* to complete it. *Dinocrates* drew a long street with porticoes on both sides, from Lake *Mareotis* to the sea, and another across it that led to *Pelusium*. He then built walls and large towers, each capable of quartering five hundred men, the noble ruins of which remain to this day; ($a$) then, by giving great privileges to *Egyptians* and *Jews*, they soon filled the quarters between the porticoes with private and public buildings. Thus were cities suddenly raised, and thus was *Tadmor* built; the ruins of which show nothing at present to travelers but incredible numbers of pillars of the *Doric* order—some yet standing, more broken—which were certainly the remains of long porticoes built to shade the streets. Now, how were *Tarsus* and *Anchiala* built in a day? That is, I suppose, the walls and gates were laid out in a day; and this way of setting out the principal streets by porticoes meant that hundreds of pillars of all sorts were to be bought ready-made at the quarries, where great numbers of artisans worked to sell what they produced. This is the reason why, even in *Rome*, the dimensions are not always found to be conformable to the rules, especially in hurried works; for instance, in the portico of the *Pantheon*, there are scarcely two columns of the same diameter. Some of the columns are six *Roman palms* and ten inches [*pollices*] in diameter, while others are six palms and five inches. However, as it is a colossal work and most wonderfully rich, consisting of sixteen huge columns of the *Corinthian* order—each column being one solid stone of oriental granite—the eye cannot readily discern any disproportion. And thus, in the great pillar of *London*, as the height exceeds the due proportion of the order, one module is imperceptible to the eye.

<margin>*Pliny's Epistles, Book 9.*</margin>
*Pliny* the Younger, proposing to repair and enlarge an old temple of *Ceres* that stood upon his estate in *Tuscany* by adding a portico, directed his architect to immediately buy four marble columns of any sort he pleased. By this method of purchasing columns of all orders and proportions at any time—ready formed at the quarries like goods in a shop or warehouse—the ancients had the advantage of erecting porticoes (the stately pride of *Roman* architecture) of any grandeur or extent in a very short time, and without being overly scrupulous about the exactness of the dimensions.

## TRACT IV.

We may gather an example of *Tyrian* architecture from the theater by whose fall *Samson* made such a vast slaughter of the *Philistines* through one stretch of his wonderful strength. In considering what this structure must have been to be demolished with one pull, I conceive it to have been an oval amphitheater with the scene in the middle, where a vast roof of cedar beams resting all around upon the walls centered upon one short architrave that united two cedar pillars in the middle. One pillar would not be sufficient to unite the ends of at least one hundred beams that converged toward the center; therefore, I say, there must have been a short architrave resting upon two pillars, upon

<margin>* Directly opposite Jerusalem to the east, in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.</margin>
The most notable monument of the *Tyrian style*, and of great antiquity, still remaining, is the Sepulcher of *Absalom*: the body of this structure is square, faced on every side with pillars, which support a solid hemispherical *tholus* <note>a dome or cupola</note>; a large architrave, frieze, and cornice lie upon the pillars, which are larger in proportion to their height than what we now allow for the *Tuscan order*; likewise, the *entablature* is larger.

This whole composition, though above 30 feet high, is all of one stone—base, pillars, and *tholus*—cut as it stood out of the adjacent cliff of white marble.

It is to be wished that some skillful artist would give us the exact dimensions to the inch, by which we might have a true idea of the ancient *Tyrian manner*; for it is most probable *Solomon* employed the *Tyrian architects* in his Temple, from his correspondence with King *Hiram*; and from these *Phoenicians* I derive both the arts and the letters of the *Grecians*, though it may be the *Tyrians* were imitators of the *Babylonians*, and they of the *Egyptians*.

Great monarchs are ambitious to leave great monuments behind them; and this occasions great inventions in the mechanical arts.

What the architecture was that *Solomon* used, we know but little of, though Holy Writ has given us the general dimensions of the Temple, by which we may, in some measure, determine the plan, but not that of all the courts.

*Villalpandus* has made a fine romantic piece after the *Corinthian order*, which in that age was not used by any nation; for the early ages used much thicker pillars than the *Doric*. In later times, they began to refine from the *Doric*, as in the Temple of *Diana* at *Ephesus* (the united work of all *Asia*), and at length improved into a slenderer pillar and leafy capital of various inventions, which was called *Corinthian*; so that if we go back to the age of *Solomon*, we may reasonably believe they used the *Tyrian manner*, at least as thick as, if not more than, the *Doric*, and that the *Corinthian manner* of *Villalpandus* is mere fancy.

### Of the Temple of *Diana* at *Ephesus*, according to the Account of *Pliny*.

THE Temple of *Diana* at *Ephesus*, a most surprising example of *Grecian* magnificence, introduced the *Ionic order*: it was two hundred and twenty years in building, at the joint expense of all the states of *Asia*, with each government contributing a pillar. In this structure, the capitals were first formed with volutes, and the proportions changed from the *Doric* to a slenderer pillar. The description in *Pliny* is short, and something that no authors, ancient or modern, seem to explain sufficiently. The account, therefore, of this prodigious fabric—the first instance of the use of the *Ionic order*—requires to be as fully and clearly illustrated as the most authentic aid we can have from antiquity will allow.

The length of the whole temple was 425 feet, the breadth 220 feet. The pillars were 127 in number, each 60 feet high. To make out this number of pillars, the arrangement must be *decastyle-dipteron* <note>a temple with ten columns in the front and two rows of columns on the sides</note>, and the columns are reckoned thus: 40 in the fronts (fore and aft), and 60 in the aisles; so this *peribole* <note>the enclosure around a temple</note> makes exactly 100. Besides these, there are 16 in the *pronaos* <note>the inner area of the portico</note> and the 4 *antae* <note>pillars at the end of a wall</note>, making 120 in all. The colonnade affords no more, but the tabernacle, or

<page-num>361</page-num>
<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>
<sig>zz</sig>
<meta>catchword: Observations</meta>

The shrine, situated in the middle of the *cella* <note>the inner chamber of a temple</note>, in which stood the colossal image of *Diana Multimammea* <note>Diana of many breasts</note>, contains seven pillars and matches the number mentioned by *Pliny*.

This strange idol (which is represented on the coins of *Ephesus* and other *Asiatic* cities) had as odd a figure as any *Indian* pagoda (the remains of a very ancient superstition from before the *Ionic* migration, which it seems the *Greeks* still wished to preserve, believing it fell out of heaven and was sent by *Jupiter*). It was made of cedar, and the *cella* had a flat roof of cedar; for it could not easily be vaulted for lack of abutment, being 115 feet broad, nearly as high, and 230 feet long. Thus the Huntress was placed, as it were, in a grove of marble pillars.

All ancient idols were encircled by groves; and this seems to be the reason for the perpetual adherence of all architecture to this form, and no other, of colonnades around temples. They were meant to represent the original groves, just as the capitals and all the ornaments still carry the figures of leaves.

<margin>*Acts of the Apostles, chapter 19, verse 24.*</margin>
*Diana Artemis* was the moon, and her ceremonies were held at night. The nineteen pillars in the aisles represented her orbital period; the seven pillars of the chapel in the middle of the *cella* represented the quarters of her monthly cycle. This, I suppose, was the <term>naiskos</term>, which we translate as the shrine of *Diana*. It is supposed that the silversmiths of *Ephesus* formed models of this representation, and not of the entire structure, to sell to strangers, "which brought no small gain to the craftsmen." In the same way today, small wooden models of the Holy Sepulchre at *Jerusalem*, decorated with mother-of-pearl, are usually made for sale to pilgrims and foreigners.

Since the columns were 60 feet high, the diameter, according to the rules, must be 6 feet 8 inches (that is, a ninth part). Thus, every column would contain at least 110 tons of marble, besides the base and capital and the vast stones of the entablature. This was especially true of the middle intercolumniation <note>the space between columns</note>, which was wider than the rest to provide a larger entrance, as was usual in *Greek* temples. It was about 22 feet wide and could not bear its own weight unless the architrave and frieze were both made of one stone, which together would weigh over 150 tons. The setting of this stone (for it seems the architect despaired) was miraculously attributed to the goddess herself, as being beyond the reach of human skill.

Thirty-six of the columns were carved by *Scopas*, a famous sculptor of the school of *Praxiteles*; and the outer walls of the *cella* were adorned with paintings from about the time of *Apelles*.

Modern travelers tell us there are great heaps of ruins today, and large vaults, which were probably the foundations of the colonnades.

I imagine the ascent to it was easy, without many steps, so that the <term>thensa sacra</term> <note>sacred chariot</note> could pass conveniently. This was a covered wagon drawn by two mules, in which the idol was placed and carried through the streets to the circus during grand ceremonies.

[We often see this temple represented on medals with the figure of *Diana*; but the front view, because of the small space left on these types of monuments, is never shown with more than eight pillars—sometimes with six, four, or only two.]

## Observations on the Temple of Peace, built by the Emperor Vespasian.

<margin>
\* 300 Feet long, 200 Feet broad.
† 228 Feet long, 66 Feet broad.
</margin>

1. THE magnitude of this \* Temple, the most magnificent of old *Rome*, is prodigious; it is longer than our † *Westminster Hall*, and the middle nave alone, besides the aisles, is more than a seventh part broader; in height it exceeds the highest cathedral now in the world.

2. The walls are thin where the roof does not press; but they are admirably secured where the weight lies. First, by the piers behind the pillars, which are of such thickness toward the rear that they provide sufficient abutment for the arch of the aisles. (This not being observed in *Gothic* cathedrals, the vault of the aisles resting against the middle of the pillars of the nave bends them inward; and therefore, in *Westminster Abbey*, they are reinforced in some places across the aisle to the outward wall with vast iron bars to prevent the vault of the aisle from spreading.) Secondly, the weight of the roof above has a mighty abutment from the sloping walls between the windows, which correspond to the half-frontispieces of the aisles; from which the flying buttresses of *Gothic* structures seem to have taken their origin.

3. This temple ascends to its vast height on each side by three stages; the mighty nave is abutted by the aisles, and the aisles by the tribunals and small rooms outside; which we may well suppose to be those archives where the *Sibyl's* books, the spoils of the *Jewish* Temple, and the records of *Rome*—the most sacred for their antiquity—were kept.

4. Thus it rises to a height equal to half the total breadth between the side tribunals; and a line drawn from the keystone of the vault of the nave to the keystone of the arch of the aisle determines the breadth of the aisle. So it is that in the farthest part, you always see half the vault of the nave, which makes it seem free and spacious, containing more than an acre of ground in its pavement, and it might well contain an assembly of 20,000 people. Its common use was as a Hall of Justice, and for that reason it was made very well-lit, whereas consecrated temples were generally very dark.

5. I have admired the greatness and firmness of this structure, but I cannot commend the architect's judgment for obscuring its majestic stature with a humble portico and low wings, which cause the visual ray to cut off much of the height. Consequently, in perspective, the front will look exceedingly broad and flat, and to those approaching the entrance, it will seem as if grafted upon the low portico; though the grace in the double frontispiece and acroteria does somewhat make amends by dividing the mighty breadth into several parts.

6. But shall I accuse the ancients of a lack of skill in optics, of which they everywhere show such admirable proof? Particularly here, the architect has given great testimony of it in the design of his cornice, wherein he has left out the *corona*, or "hanging-square," following an unusual example. The *corona* seems an essential part in all cornices, as that which gives its name to the whole and is necessary to the beauty of a cornice; because, by its projection, it shades all the lower members, receiving upon its flat surface a clear light from above. This gives the prominence and distinct appearance that we see in the parts of a cornice at a distance. But the artist here, ingeniously realizing that his light sources in this structure stood level with his cornice, and therefore it would lack the effect for which it is intended, and that the hanging-face of it

<summary>This text provides a detailed architectural analysis of the Temple of Peace in Rome, comparing its massive dimensions and superior structural engineering—specifically its use of abutments—to Gothic cathedrals like Westminster Abbey. The author also critiques the building's aesthetic proportions and the architect's unconventional use of optics in the design of the cornice.</summary>
<keywords>Temple of Peace, Emperor Vespasian, Rome, architecture, Westminster Hall, Gothic architecture, abutment, nave, aisles, flying buttresses, Sibylline Books, Jewish Temple spoils, optics, corona, cornice</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the architectural analysis of the Temple of Peace in Rome, explaining why certain elements were omitted for visual effect and defending the design's integrity against critics who suggest a decline in Roman architectural standards during the reign of Vespasian.</meta>

<page-num>363</page-num>
<header>SIR CHRISTOPHER WREN, KNT.</header>

...would be foreshortened to nothing to the eye that beholds it from below, wisely left out this member. If these optical reasons did not prevail, it would never have been used; for of all members, this is the one that most burdens the cornice. It makes us—for lack of stones of such vastness and money to move them—despair in these days of coming near the greatness of such a pillar and entablature as is used here, where the projection of the cornice is nearly five feet.

7. It was not, therefore, unskillfulness in the architect that made him choose this flat kind of appearance for his temple; it was his wit and judgment. Each deity had a peculiar gesture, face, and dress symbolically proper to it, just as their stories were but morals involved; and not only were their altars and sacrifices mystical, but the very forms of their temples were as well. No language, no poetry can so describe Peace and its effects on men’s minds as the design of this temple naturally depicts it, without any affectation of allegory. It is easy to access and open, carries a humble front but embraces widely, is luminous and pleasant, and, content with an internal greatness, despises an envious appearance of all that height it might otherwise justly boast of; instead, fortifying itself on every side, it rests secure on a square and ample basis.

8. I know very well that the critics in architecture will scarcely allow this temple to be accurate, doubting a decay of the art in the time of Vespasian, who finished this temple; but it was Claudius who began it, a time when we need not suspect corruption. Nor need we be concerned that the entablature of the columns is not continued, or that the arches of the aisles rise higher than the architraves; for these arches resemble so many tribunals, which are usually made in the form of niches with a vaulted head, adorned with reticulated work, but are not frequently set upon any imposts like the arches of a gate. However, in the interior of the best works, the whole entablature is seldom precisely maintained. Sometimes the architrave is not expressed, as within the portico of the Temple of Vesta at Tivoli; most frequently the frieze is omitted; and in the interior of temple porticoes, the cornice is always omitted, unless you choose to call the moldings of the listels a cornice. Within the portico of the Pantheon, over the capitals, runs a compound molding of architrave and cornice combined in one, yet together they do not make up the proper size of a cornice. In the open air, the cornice serves as protection from the weather as well as the crown of the building, and therefore should not be interrupted or broken forward without just reason. Inside, where it is an impediment, it is often omitted, as in this case where, by its great projection, it would have obscured the descent of light. The same order of arches without imposts is observed throughout: in the portico before the temple, in the windows of the fronts, in the passages through the tribunals, and in the niches. Although we have no more surviving examples of the like, I am inclined to believe the basilicas, which were vaulted with stone, followed this kind of structure. As it is vast and well-poised, so it is true, well-proportioned, and beautiful, and was deservedly esteemed by the Romans themselves as one of the most significant structures of Rome.

<summary>Wren explains that the Temple of Peace’s design reflects the nature of Peace through its open and grounded form, while also defending its architectural irregularities as practical choices for lighting and interior aesthetics. He notes that the temple was begun under Claudius, predating the supposed decline of Roman art, and shares similarities with vaulted basilicas.</summary>

### Observations on the Temple of Mars Ultor, built by *Augustus*; the ruins of which are seen near the Torre de Conti, in Rome.

> ->*Templa feres, et me victore, vocaberis Ultor.* <note>You shall have temples, and with me as victor, you shall be called the Avenger.</note> OVID, *FASTI*, Book 5.<-

->I.<-

Just as carefully as the appearance of the Temple of Peace was designed in reference to Peace and its attributes, so is this temple of *Mars* suited to War: a strong and stately temple shows itself prominently; and, so that it might not lose any of its perceived size, a vast wall nearly 100 feet high is placed behind it (because, as *Vitruvius* notes, things appear smaller in the open air). And though it is a single wall, erected chiefly to add glory to the building and to present at once a formidable front of trophies and statues which stand here in double ranks, yet an ingenious use is made of it to hide two irregular entrances that come from a winding street. To adapt both to the location and to give strength to the wall (which is only five feet thick), it is built with various curves (because a straight wall is more easily ruined by storms). These curves provide the opportunity to form two other facades, in which are seen niches much larger than

### II.

In this court we have an example of circular walls; and certainly no enclosure looks as graceful as a circular one. It is the circle that equally bounds the eye and is everywhere uniform; but being perfect in itself, it is not easily joined to any other area and therefore can seldom be used. A semicircle joining an oblong, as in the tribunal at the end of this temple, is a graceful composition.

### III.

If I might speculate on architecture, I would say that the two porticoes that made up the court were directly opposite the two side-frontispieces, and that the walls of the court might continue on the other side of a street, leaving open the passages A and B; and this might be the reason that *Palladio* sought no further for them, finding foundations that ended at A and B. By this means, those who walk in either portico will have the prospect of a side-frontispiece before them; those who walk in the ante-temple will have that splendid circuit of statues spread around them; and those who enter the court will have an excellent perspective of the whole. Those who come down from the temple will have the view of the Temple of *Neptune*, which *Palladio* says stood opposite it. The *Romans* guided themselves by perspective in all their structures; and why should not perspective lead us back again to what was *Roman*? If I presumed to do so, it was *Tully* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> who encouraged me, who assures us that reason is the best art of divination.

I cannot omit commending the fronts of the porticoes: the listels are designed to make roofs that are too narrow for a vault appear airy and light. The ornaments between them, consisting of a trail of fillets continuing in square angles, seem to me to have been borrowed from garden beds, and would very properly suit that purpose.

### IV.

The cornice of the wall suggests what cornice to use in plainer works; and the base of the columns is gracefully made into a continuous base for the entire temple. But the pillar with the capital of horses' heads (supposed by *Palladio*)...

(Palladio to be one of the interior decorations) belongs not to this, but the other neighboring Temple of *Neptune*; for it was *Neptune* who was called *Dominator Equorum*. This, and the Temple of *Peace*, and the *Pantheon*, are those which *Pliny* particularly mentions among the most remarkable works of *Rome*.

### V.

The squares in the wall of the *cella* opposite to the intercolumniations show us how extremely the ancients were addicted to square and geometrical figures, which are the only natural foundation of beauty.

### VI.

We find the most adorned temples of the *Corinthian* order have the walls of the *cella* channeled; they so favored the display of great stones that, where there were joints, they did not try to hide them, so that the shafts of the pillars might better appear whole and to provide a darker background behind them. Their proper proportion is double in length to their breadth; the appearance is best where many are together.

## Of the Sepulchre of Mausolus King of Caria.

The Sepulchre of *Mausolus* is so well described by *Pliny* that I have attempted to design it accordingly, and also very open, consistent with the description in *Martial*:

> ->*Aëre vacuo pendentia Mausolea.*<-
<note>Mausoleums hanging in the empty air.</note>

And yet it did not lack the solidity of the *Doric Order*, which I would rather call the *Tyrian*, as it was used in that age.

<margin>* Otherwise 106.</margin>
The skill of four famous artists—*Scopas*, *Briaxes*, *Timotheus*, and *Leochares*, all from the school of *Praxiteles*—caused this monument to be esteemed one of the seven Wonders of the World. Since these architects lived before the time of *Alexander* and before the beginning of the Temple of *Diana* at *Ephesus* (for *Mausolus* died, according to *Pliny*, in the second year of the hundredth Olympiad, which was before the *Ionic Order* was first in use), I conclude this work must be the most exact form of the *Doric*. It appeared from the city of *Halicarnassus* to the sea—that is, north and south—to be 64 feet wide, and the same in every direction, for each craftsman took a side. Being hexastyle, it contained 36 pillars in total: 20 for the four fronts and 16 within, which supported the *Pteron* (as *Pliny* calls it), in the manner shown in the plan.

*Pteron* is an unusual term and is not, I think, to be found in the authors available to us. *Harduin*, in his notes on *Pliny*, and others consider the word to be in the plural number, *Ptera* (ΠΤΕΡΑ), "wings," and think it carries the same meaning as *Pteromata* in *Vitruvius*: *Muri duo in altitudinem consurgentes alarum instar* <note>Two walls rising up in height like wings</note>. But if we take it as it is, in the singular number, it cannot carry that meaning here; instead, it may relate, as I conclude, to what we now call an *Attic Order*. I believe whatever rose above the cornice was called by this term in Greek architectural writings that are now lost.

This *Pteron* was raised here twice as high as the order below it to carry the triumphal chariot of King *Mausolus*. The *Romans* did something similar in their triumphal arches; but in this case, it is raised so high because it stands upon a second row of columns inside, and so that the chariot might be seen from the sea. Such was the situation of *Caria*, where all the ships rounding this southwest cape of *Asia* must follow the usual route to *Rhodes*.

Suppose then an order which *Vitruvius* calls *Systyle* (where the space between columns is double the diameter of the column); if the column is 4 feet in diameter and the space between columns is 8 feet, the entire facade will be 64 feet. The height of columns of 7.5 diameters will be 30 feet, and with the *Doric entablature* at a fourth of the column's height, it will reach 37.5 feet—which is exactly 25 cubits, the height *Pliny* gives for the first story. Above the *cyma* of the cornice must be a *zocle* <note>pedestal or block</note> of 2.5 feet for mounting the statues, making the total 40 feet from the floor. Upon the 16 inner columns rose the *Pteron* (the ancient Greek term, as I have noted, for whatever was erected above the cornice, which we now call an *Attic story*). Its pilasters were supported on a substructure, or pedestal, of 20 feet, so that they were elevated enough to be seen above the 7-foot statues; being set 14 feet back from the *cyma* of the outer columns, they could not easily be lower. The pilasters of the *Pteron*, being 24 feet high, added 30 feet more including their cornice. Upon this, the stone covering rose 24 feet more, *in metæ cacumen* <note>in the peak of a pyramid</note>, as *Pliny* phrases it, making the entire *Pteron* 74 feet. Now, if a ten-foot flight of steps (one-third the height of the pillar) is added around the lower colonnade, the height to the platform on the top—upon which stood the triumphal chariot—would be 124 feet.

<summary>Sir Christopher Wren provides an architectural reconstruction of the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, interpreting Pliny’s descriptions through the lens of the Doric order. He defines the technical term "Pteron" as an Attic story and calculates the monument's dimensions to reach a total height of 124 feet.</summary>
<keywords>Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, King Mausolus, Pliny, Doric Order, Pteron, Vitruvius, architecture, Seven Wonders of the World, Halicarnassus</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Sir Christopher Wren’s detailed architectural analysis and reconstruction of the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, transitioning from his discussion of the Pteron to the final dimensions and decorative elements of the monument.</meta>

<page-num>368</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

of *Mausolus*, in marble, 16 feet high; so the whole height will be 140 feet, according to *Pliny*. The whole circumference I have computed to be 416 feet, which exceeds *Pliny's* by 5 feet. The bottom and façade, which *Pliny* reported as he was informed by *Greek* measure, I have computed by exact proportions, which indeed are very fine. First, the ascent in height is a third part of the pillar; then the column with the architrave being 32 [feet], will be half the façade of 64 [feet], and the face of the *Pteron* and pedestal will have the appearance of being as high as they are broad over the heads of the statues. The ascent of steps up to the platform is only the proper stone covering, the stones being 12 inches high and 6 inches projecting <note>Wren uses the term "saile" to describe the projection or overhang of the steps.</note>. The breadth at the lower steps compared to the whole height is in a ratio of 3 to 4, which are the sides of *Pythagorean* right-angled triangles. The arrangement of the whole turns out so wonderfully—and since the artists were contemporary with the school of *Plato*—I suspect they might have drawn some practices from that school in this harmonic disposition. I have joined the 16 inward pillars into four solid structures and continued these to the top, also opening the middle space between the columns of the *Pteron* so that solid structure sits upon solid, and empty space upon empty space; thus, everything is firm, yet airy. I have omitted *triglyphs* in the *frieze*, which I consider to be the only place for the inscription, and monuments were never without one. I believe *triglyphs* are chiefly appropriate for porticoes, as an imitation of timber entablatures. There might be 20 statues around the first order, 16 more below in niches upon the solid structures, and 12 in niches of the *Pteron*—48 in total, with each sculptor responsible for 12. *Pythis*, a fifth artist (says *Pliny*), made the colossal figure of *Mausolus* in a chariot drawn by four horses.
